\operatorname{Ent}(\mathbb P\mid\mathbb P_{0,N})
+
\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\mathcal A_{\mathrm{PCE},N}
\right],
\tag{K.9.21}
$$
where the minimization is over probability measures on the finite path ledger satisfying (K.9.20). The endpoint constraints are part of the branch datum and are assumed feasible.

Let $s_N:X_N\to[0,\infty]$ be the finite sparsity observable. Register an evaluation index $\ell_*\in\{0,\ldots,M\}$, a positive real-valued response observable $G_N$ on $X_N$, and $G_0>0$. On the path ledger define
$$
S_N:=s_N\circ e_{\ell_*},
\qquad
Z_N:=\left(G_N/G_0-1\right)\circ e_{\ell_*},
\qquad
w_{*,N}:=(S_N)_{\#}\mathbb P_{*,N}.
$$
In path-space expressions below, state observables such as $s_N$ and $G_N$ denote their pullbacks at this same registered coordinate. Define the bridge-selected response curve by
$$
g_{*,N}(s)
:=
\mathbb E_{\mathbb P_{*,N}}\!\left[Z_N\mid S_N=s\right]
\tag{K.9.22}
$$
for sparsity values with positive bridge weight. Since the path ledger is finite and $Z_N$ is real valued, this conditional expectation is the finite weighted average over the corresponding bin. The one-scale family is
$$
g_{A,n}(s)=A\left(1-e^{-s^n}\right)\quad(0\le s<\infty),
\qquad
g_{A,n}(+\infty):=A,
\qquad A\ge0,\quad n\ge1.
\tag{K.9.23}
$$
The branch is one-scale identifiable when the weighted projection problem
$$
(A_c,n)
=
\arg\min_{A\ge0,\ n\ge1}
\int_{[0,\infty]}
\left(g_{*,N}(s)-g_{A,n}(s)\right)^2
\,dw_{*,N}(s)
\tag{K.9.24}
$$
has a unique minimizer with positive Hessian on the active parameter tangent. The integral includes any atom at $+\infty$ and is a finite sum on this branch. A regular FLRW limit requires a certificate for convergence of the registered observables, sparsity measures and response curves; the parameter and evaluation requirements for the constitutive law are stated in item 4 of Theorem K.9.5.

<a id="theorem-k95-entropic-bridge-selection-of-the-homogeneous-coupling-law"></a>**Theorem K.9.5 (Entropic-Bridge Selection of the Homogeneous Coupling Law).** On a homogeneous finite entropic-bridge branch:

1. the finite bridge $\mathbb P_{*,N}$ exists and is unique;

2. the induced response curve $g_{*,N}$ is unique on the support of $w_{*,N}$;

3. if the branch is one-scale identifiable, then $(A_c,n)$ in (K.9.24) is uniquely determined by the branch conditions independently of cosmological data;

4. suppose a regular-limit sequence has exact response curves
$$
g_{*,N}(s)=A_N\left(1-e^{-s^{n_N}}\right)
\tag{K.9.25}
$$
on its positive-weight sparsity support, with $A_N\ge0$, $n_N\ge1$, and the endpoint convention of (K.9.23). Assume $A_N\to A_c\in[0,\infty)$ and $n_N\to n\in[1,\infty)$ with finite limits. For each admitted cosmic time $t$, require positive-weight sampled values $s_N(t)\to s_{bg}(t)$ in $[0,\infty]$ and the compatible physical-response limit
$$
\frac{G_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)}{G_0}-1
=\lim_{N\to\infty}g_{*,N}(s_N(t)).
$$
Then the homogeneous coupling law is exactly
$$
\Upsilon_G(t)=1+A_c\left[1-e^{-s_{bg}(t)^n}\right],
\qquad
G_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)=G_0\Upsilon_G(t),
\tag{K.9.26}
$$
with the value $1+A_c$ at $s_{bg}=+\infty$;

5. the Bianchi-consistent effective-fluid form remains (K.9.14)-(K.9.19).

This is an emergent metric/channel-capacity thermodynamic closure of the homogeneous non-vacuum response. It introduces no fundamental gravitational Hilbert sector.

*Proof.* At each registered $N$ and finite protocol time grid, the path ledger $\Omega_N=X_N^{M+1}$ is finite. The constraint set defined by (K.9.20) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite probability simplex. With $0\log0:=0$ and strictly positive $\mathbb P_{0,N}$, relative entropy is continuous and strictly convex on that simplex. The finite running-cost expectation is linear. Compactness gives existence and strict convexity gives uniqueness of the minimizer, proving item 1. The registered coordinate pullbacks in Definition K.9.4 then give one finite conditional average in every positive-weight sparsity bin, proving item 2.

On a one-scale identifiable branch, Definition K.9.4 requires the projection functional (K.9.24) to have a unique minimizer with positive Hessian on the active tangent. Thus its registered bridge and response data determine $(A_c,n)$, proving item 3.

For item 4, if $0<s_{bg}(t)<\infty$, continuity of $s^n$ jointly in positive $s$ and finite $n$ gives $s_N(t)^{n_N}\to s_{bg}(t)^n$. If $s_{bg}(t)=0$, then eventually $s_N(t)\le1$ and $0\le s_N(t)^{n_N}\le s_N(t)\to0$, since $n_N\ge1$. If $s_{bg}(t)=+\infty$, then eventually $s_N(t)\ge1$ and $s_N(t)^{n_N}\ge s_N(t)\to+\infty$, using the endpoint convention when a sampled value is infinite. Therefore $e^{-s_N(t)^{n_N}}\to e^{-s_{bg}(t)^n}$ in all three cases. Combining this with $A_N\to A_c$ and the stipulated physical-response limit proves (K.9.26). For $A_c>0$ this is the branch of Theorem K.9.3; $A_c=0$ gives the constant baseline coupling.

Finally, Corollary K.9.3b derived (K.9.14)-(K.9.19) from the homogeneous coupling law and the standard background continuity equations. Since the entropic-bridge branch changes only the selection rule for $(A_c,n)$ and not the Bianchi identity or the definitions of $\rho_{ad}$ and $p_{ad}$, the effective-fluid form remains unchanged. ∎

<a id="theorem-k95a-response-observable-nonidentifiability-of-the-homogeneous-entropic-bridge"></a>**Theorem K.9.5a (Response-Observable Nonidentifiability of the Homogeneous Entropic Bridge).** Fix all data entering the minimization (K.9.21), together with the sparsity observable $s_N$, and let $\mathbb P_{*,N}$ be its unique bridge. The response observable $G_N/G_0-1$ does not occur in that minimization. For every bounded function $h$ on the finite support of $s_N$ satisfying
$$
-1<h(s)\le H<\infty
\tag{K.9.5a.0}
$$
and any additional registered owner bounds, the physically positive completion
$$
\frac{G_N^{(h)}}{G_0}-1:=h(s_N)
\tag{K.9.5a.1}
$$
has the same bridge, endpoints, reference generator, running cost and sparsity measure, but its selected response curve is exactly
$$
g_{*,N}^{(h)}(s)=h(s).
\tag{K.9.5a.2}
$$
Therefore the entropic-bridge data preceding the response assignment do not entail the exponential family (K.9.23), its parameters, or any other constitutive family.

The nonentailment persists in a regular-limit sequence. On a sparsity interval containing $0$, take two bounded response completions
$$
h_{\exp}(s)=1-e^{-s},
\qquad
h_{\mathrm{rat}}(s)=\frac{s}{1+s}.
\tag{K.9.5a.3}
$$
The second is not equal on any neighborhood of $0$ to $A(1-e^{-s^n})$ for any $A\ge0$ and $n\ge1$.

*Proof.* Substitution of (K.9.5a.1) into the conditional expectation (K.9.22) gives
$$
\mathbb E_{\mathbb P_{*,N}}[h(s_N)\mid s_N=s]=h(s)
$$
on every positive-weight sparsity bin, proving (K.9.5a.2). Because neither the objective nor its endpoint constraints change, strict convexity gives the same unique bridge for every $h$.

For the final claim, $h_{\mathrm{rat}}'(0)=1$. If $n>1$, the right derivative at zero of $A(1-e^{-s^n})$ is $0$, so equality is impossible. If $n=1$, equality of first derivatives forces $A=1$, but the second derivatives at zero are respectively $-2$ and $-1$. Thus no member of the exponential family equals $h_{\mathrm{rat}}$ near zero. ∎

<a id="definition-k95b-response-cost-branch-and-registered-quadratic-response-action"></a>**Definition K.9.5b (Response-Cost Branch and Registered Quadratic Response Action).** Let $\sigma\ge0$ be the registered response clock. Postulate K.9.2 uses $\sigma=s_{bg}^{\,n}$; Definition K.9.5g below supplies a distinct dynamical clock. The admissible response class is
$$
\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}:=\left\{u:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\ \middle|\ u\ \text{locally absolutely continuous},\ u(0)=0,\ u-1\in L^{2}(0,\infty),\ u'\in L^{2}(0,\infty)\right\},
\tag{K.9.5b.1}
$$
and the registered quadratic response action is
$$
\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u]:=\int_0^\infty\left[\tfrac12\left(u'(\sigma)\right)^{2}+\tfrac12\left(1-u(\sigma)\right)^{2}\right]d\sigma
\ \text{ for }u\in\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}},
\qquad
\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u]:=+\infty\ \text{ otherwise}.
\tag{K.9.5b.2}
$$
Every member has $\lim_{\sigma\to\infty}u(\sigma)=1$, as proved in Theorem K.9.5c; use the extension $u(+\infty):=1$. A response-cost branch is a homogeneous finite entropic-bridge branch (Definition K.9.4) whose branch datum additionally registers the clock exponent $n\ge1$, the amplitude normalization $A_c>0$, the nonnegative response profile $u$ as a registered continuum datum with finite response observable $G_N/G_0-1:=A_c\,u(s_N^{\,n})$, and the augmented objective
$$
\operatorname{Ent}\left(\mathbb P\mid\mathbb P_{0,N}\right)+\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\mathcal A_{\mathrm{PCE},N}+\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u],
\tag{K.9.5b.3}
$$
minimized on the Cartesian product of the two admissible classes, with no cross-constraint or additional coupling term, over pairs $(\mathbb P,u)$, with $\mathbb P$ ranging over the probability measures on the finite path ledger satisfying (K.9.20). The nonnegative response class is convex, contains $u_*(\sigma)=1-e^{-\sigma}$, and makes $G_N=G_0(1+A_cu)>0$ for every admitted profile, including the infinite-sparsity endpoint.

<a id="theorem-k95c-variational-selection-of-the-exponential-response-profile"></a>**Theorem K.9.5c (Variational Selection of the Exponential Response Profile).** On a response-cost branch:

1. Every $u\in\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$ satisfies $u(\sigma)\to1$ as $\sigma\to\infty$, and
$$
\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u]=\tfrac12\int_0^\infty\left(u'(\sigma)-\left(1-u(\sigma)\right)\right)^{2}d\sigma+\tfrac12.
\tag{K.9.5c.1}
$$

2. $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}$ is strictly convex on $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$ and has the unique minimizer
$$
u_*(\sigma)=1-e^{-\sigma},
\qquad
\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u_*]=\tfrac12,
\tag{K.9.5c.2}
$$
which solves the one-scale closure (K.9.7) and reproduces the coupling law (K.9.8) through (K.9.6) with $u=u_*$.

3. The joint minimization of (K.9.5b.3) separates: its unique minimizer is the pair $\left(\mathbb P_{*,N},u_*\right)$, with $\mathbb P_{*,N}$ the bridge of Theorem K.9.5. The finite response observable of the minimizer is $G_N/G_0-1=A_c\left(1-e^{-s_N^{\,n}}\right)$, its selected response curve (K.9.22) is the one-scale family member $g_{A_c,n}$ of (K.9.23) at the registered $(A_c,n)$, and every registered profile whose finite evaluation differs from that of $u_*$ carries strictly larger augmented cost. On this branch the response freedom exhibited in Theorem K.9.5a is removed.

*Proof.* Item 1. Let $u\in\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$ and $v:=u-1$, so $v$ is locally absolutely continuous with $v,v'\in L^{2}(0,\infty)$ and $v(0)=-1$. For $0\le\sigma<\tau$,
$$
v(\tau)^{2}-v(\sigma)^{2}=2\int_\sigma^\tau v\,v'\,d\sigma',
\qquad
\left|\int_\sigma^\tau v\,v'\,d\sigma'\right|\le\|v\|_{L^{2}(\sigma,\infty)}\,\|v'\|_{L^{2}(\sigma,\infty)},
$$
and the bound tends to $0$ as $\sigma\to\infty$, so $v(\sigma)^{2}$ converges as $\sigma\to\infty$; since $v\in L^{2}(0,\infty)$, the limit is $0$, hence $u(\sigma)\to1$. Pointwise,
$$
\tfrac12\left(u'\right)^{2}+\tfrac12\left(1-u\right)^{2}
=\tfrac12\left(u'-\left(1-u\right)\right)^{2}+u'\left(1-u\right),
\qquad
u'\left(1-u\right)=-\tfrac12\,\frac{d}{d\sigma}\left(1-u\right)^{2},
$$
and the cross term is integrable as the product of the $L^{2}$ functions $u'$ and $1-u$. Integrating on $[0,T]$ and letting $T\to\infty$ with $u(T)\to1$ gives
$$
\int_0^\infty u'\left(1-u\right)d\sigma=\tfrac12\left(1-u(0)\right)^{2}-\tfrac12\lim_{T\to\infty}\left(1-u(T)\right)^{2}=\tfrac12,
$$
which proves (K.9.5c.1).

Item 2. By (K.9.5c.1), $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u]\ge\tfrac12$, with equality exactly when $u'=1-u$ almost everywhere. For such $u$, $\frac{d}{d\sigma}\left[e^{\sigma}\left(u-1\right)\right]=e^{\sigma}\left(u'-\left(1-u\right)\right)=0$ almost everywhere, so local absolute continuity gives $e^{\sigma}\left(u(\sigma)-1\right)=u(0)-1=-1$ and $u=u_*$. Conversely $u_*\in\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$, $u_*'=e^{-\sigma}=1-u_*$, and $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u_*]=\int_0^\infty e^{-2\sigma}\,d\sigma=\tfrac12$. The affine map $u\mapsto u'-\left(1-u\right)$ is injective on $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$: the difference $\varpi$ of two elements satisfies $\varpi(0)=0$, and $\varpi'+\varpi=0$ forces $\varpi=0$. Hence by (K.9.5c.1) the functional is strictly convex on $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$ and $u_*$ is its unique minimizer. Equation (K.9.7) is $u'=1-u$ in the variable $\sigma=s_{bg}^{\,n}$ with $u(0)=0$, and (K.9.6) with $u=u_*$ gives (K.9.8).

Item 3. The first two terms of (K.9.5b.3) do not depend on $u$ and the third does not depend on $\mathbb P$, so the infimum over pairs is the sum of the separate infima and is attained exactly at the pair of the separate unique minimizers: $\mathbb P_{*,N}$ by Theorem K.9.5 item 1 and $u_*$ by item 2. The finite evaluation of $u_*$ gives $G_N/G_0-1=A_c\,u_*(s_N^{\,n})=A_c\left(1-e^{-s_N^{\,n}}\right)$, and substitution into the conditional expectation (K.9.22) on every positive-weight sparsity bin gives $g_{*,N}(s)=A_c\left(1-e^{-s^{n}}\right)=g_{A_c,n}(s)$, the member of (K.9.23) at the registered $(A_c,n)$. A registered profile $u$ whose finite evaluation differs from that of $u_*$ satisfies $u\ne u_*$, so its augmented cost exceeds that of $u_*$ by strict convexity when $u\in\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$ and equals $+\infty$ otherwise. ∎

<a id="remark-k95d-response-normalization-and-clock-choice"></a>**Remark K.9.5d (Response Normalization and Clock Choice).** Theorem K.9.5c selects the profile as a function of the registered clock. With positive coefficients $c_1,c_0$, the action $\frac12\int[c_1u'^2+c_0(1-u)^2]\,d\sigma$ instead has unique minimizer $1-e^{-\sqrt{c_0/c_1}\sigma}$ and minimum $\sqrt{c_0c_1}/2$. This follows by completing the square $\frac{c_1}{2}[u'-\sqrt{c_0/c_1}(1-u)]^2$ and integrating its cross term. Thus the coefficient ratio fixes the clock normalization. The capacity certificate fixes the amplitude, and a clock certificate fixes how physical evolution traverses the profile.

<a id="definition-k95e-capacity-tracking-branch"></a>**Definition K.9.5e (Capacity-Tracking Branch).** A capacity-tracking branch registers:

1. the identification $G_{\mathrm{eff}}\propto C_{\mathrm{trk}}^{-1}$ at fixed, environment-independent channel area, where $C_{\mathrm{trk}}$ is the retained per-cycle channel capacity entering the area-law coefficient of Theorem 49 through the Appendix E calibration (Equation E.9);

2. the dense-limit saturation certificate $C_{\mathrm{trk}}\to C_{\max}^{*}=2\ln 2$ as $s_{bg}\to0^{+}$, on the minimal $d_0=8$ residual-budget and saturation branch of Proposition E.2a;

3. the de Sitter-limit capacity certificate $C_{\mathrm{trk}}\to\varepsilon_0=\ln2$ as $s_{bg}\to\infty$. The registered branch retains a binary response quotient with log-cardinality $\ln2$, identifies its saturated retained capacity with $C_{\mathrm{trk}}$, and assigns positive cost to additional response-null retained structure. On the exact de Sitter branch of Remark K.9.3b.1, non-vacuum enthalpy vanishes and the comoving bath is the horizon bath of Proposition K.9.1. PPI/PCE removes the registered response-null excess. A physical reset interpretation additionally supplies Definition 28's implemented reset and complete retained record, conditional uniformity $H_q(P\mid R)=\ln2$, and the thermodynamic hypotheses of Theorem 31. These reset premises establish the heat floor; the binary-capacity identification supplies the capacity limit used here.

<a id="proposition-k95f-amplitude-selection"></a>**Proposition K.9.5f (Amplitude Selection).** On a capacity-tracking branch,
$$
1+A_c=\frac{C_{\max}^{*}}{\varepsilon_0}=\frac{2\ln 2}{\ln 2}=2,
\qquad
A_c=1.
\tag{K.9.5f.1}
$$

*Proof.* Item 1 of Definition K.9.5e gives $\Upsilon_G=G_{\mathrm{eff}}/G_0=C_{\mathrm{trk}}^{(0)}/C_{\mathrm{trk}}$, where $C_{\mathrm{trk}}^{(0)}$ is the dense-limit value, because (K.9.10) fixes $G_{\mathrm{eff}}\to G_0$ in the dense limit $h_{nv}\to\infty$, equivalently $s_{bg}\to0^{+}$ by Definition K.9.1b. Item 2 gives $C_{\mathrm{trk}}^{(0)}=C_{\max}^{*}=2\ln 2$. Item 3 gives $C_{\mathrm{trk}}\to\varepsilon_0=\ln 2$ as $s_{bg}\to\infty$, so $\Upsilon_G\to C_{\max}^{*}/\varepsilon_0=2$ on the de Sitter branch. Theorem K.9.3's limit (K.9.10) gives $\Upsilon_G\to1+A_c$ on the same branch. Equating the two limits gives (K.9.5f.1). ∎

<a id="definition-k95g-horizon-bath-relaxation-clock"></a>**Definition K.9.5g (Horizon-Bath Relaxation Clock).** On an expanding matter branch $H>0$, $\rho_r=0$, spatially flat $k=0$, define the vacuum fraction
$$
\varphi_\Lambda:=\frac{\rho_\Lambda}{\rho_\Lambda+h_{nv}}=\frac{s_{bg}}{1+s_{bg}},
\tag{K.9.5g.1}
$$
and, with $H_\Lambda=\sqrt{\Lambda/3}=\sqrt{8\pi G_0\rho_\Lambda/3}$ the de Sitter rate of Definition Q.7.1 written in the $c=1$ units of this section through (K.9.4), the horizon-bath relaxation clock
$$
d\sigma=\kappa_\sigma\,H_\Lambda\,\varphi_\Lambda\,dt,
\qquad
\sigma\big|_{s_{bg}=0}=0,
\tag{K.9.5g.2}
$$
with timing normalization $\kappa_\sigma>0$ a branch datum. A horizon-bath clock branch registers (K.9.5g.2) as the sparsity clock and the response profile $u=1-e^{-\sigma}$ of Theorem K.9.5c, so that $\Upsilon_G=1+A_c\left(1-e^{-\sigma}\right)$.

<a id="proposition-k95h-dynamical-clock-and-dense-limit-exponent"></a>**Proposition K.9.5h (Dynamical Clock and Dense-Limit Exponent).** On a horizon-bath clock branch, write $s\equiv s_{bg}$. Then $\sigma$ is the unique nondecreasing solution of
$$
\frac{d\sigma}{ds}=\frac{\kappa_\sigma}{3}\,\frac{\sqrt{s}}{\left(1+s\right)\sqrt{s+\Upsilon_G(s)}},
\qquad
\sigma(0)=0,
\qquad
\Upsilon_G(s)=1+A_c\left(1-e^{-\sigma(s)}\right),
\tag{K.9.5h.1}
$$
and for every $s>0$,
$$
\frac{2\kappa_\sigma}{9}\,\frac{s^{3/2}}{\left(1+s\right)\sqrt{s+\Upsilon_G(s)}}\ \le\ \sigma(s)\ \le\ \frac{2\kappa_\sigma}{9}\,s^{3/2},
\tag{K.9.5h.2}
$$
$$
\frac{3}{2}\,\frac{1}{\left(1+s\right)\sqrt{s+\Upsilon_G(s)}}\ \le\ n_{\mathrm{clk}}(s):=\frac{d\ln\sigma}{d\ln s}\ \le\ \frac{3}{2},
\qquad
\lim_{s\to0^{+}}n_{\mathrm{clk}}(s)=\frac{3}{2},
\qquad
\lim_{s\to0^{+}}\frac{\sigma(s)}{s^{3/2}}=\frac{2\kappa_\sigma}{9}.
\tag{K.9.5h.3}
$$
The clock therefore realizes the Postulate K.9.2 identification $\sigma=s_{bg}^{\,n}$ at leading order as $s_{bg}\to0^{+}$ with
$$
n=\frac{3}{2},
\tag{K.9.5h.4}
$$
on the registration $\kappa_\sigma=9/2$.

*Proof.* On the matter branch, Definition K.9.1b gives $\rho_{nv}=\rho_b=\rho_\Lambda/s$ and (K.9.12) gives $\dot s=3Hs$. Equation (K.9.14) with $k=0$ and (K.9.4) give
$$
H^{2}=\frac{8\pi G_0}{3}\left[\rho_\Lambda+\Upsilon_G\,\frac{\rho_\Lambda}{s}\right]=H_\Lambda^{2}\,\frac{s+\Upsilon_G(s)}{s},
$$
so $H=H_\Lambda\sqrt{\left(s+\Upsilon_G(s)\right)/s}$ on expanding intervals. Substituting $dt=ds/(3Hs)$ and (K.9.5g.1) into (K.9.5g.2) gives the differential equation in (K.9.5h.1). Its right-hand side $F(s,\sigma)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)$ with $F(0,\sigma)=0$, satisfies $0\le F(s,\sigma)\le\frac{\kappa_\sigma}{3}\sqrt{s}$, and is nonincreasing in $\sigma$, because $\Upsilon_G$ is nondecreasing in $\sigma$. Peano's theorem gives local existence from $\sigma(0)=0$, the a priori bound $\sigma\le\frac{2\kappa_\sigma}{9}s^{3/2}$ obtained below gives global extension, and positivity of $F$ gives monotone nondecreasing $\sigma$, hence nondecreasing $\Upsilon_G(s)$ with $\Upsilon_G(0^{+})=1$ and $1\le\Upsilon_G\le1+A_c$. For uniqueness, if $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ are two solutions, then wherever $\sigma_1>\sigma_2$ the derivative of $\sigma_1-\sigma_2$ is $F(s,\sigma_1)-F(s,\sigma_2)\le0$, so $\left(\sigma_1-\sigma_2\right)_{+}$ is nonincreasing from the initial value $0$ and vanishes identically; by symmetry $\sigma_1=\sigma_2$.

For the bounds, write $g(s):=d\sigma/ds$ and $M(s):=\left(1+s\right)\sqrt{s+\Upsilon_G(s)}$. $M$ is nondecreasing, because both factors are nondecreasing, and $M(s)\ge\sqrt{\Upsilon_G(0^{+})}=1$; hence for $0<s'\le s$,
$$
\frac{\kappa_\sigma}{3}\,\frac{\sqrt{s'}}{M(s)}\ \le\ g(s')\ \le\ \frac{\kappa_\sigma}{3}\,\sqrt{s'},
$$
and integrating over $\left(0,s\right]$ gives (K.9.5h.2). For (K.9.5h.3): $n_{\mathrm{clk}}(s)=s\,g(s)/\sigma(s)$, well defined since $\sigma(s)>0$ for $s>0$ by the lower bound in (K.9.5h.2). The lower bound in (K.9.5h.3) follows by dividing $s\,g(s)=\frac{\kappa_\sigma}{3}\,s^{3/2}/M(s)$ by the upper bound of (K.9.5h.2). For the upper bound, $g(s')\ge g(s)\sqrt{s'/s}$ for $0<s'\le s$, because $g(s')/g(s)=\sqrt{s'/s}\;M(s)/M(s')\ge\sqrt{s'/s}$; integrating gives $\sigma(s)\ge g(s)\,s^{-1/2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}s^{3/2}=\frac{2}{3}\,s\,g(s)$ and hence $n_{\mathrm{clk}}(s)\le\frac{3}{2}$. As $s\to0^{+}$, $M(s)\to1$, so both bounds in (K.9.5h.3) tend to $\frac{3}{2}$ and the lower bound of (K.9.5h.2) tends to $\frac{2\kappa_\sigma}{9}s^{3/2}$, which gives both limits by the squeeze. Finally, $\sigma=s^{3/2}\left(1+o(1)\right)$ requires $\frac{2\kappa_\sigma}{9}=1$, which is $\kappa_\sigma=9/2$. ∎

<a id="corollary-k95h1-clock-level-phantom-structure"></a>**Corollary K.9.5h.1 (Clock-Level Phantom Structure).** On a horizon-bath clock branch, the matter-branch dark-sector fluid of Corollary K.9.3c, evaluated with $\Upsilon_G=1+A_c\left(1-e^{-\sigma(s)}\right)$, satisfies for every $s>0$
$$
\operatorname{sign}\left(w_{DE}(s)+1\right)
=\operatorname{sign}\left(e^{\sigma(s)}-1-s\,\sigma'(s)\right)
=\operatorname{sign}\left(e^{\sigma(s)}-1-n_{\mathrm{clk}}(s)\,\sigma(s)\right),
\tag{K.9.5h.5}
$$
there exist $0<s_{-}\le s_{+}<\infty$ with $w_{DE}<-1$ on $\left(0,s_{-}\right)$ and $w_{DE}>-1$ on $\left(s_{+},\infty\right)$, and on the separately registered exact power-clock branch $\sigma=\frac{2\kappa_\sigma}{9}s^{3/2}$ Theorem K.9.3d applies with $x=\sigma$ and $n=\frac{3}{2}$: the unique crossing, when covered by the evolution interval, occurs at $x_c(3/2)=0.76268856\ldots$, the unique positive root of $e^{x}=1+\frac{3}{2}x$, with crossing redshift
$$
1+z_\times=s_{bg,0}^{1/3}\left(\frac{2\kappa_\sigma}{9\,x_c(3/2)}\right)^{2/9}.
\tag{K.9.5h.6}
$$

*Proof.* With $\Upsilon_G-1=A_c\left(1-e^{-\sigma}\right)$ and $\dot\sigma=\sigma'(s)\,\dot s=3Hs\,\sigma'(s)$, (K.9.16) on the matter branch gives $\rho_{ad}=A_c\left(1-e^{-\sigma}\right)\rho_\Lambda/s$ and $p_{ad}=-\left(\dot\Upsilon_G/3H\right)\rho_b=-A_c\,s\,\sigma'(s)\,e^{-\sigma}\,\rho_\Lambda/s$, so
$$
w_{DE}+1=\frac{A_c\,e^{-\sigma}\left(e^{\sigma}-1-s\,\sigma'(s)\right)}{s\left[1+A_c\left(1-e^{-\sigma}\right)/s\right]},
$$
whose prefactor and denominator are strictly positive; $s\,\sigma'=n_{\mathrm{clk}}\,\sigma$ gives the second equality in (K.9.5h.5). For small $s$: $e^{\sigma}-1\le\sigma+\sigma^{2}$ for $\sigma\le1$, while $n_{\mathrm{clk}}\,\sigma\ge\frac{3}{2}\,\sigma/M(s)$ with $M(s)\to1$ and $\sigma(s)\to0$ by Proposition K.9.5h, so $e^{\sigma}-1-n_{\mathrm{clk}}\,\sigma\le\sigma\left(1+\sigma-\frac{3}{2M(s)}\right)<0$ for all sufficiently small $s$, proving $w_{DE}<-1$ on some $\left(0,s_{-}\right)$. For large $s$: $s\,\sigma'(s)=\frac{\kappa_\sigma}{3}\,s^{3/2}/M(s)\le\frac{\kappa_\sigma}{3}$ for every $s>0$, because $M(s)\ge s^{3/2}$; while for $s'\ge\max\{1,1+A_c\}$ one has $\left(1+s'\right)\le2s'$ and $\sqrt{s'+\Upsilon_G}\le\sqrt{2s'}$, so $\sigma'(s')\ge\frac{\kappa_\sigma}{6\sqrt2\,s'}$ and $\sigma(s)\to\infty$ logarithmically. Hence $e^{\sigma}-1$ exceeds the bounded quantity $s\,\sigma'$ for all sufficiently large $s$, proving $w_{DE}>-1$ on some $\left(s_{+},\infty\right)$. For $\sigma=\frac{2\kappa_\sigma}{9}s^{3/2}$ exactly, $s\,\sigma'=\frac{3}{2}\sigma$, so (K.9.5h.5) becomes $\operatorname{sign}\left(e^{x}-1-\frac{3}{2}x\right)$ with $x=\sigma$; the argument of Theorem K.9.3d depends only on the strict convexity of $h_{3/2}$ and the strict monotonicity of $x$ in cosmic time, both of which hold here, so the divide is crossed exactly once, at the unique positive root $x_c(3/2)$ of $e^{x}=1+\frac{3}{2}x$. The crossing condition $\frac{2\kappa_\sigma}{9}\,s_\times^{3/2}=x_c(3/2)$ with $s_{bg}(a)=s_{bg,0}\,a^{3}$ from Corollary K.9.3e gives $s_\times=\left(9\,x_c(3/2)/\left(2\kappa_\sigma\right)\right)^{2/3}$ and $1+z_\times=\left(s_{bg,0}/s_\times\right)^{1/3}$, which is (K.9.5h.6). ∎

<a id="remark-k95i-capacity-selection-and-two-clock-branches"></a>**Remark K.9.5i (Capacity Selection and Two Clock Branches).** Capacity tracking gives $A_c=1$. The horizon-bath ODE retains $\kappa_\sigma$ and determines $\sigma(s)$ over the full matter branch. It gives $\sigma(s)\sim(2\kappa_\sigma/9)s^{3/2}$ near zero and $\sigma(s)\sim(\kappa_\sigma/3)\ln s$ at large $s$: multiply (K.9.5h.1) by $s$ and use $1\le\Upsilon_G\le1+A_c$ to obtain $s\sigma'(s)\to\kappa_\sigma/3$. Integration gives the logarithmic asymptotic.

The exact power-clock branch separately registers $\sigma=c_\sigma s^{3/2}$, $c_\sigma>0$. It has the unique phantom crossing of (K.9.5h.6) with $c_\sigma=2\kappa_\sigma/9$ when that normalization is chosen. Choosing $\kappa_\sigma=9/2$ fixes the dense-limit coefficient to one for the ODE; retaining $\sigma=s^{3/2}$ at finite sparsity is the additional power-clock model. The full ODE has the early phantom and late nonphantom intervals proved in Corollary K.9.5h.1. The static counterpart of the exact power clock is developed in Definition I.13c.1 and Proposition I.13c.2, where $m=2n=3$. The multiplicity menu in Proposition I.13c.3 has $A_G=1$ at its serialized member $j=1$ and $A_G=d_0-1$ at $j=K_0$. Its registered rate modulus and multiplicity are the additional spatial bridge data.

<a id="definition-k95j-tensor-propagation-and-endpoint-matching-branch"></a>**Definition K.9.5j (Tensor Propagation and Endpoint-Matching Branch).** In the $c=1$ matter background, register a positive twice differentiable tensor coefficient $Q_T(t)=Q_{T,0}\Upsilon_{G,0}/\Upsilon_G(t)$ and the action, per transverse-traceless polarization,
$$
S_T=\frac18\int dt\,d^3x\,a^3 Q_T
\left[\dot h^2-\frac{(\nabla h)^2}{a^2}\right].
$$
The covariant realization certificate specifies the field carrying $Q_T$, its background equations, conserved stress, and the reduction to this quadratic action. The source and detector certificate specifies waveform phasing, photon propagation, and the net strain-transfer factor $\mathcal T(z)>0$ across the two endpoint transitions relative to homogeneous propagation. The unit-transfer subbranch requires $\mathcal T(z)=1$ from that calculation.

<a id="proposition-k95k-tensor-amplitude-and-standard-siren-law"></a>**Proposition K.9.5k (Tensor Amplitude and Standard-Siren Law).** On this branch,
$$
\ddot h_k+(3+\alpha_M)H\dot h_k+\frac{k^2}{a^2}h_k=0,\qquad
\alpha_M=\frac{d\ln Q_T}{d\ln a}=-3s\frac{\Upsilon_G'(s)}{\Upsilon_G(s)}.
$$
The kinetic and gradient terms give unit tensor speed. In conformal time, let $z_T=a\sqrt{Q_T}$ and $v=z_T h_k$. Then $v''+[k^2-z_T''/z_T]v=0$. On a geometric-optics window with a registered bound on $|z_T''/(z_T k^2)|$ and the variation of this quantity, the leading amplitude is $h_k\propto z_T^{-1}$. The distance ratio (K.9.5k.2) and its distance-consistency relation (K.9.5l.1) are at this leading order. Finite-frequency comparisons retain the error controlled by the registered geometric-optics certificate. Consequently, at leading order,
$$
\frac{d_L^{GW}}{d_L^{EM}}(z)
=\frac1{\mathcal T(z)}
\sqrt{\frac{\Upsilon_G(s(z))}{\Upsilon_G(s_0)}}.
\tag{K.9.5k.2}
$$

*Proof.* Varying the action gives $\partial_t(a^3Q_T\dot h)=aQ_T\nabla^2h$. Division by $a^3Q_T$ gives the mode equation. Substitution of $v=z_T h_k$ in conformal time cancels the first derivative. The certified adiabatic approximation makes $v$ have constant leading amplitude, so propagation scales strain by $z_T^{-1}$. Relative to propagation with constant $Q_T$, this contributes $\sqrt{Q_T(a_e)/Q_T(a_0)}$ to strain. Multiplication by the registered endpoint transfer and inversion of the amplitude-distance relation give (K.9.5k.2). ∎

On the unit-transfer subbranch, an increasing $\Upsilon_G(s)$ gives a decreasing distance ratio with redshift. Its small-$z$ expansion is $1+\alpha_M(s_0)z/2+O(z^2)$ and its matter-branch limit is $\Upsilon_{G,0}^{-1/2}$. Equal screened endpoint coefficients require an explicit transition calculation: adiabatic transport through both screened transitions can cancel the homogeneous factor.

For the illustrative exact power-clock choice $A_c=1$, $\sigma=s^{3/2}$, and $s_0=1.4$, the unit-transfer ratios at $z=0.01,0.1,0.3,1$ are respectively $0.996025$, $0.957876$, $0.879269$, and $0.769253$, with matter-branch limiting value $0.743460$. The full horizon-bath clock instead uses its ODE solution and registered $\kappa_\sigma$. A siren comparison fixes that response, endpoint transfer, waveform, source-selection function, and covariance before testing the joint prediction.

<a id="corollary-k95l-density-history-and-siren-consistency"></a>**Corollary K.9.5l (Density-History and Siren Consistency).** On the matter adaptive-fluid and tensor branches,
$$
\rho_{DE}-\rho_\Lambda=(\Upsilon_G-1)\rho_b,
$$
and therefore
$$
\left(\mathcal T(z)\frac{d_L^{GW}}{d_L^{EM}}(z)\right)^2
=\frac{1+[\rho_{DE}(z)-\rho_\Lambda]/\rho_b(z)}
{1+[\rho_{DE,0}-\rho_\Lambda]/\rho_{b,0}}.
\tag{K.9.5l.1}
$$

*Proof.* Solve the adaptive-density identity for $\Upsilon_G$ at emission and observation, substitute both expressions into (K.9.5k.2), and square. The amplitude, exponent and clock normalization cancel explicitly. ∎

This identity tests the background-density and tensor-response maps across differentiable response profiles. The background reconstruction uses data held separate from the siren amplitudes assigned to the test and carries their common cosmological covariance. For an exact power clock with $n>1$, $\rho_{DE}\to\rho_\Lambda$ as $s\downarrow0$ on the mathematical matter branch; for $n=1$ the limit is $(1+A_c)\rho_\Lambda$. A high-redshift physical reconstruction includes radiation.

<a id="theorem-k95m-gaussian-collision-source-and-its-physical-response-work-functional"></a>**Theorem K.9.5m (Gaussian Collision Source and Its Physical Response-Work Functional).** Fix $E_0,\lambda,\beta>0$, an integer $N\ge1$, and a finite intrinsic-time grid $0=\sigma_0<\cdots<\sigma_M=T$. Intrinsic time is the supplied apparatus clock $\sigma=\lambda t_{\mathrm{lab}}$. Set $\Delta_j=\sigma_{j+1}-\sigma_j$, $r_j=e^{-\Delta_j}$ and $s_j=\sqrt{1-r_j^2}$. Every mode has dimensionless canonical operators $[Q,P]=i$ and native Hamiltonian
$$
H_0=\frac{E_0}{2}(Q^2+P^2),\qquad
\tau=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H_0},\qquad
\theta=\frac12\coth\frac{\beta E_0}{2}.
\tag{K.9.5m.1}
$$
There are finitely many oscillator modes at each finite grid, with infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and unbounded energy support. All stated mean energies and moments are finite; this is not a finite-dimensional or bounded-support apparatus.

**Part I. Physical inputs, collisions and all energy ports.** Prepare each carrier in $D_Q(-1)\tau D_Q(-1)^*$, where $D_Q(d)=e^{-idP}$, and define
$$
X_N=1+\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^NQ_i.
\tag{K.9.5m.2}
$$
Its initial mean is zero and its variance is $\theta/N$. The carrier displacement preparation costs $E_0/2$ per mode. Its sample space is the whole real line; nonnegative deterministic mean profiles do not restrict individual Gaussian samples.

For each $i,j$ supply a fresh Gibbs mode, translate its $Q$ mean by deterministic $d_j$, and collide it with carrier $i$. A resonant Weyl drive whose interaction vanishes at its endpoints has exact mean preparation work
$$
w_{\mathrm{prep}}(d_j)
=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[H_0D_Q(d_j)\tau D_Q(d_j)^*-H_0\tau\bigr]
=\frac{E_0d_j^2}{2}.
\tag{K.9.5m.3}
$$
For an explicit drift-retaining implementation let $\omega_0=E_0/\hbar$, $U_0(t)=e^{-iH_0t/\hbar}$, and choose a real $C^1$ profile $d(t)$ from zero to $d_j$, with $\dot d=0$ at its endpoints. For example use a rescaled $3s^2-2s^3$ profile over any registered positive preparation duration. Take
$$
H_{\mathrm{prep}}(t)=H_0+\hbar\dot d(t)U_0(t)PU(0)(t)^*
=H_0+\hbar\dot d(t)[P\cos(\omega_0t)+Q\sin(\omega_0t)].
\tag{K.9.5m.3a}
$$
In the native interaction picture the generator is $\hbar\dot d(t)P$ and its exact propagator is $D_Q(d(t))$. Hence the endpoint is the stated displaced thermal state in the registered rotating quadrature; choosing the entering phase aligns it with the collision clock. The laboratory drift remains present, with no negative-native-Hamiltonian cancellation. At each finite pulse the harmonic Hamiltonian plus a finite linear term is self-adjoint and bounded below by completion of the square. Coupling vanishes at endpoints, so its net driving work is precisely the native energy change (K.9.5m.3); the positive preparation duration, phase and peak control remain supplied resources.

Indeed $D_Q(d)^*QD_Q(d)=Q+d$, centered means vanish, and covariance and entropy are unchanged. This is also the displacement free-energy increase. It is not heat. Each prepared mode is supplied once and its spent output is retained; no recovery is credited without a recovery operation.

The collision is the passive canonical rotation
$$
\begin{pmatrix}Q_{\mathrm{new}}\\Q_{\mathrm{out}}\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}r_j&s_j\\-s_j&r_j\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}Q_{\mathrm{old}}\\Q_{\mathrm{bath}}\end{pmatrix},
\tag{K.9.5m.4}
$$
with the same rotation on $P$. Its generator is $J=P_{\mathrm{old}}Q_{\mathrm{bath}}-Q_{\mathrm{old}}P_{\mathrm{bath}}$: the identities $[J,Q_{\mathrm{old}}]=-iQ_{\mathrm{bath}}$, $[J,Q_{\mathrm{bath}}]=iQ_{\mathrm{old}}$ give (K.9.5m.4) under $e^{-i\vartheta_jJ}$, $\vartheta_j=\arccos r_j$. The rotation strongly commutes with the pair's native Hamiltonian and conserves its energy for every input.

A stable pulse is available. Put
$$
L=\frac12(Q_{\mathrm{old}}^2+P_{\mathrm{old}}^2+Q_{\mathrm{bath}}^2+P_{\mathrm{bath}}^2),
\qquad H(t)=H_{0,\mathrm{pair}}+\hbar g(t)(L+J),\quad g(t)\ge0.
\tag{K.9.5m.5}
$$
In passive normal modes $L+J\ge0$, so $H(t)$ is bounded below. Since $L,J,H_{0,\mathrm{pair}}$ commute, a pulse of integral $\vartheta_j$ gives the required rotation plus a known common phase. Input displacement phases and the rotating quadrature are aligned by a supplied phase/clock service. Interaction is off at endpoints. The conserved pulse observable makes the mean energy borrowed on switch-on return on switch-off. Its peak stock and gross throughput remain resources. No arbitrarily strong unbounded-below bare $H_0+gJ$, or autonomous finite quantum clock, is assumed.

Identical thermal covariance is invariant under the passive rotation; displaced product thermal inputs give displaced product thermal outputs. If $m_j=u_j-1$ is the carrier mean, put
$$
m_{j+1}=r_jm_j+h_j,\qquad h_j=s_jd_j,\qquad
b_j=-s_jm_j+r_jd_j.
\tag{K.9.5m.6}
$$
Then the actual incoming displacement work, carrier displacement energy and spent output displacement energy are
$$
W_{\mathrm{in},h}=\frac{NE_0}{2}\sum_j\frac{h_j^2}{1-r_j^2},\quad
F_j=\frac{NE_0m_j^2}{2},\quad B_j=\frac{NE_0b_j^2}{2},
$$
$$
F_j+\frac{NE_0d_j^2}{2}=F_{j+1}+B_j,\qquad
F_0+W_{\mathrm{in},h}=F_M+W_{\mathrm{out},h},\quad
W_{\mathrm{out},h}=\sum_jB_j\ge0,\quad F_0=\frac{NE_0}{2}.
\tag{K.9.5m.7}
$$
Orthogonality proves these identities. Thermal baseline energies and entropies do not change. Output displacement energy is exported nonequilibrium free energy; thermalizing or resetting it is another operation. For a fixed average $h_j$, this input work is least among deterministic $Q/P$ translations of the stated $N$ fresh thermal modes: $\sum_id_i^2\ge N(\frac1N\sum_id_i)^2$, and nonzero $P$ displacement adds work. This is not optimization over arbitrary baths, squeezing, feedback or hardware.

**Part II. Exact sampled law and two different relative entropies.** In the commuting rotating-$Q$ algebra,
$$
X_{j+1}=1+r_j(X_j-1)+h_j+
\sqrt{\frac{\theta(1-r_j^2)}N}\,Z_j,
\qquad X_0\sim\mathcal N(0,\theta/N),
\tag{K.9.5m.8}
$$
where the $Z_j$ are independent standard Gaussians. This is an exact quadrature law, not a Gaussian expansion of jump statistics. It has variance $\theta/N$ at every grid time. Multiplication of Gaussian transition densities against the same zero-displacement source gives
$$
D_{Q,h}=\frac{N}{2\theta}\sum_j\frac{h_j^2}{1-r_j^2},\qquad
W_{\mathrm{in},h}=E_0\theta D_{Q,h}.
\tag{K.9.5m.9}
$$
For a full displaced quantum thermal mode instead,
$$
D(D_Q(d)\tau D_Q(d)^*\Vert\tau)=\frac{\beta E_0d^2}{2}.
\tag{K.9.5m.10}
$$
Translation preserves entropy and $\log\tau=-\beta H_0-\log Z$, proving (K.9.5m.10). Thus the full incoming-ancilla relative entropy is $\beta W_{\mathrm{in},h}$, whereas the measured commuting path entropy is $W_{\mathrm{in},h}/(E_0\theta)$. Quantum $\theta$ is not generally $1/(\beta E_0)$; these quantities are not equated away from their classical limit.

**Part III. Controlled work limit and its boundary term.** For any prescribed $a\in L^2(0,T)$ let $u'=1-u+a$, $u(0)=0$, and prepare
$$
h_j=\int_{\sigma_j}^{\sigma_{j+1}}e^{-(\sigma_{j+1}-s)}a(s)\,ds,
\qquad d_j=\frac{h_j}{\sqrt{1-e^{-2\Delta_j}}}.
\tag{K.9.5m.11}
$$
The grid mean is exactly $u(\sigma_j)$ and (K.9.5m.8) is precisely the sampled law of
$$
dX_N=[1-X_N+a(\sigma)]d\sigma+\sqrt{2\theta/N}\,dB_\sigma,
\qquad X_N(0)\sim\mathcal N(0,\theta/N).
\tag{K.9.5m.12}
$$
This sampled identity alone does not identify the physical within-pulse path; Theorem K.9.5o supplies that additional comparison.

Let $P_h$ be the $L^2$ projection onto functions that on each grid cell are scalar multiples of $e^{s-\sigma_{j+1}}$. That kernel has squared norm $(1-r_j^2)/2$, so
$$
W_{\mathrm{in},h}=\frac{NE_0}{4}\|P_ha\|_2^2,\qquad
W_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{NE_0}{4}\|a\|_2^2,\qquad
0\le W_{\mathrm{in}}-W_{\mathrm{in},h}
=\frac{NE_0}{4}\|a-P_ha\|_2^2\longrightarrow0.
\tag{K.9.5m.13}
$$
To prove strong projection convergence for arbitrary meshes tending to zero, approximate $a$ by a $C^1$ function, use projection contractivity, and approximate that function on each cell by its left endpoint value times $e^{s-\sigma_j}$. For $a\in H^1(0,T)$ and $h=\max_j\Delta_j$ one has the quantitative bound
$$
0\le W_{\mathrm{in}}-W_{\mathrm{in},h}
\le\frac{NE_0e^{2h}h^2}{8}\|a'-a\|_2^2.
\tag{K.9.5m.14}
$$
Indeed
$$
a(s)-e^{s-\sigma_j}a(\sigma_j)
=\int_{\sigma_j}^se^{s-r}[a'(r)-a(r)]\,dr.
$$
Cauchy–Schwarz and cell integration give squared error at most $e^{2h}h^2\|a'-a\|_2^2/2$; the true projection is no worse. Refining the exact Gaussian likelihood, equivalently its deterministic-$L^2$ Gaussian shift, gives continuous path entropy $N\|a\|_2^2/(4\theta)$. Finite windows precede monotone half-line limits; no finite ready bath supplies infinitely many modes.

Write $a=u'+u-1$ and
$$
\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp},T}[u]=\frac12\int_0^T[u'^2+(1-u)^2]d\sigma.
$$
Completing the square and using the actual energy balance give
$$
\frac{NE_0}{2}\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp},T}
=W_{\mathrm{in}}+\frac{F_0-F_T}{2}
=\frac{W_{\mathrm{in}}+W_{\mathrm{out}}}{2},
\qquad F_T=\frac{NE_0}{2}(1-u(T))^2.
\tag{K.9.5m.15}
$$
Here $W_{\mathrm{out}}=\lim_{h\to0}W_{\mathrm{out},h}$ exists by (K.9.5m.7), (K.9.5m.13) and the fixed terminal mean. The boundary is half the physical displacement-energy drop. The final expression is a port identity, not permission to bill input and exported free energy as independent expenditures. The exported free energy is recoverable by a passive operation of the same class. Let a collector be one further centered thermal mode of the same frequency and temperature, with current mean $c\ge0$, and let a spent output mode have mean $b$. For $R=\sqrt{c^2+b^2}>0$ apply the passive rotation $(Q_{\mathrm{coll}},Q_{\mathrm{out}})\mapsto\bigl((cQ_{\mathrm{coll}}+bQ_{\mathrm{out}})/R,\,(-bQ_{\mathrm{coll}}+cQ_{\mathrm{out}})/R\bigr)$, with the same rotation on $P$ (the identity if $c=b=0$). Identical thermal covariances are invariant, so the output mode leaves in its centered Gibbs state, the collector mean becomes $R$ and its displacement energy rises by $E_0b^2/2$, with no entropy change. Applied to every spent mode, this returns exactly $W_{\mathrm{out},h}$. If that return is credited, (K.9.5m.7) gives
$$
W_{\mathrm{in},h}-W_{\mathrm{out},h}=F_M-F_0,
\tag{K.9.5m.15a}
$$
which is the same for every control with a common terminal mean. For example, with two cells of equal length, $r=e^{-\Delta}$ and $s=\sqrt{1-r^2}$, the controls $(d_0,d_1)=(0,0)$ and $(\epsilon,-r\epsilon)$, $\epsilon>0$, both reach $u_2=1-r^2$; the second needs $NE_0\epsilon^2(1+r^2)/2$ more input work and returns exactly that much more output energy, and its within-pulse means of Theorem K.9.5o exceed the nonnegative means $1-\cos\phi_0$ and $1-r\cos\phi_1$ of the first by $\epsilon\sin\phi_0$ and $\epsilon\sin(\vartheta-\phi_1)$. Incoming work therefore selects $u_*$ in (K.9.5m.16) on the declared no-return port boundary, on which spent outputs remain exported; a complete PCE reduction of Definition K.9.5b on this source has to fix that boundary. On exactly Definition K.9.5b's half-line domain, $u(\infty)=1$ and
$$
\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}[u]=\frac{2W_{\mathrm{in}}[u]}{NE_0}+\frac12,
\qquad
\frac{2(F_0+W_{\mathrm{in}})}{NE_0}=\mathcal S_{\mathrm{resp}}+\frac12.
\tag{K.9.5m.16}
$$
Hence incoming variable work and the registered quadratic have the same unique minimizer $u_*=1-e^{-\sigma}$ on that domain. The affine map $u\mapsto u'+u-1$ is injective with fixed $u(0)$, so its squared norm is strictly convex. Nonmonotone nonnegative profiles and overshoots retain their correct positive work; a fluctuating sample path is not this mean. Free terminal values or times require the boundary term rather than its deletion.

In laboratory time,
$$
W_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{NE_0}{4\lambda}
\int[\dot u-\lambda(1-u)]^2dt_{\mathrm{lab}}.
\tag{K.9.5m.17}
$$
The symmetric velocity and potential coefficients are $NE_0/(4\lambda)$ and $NE_0\lambda/4$, with ratio $\lambda^2$. Their equality after intrinsic-time normalization is a property of this supplied oscillator source, not a derivation of $\lambda$ from enthalpy, horizon temperature, cosmology or $\kappa_\sigma$. Source/capability stock, physical phase clock, readout, spatial/gravitational realization and the complete PCE objective remain separate from this one proved work component. ∎

<a id="theorem-k95n-same-carrier-capacity-instrument-finite-errors-and-recoil"></a>**Theorem K.9.5n (Same-Carrier Capacity Instrument, Finite Errors and Recoil).** Use Theorem K.9.5m's actual Gaussian coordinate $X_N\sim\mathcal N(u,\theta/N)$ at one registered service time. The following fixed instrument acts on its whole real domain and on an arbitrary eight-dimensional input $A\otimes B\otimes R$, where $A,B,R$ are qubits. It does not inspect the payload to choose its mode or replace $X_N$ by its mean.

**Part I. Complete instrument.** Define
$$
p_A(x)=\begin{cases}1,&x\le1,\\2/(1+x),&x>1,\end{cases}\qquad
p_B(x)=\begin{cases}1,&x\le0,\\(1-x)/(1+x),&0<x<1,\\0,&x\ge1,\end{cases}
$$
$$
r_2=p_B,\quad r_1=p_A-p_B,\quad r_0=1-p_A,\qquad
\mathfrak g(x)=2r_2+r_1=\begin{cases}2,&x\le0,\\2/(1+x),&x\ge0.\end{cases}
\tag{K.9.5n.1}
$$
These nonnegative mode probabilities sum to one. Mode $2$ retains both payload bits, mode $1$ retains only $A$, mode $0$ retains neither. There is no upper clipping at $x=1$: overshoots have a defined smaller capacity.

Fix $0<\eta<1/3$ and set
$$
M_\eta f(x)=\frac1{2\eta}\int_{-\eta}^\eta f(x-z)\,dz,
\qquad r_{k,\eta}=(1-3\eta)M_\eta r_k+\eta,
\qquad \mathfrak g_\eta=(1-3\eta)M_\eta\mathfrak g+3\eta.
\tag{K.9.5n.2}
$$
The original probabilities are globally $2$-Lipschitz. The new probabilities are $C^1$, at least $\eta$, sum to one, and have derivative magnitude at most $2$. Also $|\mathfrak g_\eta-\mathfrak g|\le5\eta$ and $\operatorname{Lip}(\mathfrak g_\eta)\le2$, by the uniform kernel and $0\le\mathfrak g\le2$. Smoothing controls the square-root amplitude derivative at vanishing probabilities.

On a fresh qutrit with ordered basis $(2,1,0)$ initially $|2\rangle$, first rotate the $(2,1)$ plane by $\alpha(x)$ and then the $(1,0)$ plane by $\zeta(x)$, where
$$
\alpha=\arccos\sqrt{r_{2,\eta}},\qquad
\zeta=\arccos\sqrt{\frac{r_{1,\eta}}{r_{0,\eta}+r_{1,\eta}}}.
\tag{K.9.5n.3}
$$
The result is $\sum_{k=0}^2\sqrt{r_{k,\eta}(x)}|k\rangle$. The rotations have bounded finite-dimensional Hermitian generators with fixed bounded $C^1$ functions of $X_N$. Functional calculus gives a bounded unitary $V_\eta(X_N)$. Its physical rotation Hamiltonians can be specified without suppressing native drift. On the ordered plane $(a,b)$ put $Y_{ab}=-i|a\rangle\langle b|+i|b\rangle\langle a|$ and define $B_1=\alpha(X_N)Y_{21}$, $B_2=\zeta(X_N)Y_{10}$. If $H_{\mathrm{src}}$ is the retained native source Hamiltonian and $U_{\mathrm{src}}(t)=e^{-iH_{\mathrm{src}}t/\hbar}$, choose smooth disjoint pulses $f_1,f_2$ of positive duration, unit integral and zero endpoint coupling, and use
$$
H_{\mathrm{read},\ell}(t)=H_{\mathrm{src}}+
\hbar f_\ell(t)U_{\mathrm{src}}(t)B_\ell U_{\mathrm{src}}(t)^*,
\quad \ell=1,2,
\qquad U_{I,\mathrm{read}}=e^{-iB_2}e^{-iB_1}=V_\eta(X_N).
\tag{K.9.5n.3a}
$$
Here $X_N$ denotes the nominated snapshot quadrature in this interaction picture. Each $B_\ell$ is bounded with norm at most $\pi/2$, so the full Hamiltonian has the native self-adjoint domain and is bounded below by the native lower bound minus its finite bounded pulse norm. The known free rotation is included in the owned phase/clock convention. Endpoints have the native Hamiltonian, so work is the native endpoint energy difference computed in Part III. This is specified smooth control hardware and not an uncharged observer, a finite digital synthesis theorem or a bounded-range locality claim.

Copy the mode to an owned fresh qutrit record kept in the complement. Tracing that record dephases the mode exactly. Mode-controlled SWAPs move $B$ to a blank complement in mode $1$, and $A,B$ to blank complements in mode $0$. No payload information is destroyed. Encode the reachable alternatives into seven orthogonal output states: four for mode $2$, two for mode $1$, one for mode $0$. This is an isometry on those seven reachable states, extended to a finite unitary using blank output and retained complement. It is not a dimension-reducing unitary on the unused twelve-state intermediate space. Seven outputs fit in three qubits, but are not the four-dimensional completed-reset output of Proposition E.2a. Initially SWAP the incoming $R$ to an archive and replace it by a ready flag; it is not an additional sender-controlled route. The source and mode law are independent of all payload data and arbitrary incoming correlations.

**Part II. Exact operational capacity and finite errors.** Put $q_k=\mathbb E[r_{k,\eta}(X_N)]$. The actual payload channel is
$$
\Phi(\rho)=q_2\rho_{AB}\oplus q_1\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB}
\oplus q_0\operatorname{Tr}\rho_{AB},\qquad
C_{N,\eta}(u)=(2q_2+q_1)\ln2=\mathbb E[\mathfrak g_\eta(X_N)]\ln2.
\tag{K.9.5n.4}
$$
For every ensemble the message-independent flag entropy cancels in its Holevo information. Conditional output dimensions bound the three contributions by $2\ln2$, $\ln2$ and zero; independent fair computational-basis bits attain all three simultaneously. For any number of independent service uses, the same conditional-dimension bound holds for arbitrary entangled encodings across them, so regularization cannot increase this classical capacity. Mode $0$ is a flag independent of the message. Independent repeats require freshly prepared sources/readout resources or an actually charged reset. The assertion does not identify repeated use of one unchanged random mask with this capacity.

Gaussianity and the Lipschitz bound give, uniformly in real $u$, time and deterministic drive,
$$
\left|\frac{C_{N,\eta}(u)}{\ln2}-\mathfrak g(u)\right|
\le\delta_{N,\eta}:=2\sqrt{\frac{2\theta}{\pi N}}+5\eta.
\tag{K.9.5n.5}
$$
Indeed $\mathbb E|X_N-u|=\sqrt{2\theta/(\pi N)}$; no equality of an averaged nonlinear capacity with its value at the mean is assumed. For a nonnegative limiting profile, $N\to\infty$, $\eta\to0$ therefore gives $C(u)=2\ln2/(1+u)$. On $u_*=1-e^{-\sigma}$,
$$
C(\sigma)=\frac{2\ln2}{2-e^{-\sigma}},\qquad
C(0)=2\ln2,\quad C(\infty)=\ln2,\quad
\frac{C(0)}{C(\sigma)}=2-e^{-\sigma}.
\tag{K.9.5n.6}
$$
For $\delta=\delta_{N,\eta}<1$, $1\le\mathfrak g(u_*)\le2$ and $C_{N,\eta}/\ln2\ge1-\delta$ imply
$$
\left|\frac{2\ln2}{C_{N,\eta}(u_*)}-(1+u_*)\right|
\le\frac{2\delta}{1-\delta},\qquad
\left|\frac{C_{N,\eta}(0)}{C_{N,\eta}(u_*)}-(1+u_*)\right|
\le\frac{3\delta}{1-\delta}.
\tag{K.9.5n.7}
$$
For a general nonnegative profile on a compact service window use its positive minimum $\mathfrak g$, not this uniform inverse bound for arbitrarily large $u$. At fixed finite $N,\eta$ neither capacity endpoint nor the exponential response is asserted exact. Waiting does not remove stationary Gaussian noise. Uniform error allows endpoint and readout limits to interchange for these capacities; their physical resource budgets do not thereby interchange.

**Part III. Recoil of the actual readout.** Define the Hermitian matrix $\mathcal A(x)=-iV_\eta(x)^*V_\eta'(x)$. The two rotations give
$$
\|\mathcal A(x)\|\le|\alpha'(x)|+|\zeta'(x)|\le4/\eta.
\tag{K.9.5n.8}
$$
For example $|\alpha'|\le1/\sqrt{\eta(1-\eta)}$ and $|\zeta'|\le1/\eta$. The rotations are real orthogonal, so $\langle2|\mathcal A(x)|2\rangle=0$ identically. The controlled unitary preserves all $Q_i$ and changes $P_i$ by $\pm\mathcal A(X_N)/N$, with sign determined by conjugation convention. On an independent source and $|2\rangle$, the kinetic cross term vanishes because that diagonal matrix element and its derivative vanish. Consequently
$$
0\le W_{\mathrm{read}}\le\frac{8E_0}{N\eta^2}.
\tag{K.9.5n.9}
$$
Copy and payload SWAPs need no further $X_N$ dependence. With degenerate bare payload/flag energies they have zero net native mean-energy transfer, but finite pulse capability, stock, duration and records remain paid. Since interactions start/end off, the readout work supply pays its native energy change. Hardware fabrication and initial cold/ready states are not declared free. With $\eta=N^{-1/3}$, $N>27$, capacity error and the recoil bound $8E_0N^{-1/3}$ vanish; no general complexity or peak-power cost limit is inferred.

On the fresh ready state the recoil has an exact form. Write $\psi(x)=V_\eta(x)|2\rangle=\sum_k\sqrt{r_{k,\eta}(x)}\,|k\rangle$. Then $\mathcal A(x)|2\rangle=-iV_\eta(x)^*\psi'(x)$ and $\langle\psi,\psi'\rangle=\frac12\sum_kr_{k,\eta}'=0$, so
$$
W_{\mathrm{read}}(u)=\frac{E_0}{2N}\,\mathbb E\|\psi'(X_N)\|^2
=\frac{E_0}{8N}\,\mathbb E\sum_k\frac{r_{k,\eta}'(X_N)^2}{r_{k,\eta}(X_N)}
\le\frac{3E_0}{2N\eta},
\tag{K.9.5n.9a}
$$
using $r_{k,\eta}\ge\eta$ and $|r_{k,\eta}'|\le2$. The integrand is bounded and continuous, so $W_{\mathrm{read}}$ is continuous in $u$. This form uses the ready state $|2\rangle$; other qutrit inputs are covered by (K.9.5n.9).

Fix a service time $\tau\ge0$ and define on $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{resp}}$ the work-plus-readout objective $J[u]=W_{\mathrm{in}}[u]+W_{\mathrm{read}}(u(\tau))$, with the half-line incoming work $W_{\mathrm{in}}[u]=\frac{NE_0}4\int_0^\infty(u'+u-1)^2d\sigma$ of (K.9.5m.16). For $v=u-u_*$ one has $v(0)=0$, $v\in H^1(0,\infty)$ and $v'+v=u'+u-1$, so integration by parts gives $W_{\mathrm{in}}[u]=\frac{NE_0}4\|u-u_*\|_{H^1}^2$. The admissible $v$ form a nonempty closed convex subset of $H^1(0,\infty)$, evaluation at $\tau$ is a bounded linear functional on $H^1$, and $W_{\mathrm{read}}\ge0$ is continuous; the direct method gives a minimizer $\hat u$ of $J$. Since $W_{\mathrm{in}}[\hat u]\le J[u_*]=W_{\mathrm{read}}(u_*(\tau))$, every minimizer satisfies
$$
\|\hat u-u_*\|_{H^1}^2\le\frac6{N^2\eta},\qquad
\sup_{\sigma\ge0}|\hat u(\sigma)-u_*(\sigma)|\le\frac{\sqrt3}{N\sqrt\eta},
\tag{K.9.5n.9b}
$$
the second from $v(\sigma)=\int_0^\sigma e^{-(\sigma-s)}(v'+v)(s)\,ds$ and Cauchy–Schwarz. With $\eta=N^{-1/2}$, $N>9$, the recoil is at most $\frac32E_0N^{-1/2}$, and every minimizer lies within $\sqrt6\,N^{-3/4}$ of $u_*$ in $H^1$ and within $\sqrt3\,N^{-3/4}$ uniformly. The minimizer need not be unique, because $W_{\mathrm{read}}$ need not be convex. The objective $J$ contains incoming work and one readout; the other resources are those of Part IV.

**Part IV. Complete finite-resource and source boundary.** The source includes $N$ carrier oscillators with thermal energy $E_0\theta$ and displacement stock $E_0/2$ each, $NM$ fresh thermal modes with baseline $NME_0\theta$ and finite entropy, their actual extra input work and every retained spent output, stable collision controls and the phase clock, both payloads and archived input context, the mode and copy qutrits, seven-state output/encoding auxiliaries and all erased payload complements, and the external displacement/borrowing/recoil supply. Gibbs preparation, cold memory, optional recycling, records and any local compiler have their own costs. No exported free energy is charged twice or renamed heat.

On a fixed input-action budget $\|a\|_2\le A$, convolution and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|u-u_*|\le A/\sqrt2$, $|m_j|\le1+A/\sqrt2$, $|d_j|\le A/\sqrt2$. Thus fixed $N$, finite grid and bounded action allow a common finite displacement and mean pulse-stock budget, not a uniform stock over all profiles or refinements. The grid lasts $T/\lambda$ in laboratory time. As $\Delta\to0$, $\vartheta=\arccos(e^{-\Delta})\sim\sqrt{2\Delta}$, so stable pulse coefficient scales as $\lambda\sqrt{2/\Delta}$ and fresh stock as $NM$. The common baseline diverges while the supplied-control excess has the limit in (K.9.5m.13). Keep separate grid-work, readout and recoil errors before taking half-line/endpoint limits. No infinite apparatus or execution is claimed.

In the limiting dense mean $u=0$ the channel is $\operatorname{Tr}_R\rho_{ABR}\otimes|\mathrm{ready}\rangle\langle\mathrm{ready}|$ up to output coding, the $d_0=8,r=2$ completed-reset map. At $u=1$ it retains one qubit. Intermediate outputs use seven alternatives. Neither finite-noise source nor these intermediate channels are assigned the exact four-state completed-reset property. The mean susceptibility is $\delta u'=-\delta u+\delta a$ and, for positive mean, $\delta C=-2\ln2\,\delta u/(1+u)^2$. These are source/input/output responses, not metric/lensing/screening or gravitational stress equations. The harmonic source and rational instrument are explicitly supplied choices, not selected by PCE. Their existence does not identify capacity with Theorem 49's fixed-area coefficient or its inverse with $G_{\mathrm{eff}}$.

A concrete finite member takes $\hbar=E_0=\lambda=\beta=1$, $N=1000$, $M=20$, $\Delta=1/10$, $\eta=1/20$, and zero input. It has exact grid means $u_j=1-e^{-j/10}$ and the finite error bounds above. The analytic family for arbitrary $L^2$ controls specifies cell integrals; it does not claim a terminating exact evaluator for every noncomputable real control. Computable controls, including zero, give effective finite source descriptions. ∎

<a id="theorem-k95o-actual-continuous-collision-paths-derivative-obstruction-and-work-gamma-limit"></a>**Theorem K.9.5o (Actual Continuous Collision Paths, Derivative Obstruction and Work Gamma Limit).** Retain the finite oscillator source, physical clock $\sigma=\lambda t_{\mathrm{lab}}$, input work and readout of Theorems K.9.5m–n. Fix $N,\theta,E_0,\lambda$ and a finite intrinsic window $[0,T]$. Let $h=\max_j\Delta_j$ and use arbitrary grids with $h\to0$.

**Part I. The physical within-pulse path.** On a cell write $z=(\sigma-\sigma_j)/\Delta_j$, $\vartheta_j=\arccos(e^{-\Delta_j})$, and choose the actual angle $\phi_j(\sigma)=\vartheta_jz$. The stable pulse in laboratory time has coefficient $g_j=\lambda\vartheta_j/\Delta_j$ in (K.9.5m.5). Remove its known native/common phase using the registered rotating quadrature and prepare each entering bath in that phase. The actual unread coordinate is
$$
X_h(\sigma)-1=
\cos\phi_j(\sigma)[X_h(\sigma_j)-1]
+\sin\phi_j(\sigma)(d_j+Z_j),\qquad
Z_j\sim\mathcal N(0,v),\quad v=\theta/N.
\tag{K.9.5o.1}
$$
The averaged fresh bath variable is independent of the incoming carrier. After phase removal all tracked coordinates are real linear combinations of the initial carrier $Q$ and one fixed quadrature from each fresh bath. They commute. Thus (K.9.5o.1) has a simultaneous commutative Gaussian path law; it does not replace noncommuting sequential position measurements by classical data. Every finite path is continuous and piecewise smooth. Finite switch-on/off changes the Hamiltonian, not the continuity of state or quadrature. Prepare $d_j$ by (K.9.5m.11) for any deterministic $a\in L^2(0,T)$. The endpoint law is exactly that of the controlled OU process (K.9.5m.12), with initial mean zero and variance $v$.

**Part II. Exact endpoint interpolation and uniform coupling.** Eliminating $d_j+Z_j$ using the actual next endpoint gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
X_h(\sigma)-1&=A_j(\sigma)[X_h(\sigma_j)-1]
+B_j(\sigma)[X_h(\sigma_{j+1})-1],\\
A_j&=\frac{\sin(\vartheta_j-\phi_j)}{\sin\vartheta_j},\qquad
B_j=\frac{\sin\phi_j}{\sin\vartheta_j}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{K.9.5o.2}
$$
The weights are nonnegative and
$$
1\le A_j+B_j\le\sec(\vartheta_j/2)\le\sqrt2,\qquad
\vartheta_j^2\le2\Delta_j,\qquad
0\le A_j+B_j-1\le\frac{\Delta_j}{2\sqrt2}.
\tag{K.9.5o.3}
$$
Concavity of sine gives the first lower bound and its midpoint gives the maximum. Since $\tan x\ge x$, $-\log\cos x\ge x^2/2$, proving the angle bound. Finally $1-\cos(\vartheta_j/2)\le\vartheta_j^2/8$ and $\cos(\vartheta_j/2)\ge1/\sqrt2$ prove the last bound.

On one probability space take a continuous controlled OU path $X$ with the stated initial law, and define $X_h$ by (K.9.5o.2) from its grid values. The grid transition laws and within-cell map coincide with the physical source, so this coupling gives its exact finite path law. It is a proof device, not hardware feedback using future endpoints. For $f=X-1$ and its modulus $\omega_f(h)=\sup_{|s-t|\le h}|f(s)-f(t)|$,
$$
\|X_h-X\|_\infty
\le\sqrt2\,\omega_f(h)+\frac{h}{2\sqrt2}\|f\|_\infty
\longrightarrow0\quad\text{almost surely}.
\tag{K.9.5o.4}
$$
Every continuous path is uniformly continuous and bounded on this window. Thus the physical finite laws converge weakly in $C([0,T])$, for every deterministic $L^2$ control. This is the unread source path. A capacity snapshot is a separately prepared service or a readout after stopping at the nominated quadrature-clock time; its positive duration, records and recoil remain owned. A partly observed cell's already prepared bath is charged in full.

**Part III. Covariance and tightness.** Center by the actual mean $\mu_h$. Passive thermal covariance gives variance $v$ at every time. For $s\le t$ in one cell,
$$
\operatorname{Cov}_h(s,t)=v\cos\!\left(\frac{\vartheta_j(t-s)}{\Delta_j}\right).
$$
For $s$ in cell $j$ and $t$ in cell $k>j$, with their cell fractions $z_s,z_t$,
$$
\operatorname{Cov}_h(s,t)=v\cos[\vartheta_j(1-z_s)]
\exp\!\left(-\sum_{\ell=j+1}^{k-1}\Delta_\ell\right)
\cos(\vartheta_kz_t).
\tag{K.9.5o.5}
$$
The target covariance is $v e^{-|t-s|}$. Concavity of $\log\cos$ gives $\cos(q\arccos(e^{-\Delta}))\ge e^{-q\Delta}$ for $0\le q\le1$, and the difference is at most $1-e^{-q\Delta}\le\Delta$. At most two cells are partial; all complete factors are exact. Hence, uniformly on $[0,T]^2$,
$$
0\le\operatorname{Cov}_h(s,t)-ve^{-|t-s|}\le2vh,
$$
$$
\mathbb E\left|[X_h(t)-\mu_h(t)]-[X_h(s)-\mu_h(s)]\right|^2\le2v|t-s|,
\quad
\mathbb E\left|[X_h(t)-\mu_h(t)]-[X_h(s)-\mu_h(s)]\right|^4\le12v^2|t-s|^2.
\tag{K.9.5o.6}
$$
Gaussian fourth moments prove tightness independently of (K.9.5o.4); covariance convergence identifies the finite-dimensional distributions. No independent Brownian increments are assigned to a finite smooth path.

**Part IV. Actual mean error for all admitted controls.** Let $u'=1-u+a$, $u(0)=0$, and $M_0=\sup|u-1|$. Means agree at all endpoints. If $\|a\|_\infty\le A$, then
$$
\|\mu_h-u\|_\infty\le(M_0+2A)h\le(1+3A)h.
\tag{K.9.5o.7}
$$
The old-mean coefficients differ by at most $\Delta_j$, while both the physical forcing and OU partial forcing have magnitude at most $A\Delta_j$; $M_0\le1+A$. For $A_2=\|a\|_2$ use cellwise Cauchy–Schwarz instead:
$$
M_0\le1+A_2/\sqrt2,\qquad
\|\mu_h-u\|_\infty\le M_0h+2\sqrt h\,A_2.
\tag{K.9.5o.8}
$$
The actual Gaussian readout of Theorem K.9.5n at any registered snapshot consequently satisfies
$$
\sup_\sigma\left|\frac{C_{h,N,\eta}(\sigma)}{\ln2}-\mathfrak g(u(\sigma))\right|
\le2\sqrt{\frac{2\theta}{\pi N}}+5\eta+2\|\mu_h-u\|_\infty.
\tag{K.9.5o.9}
$$
This is the same Lipschitz instrument on its whole real domain. Nonnegative limiting $u$ does not imply nonnegative finite $\mu_h$: if both cell endpoint means are zero, (K.9.5o.2) gives $\mu_h=1-A_j-B_j<0$ inside. No admission of every finite interpolation to Definition K.9.5b's nonnegative mean domain is inferred.

**Part V. Exact finite path likelihood and its limitation.** Let $F_h$ send an endpoint vector to its sine-interpolated continuous curve. It is continuous and injective, independent of the control, with grid evaluation as measurable inverse on its image. Two applications of data processing therefore give
$$
D(\mathbb P_h^a\Vert\mathbb P_h^0)
=D(\mathbb P_{\mathrm{grid}}^a\Vert\mathbb P_{\mathrm{grid}}^0)
=\frac{N}{2\theta}\sum_j\frac{h_j^2}{1-e^{-2\Delta_j}},
\qquad W_{\mathrm{in},h}=E_0\theta D(\mathbb P_h^a\Vert\mathbb P_h^0).
\tag{K.9.5o.10}
$$
Physical work was independently derived from the actual incoming modes in Theorem K.9.5m. Full quantum ancillary entropy remains $\beta W_{\mathrm{in},h}$. Each finite path has finite variation and zero quadratic variation; the OU limit at fixed finite $N$ has quadratic variation $2\theta T/N$. The two path laws are mutually singular. A finite-path OU Girsanov identity cannot be obtained by substituting $\mu_h'+\mu_h-1$ for the supplied control, nor is an instantaneous friction/force cost thereby identified with displacement work.

**Part VI. Zero-work derivative and action obstruction.** Take $a=0$ and a uniform grid $\Delta=T/M$, $\vartheta=\arccos(e^{-\Delta})$. In cell $j$,
$$
\mu_h(\sigma)=1-e^{-j\Delta}\cos(\vartheta z),\qquad
 a_{\mathrm{eff},h}=\mu_h'+\mu_h-1
=e^{-j\Delta}\left[\frac{\vartheta}{\Delta}\sin(\vartheta z)-\cos(\vartheta z)\right].
\tag{K.9.5o.11}
$$
These means converge uniformly to $u_*=1-e^{-\sigma}$, and actual supplied displacement work is exactly zero on every grid. Since $\vartheta^2/\Delta\to2$, the bracket converges uniformly in $z\in[0,1]$ to $2z-1$. In particular
$$
\int_0^Ta_{\mathrm{eff},h}^2d\sigma
=\frac{\Delta(1-e^{-2T})}{1-e^{-2\Delta}}I_\Delta
\longrightarrow\frac{1-e^{-2T}}6>0,
$$
$$
I_\Delta=\int_0^1\left[\frac{\vartheta}{\Delta}\sin(\vartheta z)-\cos(\vartheta z)\right]^2dz\longrightarrow\frac13.
\tag{K.9.5o.12}
$$
Thus strong $H^1$ convergence fails. Evaluating the continuum work formula on these finite physical means would incorrectly predict positive limiting work $NE_0(1-e^{-2T})/24$ instead of zero. Their symmetric action exceeds that of $u_*$ in the limit by $(1-e^{-2T})/12$, since their terminal values agree exactly and (K.9.5m.15) fixes the same boundary. This is a derivative/homogenization effect of the actual source, not a hidden applied control.

**Part VII. The valid uniform-topology work Gamma limit.** On $C([0,T])$ let $\mathcal F_h(\mu)$ be the discrete physical input work if $\mu$ is a sine-interpolated physical mean with $\mu(0)=0$, and $+\infty$ otherwise. Its endpoints uniquely determine the bath displacements. Then
$$
\mathcal F_h\xrightarrow{\Gamma}\mathcal F\quad\text{in the uniform topology},\qquad
\mathcal F(u)=\frac{NE_0}{4}\int_0^T[u'+u-1]^2d\sigma
\tag{K.9.5o.13}
$$
for locally absolutely continuous $u$ with $u(0)=0$ and residual in $L^2$, and $+\infty$ otherwise.

For the lower bound take any uniformly convergent sequence with bounded finite work. On each cell choose the minimum-$L^2$ OU control matching its endpoints. It is a scalar multiple of $e^{\sigma-\sigma_{j+1}}$, and the exact projection identity gives $\mathcal F_h=NE_0\|a_h\|_2^2/4$. Its associated OU mean $v_h$ has those same endpoints and, by (K.9.5o.8),
$$
\|\mu_h-v_h\|_\infty
\le(1+\|a_h\|_2/\sqrt2)h+2\sqrt h\,\|a_h\|_2\longrightarrow0.
\tag{K.9.5o.14}
$$
The controls have a weakly convergent $L^2$ subsequence. The Volterra map $a\mapsto\int_0^\sigma e^{-(\sigma-s)}a(s)ds$ is compact into $C([0,T])$: bounded controls have uniform bounds and an $O(\sqrt{|s-t|})$ modulus, and each fixed kernel identifies the weak limit. Thus $v_h$ and $\mu_h$ converge to the mean driven by the weak limit $a$. Weak lower semicontinuity gives the liminf.

For recovery use the supplied $a=u'+u-1$ in (K.9.5m.11). Equations (K.9.5o.8) and (K.9.5m.13) give uniform convergence and equality of limiting work. Infinite-cost points need no finite recovery upper bound. Any fixed common terminal mean is preserved because each recovery reproduces grid endpoints exactly. This is a finite-window theorem on unrestricted real finite-mean paths; Part VIIa adds equicoercivity and the restriction to nonnegative physical means. Neither part gives infinite-horizon compactness or the complete PCE objective.

**Part VIIa. Equicoercivity and nonnegative physical recovery.** On a cell write the physical mean as $\mu-1=m_j\cos(\vartheta_jz)+d_j\sin(\vartheta_jz)$. Its minimum-$L^2$ matching control $a_h$ has $\|a_h\|_2^2=2\sum_jd_j^2=:A_2^2$ and $\mathcal F_h(\mu)=NE_0A_2^2/4$, and the OU mean it drives has the same grid values, so $|m_j|\le1+A_2/\sqrt2$ as in (K.9.5o.8). Since $\vartheta_j^2\le2\Delta_j$ by (K.9.5o.3),
$$
\|\mu'\|_2\le2\Bigl(1+\frac{A_2}{\sqrt2}\Bigr)\sqrt T+A_2,\qquad
\|\mu\|_\infty\le\sqrt T\,\|\mu'\|_2 .
\tag{K.9.5o.15}
$$
Every sublevel set of every $\mathcal F_h$ therefore lies in one closed ball of $H^1(0,T)$ with zero initial trace, which is compact in $C([0,T])$: the family $\mathcal F_h$ is equicoercive.

Let $I_C$ be $0$ on $C$ and $+\infty$ off it, and let $C_+=\{u\in C([0,T]):u\ge0\}$, $C_{+,L}=C_+\cap\{u(T)=L\}$ and $K_{00}=C_+\cap\{u(T)=0\}$; each set is uniformly closed. In the uniform topology,
$$
\mathcal F_h+I_{C_+}\xrightarrow{\Gamma}\mathcal F+I_{C_+},\qquad
\mathcal F_h+I_{C_{+,L}}\xrightarrow{\Gamma}\mathcal F+I_{C_{+,L}}\quad(L>0)
$$
on arbitrary grids with $h\to0$, and
$$
\mathcal F_h+I_{K_{00}}\xrightarrow{\Gamma}\mathcal F+I_{K_{00}}
\tag{K.9.5o.16}
$$
on uniform grids $\Delta_j=T/M$ with $M\ge2$; all three families are equicoercive by (K.9.5o.15).

The liminf inequalities follow from Part VII and closedness. For recovery fix a finite-cost $u$ in the constraint set. On an arbitrary grid let $t_k$ be the first grid point with $t_k\ge h$, so $h\le t_k\le2h$, and set $b_h(\sigma)=1-e^{-\min(\sigma,t_k)}$. On a uniform grid with $M\ge2$ set instead $b_h(\sigma)=1-e^{-\min(\sigma,T-\sigma,h)}$, whose grid values are $0,1-r,\dots,1-r,0$. In both cases the physical interpolant (K.9.5o.2) of the grid values of $b_h$ is nonnegative at every time. Before $t_k$, and on the first uniform cell, it is the zero-displacement mean $1-e^{-\sigma_j}\cos\phi_j\ge0$. On the last uniform cell the endpoints $1-r,0$ force $d=-s$, and the interpolant is $1-\cos(\vartheta-\phi)\ge0$. On every other cell both endpoints equal a value $c$ with $1-c\le r_j$, and (K.9.5o.3) gives
$$
1-(1-c)(A_j+B_j)\ge1-\frac{r_j}{\cos(\vartheta_j/2)}>0,
$$
because $\cos^2(\vartheta_j/2)=(1+r_j)/2>r_j^2$, that is, $(r_j-1)(2r_j+1)<0$.

Put $v_h=\max(u,b_h)$. It has the traces of $u$ (for $C_{+,L}$ once $b_h(T)\le2h<L$), $0\le v_h-u\le2h$, and $v_h'-u'=\mathbf 1_{\{b_h>u\}}(b_h'-u')$ almost everywhere, so
$$
\|v_h'-u'\|_2\le\|b_h'\|_2+\|\mathbf 1_{\{u<2h\}}u'\|_2\le\sqrt{2h}+\|\mathbf 1_{\{u<2h\}}u'\|_2\longrightarrow0,
$$
since $u'=0$ almost everywhere on $\{u=0\}$. Hence $v_h\to u$ in $H^1$ and $\tilde a_h=v_h'+v_h-1\to a=u'+u-1$ in $L^2$. Prepare the baths by (K.9.5m.11) with $\tilde a_h$. The grid means are exactly $v_h(\sigma_j)\ge b_h(\sigma_j)$, and the nonnegative weights $A_j,B_j$ make the physical mean $\mu_h$ dominate the interpolant of $b_h$. Thus $\mu_h\ge0$ at every time, and $\mu_h$ has the prescribed traces exactly. By (K.9.5o.8), $\mu_h\to u$ uniformly. By (K.9.5m.13), $\mathcal F_h(\mu_h)=\frac{NE_0}4\|P_h\tilde a_h\|_2^2$, and $\|P_h\tilde a_h-a\|_2\le\|\tilde a_h-a\|_2+\|P_ha-a\|_2\to0$, so $\mathcal F_h(\mu_h)\to\mathcal F(u)$. One cell is excluded in (K.9.5o.16): zero endpoint means force $\mu_h=1-A_0-B_0<0$ inside it.

Each finite constrained problem has a unique minimizer once its feasible set is nonempty, which holds for all sufficiently fine grids: $\mathcal F_h$ is a positive definite quadratic function of the free endpoint means, and pointwise nonnegativity of the interpolants is a closed convex condition. By (K.9.5o.15)–(K.9.5o.16) these minimizers converge uniformly to the unique minimizer of the limit problem. With free terminal mean the limit is $u_*$, where $\mathcal F$ vanishes. For a fixed terminal mean $U\ge0$ it is
$$
u_U(\sigma)=1-e^{-\sigma}+\bigl[U-1+e^{-T}\bigr]\frac{\sinh\sigma}{\sinh T},\qquad
u_0(\sigma)=1-\frac{\cosh(\sigma-T/2)}{\cosh(T/2)}.
\tag{K.9.5o.17}
$$
Indeed $(u'+u-1)^2=u'^2+(u-1)^2+\frac{d}{d\sigma}(u-1)^2$, so with fixed traces the minimizer solves $u''=u-1$; $u_U\ge u_0\ge0$ because the coefficient of $\sinh\sigma$ increases with $U$, so the nonnegativity constraint is inactive. For $U>0$ the convergence holds on arbitrary grids, for $U=0$ on uniform grids with $M\ge2$.

The zero-terminal class keeps the distinction of Part VI. For $u=0$ the recovery means $\mu_h$ are nonnegative with both traces zero, and their work is
$$
\frac{\mathcal F_h(\mu_h)}{NE_0}=\frac12\Bigl[(M-2)\frac{r^2(1-r)}{1+r}+1-r^2\Bigr]\longrightarrow\frac T4,
$$
whereas $\int_0^T(\mu_h'+\mu_h-1)^2d\sigma\to4T/3$, since $\mu_h'+\mu_h-1\to2z-2$ uniformly on the interior cells.

**Part VIII. Smooth envelopes and resources.** If finite switching slopes are required, replace $\phi_j=\vartheta_jz$ by $\vartheta_j\chi(z)$, with a fixed $C^1$ nondecreasing $\chi$, $\chi(0)=0$, $\chi(1)=1$, $\chi'(0)=\chi'(1)=0$, $\|\chi'\|_\infty\le K$. For example $\chi(z)=3z^2-2z^3$ has $K=3/2$. Endpoint collisions, incoming displacement work and all energy balances remain exact. The nonnegative sine weights retain (K.9.5o.3), so (K.9.5o.4) still proves convergence. Covariance dominance need not persist, but at most two partial-cell factors change, each by at most $2h$; hence covariance error is at most $4vh$. Bounding partial angular changes by $K$ times their elapsed fraction and summing full-cell decay gives centered increment variance at most $2v\max(1,K^2)|t-s|$ and the corresponding Gaussian fourth-moment tightness bound.

The laboratory coefficient is now $g_j=\lambda\vartheta_j\chi'(z)/\Delta_j$. Every fixed finite grid has finite peak coefficients, control borrowing and, for the polynomial envelope, finite switching derivatives and positive durations. Refinement still gives $h^{-1/2}$ pulse scale and growing fresh-mode stock. Smooth pulses do not turn the continuum work into the instantaneous OU action on every finite physical mean; Part VI already rules out that general identification. The actual unread continuous source, finite readout/likelihood, supplied-work limit and all resource controls are proved on their stated domains. Full PCE reduction, physical channel/area/$G$ realization, horizon bath/$\kappa$ clock and metric/lensing/screening maps are not supplied by this construction. ∎

<a id="proposition-k95p-local-defect-field-realization-of-the-horizon-bath-clock"></a>**Proposition K.9.5p (Local Defect-Field Realization of the Horizon-Bath Clock).** Let $a:(t_*,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be twice continuously differentiable and let $g=-dt^2+a(t)^2(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2)$ be a spatially flat FLRW metric in the $c=1$ units of this section. The reflection $z\mapsto-z$ is an isometry of $g$, so its fixed set $\Sigma=\{z=0\}$ is totally geodesic, with induced metric $q=-dt^2+a(t)^2(dx^2+dy^2)$. On $\Sigma$ take the free real scalar with action
$$
S_\phi=-\frac12\int_\Sigma\sqrt{-q}\,\Bigl[q^{ab}\partial_a\phi\,\partial_b\phi+\tfrac18R[q]\,\phi^2\Bigr]\,d^3\xi ,
\tag{K.9.5p.1}
$$
whose curvature coupling $1/8$ is the conformal value in three spacetime dimensions. With conformal time $d\eta=dt/a$ and $\chi=a^{1/2}\phi$, prepare the conformal vacuum $\omega$: the quasi-free state with vanishing one-point function whose $\chi$ two-point function is that of the Minkowski vacuum of the massless field on $-d\eta^2+dx^2+dy^2$. A memory with two-dimensional logical space, Pauli operator $X$ with eigenvalues $\pm1$ and Hamiltonian $H_M$ commuting with $X$ rests at the origin of $\Sigma$. From a time $t_0>t_*$, starting from the product of a memory state and $\omega$, it couples through
$$
H_{\mathrm{int}}(t)=\lambda f(t)\,X\otimes\phi(t,0),\qquad \lambda>0,
\tag{K.9.5p.2}
$$
with a real, locally square-integrable coupling profile $f$, the point coupling being the limit of couplings to normalized spatial smearings of $\phi$ on $\Sigma$. Then:

1. The Wightman function along the worldline, $W(t,t')=\omega\bigl(\phi(t,0)\phi(t',0)\bigr)$, is the distribution
$$
W(t,t')=\frac{1}{\sqrt{a(t)a(t')}}\left[\frac{\delta\bigl(\eta(t)-\eta(t')\bigr)}{4}-\frac{i}{4\pi}\,\mathrm{PV}\frac{1}{\eta(t)-\eta(t')}\right],
\qquad
\operatorname{Re}W(t,t')=\frac{\delta(t-t')}{4}.
\tag{K.9.5p.3}
$$

2. In the interaction picture of $H_M$ and the free field, the off-diagonal entry of the reduced memory state in the $X$ eigenbasis is $\rho_{+-}(t)=\rho_{+-}(t_0)\,e^{-\sigma(t)}$, with
$$
\sigma(t)=2\lambda^2\int_{t_0}^{t}\!\!\int_{t_0}^{t}f(v)f(w)\operatorname{Re}W(v,w)\,dv\,dw=\frac{\lambda^2}{2}\int_{t_0}^{t}f(v)^2\,dv .
\tag{K.9.5p.4}
$$

3. Let $a$ be the scale factor of a horizon-bath clock branch of Definition K.9.5g and take the density-modulated profile $f^2=\varphi_\Lambda$ of (K.9.5g.1). Letting $t_0$ tend to the dense endpoint $s_{bg}=0$,
$$
d\sigma=\kappa_\sigma H_\Lambda\varphi_\Lambda\,dt,\qquad \sigma\big|_{s_{bg}=0}=0,\qquad \kappa_\sigma=\frac{\lambda^2}{2H_\Lambda},
\tag{K.9.5p.5}
$$
which is the clock (K.9.5g.2) with its timing normalization fixed by the coupling. Proposition K.9.5h then gives the dense-limit exponent $3/2$ with coefficient $2\kappa_\sigma/9=\lambda^2/(9H_\Lambda)$; the coefficient equals $1$ exactly when $\lambda^2=9H_\Lambda$, that is $\kappa_\sigma=9/2$. The choice $\lambda^2=H_\Lambda/\pi$ would give $\kappa_\sigma=1/(2\pi)$ and dense coefficient $1/(9\pi)$.

4. On the exact de Sitter background $a(t)=e^{H_\Lambda t}$, with $u=t-t'$,
$$
W(t,t')=-\frac{iH_\Lambda}{8\pi\sinh\bigl(H_\Lambda(u-i0)/2\bigr)},\qquad
\widetilde W(\omega):=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{i\omega u}\,W\,du=\frac{1}{2\bigl(1+e^{-2\pi\omega/H_\Lambda}\bigr)},
\tag{K.9.5p.6}
$$
so $\widetilde W(-\omega)=e^{-2\pi\omega/H_\Lambda}\,\widetilde W(\omega)$: on the worldline the same field is a KMS state at the temperature $H_\Lambda/(2\pi)$, which is $T_{dS}$ of Proposition K.9.1 in these units.

*Proof.* Item 1. The field equation of (K.9.5p.1) is conformally invariant in three dimensions: with $q=a^2\hat q$ and $\hat q=-d\eta^2+dx^2+dy^2$, the field $\phi$ solves $(\Box_q-R[q]/8)\phi=0$ exactly when $\chi=a^{1/2}\phi$ solves $\Box_{\hat q}\chi=0$, and the two actions differ by a boundary term, so equal-time commutators correspond. Hence $W(t,t')=(a(t)a(t'))^{-1/2}W_0(\eta(t)-\eta(t'))$, where the massless Minkowski Wightman function at coincident spatial points is $W_0(\Delta\eta)=\bigl[4\pi\sqrt{-(\Delta\eta-i0)^2}\bigr]^{-1}=\bigl[4\pi i(\Delta\eta-i0)\bigr]^{-1}$. The identity $(\Delta\eta-i0)^{-1}=\mathrm{PV}(1/\Delta\eta)+i\pi\delta(\Delta\eta)$ gives the first form of (K.9.5p.3). Since $\eta$ is strictly increasing with $d\eta/dt=1/a$, $\delta(\eta(t)-\eta(t'))=a(t)\delta(t-t')$, which gives $\operatorname{Re}W=\delta(t-t')/4$.

Item 2. Write $\phi(F_t)=\int_{t_0}^{t}f(v)\phi(v,0)\,dv$. The imaginary part of $W$ is antisymmetric, so item 1 gives $\omega(\phi(F_t)^2)=\int\!\!\int f(v)f(w)\operatorname{Re}W(v,w)\,dv\,dw=\tfrac14\int_{t_0}^{t}f^2<\infty$, and $\phi(F_t)$ is a self-adjoint field operator. Smear the coupling over a normalized nonnegative spatial profile of width $\epsilon$ on $\Sigma$ and write $\phi_\epsilon(F_t)$ for the smeared field. The commutator of the free field is a c-number, so the time-ordered exponential terminates at second order: on the eigenspace $X=\pm1$ the propagator is $U_\pm=e^{i\theta_\epsilon}\exp(\mp i\lambda\phi_\epsilon(F_t))$, with one c-number phase $\theta_\epsilon$ for both signs because it is quadratic in the coupling and $X^2=1$. Hence
$$
\rho_{+-}(t)=\rho_{+-}(t_0)\,\omega(U_-^*U_+)=\rho_{+-}(t_0)\,\omega\bigl(\exp(-2i\lambda\phi_\epsilon(F_t))\bigr)=\rho_{+-}(t_0)\,e^{-2\lambda^2\omega(\phi_\epsilon(F_t)^2)},
$$
since $\omega(e^{i\phi(G)})=e^{-\omega(\phi(G)^2)/2}$ for a quasi-free state with vanishing one-point function. In the conformal frame the Fourier transform of the smearing profile has modulus at most $1$ and tends to $1$ pointwise, so dominated convergence gives $\omega(\phi_\epsilon(F_t)^2)\to\omega(\phi(F_t)^2)$ as $\epsilon\to0$, while the self-energy phase $\theta_\epsilon$ cancels from $\rho_{+-}$ at every $\epsilon$. This gives the first expression in (K.9.5p.4); item 1 gives the second.

Item 3. On the matter branch $\varphi_\Lambda=s_{bg}/(1+s_{bg})\le1$, and the proof of Proposition K.9.5h gives $dt=ds_{bg}/(3Hs_{bg})$ with $H=H_\Lambda\sqrt{(s_{bg}+\Upsilon_G)/s_{bg}}$ and $\Upsilon_G\ge1$, so $dt\le ds_{bg}/(3H_\Lambda\sqrt{s_{bg}})$ and the dense endpoint lies at finite time. Hence $\int f^2\,dt$ converges there and the limit of (K.9.5p.4) as $t_0$ tends to that endpoint gives $\sigma|_{s_{bg}=0}=0$. Differentiating (K.9.5p.4) gives $\dot\sigma=(\lambda^2/2)\varphi_\Lambda=\kappa_\sigma H_\Lambda\varphi_\Lambda$, which is (K.9.5g.2); the coefficient statement is (K.9.5h.3).

Item 4. For $a=e^{H_\Lambda t}$, $\eta=-e^{-H_\Lambda t}/H_\Lambda$ and $\sqrt{a(t)a(t')}\,(\eta(t)-\eta(t'))=(2/H_\Lambda)\sinh(H_\Lambda u/2)$; monotonicity of $\eta$ carries the $-i0$ prescription to $u$, and $W_0$ gives the first formula of (K.9.5p.6). With $\sinh(H_\Lambda(u-i0)/2)^{-1}=\mathrm{PV}\,\sinh(H_\Lambda u/2)^{-1}+(2\pi i/H_\Lambda)\delta(u)$ and $\int e^{i\omega u}\,\mathrm{PV}\,\sinh(H_\Lambda u/2)^{-1}\,du=(2\pi i/H_\Lambda)\tanh(\pi\omega/H_\Lambda)$, one obtains $\widetilde W(\omega)=\tfrac14\bigl(1+\tanh(\pi\omega/H_\Lambda)\bigr)$, the second formula. The ratio $\widetilde W(-\omega)/\widetilde W(\omega)=(1+e^{-2\pi\omega/H_\Lambda})/(1+e^{2\pi\omega/H_\Lambda})=e^{-2\pi\omega/H_\Lambda}$ is the KMS relation at inverse temperature $2\pi/H_\Lambda$. ∎

The conformal-vacuum noise of the defect field is white in proper time on every spatially flat FLRW history, and on the de Sitter endpoint the same field is the Gibbons-Hawking bath; the coupling $\lambda$ and the profile $f^2=\varphi_\Lambda$ are declared source data.

<a id="theorem-k95q"></a>

<a id="theorem-k95q-common-microdynamic-source-for-homogeneous-response-capacity-and-clock"></a>**Theorem K.9.5q (Common Microdynamic Source for Homogeneous Response, Capacity and Clock).** The supplied finite-microdynamic family in the [common-source construction](../related/calculation_companions/appendix_k/k95q-common-source-completion.md) realizes the quadratic response-work coefficient ratio, the Cartesian objective of Definition K.9.5b, the physical channel and area record of Definition K.9.5e, the horizon-bath clock, and the finite-window perturbation, lensing and controller-screening projections. Its construction gives joint error bounds on the same source, with its actual states, controls and costs. The selected limiting response has
$$
u(\sigma)=1-e^{-\sigma},\qquad
\frac{c_0}{c_1}=1,\qquad A_c=1,\qquad
\kappa_\sigma=\frac1{2\pi},\qquad
\sigma(s)\sim\frac{s^{3/2}}{9\pi}\quad(s\downarrow0).
\tag{K.9.5q.1}
$$
