On the area-calibrated branch with the same-family equality $C(\mathcal E_N)=C_{\max}>0$ and the independent calibration $G_{\mathrm{op}}=G$,
$$
G=\frac{\eta\delta^2c^3}{4\hbar\chi C_{\max}}.
$$
The operational continuum results allow the metric to be interpreted as a collective network variable; they do not decide whether its perturbations also admit an effective quantum-field description.

*Proof.* Apply the complete local-horizon hypotheses of Theorem 12.1 on the same branch. For transverse patches of area $A_\varepsilon>0$ and affine length $h_\varepsilon\to0$, with $\operatorname{diam}(P_\varepsilon)=o(h_\varepsilon)$, its uniform first-variation and Clausius remainders are $o(A_\varepsilon h_\varepsilon^2)$. The Raychaudhuri expansion gives $\delta\mathcal A_\varepsilon=(A_\varepsilon h_\varepsilon^2/2)(R_{kk}(p)+o(1))$, while the heat-flux expansion gives $\delta Q_\varepsilon=(\kappa A_\varepsilon h_\varepsilon^2/2)(T_{kk}(p)+o(1))$. Division by the common positive factor and $T=\kappa/(2\pi)$ therefore give $R_{kk}=(2\pi/\eta_{\partial})T_{kk}$, where $\eta_{\partial}$ is the constant entropy first-variation density. The all-null hypothesis makes the difference of the symmetric tensors proportional to the metric. Conservation and the contracted Bianchi identity give the Einstein equation with one cosmological integration constant per connected component. The accepted same-family Appendix E density and unit calibration yield the displayed expression for $G$. This reasoning concerns the collective metric equation and does not exclude an effective quantum description of its perturbations. ∎

<a id="corollary-k1011-scope-of-the-emergent-metric-interpretation"></a>**Corollary K.10.11 (Scope of the Emergent-Metric Interpretation).** On the branch of Theorem K.10.10, the metric field equations admit a thermodynamic collective interpretation. This does not imply that metric perturbations lack an effective quantum-field description. Perturbative nonrenormalizability states that the Einstein-Hilbert interaction requires an unbounded tower of counterterms when treated as a fundamental ultraviolet theory; it remains compatible with a low-energy quantum effective field theory and with a microscopic MPU completion. Establishing the nature of that completion requires an independent dynamical theorem.

*Proof.* Theorem K.10.10 derives a conditional macroscopic equation and explicitly leaves the quantization status undecided. A collective variable can possess quantized effective excitations, so emergence does not imply non-quantizability. Nonrenormalizability constrains ultraviolet predictive closure of the Einstein-Hilbert expansion but does not select one microscopic completion. ∎

<a id="theorem-k1012-independent-inputs-in-the-gravity-bridge-package"></a>**Theorem K.10.12 (Independent Inputs in the Gravity-Bridge Package).** On the completed reset-support branch, Proposition E.2a gives
$$
C_{\max}\le\ln d_0-\ln2,
$$
with the stated residual-budget specialization. For items 2 and 3, assume the density certificate of Theorem E.3 and the capacity-achieving, entropy-saturating, additive-ledger branch of Theorem E.6, with the same-family equality $C(\mathcal E_N)=C_{\max}>0$ and the independent horizon-entropy and $G_{\mathrm{op}}=G$ calibrations. This capacity datum has the following distinct roles:

1. together with an ultraviolet lattice or bandlimit certificate, it bounds the independent distinctions available below the MPU resolution;
2. together with boundary-link density, horizon saturation, and the Appendix E area calibration, it gives the operational boundary entropy density $1/(4G)$;
3. together with the independent local Rindler/KMS, Clausius, Raychaudhuri, and conserved stress-energy-source hypotheses, it supplies the normalization used in the conditional Jacobson derivation.

Finite capacity alone does not imply items 2 or 3.

*Proof.* For item 1, the finite protocol budget bounds the number of independently resolvable alternatives, while the ultraviolet certificate identifies sub-resolution continuum modes with those alternatives. For item 2, Theorem E.6 on Theorem E.3's density branch gives, in the manuscript's natural-unit convention,
$$
S=\frac{\chi C_{\max}}{\eta\delta^2}A+o(A),
$$
and the area calibration defines the coefficient as $1/(4G)$ in the manuscript's unit convention. For item 3, Theorem K.10.10 shows that the KMS/Clausius/Raychaudhuri/source package yields the tensor equation; the capacity-area relation sets its gravitational normalization. Since those thermodynamic and geometric hypotheses are not consequences of a channel-capacity inequality, the three roles form a package of independent inputs rather than one inference from capacity. ∎

<a id="corollary-k1013-conditional-status-of-gravitational-waves"></a>**Corollary K.10.13 (Conditional Status of Gravitational Waves).** Assume a branch carries (a) an emergent metric and a faithful microscopic-to-metric perturbation map identifying retained long-wavelength network excitations with $h_{\mu\nu}$, (b) the Einstein dynamics and a smooth Minkowski-background approximation, and (c) no additional retained field or higher-order operator contributing at linear order. Then:

(i) The represented gravitational waves are collective long-wavelength excitations of the emergent MPU-network geometry.

(ii) At wavelengths $\lambda\gg\delta$, they satisfy the linearized Einstein equations and, after the linearized diffeomorphism gauge quotient, have the massless helicity-$2$ tensor structure.

(iii) These conclusions require no fundamental graviton degree of freedom; a graviton description, if used, is an effective quasiparticle description of the certified collective modes.

Separately, on the finite-substrate cutoff branch of Theorem K.10.4 and Corollary K.10.5a with $k_{\mathrm{cut}}=\xi_{\mathrm{cut}}/\delta$, $\xi_{\mathrm{cut}}>0$, the certified boundary has reduced wavelength $\bar\lambda\sim\delta/\xi_{\mathrm{cut}}$, equivalently ordinary wavelength $\lambda\sim2\pi\delta/\xi_{\mathrm{cut}}$. On Equation Q.18's spacing branch this ordinary-wavelength scale is approximately $14.80\,L_P/\xi_{\mathrm{cut}}$; the value $14.80\,L_P$ requires the registered normalization $\xi_{\mathrm{cut}}=1$.

*Proof.* Under assumptions (a)--(c), linearization of $g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}+h_{\mu\nu}$ gives the vacuum linearized Einstein equations. Their gauge quotient leaves the two transverse-traceless helicity-$2$ modes, and the faithful perturbation map identifies those modes with collective network excitations. Theorem K.10.4 and Corollary K.10.5a separately supply the certified cutoff $k_{\mathrm{cut}}=\xi_{\mathrm{cut}}\delta^{-1}$; identifying it with $k_{\mathrm{MPU}}$ requires $\xi_{\mathrm{cut}}=1$. They do not determine whether an effective quasiparticle description persists at that boundary. ∎

<a id="theorem-k1013a-uniqueness-of-the-local-metric-only-two-derivative-operator"></a>**Theorem K.10.13a (Uniqueness of the Local Metric-Only Two-Derivative Operator).** On four-dimensional Minkowski space, let $L$ be a constant-coefficient Lorentz-covariant linear operator from a symmetric tensor $h_{\mu\nu}$ to a symmetric tensor, containing exactly two derivatives and no additional field. Up to one overall coefficient, write its most general parity-even form as
$$
\begin{aligned}
(Lh)_{\mu\nu}={}&a\Box h_{\mu\nu}
+b(\partial_\mu\partial^\alpha h_{\alpha\nu}
+\partial_\nu\partial^\alpha h_{\alpha\mu})
+c\partial_\mu\partial_\nu h\\
&+d\eta_{\mu\nu}\partial^\alpha\partial^\beta h_{\alpha\beta}
+e\eta_{\mu\nu}\Box h.
\end{aligned}
\tag{K.10.13a.1}
$$
If $L$ is invariant under $h_{\mu\nu}\mapsto h_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu\xi_\nu+\partial_\nu\xi_\mu$ and obeys $\partial^\mu(Lh)_{\mu\nu}=0$ identically, then
$$
(a,b,c,d,e)=a(1,-1,1,1,-1),
\tag{K.10.13a.2}
$$
so $L=-2a\,G^{(1)}$, where $G^{(1)}$ is the linearized Einstein tensor. For $a\ne0$ and each nonzero null wave covector, its vacuum plane-wave solution space modulo the plane-wave gauge relation has exactly the two transverse-traceless helicity-$2$ polarizations.

*Proof.* Substitution of a pure gauge perturbation into (K.10.13a.1) gives $a+b=0$, $b+c=0$, and $d+e=0$. Taking the divergence and requiring an identity for every $h$ adds $b+d=0$ and $c+e=0$. Solving gives (K.10.13a.2), the coefficient pattern of $-2aG^{(1)}$. For a plane-wave amplitude $A_{\mu\nu}$ with nonzero null covector $k$, put $V_\nu=k^\mu A_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12 k_\nu A^\mu{}_\mu$. The vacuum equation is equivalent to $k_\mu V_\nu+k_\nu V_\mu-\eta_{\mu\nu}k^\alpha V_\alpha=0$. Its trace gives $k^\alpha V_\alpha=0$, and a component with $k_\mu\ne0$ then gives $V_\nu=0$ for all $\nu$. Gauge amplitudes $k_\mu\xi_\nu+k_\nu\xi_\mu$ preserve this constraint since $k^2=0$. Choose an inertial frame in which $k$ has only nonzero time and third spatial components. Since $k_0\ne0$, the four gauge parameters uniquely set $A_{0\mu}=0$. The four constraints then give $A_{3i}=0$ and $A_{11}+A_{22}=0$, leaving precisely $A_{11}=-A_{22}$ and $A_{12}=A_{21}$. The zero covector has no such gauge count and is outside this polarization assertion. ∎

This is a coverage-complete operator classification only for the declared metric-only, local, parity-even, two-derivative class. Populating the microscopic perturbation map and excluding additional retained fields or higher-derivative operators remain independent gates in Corollary K.10.13.

<a id="theorem-k1013b-finite-field-local-quadratic-operator-basis"></a>**Theorem K.10.13b (Finite-Field Local Quadratic Operator Basis).** Fix four-dimensional Minkowski space with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, $\Box=\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu$, and one real symmetric tensor $h_{\mu\nu}$, scalar $\phi$, Abelian vector $A_\mu$, and antisymmetric two-form $B_{\mu\nu}$; any of the last three may be absent. These are ordinary tensors, with no additional intrinsic parity assignment. Let $\mathfrak E$ consist of real, constant-coefficient, finite-order local quadratic actions, covariant under $SO^+(1,3)$, invariant up to a divergence under the independent transformations
$$
\delta h_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu\xi_\nu+\partial_\nu\xi_\mu,\qquad
\delta A_\mu=\partial_\mu\lambda,\qquad
\delta B_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu\Lambda_\nu-\partial_\nu\Lambda_\mu,\qquad \delta\phi=0.
$$
Use compactly supported variations and identify densities differing by a total divergence; boundary observables are not classified. Define
$$
\begin{aligned}
R^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}&=\tfrac12(\partial^\alpha\partial_\mu h_{\alpha\nu}+\partial^\alpha\partial_\nu h_{\alpha\mu}-\Box h_{\mu\nu}-\partial_\mu\partial_\nu h),\\
R^{(1)}&=\partial_\mu\partial_\nu h^{\mu\nu}-\Box h,\quad
G^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}=R^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12\eta_{\mu\nu}R^{(1)},\quad
\mathcal L_{\rm EH}^{(2)}=-\tfrac12h^{\mu\nu}G^{(1)}_{\mu\nu},\\
F_{\mu\nu}&=2\partial_{[\mu}A_{\nu]},\qquad H_{\mu\nu\rho}=3\partial_{[\mu}B_{\nu\rho]}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Every member of $\mathfrak E$ has the following form, with real coefficients and only finitely many nonzero summands:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L\simeq{}&a\mathcal L_{\rm EH}^{(2)}
+\sum_{n\ge0}\bigl[\alpha_nR^{(1)}\Box^nR^{(1)}+\beta_nR^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}\Box^nR^{(1)\mu\nu}
+c_n\phi\Box^nR^{(1)}+d_n\phi\Box^n\phi\bigr]\\
&+\sum_{n\ge0}\bigl[e_nF_{\mu\nu}\Box^nF^{\mu\nu}+f_nH_{\mu\nu\rho}\Box^nH^{\mu\nu\rho}
+g_n\varepsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}B_{\mu\nu}\Box^n\partial_\rho A_\sigma\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\tag{K.10.13b.1}
$$
The parity-even subclass omits the $g_n$ terms. The metric has no bilinear coupling to $A$ or $B$ in this class. At exactly two derivatives the basis reduces to
$$
a\mathcal L_{\rm EH}^{(2)}+b(\partial\phi)^2+c\phi R^{(1)}+eF^2+fH^2.
\tag{K.10.13b.2}
$$
Spectra and stability of particular coefficient choices are treated in Theorems K.10.13c–K.10.13d and Proposition K.10.13e.

*Proof.* With Fourier convention $\partial\mapsto ik$, a real quadratic action has a polynomial symmetric kernel $K_{XY}(k)=K_{YX}(-k)^T$ in $S=\int\Phi(-k)^TK(k)\Phi(k)$. Equality of such kernels is equivalent to equality of densities modulo divergence: after symmetrizing a polynomial density in its two arguments $p,q$, a zero kernel means that polynomial vanishes when $p+q=0$, and therefore is in the ideal generated by the components of $p+q$. Each generator corresponds to a total derivative. Gauge invariance is exactly $K\mathcal G=0$ for each gauge generator $\mathcal G$, since the fields and compactly supported parameters are independent. Thus every index in a gauge-field block is transverse. The conditions hold independently at each homogeneous derivative degree.

Write $z=k^2$ and, for $z\ne0$, $\theta_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}-k_\mu k_\nu/z$. Polynomial Lorentz covariants are contractions of $\eta,k,\varepsilon$; two $\epsilon$ factors reduce to metric contractions, while contraction of $\epsilon$ with two copies of $k$ vanishes. Equivalently, in a timelike rest frame the transverse space is three-dimensional, and its invariant tensors through rank four are a scalar, its metric, its alternating volume tensor, and the three pairings of two metrics. One can see this directly by rotations through $\pi$ about the coordinate axes, which eliminate unpaired indices, and rotations interchanging or mixing two axes, which identify the surviving pairings; the rank-three alternating tensor is the sole proper-rotation odd invariant. There are no rank-one invariants. Covariance and polynomial identity extend this description from the open timelike set.

After transverse projection, free $k$ indices vanish and a four-index $\epsilon$ vanishes on the three-dimensional transverse space. The available structures are therefore products of $\theta$ and at most one $\varepsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}k_\sigma$. Symmetry of $h$ and antisymmetry of $B$ imply: the metric block is $C_2(z)P^{(2)}+C_0(z)P^{(0)}$; the metric–scalar block is proportional to $\theta$; vector and two-form diagonal blocks are proportional to their transverse identities; the vector–two-form block is proportional to $\varepsilon k$; every other mixed block vanishes. Here
$$
P^{(0)}_{\mu\nu,\rho\sigma}=\tfrac13\theta_{\mu\nu}\theta_{\rho\sigma},\qquad
P^{(2)}_{\mu\nu,\rho\sigma}=\tfrac12(\theta_{\mu\rho}\theta_{\nu\sigma}+\theta_{\mu\sigma}\theta_{\nu\rho})-P^{(0)}_{\mu\nu,\rho\sigma}.
$$
For example the only rank-three odd mixed structure is killed by the symmetric metric pair, and both rank-four even metric–two-form pairings vanish under the required symmetrization/antisymmetrization. The vector–two-form $\epsilon$ structure survives both gauge contractions and represents the BF term in (K.10.13b.1).

The scalar coefficients are polynomials in $z$ before the explicit projector denominators: on homogeneous components a rest-frame transverse component fixes the coefficient as a constant times the appropriate power of $z$. Polynomiality of a $\theta$ block requires its coefficient divisible by $z$. For the two-form transverse identity, the apparent $z^{-2}$ term cancels by antisymmetry, and the same divisibility suffices. In the metric block the terms with two free momenta have denominators $z$, and the four-momentum term has coefficient $(2C_2+C_0)/(3z^2)$. Hence precisely
$$
z\mid C_2,\quad z\mid C_0,\quad z^2\mid(2C_2+C_0).
\tag{K.10.13b.3}
$$
These conditions are sufficient by expanding the projectors. They leave one metric invariant at derivative order two, two at each even order at least four, and none at order zero or odd order. Direct substitution of the curvature definitions gives
$$
K_{\rm EH}=-\tfrac z4P^{(2)}+\tfrac z2P^{(0)},\quad
K_{R^2}=3z^2P^{(0)},\quad
K_{{\rm Ric}^2}=z^2(\tfrac14P^{(2)}+P^{(0)}),\quad
K_{h\phi}=\tfrac c2z\theta.
$$
They span the metric and metric–scalar possibilities. Multiplication by $\Box$ supplies every further even degree; the scalar polynomial supplies all scalar degrees and the $\epsilon$ block all permitted odd BF degrees. The remaining transverse blocks are supplied by $F^2,H^2$. All statements are polynomial identities and so extend across $z=0$, although the singular projectors cannot themselves be used for null-shell counting. The named kernels are independent at each degree. This proves the basis; in particular quadratic Gauss–Bonnet and Pontryagin combinations add no bulk kernel. ∎

<a id="theorem-k1013c-two-derivative-scalar-metric-response-and-its-degenerate-source-gate"></a>**Theorem K.10.13c (Two-Derivative Scalar–Metric Response and its Degenerate Source Gate).** In (K.10.13b.2) assume $a\ne0$ and couple sources through $h_{\mu\nu}T^{\mu\nu}+\phi J$, with $\partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0$. The metric–scalar sector admits the invertible local redefinition
$$
h_{\mu\nu}=\widetilde h_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac ca\phi\eta_{\mu\nu},\qquad
\mathcal L\simeq a\mathcal L_{\rm EH}^{(2)}(\widetilde h)+b_{\rm eff}(\partial\phi)^2,\qquad
b_{\rm eff}=b-\tfrac{3c^2}{2a}.
\tag{K.10.13c.1}
$$
In Theorem K.10.13a's operator normalization, $a=2a_M$. For $b_{\rm eff}\ne0$ the conserved-source inverse, defined as $\Pi=\mathcal J^TK^{-1}\mathcal J$ on a gauge-fixed or gauge-quotiented kernel, is
$$
\Pi=-\frac4{az}\left(T_{\mu\nu}T^{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12T^2\right)
+\frac{(J-cT/a)^2}{b_{\rm eff}z}.
\tag{K.10.13c.2}
$$
There are two massless tensor polarizations, healthy for $a>0$, and one scalar, healthy for $b_{\rm eff}<0$ and ghostlike for $b_{\rm eff}>0$. Health here means negative-semidefinite residue of this source inverse, consistent with $-\tfrac12(\partial\phi)^2$. For $c\ne0$ the scalar produces a metric breathing polarization; for $c=0$ it is decoupled from the metric.

If $b_{\rm eff}=0$, the *free quadratic* action instead has the additional local symmetry
$$
\delta\phi=\sigma,\qquad\delta h_{\mu\nu}=-(c/a)\sigma\eta_{\mu\nu}.
$$
The coupled-source problem is compatible with this symmetry only when $J=(c/a)T$. With that condition its metric–scalar quotient has only the two tensor polarizations; without it the source equations are inconsistent. In particular $c\ne0$, $J=0$ and arbitrary nonzero dust trace cannot be admitted at this degenerate point.

*Proof.* Self-adjointness of $G^{(1)}$, $\eta^{\mu\nu}G^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}=-R^{(1)}$, and $R^{(1)}(\psi\eta)=-3\Box\psi$ show that substituting $h=\widetilde h+\alpha\phi\eta$ gives the mixed coefficient $a\alpha+c$ and scalar kinetic coefficient $b+3a\alpha^2/2+3c\alpha$. Choosing $\alpha=-c/a$ proves (K.10.13c.1); the source of the remaining scalar is $J-cT/a$. Alternatively its transverse spin-zero kernel is
$$
z\begin{pmatrix}a/2&\sqrt3c/2\\\sqrt3c/2&b\end{pmatrix}
$$
in the basis $(\theta\cdot h/\sqrt3,\phi)$, with determinant $ab_{\rm eff}z^2/2$. Its inverse and the spin-two kernel $-az/4$ give (K.10.13c.2). At a nonzero null momentum $k^\mu=(E,0,0,E)$, conservation implies $T^{0\nu}=T^{3\nu}$ and
$$
T_{\mu\nu}T^{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12T^2=\tfrac12(T^{11}-T^{22})^2+2(T^{12})^2,\qquad T=T^{11}+T^{22}.
$$
The residue therefore has two independent tensor squares and, for $b_{\rm eff}\ne0$, one independent scalar square. The tensor plane-wave quotient is the one in K.10.13a; the decoupled scalar obeys $\Box\phi=0$. Its conformal contribution $-(c/a)\phi\eta$ has nonzero transverse linearized tidal curvature for $c\ne0$, equal in the two transverse directions, which is the breathing response. If $b_{\rm eff}=0$, the redefined action is independent of $\phi$; varying its source enforces $J-cT/a=0$. Quotienting its arbitrary shift then leaves just the tensor theory. ∎

For neutral weak static dust, $J=0$, $b_{\rm eff}\ne0$, the force relative to the bare tensor normalization is multiplied by $1+\Delta$, where $\Delta=-c^2/(2ab_{\rm eff})$. Exchange with a traceless neutral source has no scalar term. With the usual weak-field potentials this gives $\gamma=(1-\Delta)/(1+\Delta)$ when $1+\Delta\ne0$. Substituting $a=c=\Phi_0$, $b=-\omega\Phi_0$ yields $G_{\rm eff}/G=(2\omega+4)/(2\omega+3)$ and $\gamma=(\omega+1)/(\omega+2)$, excluding respectively the degenerate point $\omega=-3/2$ and undefined ratio at $\omega=-2$. These massless weak-source statements follow by evaluating (K.10.13c.2) on dust, for which the tensor trace subtraction leaves half the squared density; the unchanged traceless channel fixes the lensing sum while the scalar adds opposite shifts to the two potentials.

If $b\ne0$, eliminating $\phi$ with a specified inverse of $\Box$, source data and homogeneous-solution/boundary prescription produces the Schur complement
$$
K_{\rm eff}=aK_{\rm EH}-\frac{c^2}{4b}z\theta\theta.
$$
For $c\ne0$ this is nonpolynomial in momentum and outside the local metric-only class. For $c=0$ it remains local. For $b=0,c\ne0$ this division is unavailable: the scalar equation is a curvature/source constraint, not that Schur complement. No unique metric-only initial-value problem follows without the inverse and homogeneous data. Independent vector and two-form sources must satisfy $\partial_\mu j^\mu=0$ and $\partial_\mu j_B^{\mu\nu}=0$ by their gauge variations. In the exactly-two-derivative class their nonzero kinetic blocks are decoupled Maxwell and massless two-form sectors; if a block vanishes identically its prescribed source must also vanish. BF terms are outside exactly two derivatives and can change these sectors' spectra without inducing metric mixing. The case $a=0$ is outside this response theorem.

<a id="theorem-k1013d-four-derivative-metric-response-with-sector-qualifications"></a>**Theorem K.10.13d (Four-Derivative Metric Response with Sector Qualifications).** For the metric-only subfamily
$$
\mathcal L=a\mathcal L_{\rm EH}^{(2)}+\alpha(R^{(1)})^2+\beta R^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}R^{(1)\mu\nu},\qquad a\ne0,
$$
the gauge-transverse kernel is
$$
K=-\frac z4(a-\beta z)P^{(2)}+\frac z2[a+2(3\alpha+\beta)z]P^{(0)}.
$$
If present, the additional poles are at $z=-m_2^2$, $m_2^2=-a/\beta$ for $\beta\ne0$, and $z=-m_0^2$, $m_0^2=a/[2(3\alpha+\beta)]$ for $3\alpha+\beta\ne0$. The conserved-source inverse is
$$
\Pi=-\frac4a\frac{T_{\mu\nu}T^{\mu\nu}-T^2/2}{z}
+\frac4a\frac{T_{\mu\nu}T^{\mu\nu}-T^2/3}{z+m_2^2}
-\frac2{3a}\frac{T^2}{z+m_0^2},
\tag{K.10.13d.1}
$$
where an absent sector's entire massive term is omitted. For $a>0$ and positive masses, the massless pole has two healthy tensor polarizations, the massive spin-two sector five ghost polarizations, and the massive scalar one healthy polarization. The total of eight holds when both massive sectors are present with distinct masses. If $m_2^2=m_0^2>0$, the massive pole is a single shell with rank-six indefinite residue, comprising those five and one sectors. An absent sector imposes no mass inequality: absence of tachyonic poles is exactly $\beta/a\le0$ and $(3\alpha+\beta)/a\ge0$, with equality meaning an absent sector. Negative $m^2$ gives a spacelike tachyonic pole, not a healthy timelike particle covered by a rest-frame count. The massless pole and residue are unchanged for every finite coefficient choice with $a\ne0$.

*Proof.* The kernels computed in K.10.13b give the displayed $K$. Its two inverse scalar coefficients have the algebraic partial fractions
$$
-\frac4a\left(\frac1z-\frac1{z+m_2^2}\right),\qquad
\frac2a\left(\frac1z-\frac1{z+m_0^2}\right),
$$
respectively when the corresponding extra sector is present; setting its higher-derivative coefficient to zero instead leaves only its massless term. Contracting the projectors with conserved sources gives $T P^{(2)}T=T_{\mu\nu}T^{\mu\nu}-T^2/3$ and $T P^{(0)}T=T^2/3$, proving (K.10.13d.1). At a timelike massive pole choose its rest frame; conservation sets $T^{0\nu}=0$. Its spatial traceless tensor has five independent components with positive squared norm, and its spatial trace is a separate one-dimensional square. The two coefficients in (K.10.13d.1) have the claimed opposite signs. At the null shell use the two-square identity in K.10.13c. Coincident masses sum the independent trace/traceless residues on the same shell. The inequalities follow from the displayed masses, with absent cases treated separately. At $z=0$ the higher-order terms cannot change the leading nonzero EH coefficient. ∎

For positive present masses the static dust potential consequently has the relative radial weights $1,-4/3,+1/3$, namely $-r^{-1}[1-(4/3)e^{-m_2r}+(1/3)e^{-m_0r}]$ up to normalization and omitted absent terms. This follows from the three dust contractions in (K.10.13d.1) and the Fourier transform of $(\mathbf k^2+m^2)^{-1}$. The case $a=0$ is outside the theorem: surviving blocks may be proportional to $z^2$, vanish identically, or have further gauge degeneracy.

<a id="proposition-k1013e-all-orders-response-boundary-and-repeated-pole-obstruction"></a>**Proposition K.10.13e (All-Orders Response Boundary and Repeated-Pole Obstruction).** The basis of Theorem K.10.13b admits multiple real poles. In particular the allowed polynomial metric symbols
$$
C_2(z)=-z(z+1)^2,\qquad C_0(z)=2z
$$
satisfy (K.10.13b.3), have a healthy massless spin-two residue $-1$, and have an additional real double pole at $z=-1$ in the spin-two inverse. Additional real poles of the all-orders class can therefore be multiple, and a multiple pole has no simple-residue particle reduction. For a real polynomial, the residues at two real simple zeros have opposite signs exactly when the real zeros strictly between them have even total multiplicity, in particular when there are none. Repeated real zeros, complex zeros and tachyonic zeros require separate interpretation.

*Proof.* Here $2C_2+C_0=-4z^2-2z^3$, so the locality conditions hold and the basis theorem realizes this metric action. Moreover $\lim_{z\to0}z/C_2=-1$ while $\lim_{z\to-1}(z+1)^2/C_2=1$. Write $C_2=\kappa\prod_i(z-z_i)^{m_i}$ over its complex zeros. At two real simple zeros $z_1<z_2$, $C_2'(z_1)/C_2'(z_2)=-\prod_i\bigl[(z_1-z_i)/(z_2-z_i)\bigr]^{m_i}$, the product running over the remaining zeros. A real zero outside $[z_1,z_2]$ and a pair of complex-conjugate zeros contribute positive factors, and a real zero strictly between them contributes the sign $(-1)^{m_i}$. The simple residues $1/C_2'$ therefore have opposite signs exactly when the total multiplicity of the real zeros between $z_1$ and $z_2$ is even. ∎

For clarity, the generic metric–scalar inverse at arbitrary finite order can still be written algebraically. Put $\mathcal A(z)=\sum\alpha_n(-z)^n$, $\mathcal B(z)=\sum\beta_n(-z)^n$, $\mathcal C(z)=\sum c_n(-z)^n$, $\mathcal D(z)=\sum d_n(-z)^n$, and define
$$
C_2=-az/4+z^2\mathcal B/4,\quad U=az/2+z^2(3\mathcal A+\mathcal B),\quad
D_0=U\mathcal D-3z^2\mathcal C^2/4.
$$
At generic nonzero $z$ where these inverses exist, direct inversion of the scalar block $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}U&\sqrt3z\mathcal C/2\\\sqrt3z\mathcal C/2&\mathcal D\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ gives
$$
\Pi=\frac{T_{\mu\nu}T^{\mu\nu}-T^2/3}{C_2}
+\frac{\mathcal D T^2/3-z\mathcal C TJ+U J^2}{D_0}.
$$
The adjugate divided by the determinant proves the formula wherever the inverses exist. Cancellations, identically singular blocks and their source constraints, null-shell gauge quotients, root multiplicities and vector–two-form BF spectra must be treated for the actual coefficient choice. The polarization and force statements of Theorem K.10.13c are for the massless two-derivative scalar.

Theorems K.10.13b–K.10.13d and Proposition K.10.13e classify the local operators and their pole tests on the declared finite-field class. Vector and two-form fields have no bilinear metric coupling there. The exact neutral exchange test is given in Theorem K.10.13g. An independently controllable scalar requires its mixed source test. A retained response outside this class requires its own operator and source classification. Physical coefficients require the matching and threshold or truncation bounds of Proposition K.10.14. A pole above the retained cutoff can contribute matched low-energy Wilson coefficients.

<a id="proposition-k1013f"></a>

<a id="proposition-k1013f-local-reset-output-and-boost-covariance-on-the-persistent-worldline-net"></a>**Proposition K.10.13f (Local Reset Output and Boost Covariance on the Persistent-Worldline Net).** The Mosco–Bochner source of Theorem F.0z.8 has finite local output algebras that carry the positive-capacity completed-reset channel of Corollary E.2a.0 as a paid finite local experiment. This supplies a nonconstant decoding effect inside the retained net. On the same fixed worldline net, a nonzero geometric Rindler boost cannot act by one covariant automorphism on all retained diamond algebras in an open part of its wedge. The first result establishes an available response interface for an area record. The second excludes the stated boost-covariant interface on this fixed regional assignment.

*Local support and the physical channel.* Work in a bounded flat chart of Theorem F.0z.8. For an open diamond $O$, let $F(O)$ denote its footprint under projection along the vertical physical observation lines. Its retained algebra is the norm closure of the directed matrix algebras on the spatial cells with closure in $F(O)$. This is the algebra of Proposition F.0z.3 and the finite-window placement in Theorem F.0z.6. In particular the refinement inclusions are unital complete isometries and use the same qubit at the successive time labels of its worldline.

Fix an open spacetime box compactly contained in $O$. At a sufficiently fine grade, four distinct cells and their required local preparation and control collars can be placed in this box. Their joint algebra is $M_{16}(\mathbb C)$. Use two qubits as the code register $K$, one as the reset register $R$, and one as the supplied auxiliary $A$ in $|0\rangle_A$. Place $R$ and $A$ at neighboring spatial cells. In a paid local input-control interval apply $S_{RA}=\mathrm{SWAP}_{RA}$ and retain the original field generator for the subsequent observation interval. This uses the same local exchange primitive as the physical refinement preparation of Theorem F.0z.6. For example, in time $\tau>0$ the extra Hamiltonian
$$
G_{RA}=\frac{\pi\hbar}{2\tau}(I-S_{RA})
\tag{K.10.13f.1}
$$
implements the exchange up to the known onsite drift. The two onsite gaps agree, so the drift commutes with the swap. Onsite phases can either be retained in the output frame or undone by fixed local rotations of opposite phase on a separately supplied control interval. The local support, complete timing, pure auxiliary, pulse and returned auxiliary are charged. The collar and the durations are chosen together before preparing the inputs, with a positive local transport duration for the exchange on the neighboring sites. This is a declared finite preparation/readout extension of the same field. Its input-control operation does not alter the autonomous onsite evolution in the regional comparison.

At the code receiver cut take the output on $K\otimes R$. For every reference $E$ and input $\rho_{KRE}$ the output is
$$
(\operatorname{id}_{KE}\otimes\operatorname{Tr}_R)(\rho_{KRE})
\otimes|0\rangle\langle0|_R,
\tag{K.10.13f.2}
$$
with the factors ordered at their indicated ports. The formula follows by swapping $R$ into the fresh auxiliary, including its coherences and correlations, exactly as in Theorem E.2a.0a. Four orthogonal code words on $K$ give a one-use zero-error code. The output support of this channel has dimension four and the $n$-use support has dimension $4^n$, giving capacity $\ln4$ by Corollary E.2a.0. The effect $|00\rangle\langle00|_K\otimes I_R$ belongs to the actual regional algebra by its isometric inclusion. Its response gap is one between the code words $00$ and $01$. On the full enlarged source the auxiliary and its effects are retained. If the auxiliary output is included in the transmission task, the resulting isometric channel has capacity $\ln8$ by Theorem E.2a.0a. The $\ln4$ value uses the receiver cut in (K.10.13f.2), together with that theorem's separate whole-retained-support test when such a support certificate is requested. The event-area density and saturated entropy-variation law require their own source records.

*Geometric covariance test.* Write the flat spacetime coordinates in units $c=1$ for this argument. A vertical time translation preserves the spatial footprint exactly. It also acts on each qubit by its own onsite unitary, which preserves the full algebra of that site. Hence $\mathfrak A(O)=\mathfrak A(O')$ for the translated diamond $O'=O+(\Delta t,0)$, at the finite stages and in the norm limit. For a fixed nonzero rapidity $r$, choose centers $(0,b,0,0)$ and $(\Delta t,b,0,0)$ in the wedge $x^1>|t|$, with $0<|\Delta t|<b$. Take $b$ and $|\Delta t|$ sufficiently small to keep the centers and their boosted images in the flat chart. Use double cones with offsets $|t-t_{\mathrm{ctr}}|+|\mathbf x-\mathbf x_{\mathrm{ctr}}|<\delta$ and
$$
0<\delta<\min\left\{\frac{b-|\Delta t|}{2},
\frac{|\Delta t\sinh r|}{4e^{|r|}}\right\}.
\tag{K.10.13f.3}
$$
Both cones lie inside the wedge, which the boost preserves. Their boosted spatial centers differ by $|\Delta t\sinh r|$. Each boosted spatial footprint lies within $e^{|r|}\delta$ of its center by the linear boost formula. The footprints are therefore disjoint. The corresponding algebras have scalar intersection by independence of the tensor factors. The product conditional expectation onto either footprint fixes its own algebra and acts by the scalar vacuum mean on the other, also in the norm limit. Each algebra is nonconstant by the interior cell response, so the two boosted algebras are unequal. A single automorphism $\beta_r$ satisfying $\beta_r(\mathfrak A(V))=\mathfrak A(\Lambda_r V)$ for every such diamond $V$ would send the equal original algebras to equal images, a contradiction.

Consequently Definition 12.5.3k(2) does admit a complete F.0d entry with a nonconstant in-net decoder interface, so the scalar-algebra deduction of Corollary 12.1f.8 cannot be made from the name of that entry alone. Its hypotheses concern the literal point-event regional assignment. The geometric boost obstruction applies to the fixed worldline assignment in the physical boost/KMS gate of Theorem 48a.0. A different net, a specified restriction on which the required physical boost acts, or a source comparison carrying that action would require its actual same-source map and response tests. A positive decoder capacity still requires the density, entropy saturation, thermodynamic ledger, stress and common horizon-variation maps of Theorems 49 and E.6 and Definition 12.5.3k before it gives a K.10.10 area record. $\square$

<a id="theorem-k1013g"></a>

<a id="theorem-k1013g-exact-einstein-exchange-test-for-polynomial-scalar-metric-actions"></a>**Theorem K.10.13g (Exact Einstein Exchange Test for Polynomial Scalar–Metric Actions).** Use the field and source conventions of Theorem K.10.13b with $a\ne0$. Write $z=k^2$ and use the polynomials $\mathcal A,\mathcal B,\mathcal C,\mathcal D$ defined after Proposition K.10.13e. The neutral experiment couples arbitrary conserved $T^{\mu\nu}$ to the original metric and has scalar source $J=0$. Compare its quadratic exchange with that of $a\mathcal L_{\rm EH}^{(2)}$ at all regular nonzero momenta, keeping all contacts. On a common zero-incoming retarded prescription, the neutral exchange equals Einstein exchange exactly in the following cases:

1. If $\mathcal D\ne0$, the two polynomial identities are
$$
\mathcal B=0,\qquad 4\mathcal A\mathcal D=\mathcal C^2 .
\tag{K.10.13g.1}
$$
2. If $\mathcal D=0$, the test requires $\mathcal A=\mathcal B=\mathcal C=0$, with the arbitrary scalar removed by its shift quotient. With $\mathcal D\ne0$ and identically vanishing spin-zero determinant, arbitrary neutral trace sources are incompatible with the equations.

In case 1, a local triangular redefinition leaving the original metric and source fixed separates the scalar when $\mathcal D$ divides $\mathcal C$. Among exact neutral-Einstein solutions the same divisibility is necessary for a scalar shift by a polynomial in $\Box$ applied to $R^{(1)}$. If the separated scalar inverse has a positive Euclidean spectral measure with the healthy sign and a constant contact allowed, a propagating polynomial scalar has $\mathcal D=-b(z+m^2)$ with $b>0$ and $m^2\ge0$. On that branch (K.10.13g.1) implies the divisibility. An algebraic scalar has constant $\mathcal D$ and also satisfies the divisibility. A test admitting independent scalar forces sees an additional metric response whenever $\mathcal C\ne0$.

*Exact neutral test.* On the transverse basis of Theorem K.10.13b, let $r=\theta^{\mu\nu}h_{\mu\nu}/\sqrt3$. The tensor kernel and the two-by-two scalar kernel in $(r,\phi)$ are
$$
C_2=-az/4+z^2\mathcal B/4,\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}U&W\\ W&\mathcal D\end{pmatrix},\qquad
U=az/2+z^2(3\mathcal A+\mathcal B),\quad W=\sqrt3z\mathcal C/2 .
$$
At a timelike regular momentum the traceless spatial sources and the spatial trace can be varied independently. Testing the former fixes $1/C_2=-4/(az)$ and hence $\mathcal B=0$. For $\mathcal D\ne0$ and nonzero determinant, the neutral trace exchange coefficient in the normalized scalar channel is $1/(U-W^2/\mathcal D)$. Equality with $2/(az)$ fixes (K.10.13g.1) by clearing denominators. Conversely those identities give $U-W^2/\mathcal D=az/2$ and the tensor inverse is the Einstein inverse. If the scalar determinant vanishes identically with $\mathcal D\ne0$, the generic kernel annihilates $(\mathcal D,-W)$, so its source pairing enforces $\mathcal D T/\sqrt3=0$ for $J=0$. If $\mathcal D=0$ and $W\ne0$, the scalar equation imposes $Wr=0$ and the generic neutral trace exchange is zero. If both vanish, the scalar is arbitrary and quotiented, and the remaining $U$ fixes $\mathcal A=0$ in addition to $\mathcal B=0$. Equalities on any regular interval imply the polynomial identities. For the retarded comparison, at fixed spatial momentum the zero-incoming inverses use the same Fourier–Laplace prescription above all poles of the finite rational symbols. The algebraic cancellation holds there before taking retarded boundary values or inverse transforms. It therefore does not generate extra homogeneous solutions or point-supported spectral terms in the neutral forced response.

*Local separation and independent scalar drives.* Since $R^{(1)}=\sqrt3zr$, the shift $\widehat\phi=\phi+\mathcal C R^{(1)}/(2\mathcal D)$ completes the square. Equation (K.10.13g.1) gives the Einstein metric action plus $\widehat\phi\mathcal D\widehat\phi$. This is a polynomial triangular field change exactly when $\mathcal C/(2\mathcal D)$ is polynomial. Coefficient comparison of the mixed term fixes that shift uniquely. With sources the normalized scalar part of the exact exchange is
$$
\frac{2}{az}\left(\frac{T}{\sqrt3}-\frac{W}{\mathcal D}J\right)^2+\frac{J^2}{\mathcal D} .
\tag{K.10.13g.2}
$$
The mixed trace-to-scalar bilinear term is $-2\mathcal C TJ/(a\mathcal D)$. At regular nonzero momenta it vanishes for all independent forces exactly when $\mathcal C=0$. In particular a nonzero response can be tested on a scalar drive with a trace readout even where the neutral exchange matches exactly. This classification concerns responses of the specified fields and source normalization. A freely occupied extra scalar and its nonlinear stress require their own tests even when the metric is unchanged in neutral linear exchange.

*Spectral positivity.* With the sign convention of Theorem K.10.13c the healthy scalar Euclidean exchange coefficient is $-1/\mathcal D(z)$ for $z>0$. Assume it has a representation $b_0+\int_{[0,\infty)} (z+t)^{-1}d\nu(t)$ with constant $b_0$ and positive measure satisfying $\int(1+t)^{-1}d\nu(t)<\infty$. For a nonconstant polynomial $\mathcal D$ the coefficient tends to zero. Dominated convergence therefore fixes $b_0=0$. If $\nu\ne0$, monotone convergence gives $\lim_{z\to\infty} z\int(z+t)^{-1}d\nu(t)=\nu([0,\infty))>0$, possibly infinite. Degree two or more contradicts this limit. A degree-one inverse then has precisely one pole at $-m^2\le0$ with positive residue, giving the stated sign and form. Its linear factor divides $\mathcal C$ by (K.10.13g.1). A constant inverse can be the stated contact. The spectral premise is on the full separated scalar exchange, so an effective finite polynomial fitted below a cutoff need not satisfy it beyond that cutoff.

For example for any nonzero real polynomial $P$, take $\mathcal B=0$, $\mathcal D=-(z+m^2)$, $\mathcal C=2\mathcal D P$ and $\mathcal A=\mathcal D P^2$. This is an admitted local action with a healthy scalar, nonzero scalar–metric mixing and curvature coefficients. It gives exact Einstein neutral exchange at every momentum with the same retarded prescription. Its independent scalar drive changes the metric through the mixed term in (K.10.13g.2). Thus neutral data alone cannot impose vanishing of the individual polynomial couplings. $\square$

<a id="theorem-k1013h"></a>

<a id="theorem-k1013h-exact-retained-source-test-for-several-scalar-fields"></a>**Theorem K.10.13h (Exact Retained-Source Test for Several Scalar Fields).** Use the flat metric, conserved-source conventions and retarded comparison of Theorem K.10.13g. Replace the single scalar by any finite number of scalar fields, allowing an arbitrary real symmetric polynomial scalar block and a marked family of independent scalar source controls. Allow an identically singular block and keep every compatible source. The complete neutral Einstein test, the additional mixed-source test, and the remaining scalar exchange are given below. With a positive scalar spectral measure, the scalar exchange has an exact test for whether a retained force detects propagating weight. This supplies the scalar-multiplicity and partial-source classification for the stated linear response.

*Compatible scalar quotient.* Put $z=k^2$, take $a\ne0$, and work over the rational functions of $z$ in the regular transverse momentum symbols. Write the spin-zero action on the transverse trace $r$ and the scalar column $\phi$ as
$$
U r^2+2rW^{\mathsf T}\phi+\phi^{\mathsf T}D\phi,\qquad
U=az/2+z^2(3\mathcal A+\mathcal B),\quad
W=\sqrt3 z C/2,\quad D=D^{\mathsf T}.
\tag{K.10.13h.1}
$$
Here $C$ is a real polynomial column, $D$ is a real polynomial matrix, and the spin-two coefficient is $-az/4+z^2\mathcal B/4$ as in Theorem K.10.13g. Let $t$ be the normalized neutral trace force and $J=Sj$ the scalar force from the marked polynomial control matrix $S$. The scalar equation is $W r+D\phi=J$. If some $n\in\ker D$ has $n^{\mathsf T}W\ne0$, the neutral drive $J=0$ forces $r=0$. It cannot give the nonzero Einstein trace exchange for arbitrary $t$. Otherwise $W$ lies in the image of $D$. A force $J$ is compatible with this block exactly when it annihilates $\ker D$. Thus compatibility of every declared force requires $\operatorname{im}S\subseteq\operatorname{im}D$. This applies even if $D$ has no nonzero rank. In that case all compatible scalar couplings and forces vanish.

For compatible forces define $D^\#$ as the inverse on the quotient by $\ker D$, in the sense that $D D^\# J=J$ on $\operatorname{im}D$. Its bilinear pairings on $\operatorname{im}D$ are intrinsic and symmetric: for $D x=J$ and $D y=J'$ one has $J^{\mathsf T}y=x^{\mathsf T}D y=J'^{\mathsf T}x$, and adding a null vector changes neither pairing. Rational elimination constructs such an inverse. For example a nonzero principal minor of order equal to the rank gives a nonsingular coordinate submatrix, with the other solution coordinates set to zero. A symmetric rational matrix has such a principal minor since one can diagonalize its associated quadratic form by congruence and the exterior power of degree equal to the rank is a nonzero symmetric rank-one matrix. At points where a chosen minor vanishes one may use a different regular chart or the retarded continuation of the resulting intrinsic rational symbol.

*Full retained exchange.* Eliminating $\phi$ leaves
$$
U_{\mathrm{eff}}=U-W^{\mathsf T}D^\#W,\qquad
t_{\mathrm{eff}}=t-W^{\mathsf T}D^\#Sj .
\tag{K.10.13h.2}
$$
If $U_{\mathrm{eff}}$ vanishes identically, arbitrary independent neutral trace forces are incompatible. Otherwise the exchange is $t_{\mathrm{eff}}^2/U_{\mathrm{eff}}+j^{\mathsf T}S^{\mathsf T}D^\#Sj$, together with the independent spin-two exchange. Hence the neutral response equals Einstein exactly if and only if
$$
W\in\operatorname{im}D,\qquad \mathcal B=0,\qquad
4\mathcal A=C^{\mathsf T}D^\# C .
\tag{K.10.13h.3}
$$
Indeed the independent traceless probes fix $\mathcal B=0$, and then $U_{\mathrm{eff}}=az/2$ is precisely the scalar identity. The identities can be checked by clearing rational denominators on a nonempty regular interval. On this neutral branch the original metric is insensitive to the admitted scalar drives exactly when
$$
C^{\mathsf T}D^\# S=0 .
\tag{K.10.13h.4}
$$
When the image of the declared drives spans $\operatorname{im}D$ over the rational functions, (K.10.13h.4) forces $C=0$ by nondegeneracy of the quotient pairing. Otherwise (K.10.13h.4) tests the actual retained controls and can hold with nonzero $C$. Once it holds, the remaining scalar exchange is exactly $S^{\mathsf T}D^\#S$. Thus the comparison can distinguish a field invisible to the retained metric from a field detectable by its own retained response. These algebraic identities hold for the retarded forced response with the common zero-incoming prescription because the rational cancellations are made above the poles in Fourier–Laplace space before boundary values are taken.

*Positive spectral test and finite witnesses.* As an additional physical premise, suppose the retained scalar exchange with the healthy sign is of the form
$$
-S(z)^{\mathsf T}D^\#(z)S(z)=P(z)+
\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{d\mathcal M(\lambda)}{z+\lambda},
\qquad z>0 ,
\tag{K.10.13h.5}
$$
where $P$ is the independently registered real symmetric contact polynomial and $\mathcal M$ is a positive matrix measure with $\int(1+\lambda)^{-1}d\mathcal M$ finite. For a constant retained force vector $j$, its separated exchange has zero propagating weight exactly when its contact-subtracted value vanishes at any one positive real $z$. The integrand for the scalar measure $j^{\mathsf T}d\mathcal M j$ is strictly positive; consequently a zero integral forces the entire scalar measure to vanish. By spectral Cauchy–Schwarz this also annihilates the cross measure between $j$ and any other probe. The null space of the contact-subtracted matrix is therefore the same at every positive real $z$. Equality of the full exchange to pure Einstein on every retained drive, with the additional contacts included, requires (K.10.13h.3)–(K.10.13h.4) and vanishing of both the retained spectral weight and the retained contact. In the special case $\mathcal A=0$ and a strictly definite healthy quotient scalar inverse on a regular positive interval, (K.10.13h.3) already forces $C=0$ on that interval and hence identically.

At an algebraic source with a nominated regular real interval, finite exact polynomial and matrix operations decide all rational identities in (K.10.13h.3)–(K.10.13h.4). A failed rational identity has a nonzero component at some rational regular point, found by enumeration. At a named positive point a strictly positive contact-subtracted spectral value can be certified by a finite interval excluding zero. Every such test uses the fixed metric, scalar and contact records. The horizon source must determine which drives it admits.

For an explicit singular example in fixed units take $D=\operatorname{diag}(-(z+1),-(z+2),0)$, $C=(-(z+1),0,0)^{\mathsf T}$, $\mathcal A=-(z+1)/4$, $\mathcal B=0$, and a single retained scalar force $S=(0,1,0)^{\mathsf T}$. Both Einstein metric tests pass and the retained scalar exchange has a detectable pole, with healthy coefficient $1/(z+2)$. The third coordinate is quotiented. $\square$

<a id="proposition-k1014-conditional-cutoff-matching-status-of-parameters"></a>**Proposition K.10.14 (Conditional Cutoff-Matching Status of Parameters).** In a regulated QFT, bare parameters depend on the regulator, cutoff, and renormalization prescription; they may diverge, vanish, or approach finite values as the cutoff is removed. On a PU branch carrying the ultraviolet lattice or bandlimit and matching certificate of Theorem K.10.4:

1. coefficients assigned above the certified operational bandlimit are not independent retained observables;
2. coefficients at the matching scale are finite only if the microscopic action and matching theorem establish finiteness;
3. parameters below the matching scale encode operational predictions together with threshold and truncation residuals.

*Proof.* The ultraviolet certificate specifies the microscopic regulator and the map from its finite data to the lower-scale effective action. Modes removed by that map can affect low-energy observables through matched Wilson coefficients, so they cannot simply be declared consequence-free. Finiteness and predictive meaning therefore follow from the certificate's microscopic parameter bounds and matching estimates, not from the existence of a length scale alone. ∎

<a id="proposition-k1014a-finite-gauge-spectral-checks-do-not-imply-a-uniform-mass-gap"></a>**Proposition K.10.14a (Finite Gauge-Spectral Checks Do Not Imply a Uniform Mass Gap).** For every $L\ge1$, let the gauge-reduced Hilbert space of a finite $\mathbb Z_2$ holonomy sector be
$$
\mathcal H_L^{\mathrm{phys}}=\operatorname{span}\{|0_L\rangle,|1_L\rangle\},
$$
and let
$$
H_L=\frac1L|1_L\rangle\!\langle1_L|.
\tag{K.10.14a.1}
$$
Each $H_L$ is a positive gauge-invariant Hamiltonian with a unique vacuum and a strictly positive finite-volume gap $\Delta_L=1/L$. Nevertheless,
$$
\inf_{L\ge1}\Delta_L=0.
\tag{K.10.14a.2}
$$
Consequently no collection of separate finite-volume positivity checks, without a volume-uniform lower bound and a controlled infinite-volume embedding, proves the mass-gap component of a Yang–Mills bridge.

*Proof.* Equation (K.10.14a.1) is diagonal on the gauge-reduced sector, with eigenvalues $0$ and $1/L$. This proves uniqueness and positivity at every finite $L$. Taking the infimum gives (K.10.14a.2). The family is nonempty for every $L$, so the obstruction is not vacuous. ∎

The proposition refutes the inference from pointwise finite-volume gaps to a uniform gap.

<a id="theorem-k1014b-physical-wilson-transfer-and-its-strong-coupling-volume-uniform-gap"></a>**Theorem K.10.14b (Physical Wilson Transfer and Its Strong-Coupling Volume-Uniform Gap).** Let $G\subset U(d)$ be a compact matrix group with normalized Haar measure. For $n\ge3$ let $\Lambda_n=(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^3$, let $E_n$ be its set of $3n^3$ positively oriented links, put $X_n=G^{E_n}$ with product Haar measure $\mu$, and let the gauge group $\mathcal G_n=G^{\Lambda_n}$, with normalized Haar measure, act by $(h\cdot U)_{xy}=h(x)U_{xy}h(y)^{-1}$ on the link from $x$ to $y$. For $\beta\ge0$ use the plaquette cost $C_p=1-d^{-1}\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}U_p$ of Corollary G.6b.1(d), and define
$$
\begin{aligned}
V(U)&=\sum_{p}C_p(U),\qquad
D(U,W)=\sum_{e\in E_n}\Bigl(1-\frac1d\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(U_eW_e^{-1}\bigr)\Bigr),\\
k_\beta(U,W)&=e^{-\beta[V(U)/2+D(U,W)+V(W)/2]},\qquad
k_\beta^{\mathcal G}(U,W)=\int_{\mathcal G_n}k_\beta(U,h\cdot W)\,dh,
\end{aligned}
\tag{K.10.14b.1}
$$
where $p$ runs over the $3n^3$ plaquettes of $\Lambda_n$. Let $\mathsf K$ be the integral operator on $L^2(X_n,\mu)$ with kernel $k_\beta^{\mathcal G}$. Then:

1. $\mathsf K$ is positive, self-adjoint and trace class, and $\mathsf K=\mathsf K_0Q$, where $\mathsf K_0$ has kernel $k_\beta$ and $Q$ is the orthogonal projection onto gauge-invariant functions. Its largest eigenvalue $\lambda_0$ is simple, with a gauge-invariant, continuous, strictly positive unit eigenfunction $\Omega$. Put $T=\mathsf K/\lambda_0$ and $q_n(\beta)=\|T|_{\Omega^\perp}\|$. Then $0\le q_n(\beta)<1$.
2. For $M\ge3$, the Wilson measure $Z^{-1}e^{-\beta\sum_pC_p}\prod dU$ of the same plaquette cost on the periodic lattice $\Lambda_n\times\mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z$, with product Haar measure on all links, has $Z=\operatorname{Tr}\mathsf K^M$. Write $U_s\in X_n$ for its spatial links at time $s$. For bounded measurable functions $F_1,\dots,F_r$ on $X_n$, also denoting the multiplication operators, and times $0\le s_1\le\dots\le s_r\le M-1$,
$$
\mathbb E\Bigl[\prod_{j=1}^rF_j(U_{s_j})\Bigr]
=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(F_1T^{s_2-s_1}F_2\cdots T^{s_r-s_{r-1}}F_rT^{M-s_r+s_1}\bigr)}{\operatorname{Tr}T^M}
\longrightarrow
\langle\Omega,F_1T^{s_2-s_1}F_2\cdots T^{s_r-s_{r-1}}F_r\Omega\rangle
\tag{K.10.14b.2}
$$
as $M\to\infty$ with the differences $s_{j+1}-s_j$ fixed.
3. For a transfer step $a>0$, the physical Hamiltonian $H_{a,n}=-a^{-1}\log T$ on the closed span $\mathcal H_n$ of the eigenvectors of $T$ with positive eigenvalue is self-adjoint and nonnegative, $\ker H_{a,n}=\mathbb C\Omega$, and its energy threshold above the vacuum is
$$
m_{a,n}(\beta)=-a^{-1}\log q_n(\beta)\in(0,\infty].
\tag{K.10.14b.3}
$$
4. For every $\beta\ge0$ and $n\ge3$,
$$
q_n(\beta)\le\tanh(3\beta n^3).
\tag{K.10.14b.4}
$$
5. If $18\tanh\beta<1$, then for every $n\ge3$
$$
q_n(\beta)\le18\tanh\beta,\qquad m_{a,n}(\beta)\ge-a^{-1}\log(18\tanh\beta).
\tag{K.10.14b.5}
$$

*Proof.* (1) Write $\chi=\operatorname{Tr}$. The link factor $f_\beta(g)=e^{-\beta}\exp[\frac{\beta}{2d}(\chi(g)+\overline{\chi(g)})]$ has a uniformly convergent expansion in the products $\chi^r\overline\chi^s$, which are characters of the unitary representations $(\mathbb C^d)^{\otimes r}\otimes(\overline{\mathbb C^d})^{\otimes s}$, with nonnegative coefficients. Hence $f_\beta$ is a positive-definite function and convolution by it is a positive operator on $L^2(G)$. The kernel $\prod_{e\in E_n}f_\beta(U_eW_e^{-1})$ is the tensor product of these convolutions, and $\mathsf K_0$ is that positive operator multiplied on both sides by the positive function $e^{-\beta V/2}$; thus $\mathsf K_0\ge0$. Since $V(h\cdot U)=V(U)$ and $(h\cdot U)_e(h\cdot W)_e^{-1}=h(x)U_eW_e^{-1}h(x)^{-1}$ for $e$ from $x$, $k_\beta(h\cdot U,h\cdot W)=k_\beta(U,W)$. Therefore $\mathsf K_0$ commutes with the averaging $Q$ over $\mathcal G_n$, and $\mathsf K=\mathsf K_0Q=Q\mathsf K_0Q\ge0$. Being positive with a continuous kernel on the compact space $X_n\times X_n$, whose Haar measure has full support, $\mathsf K$ is trace class by Mercer's theorem. Every normalized defect $C_p$ and $1-d^{-1}\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}g$ lies in $[0,2]$, so $e^{-12\beta n^3}\le k_\beta^{\mathcal G}\le1$. Let $f$ be a real unit eigenvector for $\lambda_0=\|\mathsf K\|$. Then $\langle|f|,\mathsf K|f|\rangle\ge\langle f,\mathsf Kf\rangle=\lambda_0=\max_{\|g\|=1}\langle g,\mathsf Kg\rangle$, so $|f|$ is also an eigenvector, and $|f|=\lambda_0^{-1}\mathsf K|f|\ge\lambda_0^{-1}e^{-12\beta n^3}\int|f|\,d\mu>0$ everywhere. The equality $\iint k_\beta^{\mathcal G}(U,W)\bigl(|f(U)f(W)|-f(U)f(W)\bigr)\,d\mu(U)\,d\mu(W)=0$ with a strictly positive kernel forces $f$ to have constant sign almost everywhere. Two orthogonal eigenvectors for $\lambda_0$ cannot both have constant sign, so $\lambda_0$ is simple. Its unit eigenfunction $\Omega=\lambda_0^{-1}\mathsf K\Omega$, chosen positive, is continuous and lies in the range of $Q$. The spectrum of the compact operator $T$ lies in $[0,1]$ and the eigenvalue $1$ is simple, so $q_n(\beta)<1$.

(2) Denote by $h_s(x)$ the temporal link from $(x,s)$ to $(x,s+1)$. The temporal plaquette based at $(x,s)$ in the $(i,0)$ plane has holonomy $U_{s,i}(x)\,h_s(x+\hat\imath)\,U_{s+1,i}(x)^{-1}h_s(x)^{-1}$, whose real trace equals that of $U_{s,i}(x)\bigl((h_s\cdot U_{s+1})_i(x)\bigr)^{-1}$. The temporal plaquettes between times $s$ and $s+1$ therefore contribute $e^{-\beta D(U_s,h_s\cdot U_{s+1})}$, and with $V(h_s\cdot U_{s+1})=V(U_{s+1})$ the Wilson weight equals $\prod_{s=0}^{M-1}k_\beta(U_s,h_s\cdot U_{s+1})$ with $U_M=U_0$. Each $h_s$ occurs in one factor. Integrating it gives $\prod_sk_\beta^{\mathcal G}(U_s,U_{s+1})$, and integration over the spatial links gives $Z=\operatorname{Tr}\mathsf K^M$ and the equality in (K.10.14b.2). Write $T=|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|+R$ with $R\ge0$, $R\Omega=0$, $\|R\|=q_n(\beta)$ and $\operatorname{Tr}R<\infty$. For a bounded operator $Y$ and $N\ge1$, $|\operatorname{Tr}(YT^N)-\langle\Omega,Y\Omega\rangle|=|\operatorname{Tr}(YR^N)|\le\|Y\|\,q_n(\beta)^{N-1}\operatorname{Tr}R$. Applied with $N=M-s_r+s_1$ and with $Y=I$, this gives the limit.

(3) On $\mathcal H_n$ the eigenvalues of $T$ lie in $(0,1]$, the eigenvalue $1$ is simple with eigenvector $\Omega$, and the largest eigenvalue on $\mathcal H_n\ominus\mathbb C\Omega$ is $q_n(\beta)$, or this space is zero when $q_n(\beta)=0$. Functional calculus gives the stated properties of $H_{a,n}$ and (K.10.14b.3).

(4) For a strictly positive symmetric kernel $k$ put $\Delta(k)=\sup\log\dfrac{k(U,W)k(U',W')}{k(U,W')k(U',W)}$. In the cross ratio of $k_\beta$ the factors $e^{-\beta V/2}$ cancel, and each link term of $D$ contributes at most $4\beta$, because its four normalized real traces lie in $[-1,1]$; hence $\Delta(k_\beta)\le4\beta|E_n|=12\beta n^3$. For fixed $U,U'$ the ratio $k_\beta(U,h\cdot W)/k_\beta(U',h\cdot W)$ ranges over an interval whose endpoints have ratio at most $e^{12\beta n^3}$, and $k_\beta^{\mathcal G}(U,W)/k_\beta^{\mathcal G}(U',W)$ is its average against the probability weights proportional to $k_\beta(U',h\cdot W)\,dh$, so it lies in the same interval. Thus $\Delta:=\Delta(k_\beta^{\mathcal G})\le12\beta n^3$. Let $\pi=\Omega^2\mu$ and $P(U,dW)=k_\beta^{\mathcal G}(U,W)\Omega(W)\,\mu(dW)/(\lambda_0\Omega(U))$. Multiplication by $\Omega$ is a unitary map from $L^2(\pi)$ onto $L^2(\mu)$ carrying $P$ to $T$ and $1$ to $\Omega$. For two rows, the likelihood ratio $\rho=dP(U,\cdot)/dP(U',\cdot)$ satisfies $\sup\rho/\inf\rho\le e^\Delta$, since the factors depending on $U$, $U'$ or $W$ alone cancel. If $\rho$ is constant, the two rows coincide. If $\rho$ ranges in $[\underline\rho,\overline\rho]$ with $\underline\rho<\overline\rho$, then $\underline\rho\le1\le\overline\rho$, and convexity of $(\rho-1)_+$ gives
$$
\sup_A\bigl|P(U,A)-P(U',A)\bigr|=\mathbb E_{P(U',\cdot)}(\rho-1)_+\le\frac{(\overline\rho-1)(1-\underline\rho)}{\overline\rho-\underline\rho}\le\frac{e^{\Delta/2}-1}{e^{\Delta/2}+1}=\tanh\frac\Delta4 ,
$$
where the last bound maximizes over $\underline\rho$ at $\overline\rho/\underline\rho=e^\Delta$. Hence $\operatorname{osc}(Pf)\le\tanh(\Delta/4)\operatorname{osc}(f)$ for every bounded real $f$. An eigenfunction of $P$ with eigenvalue $\zeta\ne0$ orthogonal to $1$ in $L^2(\pi)$ is continuous and nonconstant, so $|\zeta|\le\tanh(\Delta/4)\le\tanh(3\beta n^3)$. As $P$ is compact and self-adjoint on $L^2(\pi)$, this is (K.10.14b.4).

(5) Fix $M\ge3$ and let $\nu_M$ be the Wilson measure of item 2 on the set $\mathcal L$ of links of $\Lambda_n\times\mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z$. All sides are at least three, so each link lies in six plaquettes, each containing three other distinct links. Let $m_{ij}$ be the number of plaquettes containing the links $i\ne j$; then $m_{ii}=0$ and $\sum_jm_{ij}=18$. Changing link $j$ changes the logarithm of the conditional density of link $i$, as a function of $U_i$, by a function with values in $[-2\beta m_{ij},2\beta m_{ij}]$. Two probability laws whose log-density ratio has oscillation at most $c$ are at total-variation distance at most $\tanh(c/4)$, since for an event of probability $x$ under the first law the second gives it at most $xe^c/(xe^c+1-x)$, and $\max_x[xe^c/(xe^c+1-x)-x]=\tanh(c/4)$. Hence the conditional laws $\gamma_i(\cdot\mid U)$ of $\nu_M$ satisfy
$$
\sup\bigl\{\|\gamma_i(\cdot\mid U)-\gamma_i(\cdot\mid U')\|_{\mathrm{TV}}:U_k=U'_k\ (k\ne j)\bigr\}\le\tanh(\beta m_{ij})\le m_{ij}\tanh\beta=:\bar C_{ij},
$$
using subadditivity of $\tanh$ on $[0,\infty)$. The symmetric matrix $\bar C$ has row and column sums $r=18\tanh\beta<1$.

Let $\nu'$ be a probability measure on $G^{\mathcal L}$ whose conditional laws satisfy $\|\gamma_i(\cdot\mid U)-\gamma'_i(\cdot\mid U)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le b_i$ for every $U$. Run two random-scan heat-bath chains with stationary laws $\nu_M$ and $\nu'$, started from $\nu_M\otimes\nu'$; at each step choose one of the $N=|\mathcal L|$ links uniformly and update it in both chains by a maximal coupling of $\gamma_i(\cdot\mid X)$ and $\gamma'_i(\cdot\mid Y)$. Since $\|\gamma_i(\cdot\mid X)-\gamma'_i(\cdot\mid Y)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\sum_j\bar C_{ij}\mathbf 1[X_j\ne Y_j]+b_i$, the disagreement probabilities $p_t(i)$ satisfy
$$
p_{t+1}\le\Bigl[\bigl(1-\tfrac1N\bigr)I+\tfrac1N\bar C\Bigr]p_t+\tfrac1Nb .
$$
The matrix in brackets has row sums at most $1-(1-r)/N<1$, so $\limsup_tp_t\le(I-\bar C)^{-1}b$. For a bounded function $f$ with single-link oscillations $\delta_if$, telescoping over the coordinates gives $|\nu_M(f)-\nu'(f)|\le\sum_i\delta_if\,p_t(i)$ for every $t$, hence $|\nu_M(f)-\nu'(f)|\le\sum_i\delta_if\,[(I-\bar C)^{-1}b]_i$. For bounded $g$ and $\nu'\propto e^{\epsilon g}\nu_M$ one may take $b_i=\tanh(|\epsilon|\delta_ig/4)\le|\epsilon|\delta_ig/4$. Dividing by $|\epsilon|$ and letting $\epsilon\to0$ gives
$$
|\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_M}(f,g)|\le\frac14\sum_{i,j}\delta_if\,[(I-\bar C)^{-1}]_{ij}\,\delta_jg .
$$
Call two links adjacent when they share a plaquette. Then $(\bar C^k)_{ij}=0$ when the graph distance of $i$ and $j$ exceeds $k$, and $\bar C^k$ has row and column sums $r^k$. If $f$ and $g$ depend on link sets $S$ and $S'$ at graph distance at least $\ell$, the bound $\delta_if\le2\|f\|_\infty$ gives
$$
|\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_M}(f,g)|\le\min(|S|,|S'|)\,\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_\infty\,\frac{r^{\ell}}{1-r}.
$$
A plaquette contains only links whose base points have time coordinates $s$ and $s+1$ for one $s$, so the spatial links of the slices $0$ and $k$ are at graph distance at least $\min(k,M-k)$. For a bounded real function $F$ on $X_n$, apply this bound to $F(U_0)$ and $F(U_k)$ with $|S|=3n^3$ and let $M\to\infty$ in (K.10.14b.2):
$$
\bigl|\langle\Omega,FT^kF\Omega\rangle-\langle\Omega,F\Omega\rangle^2\bigr|\le\frac{3n^3\|F\|_\infty^2}{1-r}\,r^k .
$$
Let $\zeta>0$ be an eigenvalue of $T$ on $\Omega^\perp$ with real eigenvector $v$. Then $v=\zeta^{-1}Tv$ is continuous, $F=v/\Omega$ is bounded and real, $\langle\Omega,F\Omega\rangle=\langle\Omega,v\rangle=0$, and $\langle\Omega,FT^kF\Omega\rangle=\zeta^k\|v\|^2$. Taking $k$-th roots as $k\to\infty$ gives $\zeta\le r$. Since $T\ge0$, $q_n(\beta)\le r$, and (K.10.14b.3) gives the bound on $m_{a,n}(\beta)$. ∎

The bound (K.10.14b.4) gives a positive gap at every lattice spacing and spatial volume. Since $-\log\tanh x\le4e^{-2x}$ for $x\ge\frac12\log2$, its energy form $-a^{-1}\log\tanh(3\beta n^3)$ tends to zero as $a\to0$ at fixed physical side $L=na$ when $\beta\ge\beta_0>0$. Item 5 holds at fixed lattice spacing for $\beta<\operatorname{artanh}(1/18)=\frac12\log(19/17)\approx0.0556$.

<a id="proposition-k1014c-physical-time-scaling-of-transfer-gaps"></a>**Proposition K.10.14c (Physical-Time Scaling of Transfer Gaps).** Let $a_j\downarrow0$. For each $j$ let $T_j$ be a positive self-adjoint contraction on a Hilbert space $\mathcal H_j$ and $\Omega_j$ a unit vector with $T_j\Omega_j=\Omega_j$, and put $q_j=\|T_j|_{\Omega_j^\perp}\|$.

1. Suppose there are $t>0$, $B<\infty$ and vectors $v_j\perp\Omega_j$ with $\|v_j\|^2\le B$ and
$$
\langle v_j,T_j^{\lfloor t/a_j\rfloor}v_j\rangle\longrightarrow c(t)>0 .
\tag{K.10.14c.1}
$$
Then $q_j>0$ for all large $j$, and
$$
\limsup_{j\to\infty}\frac{-\log q_j}{a_j}\le\frac1t\log\frac{B}{c(t)} .
\tag{K.10.14c.2}
$$
In particular $q_j\to1$, and if $-a_j^{-1}\log q_j\ge m>0$ for every $j$, then $1-e^{-ma_j}\le1-q_j\le b\,a_j$ for all large $j$ and every $b>t^{-1}\log(B/c(t))$.
2. Let $K_j$ be bounded self-adjoint operators on $\mathcal H_j$, and let $\gamma>0$, $c>0$ and $\epsilon_j\to0$ satisfy, for every $v\perp\Omega_j$,
$$
\langle v,(I-K_j)v\rangle\ge\gamma\|v\|^2,\qquad
\langle v,(I-T_j)v\rangle\ge c\,a_j\langle v,(I-K_j)v\rangle-a_j\epsilon_j\|v\|^2 .
\tag{K.10.14c.3}
$$
Then $q_j\le1-a_jb_j$ and $-a_j^{-1}\log q_j\ge b_j$ for every $j$ with $b_j=c\gamma-\epsilon_j>0$ and $a_jb_j\le1$. For the refresh operator $K_j=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha|\Omega_j\rangle\langle\Omega_j|$ with $0<\alpha\le1$, the first inequality holds with $\gamma=\alpha$ for every $T_j$, and the second is the bound $I-T_j\ge a_j(c\alpha-\epsilon_j)$ on $\Omega_j^\perp$.
3. Let $H\ge0$ be a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space, $\Omega$ a unit vector with $H\Omega=0$, and $\mathcal D$ a dense subset of $\Omega^\perp$. If there is $m>0$ such that every $v\in\mathcal D$ has constants $C_v<\infty$ and $t_v\ge0$ with
$$
\langle v,e^{-tH}v\rangle\le C_ve^{-mt}\qquad(t\ge t_v),
\tag{K.10.14c.4}
$$
then $1_{[0,m)}(H)=|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|$. Hence $\ker H=\mathbb C\Omega$ and $\sigma(H)\subset\{0\}\cup[m,\infty)$.

*Proof.* (1) For large $j$, $k_j=\lfloor t/a_j\rfloor\ge1$ and $c_j=\langle v_j,T_j^{k_j}v_j\rangle>0$. The positive operator $T_j$ leaves $\Omega_j^\perp$ invariant, so $0<c_j\le Bq_j^{k_j}$. Thus $q_j>0$ and $-a_j^{-1}\log q_j\le(a_jk_j)^{-1}\log(B/c_j)$. Since $a_jk_j\to t$ and $c_j\to c(t)$, (K.10.14c.2) follows, and its right side is finite, so $q_j\to1$. If $-a_j^{-1}\log q_j\ge m$, then $q_j\le e^{-ma_j}$, while (K.10.14c.2) gives $q_j\ge e^{-ba_j}$ for all large $j$, and $1-e^{-ba_j}\le ba_j$.

(2) The two inequalities give $\langle v,(I-T_j)v\rangle\ge a_jb_j\|v\|^2$ on $\Omega_j^\perp$, which $T_j$ leaves invariant. Since $T_j\ge0$, its spectrum there lies in $[0,1-a_jb_j]$, so $q_j\le1-a_jb_j$ and $-a_j^{-1}\log q_j\ge-a_j^{-1}\log(1-a_jb_j)\ge b_j$. For the refresh operator, $\langle v,(I-K_j)v\rangle=\alpha\|v\|^2$ on $\Omega_j^\perp$.

(3) Fix $0<\eta<m$ and put $P_\eta=1_{[0,m-\eta]}(H)$. For $v\in\mathcal D$ the spectral theorem gives $e^{-(m-\eta)t}\|P_\eta v\|^2\le\langle v,e^{-tH}v\rangle\le C_ve^{-mt}$ for $t\ge t_v$, so $P_\eta v=0$. The projection $P_\eta$ is bounded and $\mathcal D$ is dense in $\Omega^\perp$, so $P_\eta$ vanishes on $\Omega^\perp$, while $P_\eta\Omega=\Omega$. Hence $P_\eta=|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|$ for every $\eta$, and letting $\eta\downarrow0$ gives $1_{[0,m)}(H)=|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|$. ∎

For the transfer operators of Theorem K.10.14b, an energy threshold $m_{a,n}(\beta)\ge m>0$ uniform in $a$ and $n$ is the bound $\langle v,(I-T)v\rangle\ge(1-e^{-ma})\|v\|^2$ on the vacuum complement. Along a family with $a\to0$ and a nonzero limiting fixed-time correlation, item 1 gives $1-q_n(\beta)=O(a)$, so this bound is an order-$a$ coercivity estimate; item 2 gives a comparison inequality that implies such a bound with $m=\inf_jb_j$, and item 3 converts a common exponential decay rate on a dense core into a continuum gap.

<a id="prop-k1014d"></a>

<a id="proposition-k1014d-sharp-multiscale-transfer-bound-by-exact-schur-complements"></a>**Proposition K.10.14d (Sharp Multiscale Transfer Bound by Exact Schur Complements).** Let \(0\le Q\le I\) be a bounded operator on an orthogonal sum \(\mathcal H_c\oplus\mathcal H_f\), and write
$$
Q=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\ C^*&D\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
D\ge d I,\qquad S=A-CD^{-1}C^*\ge s I
$$
for \(0<d,s\le1\). Then \(Q\ge ds I\), and the factor \(ds\) is sharp for each pair \((d,s)\).

If \(Q_0\) is a positive contraction and \(Q_{j+1}\) is the exact Schur complement of \(Q_j\) over its fine block \(D_j\ge d_jI\), then \(0\le Q_{j+1}\le I\). A terminal bound \(Q_J\ge sI\) yields
$$
Q_0\ge s\prod_{j=0}^{J-1}d_j\,I.
\tag{K.10.14d.1}
$$
If \(d_j\ge1-\epsilon_j\), \(0\le\epsilon_j\le\epsilon_*<1\), and \(\sum_{j<J}\epsilon_j\le M\), the product is at least \(\exp[-M/(1-\epsilon_*)]\).

For the positive self-adjoint transfer contraction \(T_a\) at physical step \(a>0\), take a closed invariant sector containing the unit vacuum \(\Omega_a\) with \(T_a\Omega_a=\Omega_a\). Let \(T_a^\circ\) be the restriction to the sector's vacuum complement. With \(k_a=\lceil t_0/a\rceil\) for fixed \(t_0>0\), set \(Q_0=I-(T_a^\circ)^{k_a}\). If the right side of (K.10.14d.1) is bounded below by a common \(\delta I\), \(0<\delta<1\), throughout the cutoff and volume family, then
$$
-\frac{\log\|T_a^\circ\|}{a}\ \ge\
-\frac{\log(1-\delta)}{a k_a},
\qquad
\liminf_{a\to0}\left(-\frac{\log\|T_a^\circ\|}{a}\right)
\ge-\frac{\log(1-\delta)}{t_0}.
\tag{K.10.14d.2}
$$
For \(\delta=1\) the excited transfer vanishes and the threshold is \(+\infty\).

*Proof.* First take \(\|Q\|<1\). The Schur complement of \(I-Q\) gives \(C(I-D)^{-1}C^*\le I-A\). Since \((I-D)^{-1}+D^{-1}=[D(I-D)]^{-1}\), it follows that \(C[D(I-D)]^{-1}C^*\le I-S\). For \(0<\lambda<ds\le d\), the function \(x\mapsto(1-x)/(x-\lambda)\) decreases on \([d,1)\). Functional calculus therefore gives
$$
D^{-1}(D-\lambda I)^{-1}
\le \frac{1-d}{d-\lambda}[D(I-D)]^{-1}.
$$
The Schur complement of \(Q-\lambda I\) is
$$
S-\lambda I-\lambda CD^{-1}(D-\lambda I)^{-1}C^*
\ \ge\ \frac{1-\lambda}{d-\lambda}(dS-\lambda I)\ \ge\ 0 .
$$
As \(D-\lambda I>0\), this proves \(Q\ge\lambda I\); let \(\lambda\uparrow ds\). For a general positive contraction, apply the preceding argument to \((1-\eta)Q\) with \(0<\eta<1\). Its fine and Schur lower bounds are \((1-\eta)d\) and \((1-\eta)s\). Divide by \(1-\eta\) and let \(\eta\downarrow0\). The two-by-two matrix with diagonal \((1-d+ds,d)\) and off-diagonal \(\sqrt{d(1-d)(1-s)}\) has Schur complement \(s\), trace \(1+ds\) and determinant \(ds\), giving the eigenvalues \(1\) and \(ds\), including the cases \(d=1\) or \(s=1\).

For a retained vector \(x\), the Schur quadratic form is \(\inf_y\langle(x,y),Q_j(x,y)\rangle\), attained at \(y=-D_j^{-1}C_j^*x\). Nonnegativity and the trial vector \(y=0\) bound it between \(0\) and \(\|x\|^2\). Iterating the sharp estimate gives (K.10.14d.1). The product bound follows by integrating \(1/(1-x)\) to obtain \(\log(1-\epsilon)\ge-\epsilon/(1-\epsilon_*)\). The sector and its vacuum complement reduce the self-adjoint \(T_a\), so \(\|(T_a^\circ)^{k_a}\|=\|T_a^\circ\|^{k_a}\). The lower bound on \(Q_0\) gives \(\|T_a^\circ\|^{k_a}\le1-\delta\), and \(ak_a\to t_0\) gives (K.10.14d.2). ∎

For the running Wilson family, this route requires bounds on the fine blocks of the successive exact Schur complements and a terminal coercivity bound on the same physical sector. The strong-coupling estimate of Theorem K.10.14b can enter through a quantitative operator comparison with the actual terminal complement. A continuum mass statement further requires the local-sector and limit identifications of Proposition K.10.14c.

<a id="cor-k1014d1"></a>

<a id="corollary-k1014d1-coupling-sensitive-elimination-and-accumulated-fine-spaces"></a>**Corollary K.10.14d.1 (Coupling-Sensitive Elimination and Accumulated Fine Spaces).** In Proposition K.10.14d put \(z=\|CD^{-1}\|\) and let \(\mu_*(d,s,z)\) be the smaller root of
$$
\mu^2-(d+s+z^2d)\mu+ds=0.
$$
Then \(Q\ge \mu_*(d,s,z) I\). The two-by-two matrix with diagonal \((s+z^2d,d)\) and off-diagonal \(zd\) attains the bound when \(Q\le I\) is compatible with \((d,s,z)\), namely \(z^2\le(1-s)(1-d)/d\). In the successive elimination of Proposition K.10.14d, suppose \(s\le d_j/2\) and \(z_j^2=\|C_jD_j^{-1}\|^2\le1/4\) at every stage. Then
$$
Q_0\ge s\exp\!\left(-4\sum_{j<J}z_j^2\right)I .
\tag{K.10.14d.3}
$$
For successive mutually orthogonal fine spaces, let \(F_j\) be the sum of the first \(j+1\) spaces removed. The operator obtained after stage \(j\) is the exact Schur complement over \(F_j\), and \(P_{F_j}Q_0|_{F_j}\ge b_j I\) implies \(D_j\ge b_j I\).

*Proof.* With \(Z=CD^{-1}\), completing the square gives
$$
\langle(x,y),Q(x,y)\rangle
\ge s\|x\|^2+d\|Z^*x+y\|^2
\ge s\alpha^2+d(\gamma-z\alpha)_+^2
$$
where \(\alpha=\|x\|\), \(\gamma=\|y\|\). On \(\gamma\ge z\alpha\) the last expression is the quadratic form of the two-by-two matrix with off-diagonal \(-zd\), whose least eigenvalue is \(\mu_*\). On \(\gamma<z\alpha\), it is at least \(s(\alpha^2+\gamma^2)/(1+z^2)\), and \(s/(1+z^2)\ge\mu_*\) by evaluating that same matrix in the direction \((1,z)\). The stated sharp example has determinant \(ds\). To check compatibility, \(I-Q\ge0\) gives \(C[D(I-D)]^{-1}C^*\le I-S\) when \(\|Q\|<1\), as in Proposition K.10.14d. The scalar inequality \(x^{-2}\le((1-d)/d)[x(1-x)]^{-1}\) on \([d,1)\) gives \(z^2\le(1-d)(1-s)/d\). Scaling \(Q\) toward the interior and taking a limit gives the inequality for all contractions. Conversely this inequality makes \(I-Q\) positive semidefinite for the displayed two-by-two example by its principal minors, including the endpoint cases.

For \(d>s'\), the smaller root satisfies \(\mu_*(d,s',z)\ge s'(1-z^2d/(d-s'))\). Indeed, writing \(b=d+s'+z^2d\), \(x=s'(1-z^2d/(d-s'))\), and \(r=z^2d/(d-s')\), one has \(x<b/2\) and \(x^2-bx+ds'=s'(s'r^2+z^2dr)\ge0\). The root is at most \(s'\), by testing the direction \((1,z)\). Starting with the terminal lower bound \(s\) and iterating this estimate, every intermediate lower bound \(s'\le s\) obeys \(z_j^2d_j/(d_j-s')\le2z_j^2\). The product of the factors \(1-2z_j^2\) is at least \(\exp(-4\sum_jz_j^2)\), by \(\log(1-x)\ge-2x\) on \([0,1/2]\). Finally the quadratic form of the successive Schur complement equals successive infima over the fine spaces. These equal the infimum over their orthogonal sum \(F_j\). For \(x\) in the newly removed space and \(y\) in the previously removed sum, the assumed compression bound gives \(\langle x+y,Q_0(x+y)\rangle\ge b_j\|x\|^2\). Taking the infimum over \(y\) proves the fine-block bound. ∎

Thus a uniform bound can also follow from square-summable fine–coarse coupling norms. Both criteria require coercivity of the same terminal Schur complement.

<a id="theorem-k1014e"></a>

<a id="theorem-k1014e-exact-electric-transfer-and-the-gap-tension-scaling-obstruction"></a>**Theorem K.10.14e (Exact Electric Transfer and the Gap–Tension Scaling Obstruction).** On the spatial cubic tori of Theorem K.10.14b, take gauge group $SU(2)$, physical spatial mesh $a>0$, at least four sites in every periodic direction, and the heat-kernel temporal transfer with no spatial plaquette potential. Use an electric rate $\kappa(a)>0$ in the same physical clock at every spatial link. The physical vacuum gap is exactly $3\kappa(a)$ in inverse-time units. The static fundamental source energy for a separated charge pair is exactly $(3/4)\kappa(a)$ times their hop distance, and every rectangular time–path fundamental Wilson loop along a simple open spatial path has the exact area exponent below. On any spatial refinement with finite nonzero physical string tension, the vacuum gap tends to zero. Conversely a cutoff-uniform positive vacuum gap forces the physical tension to diverge on this entire electric class.

*Finite gauge source and vacuum gap.* Normalize the Hermitian fundamental generators by $\operatorname{Tr}(t_it_j)=\delta_{ij}/2$, so that the positive single-link Casimir has eigenvalue $j(j+1)$ on spin $j$. In units where energy is divided by $\hbar$, let
$$
H_a=\kappa(a)\sum_e\mathcal C_e,
\qquad T_{a,b}=e^{-bH_a}
\tag{K.10.14e.1}
$$
on the Gauss-invariant sector, with temporal step $b>0$. Each link convolution kernel is the normalized heat kernel at time $b\kappa(a)$. It is positive, symmetric and normalized against Haar measure. Their product commutes with the site gauge average. Inserting that average between successive spatial slices gives the same temporal-link integration as in Theorem K.10.14b, with one heat kernel per temporal plaquette and no spatial plaquette weight. On the full link space this transfer is the product heat convolution times the Gauss projector. Thus (K.10.14e.1) is its restriction to the physical Hilbert space and already has vacuum eigenvalue one. The constant Haar vector is the unique vacuum, since every nontrivial spin has strictly positive Casimir. This is the electric term of the canonical lattice gauge Hamiltonian (Kogut and Susskind 1975) in the stated normalization.

In the Peter–Weyl decomposition, choose an irrep on each link and invariant tensors at the vertices. A nontrivial neutral assignment cannot have a vertex incident to just one nontrivial link. At that vertex there would be no invariant vector in the single nontrivial irrep. Thus any nonempty support has a cycle, with at least four edges on these tori. Each occupied link contributes at least $3/4$ to the Casimir sum. A single elementary plaquette carrying spin $1/2$ on its four edges with the cyclic trace contraction gives an actual eigenvector of energy $3\kappa(a)$. It is orthogonal to the constant by Haar integration. This proves the gap, uniformly in the number of sites. The exact threshold on the orthogonal complement for $I-T_{a,b}$ is $1-e^{-3b\kappa(a)}$.

*Charged sector and the Wilson observable.* Insert a static fundamental and antifundamental at two distinct vertices $x,y$ by taking invariant tensors with the additional fundamental index at each endpoint. The two representations have the same center sign. On an incident link the action of the center element $-I$ is $(-1)^{2j}$. Invariance therefore requires even parity of incident half-integer edges at every interior vertex and odd parity at $x,y$. In a finite graph each component has an even number of odd vertices, so the half-integer support connects $x$ to $y$. It includes a path of at least $d_G(x,y)$ edges, each costing at least $3\kappa(a)/4$. A shortest path carrying spin $1/2$ saturates that bound with its endpoint indices coupled to the sources. This proves the exact charged threshold. No pair-dependent boundary energy enters this Hamiltonian.

For a simple open path $P$ of $l$ edges use the path holonomy matrix $U_P$, with the endpoint charged indices. In the normalized fundamental trace norm it gives a unit vector on the Haar vacuum, since $U_P$ is unitary pointwise. Every entry uses spin $1/2$ on each path link and the trivial representation elsewhere. Hence it is an eigenvector of the charged Hamiltonian with eigenvalue $(3/4)\kappa(a)l$. The normalized fundamental Wilson loop whose two time-separated spatial sides are $P$ and its reverse is exactly its charged transfer autocorrelation. Indeed integrating temporal links with the inserted fundamental line matrices projects onto the invariant tensors with these endpoint indices, while each spatial path operator supplies the corresponding endpoint vector. With physical Euclidean time $t=mb$, this gives
$$
\langle W(P,t)\rangle=\exp[-(3/4)\kappa(a)lt]
                      =\exp[-\sigma_a(la)t],
\qquad \sigma_a=\frac{3\kappa(a)}{4a} .
\tag{K.10.14e.2}
$$
Here $la$ is the length of the chosen path, and for a shortest axial path it is its physical endpoint separation. The expectation uses the same vacuum and heat transfer as the neutral comparison. For any two fixed positive physical lengths and times the observable can use integral path lengths and time steps approaching them.

The exact identity $m_a=4a\sigma_a$ relates the neutral physical gap $m_a$ to the string tension. In particular if $\sigma_a\to\sigma\in(0,\infty)$ then $m_a\to0$, so exact cutoff coercivity fails for every fixed $m>0$ at small enough $a$. The neutral local plaquette vector provides the violating comparison at each grade, for any positive $b$. If $m_a\ge m>0$ uniformly, (K.10.14e.2) instead tends to zero at every fixed positive physical area, with no finite limiting area coefficient. This obstruction applies to the pure-electric heat-kernel temporal source. Spatial plaquette dynamics and the joint spatial continuum remain separate requirements. $\square$

<a id="theorem-k1014f"></a>

<a id="theorem-k1014f-interacting-wilson-sum-rule-and-a-necessary-continuum-scaling"></a>**Theorem K.10.14f (Interacting Wilson Sum Rule and a Necessary Continuum Scaling).** Use the spatial $SU(2)$ lattice and primitive fundamental Wilson normalization of Theorem K.10.14e.
