Add an arbitrary real bounded gauge-invariant multiplication potential $V$ to the Hamiltonian $H=\kappa(a)\sum_e\mathcal C_e+V$, in inverse-time units. This includes a spatial plaquette interaction of any finite coefficient at each finite lattice. Use the same multiplication potential and the same clock in the vacuum and static fundamental pair sectors. Then every simple open path of $l$ links gives a unit-mass Wilson spectral measure with exact first moment $3\kappa(a)l/4$ and an explicit second-moment bound. Its charged correlator obeys a volume-independent Jensen lower bound, which gives a necessary positive lower limit of $\kappa(a)/a$ on any refinement with a finite strictly positive continuum Wilson string tension. A local neutral plaquette trial also bounds the neutral vacuum gap using the actual interacting vacuum distribution. These statements concern the continuous-time Hamiltonian transfer generated by this sum.

*Common ground energy and charged carrier.* Let $\Omega$ be the normalized ground and $E_0$ its energy on the neutral space. On the unrestricted link Hilbert space the heat semigroup of $\kappa(a)\sum_e\mathcal C_e$ has a strictly positive smooth kernel at positive time. The Feynman–Kac weighting by real bounded $V$ preserves positivity improvement, and the resolvent remains compact. The unrestricted ground is thus unique and can be chosen strictly positive. Gauge transformations preserve the Hamiltonian and its positive ground, so it is Gauss invariant and its energy is $E_0$. Introduce the two static endpoint indices of Theorem K.10.14e. Before the Gauss restriction the extended Hamiltonian acts as the same unrestricted Hamiltonian on every index component. Its restriction to the invariant charged sector is therefore at least $E_0$. Its spectral differences on that sector are nonnegative, with no extra endpoint term.

*Exact first moment and second-moment bound.* For the oriented simple path $P$, use the equivariant matrix $U_P$ with the normalized fundamental trace norm and the paired endpoint indices. Equivalently its vector-valued multiplier $v(U)$ has pointwise norm one. It maps $\Omega$ to the actual charged unit vector $\Xi_P=\Omega v$. With the real invariant derivations $D_{e,i}$ in the convention $\mathcal C_e=-\sum_iD_{e,i}^2$, one has
\[
\sum_{e,i}|D_{e,i}v|^2=3l/4,
\qquad \sum_{e,i}D_{e,i}^2v=-(3l/4)v .
\tag{K.10.14f.1}
\]
These follow link by link by insertion of the fundamental generators with $\sum_i t_i^2=(3/4)I$. The path visits each link at most once, and endpoint orientation only changes the sign or conjugate of an inserted generator. Taking the real part of the electric form on $\Omega v$ gives no cross term, since $\operatorname{Re}\langle v,D_{e,i}v\rangle=0$ and $\Omega$ is real. The multiplication potential commutes through the insertion. The total first energy difference is therefore $\bar E_P=3\kappa(a)l/4$. The same identity follows from the exact product rule
\[
(H-E_0)\Xi_P=\bar E_P\Xi_P-2\kappa(a)\sum_{e\in P,i}(D_{e,i}\Omega)D_{e,i}v .
\tag{K.10.14f.2}
\]
All vector products are in the relevant graph or form domains because the multiplier is smooth on the compact group and the ground lies in the free operator domain. The charged spectral variance about $\bar E_P$ consequently obeys
\[
\operatorname{Var}_P(E)\le 3l\kappa(a)^2\sum_{e\in P,i}\|D_{e,i}\Omega\|^2 .
\tag{K.10.14f.3}
\]
This uses Cauchy–Schwarz pointwise and (K.10.14f.1). The vacuum trial and $\inf V$ bound the total electric energy if only a global bound is supplied. The second moment gives a certified upper tail for this charged Wilson measure at each finite grade, including all link representations. At $V=0$ the variance is zero and the measure is exactly the line of Theorem K.10.14e.

*Confinement scaling test.* By the definition of the charged Wilson insertion its same-path temporal rectangle expectation at time $t\ge0$ is $\langle\Xi_P,e^{-t(H-E_0)}\Xi_P\rangle$. In particular it is positive and at most one. Jensen's inequality and the exact first moment give
\[
1\ \ge\ \langle W(P,t)\rangle\ \ge\ \exp[-(3/4)\kappa(a)lt] .
\tag{K.10.14f.4}
\]
The coefficient in this bound uses the same fundamental normalization and area $lat$ at every cutoff. Suppose Wilson rectangles of fixed physical side lengths and times converge along the given spatial refinement, with shortest axial paths and compatible clock steps. If $\liminf_{a\downarrow0}\kappa(a)/a=0$, a subsequence of (K.10.14f.4) squeezes every such rectangle to one. Thus the assumed limiting Wilson response is identically one on those rectangles and has zero string tension. More generally for finite $b=\liminf_{a\downarrow0}\kappa(a)/a$, the limiting normalized response on each rectangle of area $A$ is at least $\exp(-3bA/4)$. Any continuum string tension extracted from the large-area exponent of those same normalized rectangles is at most $3b/4$. Convergence of the neutral correlations is a separate continuum condition.

*Local neutral gap test.* Take the normalized real fundamental trace $F$ of an elementary plaquette. With the common vacuum mean removed, $\Phi=(F-\langle F\rangle)\Omega$ is orthogonal to the neutral ground and has squared norm $\operatorname{Var}_\Omega(F)>0$ because the vacuum has full support and $F$ is nonconstant. The ground-state form identity yields
\[
\frac{\langle\Phi,(H-E_0)\Phi\rangle}{\|\Phi\|^2}
=\kappa(a)\frac{1-\langle F^2\rangle_\Omega}{\operatorname{Var}_\Omega(F)}
\le \frac{\kappa(a)}{\operatorname{Var}_\Omega(F)}.
\tag{K.10.14f.5}
\]
For the identity, subtract the ground equation tested against $(F-\langle F\rangle)^2\Omega$ from the electric form on $\Phi$. Write the plaquette holonomy as $F I+i\mathbf b\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$, with $|\mathbf b|^2=1-F^2$. Inserting $it_i$ at one link differentiates the normalized trace by a component of $\mathbf b/2$ in a rotated frame, up to the link orientation sign. Thus the sum of squares on each of its four links is $(1-F^2)/4$. A refinement with $\kappa(a)\to0$ and plaquette variances bounded below cannot satisfy a uniform positive neutral gap. The same quotient tests the transfer coercivity: for $T=e^{-b(H-E_0)}$ the Rayleigh quotient of $I-T$ on $\Phi$ is at most $1-e^{-b\langle H-E_0\rangle_\Phi}$ by Jensen, with normalized expectation in that vector. A candidate with small electric rates must therefore show concentration of its actual plaquette distribution if it is to pass the fixed-mass test. The Wilson first moment and neutral trial are evaluated on the same interacting vacuum. Joint convergence, the lower gap inequality and the continuum Wilson law retain their tests. $\square$

<a id="prop-k1014g"></a>

<a id="proposition-k1014g-twist-sectors-and-the-local-vacuum-sector-of-the-wilson-transfer"></a>**Proposition K.10.14g (Twist Sectors and the Local Vacuum Sector of the Wilson Transfer).** In the setting of Theorem K.10.14b let $Z(G)$ be the center of $G$ and $\mathcal H^{\mathcal G}_n\subset L^2(X_n,\mu)$ the subspace of gauge-invariant functions. For a spatial direction $i$, an element $c\in Z(G)$ and $s\in\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$, let $\tau^{(s)}_{i,c}$ multiply by $c$ every link $(x,i)$ with $x_i=s$ and fix the other links, and put $(S_{i,c}f)(U)=f(\tau^{(s)}_{i,c}U)$ for $f\in\mathcal H^{\mathcal G}_n$. Call a bounded Borel gauge-invariant function $F$ on $X_n$ non-wrapping if for each direction $i$ there is $s_i$ such that $F$ does not depend on the links $(x,i)$ with $x_i=s_i$. With the multiplication operators $F_i$ acting on $\mathcal H^{\mathcal G}_n$, the local vacuum sector is
$$
\mathcal L_n=\overline{\operatorname{span}}\bigl\{T^{k_0}F_1T^{k_1}F_2\cdots T^{k_{r-1}}F_r\Omega:\ r\ge0,\ k_i\ge0,\ F_i\ \text{non-wrapping}\bigr\}.
\tag{K.10.14g.1}
$$

1. $S_{i,c}$ is independent of $s$. The operators $S_{i,c}$ form a unitary representation of $Z(G)^3$ on $\mathcal H^{\mathcal G}_n$ that commutes with $T$, and $S_{i,c}\Omega=\Omega$. Its fixed subspace $\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$ is closed, contains $\Omega$ and reduces $T$.
2. Every non-wrapping function is invariant under every $\tau^{(s)}_{i,c}$. Hence $\mathcal L_n$ is a closed subspace that reduces $T$, and $\Omega\in\mathcal L_n\subset\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$. The vectors entering (K.10.14b.2) for non-wrapping slice observables lie in $\mathcal L_n$.
3. For $G=SU(2)\subset U(2)$, let $P_x$ be the $54$ links $(x+a,j)$ with $a\in\{0,1,2\}^3$ and $a_j\le1$. The closed span of the vectors $F\Omega$, with $F$ a finite product of bounded gauge-invariant functions of the links of single sets $P_x$, is $\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$. Hence $\mathcal L_n=\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$. For $G=\{\pm1\}\subset U(1)$ also $\mathcal L_n=\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$.
4. Let $G=\{\pm1\}\subset U(1)$ and $\beta>0$. For each of the seven nontrivial characters of $Z(G)^3$, the largest eigenvalue of $T$ on the corresponding isotypic subspace of $\mathcal H^{\mathcal G}_n$ is at least $\tanh(\beta)^{3n^3}$. In particular $q_n(\beta)\ge\tanh(\beta)^{3n^3}$ and $m_{a,n}(\beta)\le-(3n^3/a)\log\tanh\beta$. Define $\beta^*>0$ by $e^{-2\beta^*}=\tanh\beta$. The spectrum of $T$ on $\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$ at coupling $\beta$, with multiplicities, equals its spectrum at $\beta^*$, and for every $n\ge3$
$$
q_n^{\mathrm{tw}}(\beta):=\bigl\|T|_{\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}\ominus\mathbb C\Omega}\bigr\|\le18e^{-2\beta}\qquad\text{whenever }18e^{-2\beta}<1 .
\tag{K.10.14g.2}
$$

*Proof.* (1) A spatial plaquette whose plane contains direction $i$ contains two $i$-links with the same coordinate $x_i$, traversed in opposite directions, so the central factors cancel; the other plaquettes are unchanged. Hence $V\circ\tau^{(s)}_{i,c}=V$, $D(\tau^{(s)}_{i,c}U,\tau^{(s)}_{i,c}W)=D(U,W)$, $\tau^{(s)}_{i,c}$ commutes with the gauge action because $c$ is central, and it preserves $\mu$. Composition with $\tau^{(s)}_{i,c}$ is therefore unitary on $L^2(X_n,\mu)$ and commutes with $\mathsf K_0$, $Q$ and $\mathsf K$. Let $\gamma(x)=c$ for $x_i\in\{s'+1,\dots,s\}$, cyclically, and $\gamma(x)=1$ otherwise. Then $\gamma\cdot U$ multiplies the $i$-links with $x_i=s$ by $c$ and those with $x_i=s'$ by $c^{-1}$ and fixes all other links, so $\tau^{(s)}_{i,c}=\gamma\cdot\tau^{(s')}_{i,c}$ and $S_{i,c}$ is independent of $s$ on $\mathcal H^{\mathcal G}_n$. The relations $S_{i,c}S_{i,c'}=S_{i,cc'}$ and commutativity in $i$ are immediate. $S_{i,c}\Omega$ is a strictly positive unit eigenvector of $T$ for the eigenvalue $1$, so it equals $\Omega$ by item 1 of Theorem K.10.14b. A closed subspace fixed by a family of unitaries commuting with the self-adjoint $T$ reduces $T$.

(2) If $F$ does not depend on the $i$-links with $x_i=s_i$, then $F\circ\tau^{(s_i)}_{i,c}=F$, and gauge invariance with item 1 gives $F\circ\tau^{(s)}_{i,c}=F$ for every $s$. Multiplication by $F$ and the operator $T$ map $\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$ into itself, and $\Omega\in\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$, so every generating vector of (K.10.14g.1) lies in $\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$. The generating set is $T$-invariant, so $\mathcal L_n$ is $T$-invariant and, $T$ being self-adjoint, reduces $T$. The vacuum matrix elements in (K.10.14b.2) are inner products of such vectors.

(3) For $n\ge3$ the set $P_x$ consists of $54$ distinct links on the $27$ distinct sites $x+\{0,1,2\}^3$ and contains no $j$-link based at $x_j+2$, so its functions are non-wrapping. At a site $v$ let $A_v,B_v$ be the holonomies of the elementary plaquettes based at $v$ in the planes $(1,2)$ and $(1,3)$. Both lie in $P_v$, and for $y=x+e_i$ both $A_y$ and $B_y$ lie in $P_x$. Conditionally on all links except $(v+e_1,2)$ and $(v+e_1,3)$, each of which occurs in exactly one of the two loops, $A_v$ and $B_v$ are independent Haar elements of $SU(2)$. Two independent Haar elements commute with probability zero, since the centralizer of a noncentral element is a maximal torus of Haar measure zero, and an elementary plaquette trace vanishes with probability zero. The set $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ on which $A_v,B_v$ fail to commute for every $v$ and every elementary plaquette trace is nonzero is therefore open, invariant under gauge transformations and twists, and of full measure. Two noncommuting elements of $SU(2)$ have common centralizer $\{\pm I\}$.

Let $U\in X_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and let $U'$ have the same gauge orbit as $U$ on every $P_x$, say $U'_e=g^x(v)U_eg^x(w)^{-1}$ for every link $e$ of $P_x$ from $v$ to $w$. Put $g(v)=g^v(v)$. For the link $e$ from $x$ to $y=x+e_i$, the element $g^y(y)^{-1}g^x(y)$ conjugates both $A_y$ and $B_y$ trivially, hence is $\pm I$. Therefore $V=g^{-1}\cdot U'$ satisfies $V_e=z_eU_e$ with $z_e=\pm I$ for every link. For an elementary plaquette $p$, $\operatorname{Tr}V_p=z_p\operatorname{Tr}U_p$ with $z_p$ the product of its four signs, while $\operatorname{Tr}V_p=\operatorname{Tr}U'_p=\operatorname{Tr}U_p\ne0$, so $z_p=1$. The signs form a flat $\mathbb Z_2$ connection on $(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^3$, which is a site gauge transformation composed with twists, since the first cohomology of the three-torus with $\mathbb Z_2$ coefficients is generated by the three seam classes. Thus $U'$ is a gauge transformation of a twist of $U$. Let $Y$ be the quotient of $X_n$ by gauge transformations and twists, $Y_x$ the gauge-orbit space of the links of $P_x$, and $\Phi:Y\to\prod_xY_x$ the continuous restriction map, which is well defined because a twist restricts to a gauge transformation on $P_x$. $\Phi$ is injective on the image of $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and no point outside that image has the same value as a point inside it. By the Lusin–Souslin theorem the inverse of $\Phi$ on this Borel image is Borel. Every bounded gauge- and twist-invariant Borel function therefore agrees almost everywhere with a Borel function of the patch orbits, and finite sums of products of bounded Borel functions of single patch orbits are dense in $L^2$ of the image measure by the monotone class theorem. With $\pi=\Omega^2\mu$, this density holds in the twist-invariant subspace of $L^2(\pi)$; multiplication by $\Omega$ maps it unitarily onto $\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$. Hence the stated vectors span a dense subspace of $\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$, and item 2 gives $\mathcal L_n=\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$. For $G=\{\pm1\}$ two configurations with the same plaquette variables differ by a flat connection, which is a gauge transformation composed with twists, so a gauge- and twist-invariant function is a polynomial in the plaquette variables. Each plaquette variable is non-wrapping, so the vectors $F\Omega$ already exhaust $\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$.

(4) Write $E=3n^3$ and $t=e^{-2\beta}$. Convolution by the link factor $e^{-\beta(1-g)}$ on $L^2(\{\pm1\})$ has eigenvalues $c_0=(1+t)/2$ on constants and $c_1=(1-t)/2$ on the character, so the operator $\mathsf C$ with kernel $e^{-\beta D(U,W)}$ satisfies $c_1^E\le\mathsf C\le c_0^E$, and $\lambda_0\le\|e^{-\beta V/2}\|^2\|\mathsf C\|\le c_0^E$. For $h\in\mathbb Z_2^3$ let $O_h$ be the set of configurations with all plaquette variables equal to $1$ and cycle holonomies $h$. Each $O_h$ is one gauge orbit, $V=0$ on $O_h$, and $\tau^{(s)}_{i,-1}O_h=O_{h+e_i}$. For a character $w$ of $\mathbb Z_2^3$ put $\phi_w=\sum_hw(h)\mathbf 1_{O_h}\in\mathcal H^{\mathcal G}_n$. Then $e^{-\beta V/2}\phi_w=\phi_w$ and $S_{i,-1}\phi_w=w(e_i)\phi_w$, and the isotypic subspace of $w$ reduces $T$, so its largest eigenvalue is at least
$$
\frac{\langle\phi_w,\mathsf K\phi_w\rangle}{\lambda_0\|\phi_w\|^2}
=\frac{\langle\phi_w,\mathsf C\phi_w\rangle}{\lambda_0\|\phi_w\|^2}
\ge\Bigl(\frac{c_1}{c_0}\Bigr)^E=\tanh(\beta)^E .
$$
For nontrivial $w$ that subspace is orthogonal to $\Omega$, which gives the bound on $q_n(\beta)$, and (K.10.14b.3) gives the bound on $m_{a,n}(\beta)$.

For a set $S$ of spatial links put $\chi_S(U)=\prod_{e\in S}U_e$. These characters form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(X_n,\mu)$. $\chi_S$ is gauge invariant exactly when $S$ is a cycle modulo $2$, and in addition twist invariant exactly when its intersection with every seam is even, that is, when $S=\partial P$ is the boundary of a set $P$ of spatial plaquettes. One has $\mathsf C\chi_S=c_0^E\tanh(\beta)^{|S|}\chi_S$. With $\theta=\tanh(\beta/2)$, $e^{-\beta(1-z_p)/2}=(1+\theta z_p)/(1+\theta)$, and multiplication by $z_p=\chi_{\partial p}$ maps $\chi_{\partial P}$ to $\chi_{\partial(P+p)}$. On the dual lattice, again $(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^3$, the plaquettes are links, the links are plaquettes and the cubes are sites; a set $P$ is a dual configuration with value $-1$ on $P$. Adding the boundary of a cube is a dual gauge transformation and adding a coordinate two-torus is a dual twist, and $\partial P=\partial P'$ exactly when $P+P'$ is a $2$-cycle, which is generated by these two kinds of sets. Hence $\chi_{\partial P}\mapsto$ (normalized indicator of the class of $P$) is a unitary map $\Phi$ from $\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$ onto the dual gauge- and twist-invariant functions $\mathcal H_*^{\mathrm{tw}}$. A link lies in $\partial P$ exactly when an odd number of the four plaquettes containing it lie in $P$, so $|\partial P|$ is the number of frustrated dual plaquettes and $\tanh(\beta)^{|\partial P|}=e^{-\beta^*V_*}$, with $V_*$ the dual plaquette cost. Thus $\Phi\mathsf C\Phi^{-1}=c_0^E\mathsf A_*^2$ with $\mathsf A_*=e^{-\beta^*V_*/2}$, and $\Phi e^{-\beta V/2}\Phi^{-1}=(1+\theta)^{-E}\mathsf D$ with $\mathsf D=\prod_p(1+\theta X_p)$, $X_p$ the flip of the dual link $p$. Since $2\theta/(1+\theta^2)=\tanh\beta=e^{-2\beta^*}$, $\mathsf D^2=(1+\theta^2)^E\prod_p(1+e^{-2\beta^*}X_p)$ is a positive multiple of the dual link operator $\mathsf C_*$ at coupling $\beta^*$. Therefore $\Phi\mathsf K\Phi^{-1}$ restricted to $\mathcal H_*^{\mathrm{tw}}$ is a positive multiple of $\mathsf D\mathsf A_*^2\mathsf D=YY^*$ with $Y=\mathsf D\mathsf A_*$, while the dual transfer at $\beta^*$ restricted to $\mathcal H_*^{\mathrm{tw}}$ is a positive multiple of $\mathsf A_*\mathsf D^2\mathsf A_*=Y^*Y$. These finite-dimensional operators have the same spectrum with multiplicities. The Perron eigenvector of each transfer is twist invariant by item 1, so after normalization by the largest eigenvalue the spectra on $\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$ at $\beta$ and at $\beta^*$ coincide. Since $\tanh\beta^*=(1-\tanh\beta)/(1+\tanh\beta)=e^{-2\beta}$, item 5 of Theorem K.10.14b at $\beta^*$ gives $q_n^{\mathrm{tw}}(\beta)=q_n^{\mathrm{tw}}(\beta^*)\le q_n(\beta^*)\le18e^{-2\beta}$ when $18e^{-2\beta}<1$. ∎

For $G=\{\pm1\}$ at fixed $n$, item 4 gives $q_n(\beta)\to1$ as $\beta\to\infty$ on the full gauge-invariant space, while on $\mathcal L_n=\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$ the bound $18e^{-2\beta}$ holds uniformly in $n$. At fixed physical side $L=na$ and $\beta\ge b\log(1/a)$ with $b>2$, item 4 and $-\log\tanh\beta\le2e^{-2\beta}/(1-e^{-2\beta})$ give $m_{a,n}(\beta)\le6L^3a^{2b-4}/(1-a^{2b})\to0$ on the full gauge-invariant space. A cutoff- and volume-uniform gap is therefore a statement about the local sectors $\mathcal L_n$.

**Long-distance condition.** Let $(a_j,n_j,\beta_j)$ be a scaling family of the source of Theorem K.10.14b with $a_j\downarrow0$, transfers $T_j$, vacua $\Omega_j$ and local sectors $\mathcal L_j$. Let $\mathcal D$ be a complex vector space and $v_j:\mathcal D\to\mathcal L_j\ominus\mathbb C\Omega_j$ linear maps, for instance centered renormalized local insertions. The family satisfies the long-distance condition with rate $m>0$ on $\mathcal D$ if every $d\in\mathcal D$ has $C_d<\infty$ and $t_d\ge0$ with
$$
\limsup_{j\to\infty}\bigl\langle v_j(d),T_j^{\lfloor t/a_j\rfloor}v_j(d)\bigr\rangle\le C_de^{-mt}\qquad(t\ge t_d).
\tag{K.10.14g.3}
$$
If $\|T_j|_{\mathcal L_j\ominus\mathbb C\Omega_j}\|\le e^{-ma_j}$ for all large $j$, then (K.10.14g.3) holds for every $t_d>0$ with $C_d=e^{mt_d}\limsup_j\langle v_j(d),T_j^{\lfloor t_d/a_j\rfloor}v_j(d)\rangle$, whenever this is finite: the spectral measure of $v_j(d)$ is supported in $[0,e^{-ma_j}]$, so $\langle v,T^{k+l}v\rangle\le e^{-ma_jk}\langle v,T^lv\rangle$ for $k,l\ge0$. The prefactor is a correlation at the positive separation $t_d$, so the condition uses no norm of an unsmeared renormalized insertion. If the matrix elements in (K.10.14g.3) converge for each fixed $t$ to $\langle v(d),e^{-tH}v(d)\rangle$ for a self-adjoint $H\ge0$ with unit vacuum $\Omega$ and a linear map $v$ from $\mathcal D$ onto a dense subspace of $\Omega^\perp$, then $\langle v(d),e^{-tH}v(d)\rangle\le C_de^{-mt}$ for $t\ge t_d$, and Proposition K.10.14c(3) gives $\ker H=\mathbb C\Omega$ and $\sigma(H)\subset\{0\}\cup[m,\infty)$.

<a id="prop-k1014h"></a>

<a id="proposition-k1014h-finite-character-approximation-of-the-physical-transfer"></a>**Proposition K.10.14h (Finite Character Approximation of the Physical Transfer).** In the setting of Theorem K.10.14b let $\beta>0$, $E=3n^3$, $\chi=\operatorname{Tr}$, $f_\beta(g)=e^{-\beta(1-d^{-1}\operatorname{Re}\chi(g))}$ and, for an integer $M\ge0$,
$$
f_{\beta,M}(g)=e^{-\beta}\sum_{j=0}^{M}\frac{(\beta/2d)^j}{j!}\bigl(\chi(g)+\overline{\chi(g)}\bigr)^j .
$$
Let $\mathsf C_M$ be the integral operator on $L^2(X_n,\mu)$ with kernel $\prod_{e\in E_n}f_{\beta,M}(U_eW_e^{-1})$, $K_M$ the restriction of $e^{-\beta V/2}\mathsf C_Me^{-\beta V/2}Q$ to $\mathcal H^{\mathcal G}_n$, and $T_M=K_M/\lambda_0$. Let $0<\epsilon<1$ and $R=M+1\ge\max\{e^2\beta,\ \beta+\log(2E/\epsilon)\}$. Then:

1. $\mathsf C_M$ has finite rank and $0\le K_M\le\mathsf K|_{\mathcal H^{\mathcal G}_n}$.
2. $|f_\beta-f_{\beta,M}|\le\frac{\epsilon}{2E}f_\beta$ pointwise and $\|\mathsf K|_{\mathcal H^{\mathcal G}_n}-K_M\|\le\epsilon\lambda_0$; hence $0\le T_M\le T$ and $\|T-T_M\|\le\epsilon$.
3. Let $\lambda_{0,M}\ge\lambda_{1,M}$ be the two largest eigenvalues of $K_M$ and $q_M=\lambda_{1,M}/\lambda_{0,M}$. Then $(1-\epsilon)\lambda_0\le\lambda_{0,M}\le\lambda_0$ and $(1-\epsilon)q_M\le q_n(\beta)\le\min\{1,q_M+\epsilon\}$.
4. Write $f_{\beta,M}=\sum_\rho c_\rho\chi_\rho$ over finitely many irreducible characters, with $c_\rho\ge0$. Let $(s_\alpha)$ be an orthonormal basis of the gauge-invariant functions in the range of $\mathsf C_M$ consisting of spin networks, with link representations $\rho_e(\alpha)$ and weights $w_\alpha=\prod_ec_{\rho_e(\alpha)}/\dim\rho_e(\alpha)$. The nonzero spectrum of $K_M$ is the spectrum of the finite positive matrix
$$
F_M=W^{1/2}\mathsf GW^{1/2},\qquad \mathsf G_{\alpha\delta}=\int_{X_n}e^{-\beta V}\,\overline{s_\alpha}\,s_\delta\,d\mu,\qquad W=\operatorname{diag}(w_\alpha).
\tag{K.10.14h.1}
$$
5. Spin networks are eigenvectors of the twists $S_{i,c}$, and $\mathsf G$ and $F_M$ are block diagonal in the twist characters. With $q_M^{\mathrm{tw}}$ the ratio of the two largest eigenvalues of the twist-trivial block $F_M^{\mathrm{tw}}$,
$$
(1-\epsilon)q_M^{\mathrm{tw}}\le q_n^{\mathrm{tw}}(\beta)\le\min\{1,q_M^{\mathrm{tw}}+\epsilon\},\qquad
\bigl\|T|_{\mathcal L_n\ominus\mathbb C\Omega}\bigr\|\le q_n^{\mathrm{tw}}(\beta).
\tag{K.10.14h.2}
$$

*Proof.* (1) Each $(\chi+\bar\chi)^j$ is the character of $(\mathbb C^d\oplus\overline{\mathbb C^d})^{\otimes j}$. Hence $f_{\beta,M}$ and $f_\beta-f_{\beta,M}$ are uniformly convergent sums of irreducible characters with nonnegative coefficients, and convolution by either is a positive operator on $L^2(G)$; only finitely many irreducible representations occur in $f_{\beta,M}$, so its convolution has finite rank. For commuting positive single-link operators $0\le C_{1,M}\le C_1$, $C_1^{\otimes E}-C_{1,M}^{\otimes E}=\sum_iC_{1,M}^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes(C_1-C_{1,M})\otimes C_1^{\otimes(E-i)}\ge0$. Multiplication by $e^{-\beta V/2}$ on both sides and composition with $Q$, which commutes with all these operators, preserve the order, and $\mathsf K=e^{-\beta V/2}\mathsf Ce^{-\beta V/2}Q$ by item 1 of Theorem K.10.14b, where $\mathsf C$ has kernel $e^{-\beta D(U,W)}=\prod_ef_\beta(U_eW_e^{-1})$.

(2) Since $|\chi+\bar\chi|\le2d$ and $f_\beta\ge e^{-2\beta}$,
$$
\frac{|f_\beta-f_{\beta,M}|}{f_\beta}\le e^{\beta}\sum_{j\ge R}\frac{\beta^j}{j!}
\le e^{\beta}\frac{\beta^R}{R!}\,\frac1{1-\beta/(R+1)}
\le e^{\beta}\Bigl(\frac{e\beta}R\Bigr)^R\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi R}\,(1-e^{-2})}\le e^{\beta-R}\le\frac{\epsilon}{2E},
$$
using $R!\ge\sqrt{2\pi R}(R/e)^R$, $R\ge e^2\beta$, $R\ge1$, $\sqrt{2\pi}(1-e^{-2})>1$ and $R\ge\beta+\log(2E/\epsilon)$. The product over the $E$ links then differs from $\prod_ef_\beta$ by at most $((1+\epsilon/2E)^E-1)\prod_ef_\beta\le(e^{\epsilon/2}-1)\prod_ef_\beta\le\epsilon\prod_ef_\beta$. Gauge averaging and multiplication by $e^{-\beta[V(U)+V(W)]/2}$ preserve this pointwise bound, so the kernel of $\mathsf K-e^{-\beta V/2}\mathsf C_Me^{-\beta V/2}Q$ is dominated in absolute value by $\epsilon k_\beta^{\mathcal G}$. An integral operator dominated by a positive kernel has at most its norm, which gives $\|\mathsf K|_{\mathcal H^{\mathcal G}_n}-K_M\|\le\epsilon\lambda_0$.

(3) On $\mathcal H^{\mathcal G}_n$ one has $K_M\le\mathsf K\le K_M+\epsilon\lambda_0$, so the min–max principle gives $\lambda_{j,M}\le\lambda_j\le\lambda_{j,M}+\epsilon\lambda_0$ for the two largest eigenvalues, with $\lambda_1=q_n(\beta)\lambda_0$. Hence $(1-\epsilon)\lambda_0\le\lambda_{0,M}\le\lambda_0$, $q_n(\beta)\le(\lambda_{1,M}+\epsilon\lambda_0)/\lambda_0\le q_M+\epsilon$ and $q_n(\beta)\ge\lambda_{1,M}/\lambda_0\ge(1-\epsilon)q_M$.

(4) By Schur orthogonality, convolution by $\chi_\rho$ is $(\dim\rho)^{-1}$ times the projection onto the $\rho$-isotypic functions. A spin network with link representations $\rho_e$ is therefore an eigenvector of $\mathsf C_M$ with eigenvalue $w_\alpha$, and $Q\mathsf C_MQ=\sum_\alpha w_\alpha|s_\alpha\rangle\langle s_\alpha|$. Since $e^{-\beta V/2}$ commutes with $Q$, $K_M=XX^*$ with $X=e^{-\beta V/2}\mathsf SW^{1/2}$ and $\mathsf Se_\alpha=s_\alpha$. The nonzero spectra of $XX^*$ and $X^*X=F_M$ coincide, and $F_M$ is nonsingular: $\mathsf G$ is the Gram matrix of the linearly independent functions $s_\alpha$ in $L^2(e^{-\beta V}d\mu)$, and every $w_\alpha$ is positive.

(5) A twist multiplies each seam link by a central element, which acts on the matrix coefficients of $\rho_e$ by its central character, so each spin network is an eigenvector of every $S_{i,c}$. As $e^{-\beta V}$ is twist invariant and the $S_{i,c}$ are unitary, $\mathsf G_{\alpha\delta}=0$ when $s_\alpha$ and $s_\delta$ carry different twist characters. The link kernels are invariant under simultaneous central multiplication of both arguments, so $K_M$ commutes with the twists and the nonzero spectrum of $K_M|_{\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}}$ is the spectrum of $F_M^{\mathrm{tw}}$. The inequalities of item 3 restrict to the reducing subspace $\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$, which contains $\Omega$, and min–max there gives the bracket in (K.10.14h.2). The last inequality holds because $\mathcal L_n\subset\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{tw}}$ reduces $T$ by Proposition K.10.14g. ∎

At $\beta=0$ the truncation is exact for every $M$. The degree $M=O(\beta+\log(n^3/\epsilon))$ grows logarithmically in $1/a$ along $\beta=O(\log(1/a))$, $n=L/a$ and $\epsilon=a^\kappa$. A bound $q_M^{\mathrm{tw}}+\epsilon\le e^{-ma}$ on the twist-trivial block implies the local-sector bound that gives (K.10.14g.3). The retained matrix $F_M^{\mathrm{tw}}$ is a weighted Gram matrix of spin networks in $L^2$ of the three-dimensional Wilson measure $e^{-\beta V}d\mu$ at the same coupling.

<a id="prop-k1014i"></a>

<a id="proposition-k1014i-volume-uniform-plaquette-cost-moments-of-the-su2-wilson-law"></a>**Proposition K.10.14i (Volume-Uniform Plaquette-Cost Moments of the $SU(2)$ Wilson Law).** Let $G=SU(2)$, $\beta>0$, and let $\nu$ be the Wilson measure of the plaquette cost $C_p$ of Corollary G.6b.1(d) on a periodic four-dimensional lattice with all sides at least three, or its limit on $\Lambda_n\times\mathbb Z$ as the number of time slices tends to infinity, which exists on observables of finitely many time slabs by the trace argument in the proof of (K.10.14b.2). For every set $S$ of distinct plaquettes and $0\le t<\tfrac12$,
$$
\mathbb E_\nu\exp\Bigl(t\beta\sum_{p\in S}C_p\Bigr)\le(1-2t)^{-3|S|/4}.
\tag{K.10.14i.1}
$$
Consequently $\mathbb E_\nu C_p\le3/(2\beta)$ for every plaquette, and for every $\varepsilon>0$
$$
\nu\bigl(C_p\ge\varepsilon\ \text{for all }p\in S\bigr)\le q_\beta(\varepsilon)^{|S|},\qquad q_\beta(\varepsilon)=2^{3/4}e^{-\beta\varepsilon/4}.
\tag{K.10.14i.2}
$$
Call two plaquettes adjacent when they share a link. The connected component of $\{p:C_p\ge\varepsilon\}$ containing a fixed plaquette has at least $k$ elements with probability at most $q_\beta(\varepsilon)[80\,q_\beta(\varepsilon)]^{k-1}$.

*Proof.* *One link.* Put $c_\gamma(g)=e^{\gamma\operatorname{Tr}g/2}/Z_\gamma$ with $Z_\gamma=2I_1(\gamma)/\gamma$ the Haar integral of the numerator. By the recurrence $I_{k-1}-I_{k+1}=(2k/\gamma)I_k$, convolution by $c_\gamma$ acts on the spin-$j$ matrix coefficients by $r_j(\gamma)=I_{2j+1}(\gamma)/I_1(\gamma)$. For $k\ge2$, $y_k=\gamma I_k'/I_k$ obeys $\gamma y_k'=\gamma^2+k^2-y_k^2$, $y_k-y_1\to k-1>0$ as $\gamma\to0$, and at a zero of $y_k-y_1$ its derivative is $(k^2-1)/\gamma>0$. Hence $(\log(I_k/I_1))'=(y_k-y_1)/\gamma>0$, and convolution by $c_\gamma$ is nondecreasing in $\gamma$ in operator order. With $r=I_2/I_1$ one has $(\log Z_\gamma)'=r$ and $r'=1-r^2-3r/\gamma$; at a contact point of $r$ with $1-3/(2\gamma)$ the derivative of the difference is $3/(4\gamma^2)>0$, so $1-r(\gamma)\le3/(2\gamma)$ for $\gamma\ge3/2$, and trivially for $\gamma<3/2$.

*Boost.* For $0\le t<1$ and $q_0=\operatorname{Tr}(uw^{-1})/2$, $c_\beta(uw^{-1})e^{t\beta(1-q_0)}=b_\beta(t)\,c_{(1-t)\beta}(uw^{-1})$ with $b_\beta(t)=e^{t\beta}Z_{(1-t)\beta}/Z_\beta$, and
$$
\log b_\beta(t)=\int_{(1-t)\beta}^{\beta}\bigl(1-r(\gamma)\bigr)\,d\gamma\le-\tfrac32\log(1-t).
$$

*Temporal plaquettes.* In the transfer of Theorem K.10.14b the temporal plaquettes between two slices correspond to the spatial links, and their weights are the link factors of $\mathsf C$. The link factor of (K.10.14b.1) is $f_\beta=e^{-\beta}Z_\beta c_\beta$, and $e^{-\beta C}e^{t\beta C}=e^{-(1-t)\beta C}$ for a plaquette cost $C$. Multiplying the Wilson weight by $\exp[\beta t_{s,e}C_{(s,e)}]$, $0\le t_{s,e}<1$, for temporal plaquettes $(s,e)$ therefore replaces, in slab $s$, the normalized kernel $c_\beta$ at each boosted link $e$ by $b_\beta(t_{s,e})c_{(1-t_{s,e})\beta}$; let $L_s$ be the resulting operator, normalized by the same $\lambda_0$ as $T$. By the two previous steps $0\le L_s\le c_sT$ with $c_s=\prod_e(1-t_{s,e})^{-3/2}$, and $L_s$ commutes with the gauge action. On a lattice with $M$ slices the boosted expectation is $\operatorname{Tr}(L_0\cdots L_{M-1})/\operatorname{Tr}T^M\ge0$. Eigenvalue domination gives $\|L_s\|_{\mathcal S_M}\le c_s\|T\|_{\mathcal S_M}$ in the Schatten class $\mathcal S_M$, and Hölder's inequality gives $|\operatorname{Tr}(L_0\cdots L_{M-1})|\le\prod_sc_s\operatorname{Tr}T^M$. In the infinite-time limit the boosted expectation of finitely many slabs is $\langle\Omega,L_1\cdots L_r\Omega\rangle\le\prod_sc_s$. In particular $\mathbb E\exp(u\beta\sum_{p\in R}C_p)\le(1-u)^{-3|R|/2}$ for every set $R$ of temporal plaquettes and $0\le u<1$.

*All orientations.* Let $S_\mu$ be the plaquettes of $S$ whose plane contains the axis $\mu$, and $X_\mu=\sum_{p\in S_\mu}C_p$. Each plaquette lies in exactly two of the four sets, so $\sum_\mu X_\mu=2\sum_{p\in S}C_p$, and Hölder's inequality gives $\mathbb E e^{t\beta\sum_SC_p}\le\prod_\mu(\mathbb Ee^{2t\beta X_\mu})^{1/4}$. Items 1 and 2 of Theorem K.10.14b hold with the same proofs on rectangular spatial tori. Taking axis $\mu$ as transfer time on the same periodic lattice, every plaquette of $S_\mu$ is temporal, and the previous step with $u=2t$ gives (K.10.14i.1). For the infinite-time limit, an observable of finitely many slabs has periodic expectation $\operatorname{Tr}(T^{M-r}\mathcal O)/\operatorname{Tr}T^M$ with a bounded slab operator $\mathcal O$, which tends to $\langle\Omega,\mathcal O\Omega\rangle$ as in the proof of (K.10.14b.2); (K.10.14i.1) passes to this limit.

*Consequences.* Jensen's inequality gives $t\beta\,\mathbb EC_p\le-\tfrac34\log(1-2t)$; divide by $t\beta$ and let $t\downarrow0$. Markov's inequality with $t=\tfrac14$ gives (K.10.14i.2). A plaquette shares a link with at most $4\cdot5=20$ others, and the connected sets of $k$ plaquettes containing a fixed one number at most $(4\cdot20)^{k-1}$, by encoding a spanning tree as a plane rooted tree with at most $4^{k-1}$ shapes and at most $20^{k-1}$ neighbour labels; a union bound with (K.10.14i.2) gives the cluster estimate. ∎

Proposition K.10.14i holds at every coupling and uniformly in the volume and the time period. At large $\beta$ the Wilson law of the plaquette cost of Corollary G.6b.1(d) gives plaquette costs of at most order $1/\beta$, the regime of that corollary's smooth-field expansion, with exponentially rare connected clusters of large cost. Along $\beta=b\log(1/a)$ at fixed $\varepsilon$ and fixed $k>16/(b\varepsilon)$, the probability that a cluster of at least $k$ plaquettes of large cost meets a fixed physical region tends to zero, since such a region contains $O(a^{-4})$ plaquettes.

<a id="prop-k1014j"></a>

<a id="proposition-k1014j-short-distance-and-bounded-window-two-point-data-leave-the-gap-undetermined"></a>**Proposition K.10.14j (Short-Distance and Bounded-Window Two-Point Data Leave the Gap Undetermined).** For $s\ge0$ let $D_s(r)=\sqrt s\,K_1(\sqrt sr)/(4\pi^2r)$, with $D_0(r)=1/(4\pi^2r^2)$, be the Euclidean two-point kernel of the free scalar field of squared mass $s$ in four dimensions. Fix $d>0$, put $\kappa=d/(16\pi^2)$ and $\rho(s)=\kappa s^2\log^{-2}(e+s)\,\mathbf 1_{[1,\infty)}(s)$, and for $\epsilon\ge0$ let $\phi_\epsilon$ be the generalized free field with Källén–Lehmann density $\rho+\epsilon\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$, with Fock vacuum $\Omega_\epsilon$ and Hamiltonian $H_\epsilon$. Its Schwinger two-point function at Euclidean separation $r>0$ is $G_\epsilon(r)=\int(\rho(s)+\epsilon\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}(s))D_s(r)\,ds$. Then:

1. $\lim_{r\downarrow0}r^8\log^2(1/r)\,G_\epsilon(r)=3d/\pi^4$ for every $\epsilon\ge0$;
2. $0\le G_\epsilon(r)-G_0(r)\le\epsilon/(4\pi^2r^2)$ for every $r>0$;
3. $\ker H_\epsilon=\mathbb C\Omega_\epsilon$ for every $\epsilon\ge0$, $\sigma(H_0)=\{0\}\cup[1,\infty)$, and $\sigma(H_\epsilon)=[0,\infty)$ for $\epsilon>0$.

Hence $\phi_0$ satisfies (K.10.14c.4) with $m=1$ on all of $\Omega_0^\perp$, while for $\epsilon>0$ no dense subset of $\Omega_\epsilon^\perp$ satisfies (K.10.14c.4) for any $m>0$, by Proposition K.10.14c(3). The two fields have the same leading short-distance law, and on any range $r_{\min}\le r\le r_{\max}$ their two-point functions differ by at most $\epsilon/(4\pi^2r_{\min}^2)$. The long-distance hypothesis (K.10.14c.4), and with it the condition (K.10.14g.3), is therefore independent of these data.

*Proof.* (1) For $\epsilon=0$ put $L=\log(1/r)$ and $u=r\sqrt s$:
$$
r^8L^2G_0(r)=\frac{\kappa}{2\pi^2}\int_r^\infty u^6K_1(u)\,\frac{L^2}{\log^2(e+u^2/r^2)}\,du .
$$
For fixed $u>0$ the last factor tends to $1/4$. On $[r,\sqrt r]$, $K_1(u)\le1/u$ and $\log(e+u^2/r^2)\ge1$ bound the contribution by $L^2\int_r^{\sqrt r}u^5\,du=O(L^2r^3)$. On $[\sqrt r,\infty)$, $\log(e+u^2/r^2)\ge\log(1/r)=L$, so the factor is at most one, and $u^6K_1(u)$ is integrable. Dominated convergence and $\int_0^\infty u^6K_1(u)\,du=2^5\Gamma(4)\Gamma(3)=384$ give the limit $\kappa\cdot384/(8\pi^2)=48\kappa/\pi^2=3d/\pi^4$.

(2) $zK_1(z)$ tends to $1$ as $z\downarrow0$ and has derivative $-zK_0(z)<0$, so $0\le D_s(r)\le1/(4\pi^2r^2)$, and $G_\epsilon-G_0=\epsilon\int_0^1D_s\,ds$ lies in $[0,\epsilon/(4\pi^2r^2)]$. Multiplied by $r^8\log^2(1/r)$ this tends to zero, which gives item 1 for $\epsilon>0$.

(3) The one-particle space of $\phi_\epsilon$ is $L^2(\mathbb R^3\times[0,\infty),d^3p\,(\rho(s)+\epsilon\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}(s))\,ds)$, on which the Hamiltonian is multiplication by $\omega(p,s)=\sqrt{|p|^2+s}$, and $H_\epsilon$ is its second quantization. An $N$-particle vector of zero energy would be supported where $\sum_i\omega(p_i,s_i)=0$, a null set for $N\ge1$, so $\ker H_\epsilon=\mathbb C\Omega_\epsilon$. For $\epsilon=0$ the one-particle energies form the essential range $[1,\infty)$ on the support $s\ge1$, and $N$-particle energies are at least $N$, so $\sigma(H_0)=\{0\}\cup[1,\infty)$. For $\epsilon>0$ the one-particle energy takes values in every interval $(0,\eta)$ on sets of positive measure, so $\sigma(H_\epsilon)=[0,\infty)$. Every vector of $\Omega_0^\perp$ has spectral measure in $[1,\infty)$, which gives (K.10.14c.4) with $m=1$; for $\epsilon>0$ a dense subset satisfying (K.10.14c.4) would give a gap by Proposition K.10.14c(3). ∎

<a id="remark-k1015-distinction-from-wilsonian-effective-field-theory"></a>**Remark K.10.15 (Distinction from Wilsonian Effective Field Theory).**

PU records distinct conditional objects: a refresh-branch mixing gap, a Leech norm gap, and an action-per-update floor. None alone is a Yang--Mills particle mass gap. Proposition K.10.14c(2) states the comparison inequality, with the factor $a$ of the transfer step, under which a mixing gap bounds the physical transfer gap of Theorem K.10.14b. Converting the norm gap to an absolute physical gap requires the confinement/spectral bridge, $\mathfrak B_{mass}$, and norm--information calibration; this claim is separate from the Wilsonian continuum question.

**Connection to Horizon Thermodynamics.** On the complete protocol branch of Theorem Q.0.10 and Corollary Q.0.10c, with the declared local acceleration or surface-gravity identification, the conditional Rindler-Landauer rate is
$$
\dot{N} = \frac{a}{2\pi c}.
$$
The black-hole specialization additionally uses Theorem Q.0.12; an MPU-substrate interpretation requires a separate clock-and-scale identification. Theorem Q.0.15 places this rate beside the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, horizon-area calibration, and gravitational coupling on their joint hypothesis package. It is a compatibility ledger.

**Technical synthesis.** Within the Predictive Universe framework, renormalization extracts operational predictions from continuum approximations that, if extrapolated literally, would describe operationally inaccessible physics. On Theorem K.10.3a's finite-total-distinguishability certificate, one registered instantiation cannot support an unbounded family of independent response distinctions. A hard ultraviolet retained-mode boundary follows only on Theorem K.10.4's lattice or bandlimit and matching certificate. Theorem K.5.4 proves exit from one framed Fermi-expansion certificate.

Theorem K.10.10, Corollary K.10.11, and Theorem K.10.12 give a conditional thermodynamic interpretation of the macroscopic metric equation while leaving effective quantization of perturbations open. Perturbative nonrenormalizability of the Einstein--Hilbert action is compatible with low-energy quantum gravity.

---

<a id="theorem-k1016-operational-inertial-range-turbulence-scaling"></a>**Theorem K.10.16 (Operational Inertial-Range Turbulence Scaling).** Let an MPU-admissible fluid description possess a finite inertial range
$$
k_0\ll k\ll k_d\le k_{\mathrm{MPU}},
\tag{K.10.20}
$$
with forcing confined to $k\lesssim k_0$ and dissipation confined to $k\gtrsim k_d$. Suppose that inside the inertial range:

1. the only conserved transferred scalar relevant to the one-dimensional energy spectrum is the scale-independent energy flux per unit mass $\varepsilon_T$;
2. PCE compression removes dependence on forcing details, viscosity, molecular structure, and sub-MPU degrees of freedom from the inertial-range closure;
3. the inertial-range spectrum $E(k)$ is locally determined only by $\varepsilon_T$ and $k$.

Then the spectrum has the universal exponent
$$
E(k)=C_K\,\varepsilon_T^{2/3}k^{-5/3},
\tag{K.10.21}
$$
where $C_K$ is a dimensionless branch constant not fixed by dimensional closure alone.

*Proof.* In a statistically stationary inertial range, energy neither accumulates at an intermediate wavenumber nor is created there. The flux entering each inertial shell equals the flux leaving it, so the flux is independent of $k$ and is denoted $\varepsilon_T$. The dimensions are
$$
[E(k)]=L^3T^{-2},
\qquad
[\varepsilon_T]=L^2T^{-3},
\qquad
[k]=L^{-1}.
$$
By assumption 3, write
$$
E(k)=C_K\varepsilon_T^a k^b
$$
with dimensionless $C_K$. Matching dimensions gives
$$
L^3T^{-2}=L^{2a-b}T^{-3a}.
$$
Thus
$$
-3a=-2,\qquad 2a-b=3.
$$
The unique solution is
$$
a=\frac{2}{3},\qquad b=-\frac{5}{3}.
$$
Substitution yields (K.10.21). PCE enters by justifying the absence of additional inertial-range dimensional inputs: operationally irrelevant microscopic detail is compressed away, while the certified finite-substrate branch supplies $k_d\le k_{\mathrm{MPU}}$ rather than an all-scale continuum limit. ∎

<a id="corollary-k10161-finite-resolution-status-of-the-turbulent-cascade"></a>**Corollary K.10.16.1 (Finite-Resolution Status of the Turbulent Cascade).** PU does not require an exact continuum Navier-Stokes cascade extending to arbitrarily large $k$. The $-5/3$ exponent holds only on the finite operational band $k_0\ll k\ll k_d$, with deviations expected near forcing, dissipation, boundaries, anisotropic constraints, or $k_d\sim k_{\mathrm{MPU}}$.

*Proof.* Theorem K.10.16 assumes a finite inertial interval. If $k$ approaches $k_0$, forcing details become operationally relevant and assumption 2 fails. If $k$ approaches $k_d$, dissipation or MPU-scale discreteness becomes operationally relevant and assumption 3 fails. Therefore the exponent is a finite-band universality statement, not a claim about an exact all-scale continuum. ∎

<a id="theorem-k10162-exact-nonlinear-finite-shell-cascade-and-constant-map"></a>**Theorem K.10.16.2 (Exact Nonlinear Finite-Shell Cascade and Constant Map).** Fix shells $k_n=k_0\lambda^n$, $0\le n\le N$, with $k_0>0$, $\lambda>1$, positive shell weights $w_n$, injection $\varepsilon_T>0$, and a dimensionless transfer coefficient $A>0$. For nonnegative shell spectra $E_n(t)$ define
$$
J_n(E_n)=A k_n^{5/2}E_n^{3/2}
\tag{K.10.16.2.1}
$$
and the finite cascade
$$
\begin{aligned}
w_0\dot E_0&=\varepsilon_T-J_0(E_0),\\
w_n\dot E_n&=J_{n-1}(E_{n-1})-J_n(E_n),
\qquad 1\le n\le N.
\end{aligned}
\tag{K.10.16.2.2}
$$
The last flux $J_N$ is the registered dissipative sink. The nonnegative orthant is invariant, and (K.10.16.2.2) has the unique stationary state
$$
E_n^*=A^{-2/3}\varepsilon_T^{2/3}k_n^{-5/3}.
\tag{K.10.16.2.3}
$$
Every solution with finite nonnegative initial data converges componentwise to this state. At the limit, every interior balance residual, the injection residual $\varepsilon_T-J_0$, and the sink residual $J_N-\varepsilon_T$ vanish exactly. Thus this selected nonlinear finite dynamics has
$$
C_K=A^{-2/3}
\tag{K.10.16.2.4}
$$
as its exact constant map.

*Proof.* At a zero component the right-hand side of (K.10.16.2.2) is nonnegative, proving invariance. Stationarity first gives $J_0=\varepsilon_T$ and then recursively $J_n=J_{n-1}=\varepsilon_T$; strict monotonicity of each $J_n$ gives uniqueness and (K.10.16.2.3). The first equation is a scalar autonomous equation whose vector field points toward its unique equilibrium, so $E_0(t)\to E_0^*$. Inductively, if $J_{n-1}(E_{n-1}(t))\to\varepsilon_T$, comparison with the scalar equations having constant inputs $\varepsilon_T\pm\epsilon$ traps the liminf and limsup of $E_n$ between roots that converge to $E_n^*$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. This proves componentwise convergence. Substitution gives the residual and constant statements. ∎

The model resolves flux, boundary residuals, exponent, and constant on its complete finite shell class. It contains no velocity-increment distribution or higher moment, so it makes no intermittency claim and does not replace a Navier–Stokes realization.

<a id="definition-k10163-budgeted-cam-source-and-native-clock"></a>**Definition K.10.16.3 (Budgeted Cam Source and Native Clock).** Fix a dimensionless gear $\kappa>0$, a maximal band ratio $R_*\ge2$ and an integer clock budget $D>4\log R_*+1$ (for example $R_*=2^{30}$, $D=256$), and put $\delta_{\rm p}=1/100$, $\sigma=1/(100R_*)$. The cam class is
$$
\mathcal F=\Bigl\{f\in C^{1,1}([1,R_*]):\ f(1)=1,\ \tfrac12\le f\le2R_*,\ |f'|\le2,\ \operatorname*{ess\,sup}|f''|\le2\Bigr\},
\tag{K.10.16.3.1}
$$
with the $C^1$ topology; a cam is a budgeted dimensionless strain-rate schedule, and the class contains, for example, $f=1$ and $f(x)=x$. A source instance chooses $q>0$, $k_f>0$ and $1<R\le R_*$ and sets
$$
V_0=2\sqrt q,\qquad \gamma=\kappa k_f\sqrt q,\qquad T=D/\gamma .
\tag{K.10.16.3.2}
$$
In the dimensionless time $z=\gamma t$, one period consists of: (i) preparation, raising the transverse wave amplitude from $0$ to $V_0$ over duration $\delta_{\rm p}$ at the fixed wave number $k_I=e^{-\sigma}k_f$; (ii) a low ramp of duration $2\sigma$ with strain rate $a/\gamma=h(\theta)+2\sigma f'(1)Q(\theta)$, $\theta\in[0,1]$, where $h(t)=3t^2-2t^3$ and $Q(t)=t^2(t-1)(5t-3)/2$; (iii) the core, in which $x=k/k_f$ runs from $1$ to $R$ with
$$
\frac{dx}{dz}=xf(x),\qquad \frac a\gamma=f(x),\qquad k'=ak;
\tag{K.10.16.3.3}
$$
(iv) a high ramp of duration $2\sigma/f(R)$ with strain rate $a/\gamma=f(R)\bigl[1-h(\theta)-(2\sigma Rf'(R)/f(R))\,Q(1-\theta)\bigr]$; (v) extraction, lowering the amplitude from $V_0$ to $0$ over duration $\delta_{\rm p}/f(R)$ at $k_D=e^{\sigma}Rk_f$; (vi) return at zero amplitude with strain rate $a/\gamma=-\sin^2[\pi z/(2(\log R+2\sigma))]$ over duration $2(\log R+2\sigma)$; (vii) idle at $a=0$ and zero amplitude for the rest of the period. The stationary law of the source is the uniform law of the period age. For use with Theorem K.10.16 the instance takes $k_f\le e^{-\sigma}k_{\mathrm{MPU}}/R$, so that every wave number of the period is at most $k_D=e^{\sigma}Rk_f\le k_{\mathrm{MPU}}$, with $k_{\mathrm{MPU}}$ of Definition K.10.3.

<a id="theorem-k10164-cam-class-spectrum-flux-and-closure-classification"></a>**Theorem K.10.16.4 (Cam-Class Spectrum, Flux and Closure Classification).** Consider the transverse wave of Definition K.10.16.3, carrying fluctuation energy $q$ per unit core mass at the wave number $k(t)$ during the core.

1. For every $f\in\mathcal F$ the ramps are nonnegative and join the core in value and first derivative, each ramp has strain integral $\sigma$, the return restores the geometry, and the active duration obeys
$$
D_{\rm act}\le3\delta_{\rm p}+10\sigma+4\log R_*<1+4\log R_*<D,
\tag{K.10.16.4.1}
$$
so the period $T=D/\gamma$ is the same for every cam.

2. For every $f\in\mathcal F$, on $k_f<k<Rk_f$,
$$
\varepsilon_T:=\frac qT=\frac{\kappa k_fq^{3/2}}{D},\qquad
E_f(k)=\frac{q}{Dk\,f(k/k_f)},\qquad
J_f(k)=a(k)kE_f(k)=\varepsilon_T ,
\tag{K.10.16.4.2}
$$
and at fixed $\varepsilon_T,\kappa,D$, with $x=k/k_f$,
$$
E_f(k)=\varepsilon_T^{2/3}(\kappa^2D)^{-1/3}k^{-5/3}\,\frac{x^{2/3}}{f(x)} .
\tag{K.10.16.4.3}
$$

3. The spectral response on overlapping interior bands is independent of the forcing scale $k_f$ at fixed $\varepsilon_T,\kappa,D$ if and only if $f=f_*$, $f_*(x)=x^{2/3}$, and $f_*\in\mathcal F$.

4. For $f_*$,
$$
E(k)=C_K\varepsilon_T^{2/3}k^{-5/3},\quad C_K=(\kappa^2D)^{-1/3},\qquad
J(k)=A_{\rm eff}k^{5/2}E(k)^{3/2}=\varepsilon_T,\quad A_{\rm eff}=\kappa\sqrt D ,
\tag{K.10.16.4.4}
$$
so $C_K=A_{\rm eff}^{-2/3}$, the constant map (K.10.16.2.4) at $A=A_{\rm eff}$.

5. Fix a common interior band $\mathcal J$ and the task family consisting of $\varepsilon_T$ and the probes $L_w=\int_{\mathcal J}w(k)E(k)\,dk$ for bounded smooth $w$ supported in $\mathcal J$. On the $f_*$ source the map from source settings to $\varepsilon_T$ is a minimal sufficient coordinate for this family: two settings with equal $\varepsilon_T$ have equal responses, and every response-complete encoding determines $\varepsilon_T$. For every other cam some pair of settings with equal $\varepsilon_T$ is separated by a probe $L_w$. For fixed admissible $k_f,R$ and a compact positive interval of $\varepsilon_T$, the section $q=(\varepsilon_TD/(\kappa k_f))^{2/3}$ realizes every value.

*Proof.* Item 1. One has $Q(0)=Q(1)=Q'(0)=0$, $Q'(1)=1$, $\int_0^1Q=0$, $\int_0^1h=1/2$, and $|Q|\le h/2$ on $[0,1]$, because $Q/h=(t-1)(5t-3)/(2(3-2t))$ and $t(5t-6)\le0\le5t^2-10t+6$ there. Hence the low ramp has strain integral $2\sigma\cdot\frac12=\sigma$, ends at rate $f(1)=1$ with $z$-derivative $f'(1)$, which is the core value $xf(x)f'(x)$ at $x=1$, and is bounded below by $(1-2\sigma)h\ge0$. Since $h(1-\theta)=1-h(\theta)$, the high ramp starts at rate $f(R)$ with $z$-derivative $Rf(R)f'(R)$ and has strain integral $\sigma$, and, using $f\ge1/2$ and $|f'|\le2$, its correction relative to $f(R)(1-h)$ is at most $4\sigma R_*=1/25$. The return has strain integral $-(\log R+2\sigma)$, which cancels the forward strain $\sigma+\log R+\sigma$. Since $f\ge1/2$, the core lasts $D_{\rm core}=\int_1^Rdx/(xf(x))\le2\log R_*$, and with $1/f(R)\le2$,
$$
D_{\rm act}=\delta_{\rm p}+2\sigma+D_{\rm core}+\frac{\delta_{\rm p}+2\sigma}{f(R)}+2(\log R+2\sigma)\le3\delta_{\rm p}+10\sigma+4\log R_*,
$$
which is below $1+4\log R_*<D$.

Item 2. In the core the wave number crosses $[k,k+dk]$ once per period and spends the time $dk/(a(k)k)$ there, while every other stage carries the wave outside $(k_f,Rk_f)$ or carries none. The uniform age law therefore gives $E_f(k)=q/(Ta(k)k)=q/(Dkf(k/k_f))$, since $Ta=Df$. The flux across $k$ is the energy $q$ carried through $k$ once per period, $q/T=\varepsilon_T$, and $a(k)kE_f(k)=q/T$. Substituting $q=(\varepsilon_TD/(\kappa k_f))^{2/3}$ and $k_f=k/x$ gives (K.10.16.4.3).

Item 3. For fixed $\varepsilon_T,\kappa,D$ and $k$, the forcing scale enters (K.10.16.4.3) only through $x=k/k_f$, and admitted $k_f$ with $1<k/k_f<R\le R_*$ cover every $x\in(1,R_*)$ on overlapping bands. Independence of $k_f$ is therefore equivalent to constancy of $x^{2/3}/f(x)$ on $(1,R_*)$, and by continuity on $[1,R_*]$; the normalization $f(1)=1$ fixes the constant to $1$. The cam $f_*$ satisfies $1\le f_*\le R_*^{2/3}<2R_*$, $|f_*'|\le2/3$ and $|f_*''|\le2/9$.

Item 4. Substitute $f_*$ into (K.10.16.4.3); then $k^{5/2}E^{3/2}=\varepsilon_T(\kappa^2D)^{-1/2}$.

Item 5. By item 4 the probes depend on the settings only through $\varepsilon_T$, and $\varepsilon_T$ is itself a member of the family, so every response-complete encoding determines it. For $f\ne f_*$, item 3 supplies two forcing scales with equal $\varepsilon_T$ and different spectra on a common interior band, which a smooth probe supported there separates. The section is explicit. ∎

The selected cam has the finite algebraic presentation $y^3=x^2$, $y>0$; during its core $a'=\tfrac23a^2$, and the finite core ends before the pole of that equation. A supplied shell coefficient $A$ of Theorem K.10.16.2 is matched by the gear calibration $\kappa=A/\sqrt D$. The class $\mathcal F$ has an explicit generator: Bernstein polynomials of the rescaled cam preserve the value at $1$ and the range, first-derivative and second-derivative bounds, and obey $\|B_nf-f\|_\infty\le2(R_*-1)^2/(8n)$, so rational Bernstein coefficients with certified bounds give a dense family of finite cam presentations.

<a id="theorem-k10165-state-carried-quantum-fluid-realization"></a>**Theorem K.10.16.5 (State-Carried Quantum-Fluid Realization).** Take a neutral noninteracting quantum gas of two species $\iota\in\{+,-\}$ with particle mass $m$ on $\mathbb R_x\times S^1_y(L_y)\times\mathbb R_z$ and scalar-potential Schrödinger dynamics. Fix $K,L,Z_0,L_y>0$ with $KL=2\pi n$ for an integer $n\ge R_*$, $P=2\pi\hbar r/L_y$ for an integer $r\ge1$, $V=P/m$ and $q=V^2/4$, and the eight phases $\theta_j=\pi/16+j\pi/8$, $j=0,\dots,7$. Let $\varpi$ be a smooth envelope with $0<\varpi\le1$, equal to $1$ on the core $[-L/2,L/2]$ and on a collar of width $d=s_0/(16K)$, $s_0=\sin(\pi/16)$, and equal to $e^{-\beta u^2}$ at distance $u\ge2d$ beyond the core; let $\Theta_j$ equal $KX+\theta_j$ on the core and collar and freeze smoothly within the next distance $d$, so that it changes by at most $s_0/8$ beyond the core. Put
$$
f_+=\varpi\cos\Theta_j,\qquad f_-=\varpi\sin\Theta_j,\qquad f_+^2+f_-^2=\varpi^2,
$$
let $g$ be the analogous positive profile, equal to $1$ on $[-Z_0,Z_0]$ with Gaussian tails $e^{-\beta_zu^2}$, and let $N_\iota=\int f_\iota^2$, $N_z=\int g^2$, $E_K=\hbar^2K^2/(2m)$,
$$
W_\iota=E_K+\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{f_\iota''}{f_\iota},\qquad W_z=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{g''}{g}.
\tag{K.10.16.5.1}
$$
With $b=e^{-s}$, $c=e^{s}$ and $a=s'$ the strain rate of Definition K.10.16.3, let species $\iota$ evolve under
$$
H_\iota(t)=\frac{p^2}{2m}+b^{-2}W_\iota(x/b)+c^{-2}W_z(z/c)-\frac m2\Bigl[\frac{b''}{b}x^2+\frac{c''}{c}z^2\Bigr],
\tag{K.10.16.5.2}
$$
where on a registered finite horizon $[0,T_h]$ the tail parameters satisfy
$$
\frac{2\hbar^2\beta^2}{mb(t)^4}>\frac m2\Bigl|\frac{b''(t)}{b(t)}\Bigr|,\qquad
\frac{2\hbar^2\beta_z^2}{mc(t)^4}>\frac m2\Bigl|\frac{c''(t)}{c(t)}\Bigr|\qquad(0\le t\le T_h);
\tag{K.10.16.5.2a}
$$
such $\beta,\beta_z$ exist because $b$, $c$, $a$ and $a'$ are bounded on the horizon. Since the Gaussian tails make $b^{-2}W_\iota(x/b)$ and $c^{-2}W_z(z/c)$ grow as $2\hbar^2\beta^2x^2/(mb^4)$ and $2\hbar^2\beta_z^2z^2/(mc^4)$ to leading order, (K.10.16.5.2a) gives a potential bounded below by $c_0(x^2+z^2)-C$ with $c_0>0$ uniformly on $[0,T_h]$, so each $H_\iota(t)$ is semibounded there. Prepare $\rho=\frac{N_+}{N_++N_-}|\psi_+\rangle\langle\psi_+|\oplus\frac{N_-}{N_++N_-}|\psi_-\rangle\langle\psi_-|$ with
$$
\psi_\pm(t)=\frac{f_\pm(x/b)\,g(z/c)}{\sqrt{bc\,N_\pm N_zL_y}}\,
e^{im[(b'/b)x^2+(c'/c)z^2]/(2\hbar)}\,
e^{\pm iPy/\hbar-i[E_K\int_0^tb^{-2}du+P^2t/(2m)]/\hbar}.
\tag{K.10.16.5.3}
$$
Then:

1. $W_\iota$ and $W_z$ are smooth, vanish on the core and grow quadratically in the tails; $[-\hbar^2\partial_X^2/(2m)+W_\iota]f_\iota=E_Kf_\iota$ and $[-\hbar^2\partial_Z^2/(2m)+W_z]g=0$; each $\psi_\iota$ solves $i\hbar\partial_t\psi_\iota=H_\iota\psi_\iota$; and $H_\iota$ is $y$-independent, so $p_y$ is conserved.

2. On the material core $\Omega_t=\{x/b\in[-L/2,L/2],\ z/c\in[-Z_0,Z_0]\}\times S^1_y$ the density is the constant $n_0=1/[(N_++N_-)N_zL_y]$, the current is $n_0u$ with
$$
u=\bigl(-ax,\ V\cos(kx+\phi),\ az\bigr),\qquad k=2K/b,\quad \phi=2\theta_j,\quad k'=ak,
\tag{K.10.16.5.4}
$$
and the Hamiltonian reduces there to $p^2/(2m)+\tfrac m2[(a'-a^2)x^2-(a'+a^2)z^2]$.

3. In velocity-squared number-density units the core stress is $\Pi_{xx}=n_0\hbar^2K^2/(m^2b^2)$, $\Pi_{yy}=n_0V^2\sin^2(kx+\phi)$, all other components zero; $\nabla\!\cdot\Pi=0$, and
$$
(\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla)u=\bigl((a^2-a')x,0,(a^2+a')z\bigr),\qquad \nabla\!\cdot u=0,\qquad
\partial_tv_y+U\cdot\nabla v_y=0,
\tag{K.10.16.5.5}
$$
with $U=(-ax,0,az)$, so $\partial_t(v_y^2/2)+\nabla\!\cdot[U v_y^2/2]=0$: the transverse wave is advected with $k'=ak$ and receives no core force or work.

4. The core mass fraction $p_{\rm core}=2LZ_0/[(N_++N_-)N_z]$ is constant in time and independent of the phase, and per unit core mass the kinetic energy splits exactly as $K_U+q+q+\hbar^2K^2/(2m^2b^2)$, where $K_U=a^2(b^2L^2+4c^2Z_0^2)/24$ is the mean-strain energy, the first $q$ the transverse hydrodynamic energy, the second $q$ the counterstream variance and the last term the gradient energy, which changes at rate $2a$ times itself.

5. Let the filler $\Gamma_0$ be the same state with $p_y=0$ in both species and $\Gamma_w$ the wave state. A number-preserving swap between the active layer and a reservoir layer, generated by $\hbar\theta_{\rm sw}'(t)$ times the site-local inter-layer hopping, with equal in-plane Hamiltonians and no initial cross-layer coherence, gives the active one-body density
$$
\Gamma_{\rm active}=(1-\eta)\Gamma_0+\eta\Gamma_w,\qquad \eta=\sin^2\theta_{\rm sw},
\tag{K.10.16.5.6}
$$
with unchanged density, transverse velocity $\eta V\cos(kx+\phi)$, $p$-th increment moments $\eta^p$ times those of the wave, and per unit core mass microscopic, hydrodynamic and internal transverse energies $2\eta q$, $\eta^2q$ and $2\eta q-\eta^2q$. Injection uses this swap at $k_I$, extraction the reverse swap at $k_D$, and the return and idle stages carry the filler.

6. A phase change at the ready stage, carried out by lowering each layer's own generator to zero as $\lambda(t)H_j$ and $\lambda(t)H_{j+1}$, swapping the layers as in item 5, and restoring the generators, leaves the active density unchanged and the active current zero throughout, and advances the phase counter $j\mapsto j+1\bmod8$. Its duration fits in $D_{\rm phase}=(D-4\log R_*-1)/2$ for every cam.

7. With $q=V^2/4$ and the strain rate of Definition K.10.16.3, the core current carries the transverse wave of Theorem K.10.16.4.

*Proof.* Item 1. The profiles are exactly trigonometric on a neighbourhood of every interior zero, where $f_\iota''/f_\iota=-K^2$; beyond the core the frozen angle keeps $|\cos\Theta_j|,|\sin\Theta_j|\ge7s_0/8$, so no new zero appears. Hence $W_\iota$ is smooth, equal to $E_K-\hbar^2K^2/(2m)=0$ on the core, and quadratic where $\varpi$ is Gaussian; the eigen-equations hold by construction. The lens substitution $\psi=b^{-1/2}F(x/b,\tau)e^{imb'x^2/(2\hbar b)}$, $d\tau=b^{-2}dt$, carries $p_x^2/(2m)+b^{-2}W(x/b)-\tfrac m2(b''/b)x^2$ in the time $t$ to $p_X^2/(2m)+W(X)$ in the time $\tau$, and likewise in $z$; with the stationary reference eigenstates this gives (K.10.16.5.3) and the Schrödinger equation. No term of $H_\iota$ depends on $y$.

Item 2. The common envelope gives $\sum_\iota\frac{N_\iota}{N_++N_-}|\psi_\iota|^2=n_0(f_+^2+f_-^2)=n_0$ on the core. Both species share the chirp, which gives $u_x=\hbar\partial_x\arg\psi/m=-ax$ and $u_z=az$, while their opposite momenta give $u_y=V(f_+^2-f_-^2)/(f_+^2+f_-^2)=V\cos(2KX+2\theta_j)$ with $X=x/b$. On the core $W_\iota=W_z=0$.

Item 3. For a real amplitude $F$ the quantum stress is $(\hbar^2/(2m^2))[(\partial F)^2-F\partial^2F]$; for $\cos$ and $\sin$ of $Kx/b+\theta_j$ each bracket equals $K^2/b^2$, which gives $\Pi_{xx}$. The two species move with $\pm V$ in $y$, so the $yy$ covariance about $u_y$ is $n_0V^2-n_0V^2\cos^2(kx+\phi)$. All species share $u_x,u_z$ and have $y$-independent amplitudes, which removes the mixed terms. Thus $\Pi_{xx}$ is constant and $\Pi_{yy}$ independent of $y$, and the momentum balance reduces to the gradient of the mean potential of item 2, which is (K.10.16.5.5). Direct differentiation, with $\partial_tk=ak$, gives the advection equation.

Item 4. The fraction follows from the core volume and the constant density. The four energies are spatial averages over an integer number of periods of $\cos^2$ and $\sin^2$ and of $(ax)^2+(az)^2$; the gradient term is proportional to $b^{-2}=e^{2s}$.

Item 5. The swap is a mode rotation acting on one-body density matrices with zero initial cross-layer coherence, so the active block is $\cos^2\theta_{\rm sw}\Gamma_0+\sin^2\theta_{\rm sw}\Gamma_w$. Both states have the same density and $x,z$ currents, and only $\Gamma_w$ carries $y$ current. The wave part has microscopic transverse energy $V^2/2=2q$ per unit mass.

Item 6. Under $\lambda H_j$ each ready state is an eigenstate of its own generator and acquires only a scalar phase; during the swap both in-plane generators vanish and item 5 applies to two zero-current states of equal density; restoration again acts by scalar phases. Since $D_{\rm act}<1+4\log R_*$ by (K.10.16.4.1), the remaining time exceeds $2D_{\rm phase}$.

Item 7. Item 4 gives transverse energy $q$ per unit core mass, and item 3 gives $k'=ak$. ∎

<a id="theorem-k10166-finite-band-intermittency-of-the-selected-source"></a>**Theorem K.10.16.6 (Finite-Band Intermittency of the Selected Source).** On the $f_*$ source of Theorems K.10.16.4–K.10.16.5, run with the deterministic phase counter through the eight phases, let $r\,e_x$ be a transverse increment inside the common interior of the core. Then $\delta_rv=-2V\sin(kr/2)\sin(kx+\phi+kr/2)\,e_y$, and the eight-phase averages of $|\sin|^p$ are $c_2=1/2$ and $c_4=3/8$ at every $x$ and $k$, while $\tfrac18\sum_j\sin^8(\vartheta+\pi j/4)=(35+\cos8\vartheta)/128$. With $\alpha=2/3$, $a_r=k_fr/2$, $b_r=Rk_fr/2$, $C_l=C_h=\delta_{\rm p}+2\sigma$ and
$$
I_p=\int_0^\infty u^{-1-\alpha}|\sin u|^p\,du,\qquad
I_2=2^{\alpha-1}C_\alpha,\quad I_4=I_2(1-2^{\alpha-2}),\quad C_\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2\Gamma(1+\alpha)\sin(\pi\alpha/2)},
\tag{K.10.16.6.1}
$$
the full-period structure functions are
$$
S_p(r)=K_pr^{\alpha}(1+e_p),\qquad K_p=(2V)^pc_pD^{-1}(k_f/2)^{\alpha}I_p,
$$
$$
|e_p|\le\frac{(C_l+1/(p-\alpha))\,a_r^{p-\alpha}+(C_h+1/\alpha)\,b_r^{-\alpha}}{I_p}\qquad(p=2,4).
\tag{K.10.16.6.2}
$$
For $R=2^{30}$ and $k_fr\in[2^{-20},2^{-10}]$, $|e_2|,|e_4|<1/20$, and whenever $r$ and $2r$ lie in that band the flatness $F=S_4/S_2^2$ obeys
$$
\frac{F(r)}{F(2r)}\ge2^{2/3}\Bigl(\frac{19}{21}\Bigr)^3>1 .
\tag{K.10.16.6.3}
$$

*Proof.* The increment formula is the difference of two cosines. The phases $\phi_j=2\theta_j$ are equally spaced by $\pi/4$; expanding $\sin^2$ and $\sin^4$ in $\cos2\psi$ and $\cos4\psi$, both cosine sums vanish over the eight phases, while $\sin^8$ retains $\cos8\psi$, which gives the displayed eighth moment. In the core $dz=dk/(kf_*(k/k_f))$, and the substitution $u=kr/2$ turns the period average of $(2V)^pc_p|\sin(kr/2)|^p$ into $(2V)^pc_pD^{-1}(k_fr/2)^{\alpha}\int_{a_r}^{b_r}u^{-1-\alpha}|\sin u|^pdu$. The omitted parts of $I_p$ are at most $\int_0^{a_r}u^{p-1-\alpha}du=a_r^{p-\alpha}/(p-\alpha)$ and $\int_{b_r}^\infty u^{-1-\alpha}du=b_r^{-\alpha}/\alpha$. Preparation and the low ramp last at most $C_l$ with $k\le k_f$, so $|\sin(kr/2)|^p\le a_r^p$; the high ramp and extraction last at most $C_hR^{-\alpha}$ with $|\sin|^p\le1$; swaps multiply the amplitude by $\eta\le1$; return, idle and phase-change stages carry zero transverse current. Dividing these contributions by $K_pr^\alpha$ and using $R^{-\alpha}a_r^{-\alpha}=b_r^{-\alpha}$ gives (K.10.16.6.2). For the integrals write $\sin^2u=\tfrac12(1-\cos2u)$ and $\sin^4u=\tfrac18[4(1-\cos2u)-(1-\cos4u)]$ and use $\int_0^\infty(1-\cos\beta u)\,u^{-1-\alpha}du=\beta^{\alpha}C_\alpha$ for $0<\alpha<2$, which follows from the Laplace representation of $u^{-1-\alpha}$, Tonelli's theorem and the $\beta$ integral. With $\Gamma(5/3)\le1$ (log-convexity between $\Gamma(1)$ and $\Gamma(2)$), $\pi>3$, $\sin(\pi/3)<7/8$ and $2^{-1/3}>3/4$, one gets $I_2>9/7$, and with $1-2^{-4/3}>3/5$, $I_4>27/35$. In the stated band $a_r\le2^{-11}$ and $b_r\ge2^{9}$, so $a_r^{4/3}\le2^{-14}$, $a_r^{10/3}\le2^{-36}$, $b_r^{-2/3}\le1/64$, and $C_l=C_h\le3/100$; these give $|e_2|,|e_4|<1/20$. Then $F(r)/F(2r)=2^{\alpha}(1+e_4(r))(1+e_2(2r))^2/[(1+e_2(r))^2(1+e_4(2r))]\ge2^{2/3}(19/20)^3/(21/20)^3$, and $(21/19)^9<4$. ∎

On this source $S_2$ and $S_4$ both scale as $r^{2/3}$ in the band, so the flatness grows as $r^{-2/3}$ toward small scales. The eight-phase source is homogeneous exactly at second and fourth order, the orders the statement uses, and the margin in (K.10.16.6.3) survives every finite implementation error smaller than it.

<a id="theorem-k10167-attained-definition-15-compression-of-the-selected-source"></a>**Theorem K.10.16.7 (Attained Definition-15 Compression of the Selected Source).** Fix the $f_*$ source of Theorems K.10.16.4–K.10.16.5, a common interior band $\mathcal J$, integers $m\ge1$ and $\ell\ge0$, $M=2^m$, $N_Z=2^\ell$, $M$ distinct flux settings $\varepsilon_e$ in an admitted compact interval and $N_Z$ nuisance settings (forcing scale, input energy, endpoint, phase and tail choices) for each, selected by independent uniform binary registers $\xi\in\{0,1\}^m$ and $\zeta\in\{0,1\}^\ell$. A candidate encoder $P$ is a fixed-schedule bounded deterministic program over a finite local instruction alphabet (single-bit acquisition, copy, NOT, CNOT, Toffoli, local swaps, reset and archive) on fixed-charge two-rail registers, within frozen bounds $W_{\max},A_{\max},G_{\max}\ge m$ that admit the direct transfer schedule; lossy programs are admitted. At a deadline the input ports are disconnected; the input-dependent state of $P$ crossing that cut occupies $W$ binary cells, and $P$ then outputs a canonical $m$-bit label $\hat e$ to a common charged spectral decoder, which returns a prediction $r_{\hat e,w}\in[1/4,3/4]$ for a bounded probe $w$. Independent later preparations with the same $(\xi,\zeta)$ supply a flux outcome $Y_F$, the nearest registered label of a flux measurement with $\Pr(Y_F=e\mid e,\zeta)\ge1-\delta_F$, $\delta_F\le1/8$, and a spectral outcome $Y_S$, a randomized readout of a measured probe with success probability in $[1/4,3/4]$. Define
$$
PP(P)=\tfrac34\Pr(\hat e=Y_F)+\tfrac14\,\mathbb E\bigl[1-(Y_S-r_{\hat e,w})^2\bigr],
\tag{K.10.16.7.1}
$$
$$
C(P)=C_0+Ac_A+W(c_R+c_U+c_M+c_D)+G(c_P+c_D)+C_{\rm extra}(P),
\tag{K.10.16.7.2}
$$
where $A$, $W$ and $G$ are the acquisition events, retained cells and processing slots of $P$, the six positive prices charge acquisition, representation, processing, update, maintenance and adaptation, $C_0$ is the common cost of the source, the future measurements, the decoder and the fixed controller bank, and $C_{\rm extra}\ge0$ collects every further resource. Let $P_*$ transfer the $m$ bits of $\xi$ into $m$ cells and output them, and put $c_{\rm wire}=c_A+c_R+c_P+c_U+c_M+2c_D$ and $g=5/(16MN_Z)$. Then:

1. $7/64\le PP(P)\le61/64$ for every program.

2. Every program that mislabels at least one input satisfies $PP(P_*)-PP(P)\ge g$.

3. Every program that outputs $e$ on every input has $A,W,G\ge m$ and $C(P)\ge C_0+mc_{\rm wire}=C(P_*)$; at equality its retained code is a bijective relabeling of $\xi$, independent of $\zeta$.

4. For every $\Gamma>mc_{\rm wire}/g$, for example $\Gamma=(m+1)c_{\rm wire}/g$, the potential $V(P)=C(P)-\Gamma\,PP(P)$ attains its minimum over the whole class at $P_*$; every minimizer outputs a nuisance-free code of $\xi$, and every mislabeling program exceeds the minimum by at least $\Gamma g-mc_{\rm wire}>0$.

5. The installation map $P\mapsto P_*$, which archives the old program and loads the direct one through charged update and adaptation operations, is idempotent and does not increase $V$.

*Proof.* Item 1. For $r\in[1/4,3/4]$ the pointwise Brier term is at least $1-(3/4)^2=7/16$; for a Bernoulli target with probability $p\in[1/4,3/4]$ its expectation is at most $1-p(1-p)\le13/16$. Item 2. On an input where $P$ outputs $e'\ne e$ the flux-term difference is at least $(1-\delta_F)-\delta_F\ge3/4$ and the Brier-term difference is at least $-1$, so the conditional gap is at least $\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac34-\tfrac14=5/16$; where $P$ outputs $e$ the forecasts coincide. One of the $MN_Z$ equally likely inputs suffices. Item 3. $A$ binary answers give at most $2^A$ transcripts and $W$ cells at most $2^W$ states, while exact decoding needs $M=2^m$ of each; every acquisition needs a transfer slot, so $G\ge A$. Positivity of the prices turns equality into $A=W=G=m$ and $C_{\rm extra}=0$; the $M$ retained states then split into $M$ disjoint nonempty fibres of the decoder, each a single state. Item 4. For a mislabeling program $V(P)-V(P_*)\ge-mc_{\rm wire}+\Gamma g>0$ because $C(P)\ge C_0$; for a perfect program $PP(P)=PP(P_*)$ and item 3 applies. Item 5 follows from item 4. ∎

Theorems K.10.16.4 and K.10.16.7, with the band $k_f\le k\le Rk_f$ below $k_D\le k_{\mathrm{MPU}}$ as fixed in Definition K.10.16.3, populate the hypotheses of Theorem K.10.16 on the selected source: $\varepsilon_T$ is the transferred scalar, the spectrum is determined by $\varepsilon_T$ and $k$, and the minimizers of Definition 15 on the declared architecture retain $\varepsilon_T$ and discard the forcing and nuisance settings, whose records stay in charged archives. The benefit weight is part of the statement: at $\Gamma=0$ the constant program is cheaper. A compact flux interval is approximated by finite alphabets with $|L_w(\varepsilon)-L_w(\varepsilon')|\le\tfrac23(\kappa^2D)^{-1/3}\varepsilon_{\min}^{-1/3}\bigl[\int_{\mathcal J}|w|k^{-5/3}dk\bigr]|\varepsilon-\varepsilon'|$.

<a id="theorem-k10168-finite-physical-response-map-and-clock"></a>**Theorem K.10.16.8 (Finite Physical Response Map and Clock).** Realize the source of Theorem K.10.16.5 on a finite lattice with spacings $h_d$, open boundaries in $x,z$ and a periodic $y$ ring of $N_y>2r$ sites, one rail per species, with the Hamiltonian
$$
H_{\iota,h}=\sum_{\mathbf r,d}\kappa_d\bigl(2|\mathbf r\rangle\langle\mathbf r|-|\mathbf r\rangle\langle\mathbf r+e_d|-|\mathbf r+e_d\rangle\langle\mathbf r|\bigr)+\sum_{\mathbf r}U_{\iota,R_c}(t,\mathbf r)|\mathbf r\rangle\langle\mathbf r|,\qquad\kappa_d=\frac{\hbar^2}{2mh_d^2},
\tag{K.10.16.8.1}
$$
where $|\iota,\mathbf r\rangle$ is one particle of species $\iota$ at the site $\mathbf r$, and $U_{\iota,R_c}=\chi_{R_c}U_\iota$ is the potential of (K.10.16.5.2) multiplied by a smooth $y$-independent cutoff equal to $1$ on $|x|,|z|\le R_c$ and $0$ beyond $2R_c$. Density is the site occupation $P_{\mathbf r}$ and the link flux is $I_{(\mathbf r,\mathbf r+e_d)}=(\kappa_d/\hbar)(-i|\mathbf r\rangle\langle\mathbf r+e_d|+i|\mathbf r+e_d\rangle\langle\mathbf r|)$, read by a local hopping rotation followed by occupation readout. Then on every finite horizon $[0,T_h]$:

1. $\sup_t\|(H_{\iota,R_c}-H_\iota)\psi_\iota\|\le C(1+R_c)^pe^{-cR_c^2}$ and $\|U_{\iota,R_c}(t,0)\psi_\iota(0)-\psi_\iota(t)\|\le(T_h/\hbar)C(1+R_c)^pe^{-cR_c^2}$, with $C,c,p$ computed from the Gaussian tails of the profiles; $p_y$ remains conserved.

2. $dP_{\mathbf r}/dt+\sum_{\mathbf r'}I_{\mathbf r\to\mathbf r'}=0$; the link current per face area of sampled amplitudes is $[\hbar/(mh_d)]\operatorname{Im}(\psi(\mathbf r)^*\psi(\mathbf r+h_de_d))$, which converges to $(\hbar/m)\operatorname{Im}(\psi^*\partial_d\psi)$; and $\|H_{\iota,h}S_hv-S_hH_{\iota,R_c}v\|\le[\hbar^2\operatorname{Vol}^{1/2}/(24m)]\sum_dh_d^2\sup|\partial_d^4v|$ for the sampling $S_hv(\mathbf r)=\sqrt{\Delta V}\,v(\mathbf r)$.

3. The state error obeys $\mathcal E_h\le\delta_{\rm prep}+\delta_{\rm norm}+(T_h/\hbar)[\sup\|S_h\varrho_\iota\|+C_{FD}h^2]+\delta_{\rm time}+\delta_{\rm gates}$, where $\varrho_\iota$ is the taper and cutoff residual and a time-sliced native implementation has $\delta_{\rm time}\le T_h\Delta t[M_1/(2\hbar)+C_{\rm com}/(2\hbar^2)]$, $M_1=\sup\|\partial_tH_h\|$, $C_{\rm com}=\sum_{a<b}\sup\|[H_a,H_b]\|$. Along $R_{c,j}\propto j$ with $h_j$ comparable to $e^{-c'R_{c,j}^2}$ for small $c'$, and preparation, normalization, time and gate errors $o(h)$, one has $\mathcal E_h/h\to0$; density, current and kinetic-energy expectations then converge, since the current probes have norm at most $\sum_d\hbar\|g_d\|_\infty/(mh_d)$ and the kinetic operator $K_h$ has norm at most $4\sum_d\kappa_d$, with $|\langle\Psi_h,K_h\Psi_h\rangle-\langle S_hv,K_hS_hv\rangle|\le2\|K_h^{1/2}S_hv\|\,\|K_h\|^{1/2}\mathcal E_h+\|K_h\|\mathcal E_h^2$ for the lattice state $\Psi_h$ and a sampled reference state $S_hv$.

4. On a registered domain where the density is at least $\nu$ and its error at most $\nu/2$, $|j_{\rm est}/n_{\rm est}-j/n|\le2\delta_j/\nu+2|j|\delta_n/\nu^2$; with $N\ge2B^2\varepsilon_{\rm stat}^{-2}\log(2n_{\rm set}/\delta_{\rm fail})$ independent shots for each of $n_{\rm set}$ settings with outcomes in $[-B,B]$, all estimates are within $\varepsilon_{\rm stat}$ with probability at least $1-\delta_{\rm fail}$.

5. For observation or intervention times $t_1<\dots<t_M$ with registered normalized instruments $\{\mathcal I_{i,o}\}$, the joint outcome law is $\Pr(o_1,\dots,o_M)=\operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal I_{M,o_M}\mathcal U_M\cdots\mathcal I_{1,o_1}\mathcal U_1(\rho_0)]$, and channel errors $\delta_0,\dots,\delta_M$ change it by at most $\tfrac12\sum_i\delta_i$ in total variation.

6. With $N$ clock ticks per cycle of duration $T_c$, labels $(i,j)\in\{0,\dots,N-1\}\times\mathbb Z/8$, the implemented tick channels and the deterministic wrap $(N-1,j)\mapsto(0,j+1)$, the active marginal $\Omega_N=\frac1{8N}\sum_{i,j}|i,j\rangle\langle i,j|\otimes\rho_{i,j}$ is exactly stationary at the ticks, and for a bounded response $|F|\le B$ with $|\partial_aF|\le L_F$ away from $n_b$ boundary ages, $|\mathbb E_{\rm grid}F-\mathbb E_{\rm uniform}F|\le L_F\Delta/2+4Bn_b(w_g+\Delta)/T_c+2B\varepsilon_{\rm phase}+\varepsilon_{\rm source}$ with guard width $w_g$, tick $\Delta=T_c/N$, clock-preparation error $\varepsilon_{\rm phase}$ and source error $\varepsilon_{\rm source}$.

7. Let a fair bit $X$ select the flux $\varepsilon_0$ or $\varepsilon_1$, let $Y$ be the readout with probability $p_X=(1+L_X/B_w)/2$ of a spectral probe $L_X$, $B_w>\max(|L_0|,|L_1|)$, and let a forecast register receive $X$. Its Brier score improves over a comparator whose information excludes $X$ and every flux-reconstructing record by exactly $(p_1-p_0)^2/4$, and by at least $(p_1-p_0)^2/4-2\delta_o-4\eta_f$ under output-law error $\delta_o$ and forecast error $\eta_f$.

*Proof.* Item 1. $(H_{\iota,R_c}-H_\iota)\psi_\iota=(\chi_{R_c}-1)U_\iota\psi_\iota$, $|U_\iota|\le C(1+x^2+z^2)$, and the scaled profiles have Gaussian tails on the finite horizon, so the norm is a Gaussian incomplete-gamma integral; Duhamel's formula gives the propagator bound, and the cutoff is $y$-independent. Item 2. For the hopping amplitude $-\kappa_d$ the inflow from $\mathbf r'$ to $\mathbf r$ is $(2/\hbar)\operatorname{Im}(h_{\mathbf r\mathbf r'}\rho_{\mathbf r'\mathbf r})$, which is the stated continuity law; inserting sampled amplitudes gives the face-area current; the consistency bound is the fourth-order Taylor remainder of the second difference. Item 3. Unitary stability sums the residuals; freezing the Hamiltonian on slabs of length $\Delta t$ and splitting commuting blocks gives $\delta_{\rm time}$; on the diagonal the residual is $o(h)$, while the current and kinetic operators have norms $O(1/h)$ and $O(1/h^2)$, which the displayed inequality controls. Item 4. Expand the ratio about $(j,n)$; the shot bound is Hoeffding's inequality for range $2B$ with a union bound over the settings. Item 5. Each instrument is completely positive with trace-preserving sum, so the law is positive and normalized; errors telescope by trace-norm contractivity. Item 6. Every non-wrap block has a unique predecessor and each wrap block receives the weight $1/(8N)$ of $(N-1,j)$; the quadrature bound is cellwise Lipschitz quadrature on cells avoiding the guard layers, with the remaining cells, of total length at most $2n_b(w_g+\Delta)$, bounded by $B$. Item 7. The comparator's best forecast is $\bar p=(p_0+p_1)/2$, and $\mathbb E[(Y-\bar p)^2]-\mathbb E[(Y-p_X)^2]=\operatorname{Var}(p_X)=(p_1-p_0)^2/4$; each bounded loss moves by at most $\delta_o+2\eta_f$. ∎

The finite construction is typed on the reset-free unitary transport of Definition 26 and the registered normalized instruments of Definition 27: occupation projectors $\mathcal I_k(\rho)=P_k\rho P_k$ and, for link currents, $P_kR\rho R^\dagger P_k$ after the local rotation $R$, with zero- and two-particle outcomes included during swaps. Its length, time, mass and energy units are the physical ones of (K.10.16.5.2), so $q$ has units $L^2T^{-2}$, $\gamma$ and $a$ have units $T^{-1}$, $E$ has units $L^3T^{-2}$ and $\varepsilon_T$ has units $L^2T^{-3}$, while $\kappa$, $D$, $A_{\rm eff}$ and $C_K$ are dimensionless. Each refinement is a finite nonrelativistic apparatus with its own registered parameter domain.

### K.10.17 Finite Operational Theory-Space

<a id="definition-k1017a-operational-theory-pseudometric-at-fixed-resolution"></a>**Definition K.10.17a (Operational Theory Pseudometric at Fixed Resolution).** Fix an energy bound $E$, physical/readout scale $\ell_{\mathrm{res}}$, finite predictive capacity bound $C$, protocol depth bound $L$, and total-variation tolerance $\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}\in(0,1]$. Assume the registered protocol grammar is finite and every protocol has a finite outcome alphabet, or a bounded readout range equipped with a finite $\ell_{\mathrm{res}}$ partition. Let $\mathcal P(E,\ell_{\mathrm{res}},C,L)$ be the resulting finite protocol set. Define
$$
d_{E,\ell_{\mathrm{res}},C,L}(T_1,T_2)
=
\max_{P\in\mathcal P(E,\ell_{\mathrm{res}},C,L)}
d_{\mathrm{TV}}\bigl(\Pr_{T_1}(\cdot\mid P),\Pr_{T_2}(\cdot\mid P)\bigr).
\tag{K.10.22}
$$
If $\mathcal P(E,\ell_{\mathrm{res}},C,L)$ is empty, define $d_{E,\ell_{\mathrm{res}},C,L}\equiv0$. A family of theories is $\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}$-distinguishable when distinct members have pseudometric distance greater than $\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}$.

<a id="theorem-k1017b-finite-operational-theory-space"></a>**Theorem K.10.17b (Finite Operational Theory-Space).** Under Definition K.10.17a, every $\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}$-distinguishable family in
$$
\mathcal T(E,\ell_{\mathrm{res}},C,L)
$$
is finite. Equivalently, the induced prediction set has a finite $\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}$-cover in the operational pseudometric.

*Proof.* The protocol grammar is finite: the interface alphabet is finite at fixed MPU resolution, and the depth bound $L$ allows only finitely many finite words in that alphabet. Hence $\mathcal P(E,\ell_{\mathrm{res}},C,L)=\{P_1,\dots,P_N\}$ is finite. By Definition K.10.17a, each protocol has a finite outcome partition
$$
\Omega_i=\{\omega_{i1},\dots,\omega_{im_i}\}.
$$
A theory determines a point in the finite product of probability simplices
$$
\Delta
=
\prod_{i=1}^N\Delta(\Omega_i).
$$
Each simplex $\Delta(\Omega_i)$ is compact and finite-dimensional. Choose a finite $\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}/2$-net in each factor; their finite product is a net for the maximum total-variation metric. Assign each prediction vector to a net point within that distance. Two vectors assigned to the same point have distance at most $\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}$ by the triangle inequality, so a family with pairwise distances greater than $\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}$ has at most one member per cell and is finite. Choosing one prediction from every occupied cell also gives a finite $\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}$-cover of the prediction set. When there are no protocols, the product is a singleton and the same conclusion holds for the zero pseudometric. This argument constructs a finite cover and bounds separated families; a positive distance tolerance alone does not define equivalence classes. ∎

<a id="corollary-k1017c-operational-landscape-finiteness"></a>**Corollary K.10.17c (Operational Landscape Finiteness).** Infinite continuum parameter spaces in EFT, cosmology, or dark-sector modeling reduce at finite PU resolution to a finite atlas of distinguishable predictive cells.

*Proof.* Such parameter spaces define maps into the finite product simplex $\Delta$ of Theorem K.10.17b. The image of any set under a finite-cover has no more distinguishable cells than the finite cover of $\Delta$. ∎

### K.10.18 Predictive $c/a$-Theorem from Data Processing

<a id="definition-k1018a-predictive-distinguishability-function"></a>**Definition K.10.18a (Predictive Distinguishability Function).** Let $k_1>k_2$ denote two operational resolution scales, with $k_1$ the finer scale. Let
$$
\mathcal E_{k_1\to k_2}
$$
be the completely positive trace-preserving coarse-graining channel from the retained state space at scale $k_1$ to the retained state space at scale $k_2$. For a branch family $\mathcal S_{k_1}$, define $\mathcal S_{k_2}:=\mathcal E_{k_1\to k_2}(\mathcal S_{k_1})$ and
$$
C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k)
=
\sup_{\rho,\sigma\in\mathcal S_k}
D(\rho\Vert\sigma),
\tag{K.10.23}
$$
where
$$
D(\rho\Vert\sigma)
=
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{Tr}\rho(\log\rho-\log\sigma),
&\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma,\\
+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
Equality and Petz-recovery statements below are made only for pairs with finite relative entropy and a finite common value of $C_{\mathrm{pred}}$.
