<a id="theorem-k1018b-predictive-rg-monotonicity"></a>**Theorem K.10.18b (Predictive RG Monotonicity).** For every admissible coarse-graining channel,
$$
C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k_2)\le C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k_1).
\tag{K.10.24}
$$

*Proof.* For any $\rho,\sigma\in\mathcal S_{k_1}$, monotonicity of quantum relative entropy under completely positive trace-preserving maps gives
$$
D(\mathcal E_{k_1\to k_2}(\rho)\Vert
\mathcal E_{k_1\to k_2}(\sigma))
\le
D(\rho\Vert\sigma).
$$
Taking the supremum over $\rho,\sigma\in\mathcal S_{k_1}$ gives
$$
\sup_{\rho',\sigma'\in\mathcal S_{k_2}}
D(\rho'\Vert\sigma')
\le
\sup_{\rho,\sigma\in\mathcal S_{k_1}}
D(\rho\Vert\sigma),
$$
because every element of $\mathcal S_{k_2}$ is the coarse-grained image of an element of $\mathcal S_{k_1}$. This is (K.10.24). ∎

<a id="corollary-k1018c-endpoint-central-datum-inequality"></a>**Corollary K.10.18c (Endpoint Central-Datum Inequality).** Suppose an RG branch has conformal endpoints $k_1$ and $k_2$, and the declared normalization identifies $C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k_i)$ with central data $c_i$ at those endpoints. Then
$$
c_2\le c_1.
$$
Calling $C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k)$ the standard central function at intermediate scales requires a separate all-scale identification.

*Proof.* Theorem K.10.18b gives $C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k_2)\le C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k_1)$. Substituting the two endpoint identifications gives $c_2\le c_1$. No premise identifies the intermediate values with a conventional central function, so no stronger conclusion follows. ∎

<a id="corollary-k1018d-equality-conditions-for-predictive-rg-monotonicity"></a>**Corollary K.10.18d (Equality Conditions for Predictive RG Monotonicity).** Suppose
$$
C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k_2)=C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k_1)<\infty.
$$
If both suprema are attained, then at least one fine-scale maximizing pair maps to a coarse-scale maximizing pair and has zero data-processing loss. Petz sufficiency for the entire branch family is sufficient, but not necessary, for equality. Without attainment, equality yields a sequence of preimage pairs whose coarse values approach the common supremum and whose data-processing loss tends to zero.

*Proof.* Let $(\rho'_*,\sigma'_*)$ attain the coarse supremum. Since $\mathcal S_{k_2}=\mathcal E(\mathcal S_{k_1})$, choose preimages $\rho_*,\sigma_*\in\mathcal S_{k_1}$. Data processing and equality of the suprema give
$$
C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k_1)
=D(\rho'_*\Vert\sigma'_*)
\le D(\rho_*\Vert\sigma_*)
\le C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k_1).
$$
Both inequalities are equalities. Thus the preimage pair is fine-scale maximizing and has zero loss; equality in data processing for that pair is equivalent to pairwise Petz recovery. Without attainment, choose coarse pairs with values tending to the coarse supremum and choose preimages. If $D_n'$ and $D_n$ are their coarse and fine relative entropies, then
$$
0\le D_n-D_n'\le C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k_1)-D_n'\longrightarrow0,
$$
which proves the sequence statement.

For whole-family sufficiency, let $\mathcal R$ be a CPTP recovery map with $\mathcal R\mathcal E(\rho)=\rho$ for every $\rho$ in the family. Applying data processing to $\mathcal E$ and then to $\mathcal R$ gives
$$
D(\mathcal E(\rho)\Vert\mathcal E(\sigma))
\le D(\rho\Vert\sigma)
=D(\mathcal R\mathcal E(\rho)\Vert\mathcal R\mathcal E(\sigma))
\le D(\mathcal E(\rho)\Vert\mathcal E(\sigma)).
$$
Thus every pair and the supremum have zero loss.

For nonnecessity, consider diagonal densities on two binary registers with probability vectors
$$
p_0=(9/10,1/10)\otimes(1/2,1/2),\qquad
p_1=(1/10,9/10)\otimes(1/2,1/2),\qquad
p_2=(1/2,1/2)\otimes(3/5,2/5),
$$
and let $\mathcal E$ discard the second register. All pairwise relative entropies are finite. The two ordered pairs $(p_0,p_1)$ and $(p_1,p_0)$ have relative entropy $(4/5)\ln9$, which is preserved by $\mathcal E$. Additivity on product distributions gives, for $i\in\{0,1\}$,
$$
D(p_i\Vert p_2)
=\frac9{10}\ln\frac95+\frac1{10}\ln\frac15
+\frac12\ln\frac{25}{24}
\le\ln\frac94,
$$
$$
D(p_2\Vert p_i)
=\ln\frac53+\frac35\ln\frac65+\frac25\ln\frac45
\le\ln2.
$$
The first bound also follows from the maximal probability ratio $9/4$; the second uses $D((3/5,2/5)\Vert(1/2,1/2))\le\ln(6/5)$. Since $\ln2<\ln(9/4)<(4/5)\ln9$, the common predictive supremum is $(4/5)\ln9$. But
$$
\mathcal E(p_2)=\frac{\mathcal E(p_0)+\mathcal E(p_1)}2,
\qquad
p_2\ne\frac{p_0+p_1}2.
$$
Linearity therefore precludes a channel recovering all three states. This proves that whole-family Petz sufficiency is not necessary for equality of the predictive suprema. ∎

<a id="proposition-k1018e-endpoint-central-normalization-is-independent-of-data-processing"></a>**Proposition K.10.18e (Endpoint Central Normalization Is Independent of Data Processing).** Let the endpoint predictive data in Definition K.10.18a be finite and positive,
$$
C_i=C_{\mathrm{pred}}(k_i)>0,
\qquad C_2\le C_1.
$$
For arbitrary positive constants $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$, the assignments
$$
c_i=\alpha_iC_i,
\qquad
a_i=\beta_iC_i
\tag{K.10.18e.1}
$$
preserve the same state families, coarse-graining channel, relative entropies, and data-processing inequality. The endpoint ratios
$$
\frac{c_i}{a_i}=\frac{\alpha_i}{\beta_i}
\tag{K.10.18e.2}
$$
therefore range independently over all positive values while the predictive record is fixed. Even an endpoint-independent choice $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$ fixes neither the $a$ normalization nor a relation between the two central data.

*Proof.* The constants in (K.10.18e.1) do not occur in the definition of $C_i$ or in the CPTP channel. Hence changing them leaves every premise and conclusion of Theorem K.10.18b unchanged. Given any prescribed positive endpoint ratios $r_i$, choose $\alpha_i=r_i$ and $\beta_i=1$ to obtain (K.10.18e.2). ∎

Thus data processing supplies the ordered dimensionless predictive datum, while a common $c/a$ normalization requires an independent response-complete calibration. Equality conditions and Petz recovery do not remove this positive calibration modulus.

<a id="proposition-k1018f-predictive-diameter-of-the-accepted-gaussian-input-domain"></a>**Proposition K.10.18f (Predictive Diameter of the Accepted Gaussian Input Domain).** Use the same Fock carrier, vacuum $\Omega$ and positive regularity operator $\mathsf K=d\Gamma(1+|p|^2-\Delta_p)$ as Definition F.10.4c.12. For any $E>0$, let
$$
\mathcal S_E=\{\rho:\rho\ge0,\ \operatorname{Tr}\rho=1,\ \operatorname{Tr}(\rho\mathsf K)\le E\}.
\tag{K.10.18f.1}
$$
Then
$$
\sup_{\rho,\sigma\in\mathcal S_E}D(\rho\Vert\sigma)=+\infty.
\tag{K.10.18f.2}
$$
The supremum remains infinite on a family of faithful states in $\mathcal S_E$ for which every ordered pair has finite relative entropy. A single admitted binary final effect, the vacuum projection $P_\Omega=|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|$, witnesses the divergence. Thus neither the accepted regularity/energy budget nor the additional requirement of faithful inputs supplies the finite predictive diameter required for a finite positive normalization in Proposition K.10.18e.

*Proof.* Choose a unit one-particle Schwartz vector $f$, orthogonal to $\Omega$, and put $b_f=\langle f,\mathsf Kf\rangle\in(0,\infty)$. For $0<\eta\le\min\{1/2,E/(2b_f)\}$, the state $(1-\eta)P_\Omega+\eta|f\rangle\langle f|$ belongs to $\mathcal S_E$. Its support is not contained in that of $P_\Omega\in\mathcal S_E$, so Definition K.10.18a gives infinite relative entropy. This proves (K.10.18f.2).

For the faithful assertion, the Hermite eigenvectors of $1+|p|^2-\Delta_p$ have eigenvalues $1+d+2|\alpha|$, $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d$. Their finite bosonic occupation vectors form an orthonormal eigenbasis of $\mathsf K$; its zero-eigenvalue vector is exactly $\Omega$. Enumerate the remaining basis vectors as $e_j$, $j\ge1$, with eigenvalues $b_j>0$. Set
$$
Z=\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{2^{-j}}{1+b_j},\qquad
\nu=Z^{-1}\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{2^{-j}}{1+b_j}|e_j\rangle\langle e_j|,\qquad
B=\operatorname{Tr}(\nu\mathsf K).
\tag{K.10.18f.3}
$$
Every summand is positive, so $0<Z\le1$; also $0<B\le Z^{-1}<\infty$. The state $\nu$ has support $\Omega^\perp$. Fix $0<\eta\le\min\{1/2,E/(2B)\}$ and, for $0<t\le1$, define
$$
\rho_t=(1-t\eta)P_\Omega+t\eta\nu.
\tag{K.10.18f.4}
$$
Each $\rho_t$ has strictly positive weight on every vector of the complete eigenbasis and is therefore faithful. Its regularity budget is $t\eta B\le E/2$. The same-source Hamiltonian obeys $H=d\Gamma(\sqrt{m^2+|p|^2})\le(m+1)\mathsf K$ as a quadratic-form inequality, as in Definition F.10.4c.12; thus these states also have finite mean physical field energy.

For $s,t\in(0,1]$, the states commute. On $\Omega^\perp$ their eigenvalue ratio is exactly $s/t$, so the spectral sum in the relative entropy reduces to
$$
D(\rho_s\Vert\rho_t)
=(1-s\eta)\ln\frac{1-s\eta}{1-t\eta}+s\eta\ln\frac{s}{t}<\infty.
\tag{K.10.18f.5}
$$
Both terms are finite for every fixed positive $s,t$. Taking $s=1$ gives
$$
D(\rho_1\Vert\rho_t)
=(1-\eta)\ln\frac{1-\eta}{1-t\eta}+\eta\ln\frac1t
\longrightarrow+\infty\qquad(t\downarrow0).
\tag{K.10.18f.6}
$$
The first term converges to the finite number $(1-\eta)\ln(1-\eta)$ and the second diverges. Measuring $\{P_\Omega,I-P_\Omega\}$ gives the probability vector $(1-t\eta,t\eta)$. Its classical relative entropy is exactly (K.10.18f.5), so this admitted bounded final effect already retains the whole displayed divergence. Proposition F.10.4c.20 includes bounded final effects and the complete unconditioned output; no postselection or discarded failure record enters this witness. The states above are admissible mathematical input records of Definition F.10.4c.12. ∎

<a id="proposition-k1018g-exact-thermal-interval-loss-under-fermionic-shell-removal"></a>**Proposition K.10.18g (Exact Thermal-Interval Loss under Fermionic Shell Removal).** Let $J$ be a nonempty finite or countable set of independent fermionic excitation modes with energies $\epsilon_j>0$. In the countable case assume $\sum_j e^{-\beta\epsilon_j}<\infty$ for every $\beta>0$. On the corresponding Fock carrier let
$$
H_J=\sum_{j\in J}\epsilon_j n_j,\qquad
\rho_{J,\beta}=Z_J(\beta)^{-1}e^{-\beta H_J},\qquad
0<\beta_-<\beta_+<\infty,
\tag{K.10.18g.1}
$$
and use the entire family $\mathcal S_J=\{\rho_{J,\beta}:\beta\in[\beta_-,\beta_+]\}$ in Definition K.10.18a. Every ordered pair has finite relative entropy, and
$$
C_J=D(\rho_{J,\beta_-}\Vert\rho_{J,\beta_+})>0.
\tag{K.10.18g.2}
$$
For a partition $J=L\sqcup B$, let the actual retained channel be partial trace over $B$, followed by any fixed unitary identification $V$ of the retained carrier with its output carrier. Then
$$
\mathcal E(\rho_{J,\beta})=V\rho_{L,\beta}V^*,\qquad
C_J-C_{\mathcal E(\mathcal S_J)}=C_B.
\tag{K.10.18g.3}
$$
Set $C_\varnothing=0$. For the stated nondegenerate interval, the loss is zero exactly when $B=\varnothing$, and it is strictly positive whenever a positive-energy mode is removed. In particular, if the two independently calibrated conformal endpoint data obey $c_1=c_2>0$, a common positive scalar identification $c_i=\alpha C_i$ is incompatible with this nonempty-shell channel and full thermal family. The same conclusion holds for a common positive $a$ datum.

*Proof.* Put
$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_J(\beta)&=\log Z_J(\beta)=\sum_{j\in J}\log(1+e^{-\beta\epsilon_j}),\\
U_J(\beta)&=\sum_{j\in J}\frac{\epsilon_j}{1+e^{\beta\epsilon_j}},\\
V_J(\beta)&=\sum_{j\in J}\epsilon_j^2p_j(\beta)(1-p_j(\beta)),\qquad
p_j(\beta)=(1+e^{\beta\epsilon_j})^{-1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{K.10.18g.4}
$$
The finite formulas follow by diagonalizing the commuting occupations $n_j$. In the countable case, for every compact positive $\beta$ interval and every nonnegative integer $r$, the derivative bounds reduce to sums of $\epsilon_j^r e^{-\beta_-\epsilon_j}$, which converge because $x^r e^{-\beta_-x/2}$ is bounded and the assumed sum at $\beta_-/2$ is finite. Thus the displayed products define a trace-class Gibbs density, the sums and their needed derivatives converge uniformly, and the same identities follow by limits of finite mode sets. In particular $\ell_J'=-U_J$ and $U_J'=-V_J$.

The Gibbs logarithms give
$$
D_J(\beta,\gamma)
=(\gamma-\beta)U_J(\beta)+\ell_J(\gamma)-\ell_J(\beta).
\tag{K.10.18g.5}
$$
Every term is finite. Its partial derivatives are
$$
\partial_\beta D_J=(\beta-\gamma)V_J(\beta),\qquad
\partial_\gamma D_J=U_J(\beta)-U_J(\gamma).
\tag{K.10.18g.6}
$$
Since $V_J>0$, $U_J$ is strictly decreasing. Holding either argument fixed, the maximum over its interval occurs at an endpoint. Applying this twice leaves the two opposite corners, since the two diagonal corners have value zero.

The positive-energy assumption and $\beta>0$ give $0<p_j(\beta)<1/2$. Termwise differentiation, justified above, yields
$$
V_J'(\beta)
=-\sum_{j\in J}\epsilon_j^3p_j(\beta)(1-p_j(\beta))(1-2p_j(\beta))<0.
\tag{K.10.18g.7}
$$
Integrating $U_J'=-V_J$ in (K.10.18g.5) gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
D_J(\beta_-,\beta_+)&=\int_{\beta_-}^{\beta_+}(\beta_+-t)V_J(t)\,dt,\\
D_J(\beta_+,\beta_-)&=\int_{\beta_-}^{\beta_+}(t-\beta_-)V_J(t)\,dt.
\end{aligned}
\tag{K.10.18g.8}
$$
Write $m=(\beta_-+\beta_+)/2$ and pair the integrands at $t$ and $2m-t$. Their difference integrates to
$$
\int_{\beta_-}^{m}(\beta_-+\beta_+-2t)
\bigl[V_J(t)-V_J(\beta_-+\beta_+-t)\bigr]\,dt>0.
\tag{K.10.18g.9}
$$
Both factors are strictly positive inside that half interval. The hot-to-cold corner is therefore the unique larger corner, proving (K.10.18g.2).

The Fock tensor factorization for $J=L\sqcup B$ gives $H_J=H_L\otimes I+I\otimes H_B$ and $\rho_{J,\beta}=\rho_{L,\beta}\otimes\rho_{B,\beta}$. The partial trace has the declared output on every state; its displayed action on the family is consequently an entire channel calculation. Additivity of (K.10.18g.5), or substitution of the sums in (K.10.18g.4), gives
$$
D_J(\beta,\gamma)=D_L(\beta,\gamma)+D_B(\beta,\gamma).
$$
Equation (K.10.18g.2) selects the same ordered maximizing endpoints in each nonempty factor. Unitary invariance then proves (K.10.18g.3), including an empty factor. A nonempty $B$ has $C_B>0$ by (K.10.18g.8), proving the strict/equality criterion. Finally, a common positive $\alpha$ and $c_1=c_2$ would imply $C_1=C_2$, contradicting the strict loss. Replacing $c$ by $a$ gives the last assertion. ∎

For the antiperiodic massless Dirac torus spectrum $\epsilon_{n}=2\pi|n+(1/2,1/2,1/2)|/L$, with four excitation polarizations per Dirac species, the summability hypothesis follows from cubic lattice counting and exponential decay. A scale identification $L\mapsto L/b$, $\beta\mapsto\beta/b$ preserves all products $\beta\epsilon_n$ and hence the displayed relative entropies and diameters after its retained mode identification. Such a unitary identification cannot undo a preceding nonempty-shell loss. Taking a discarded shell to infinite energy can instead make its loss tend to zero; that regulator limit requires a separate identification of distinct operational endpoint scales and of the complete stress/metric responses.

<a id="theorem-k1018h-dirac-mass-flow-endpoint-channel-and-its-predictive-diameters"></a>**Theorem K.10.18h (Dirac Mass-Flow Endpoint Channel and Its Predictive Diameters).** Fix integers $N\ge M\ge1$, a physical mass $m>0$, a reference period $\ell>0$ and a compact inverse-temperature interval $0<\theta_-<\theta_+$. The source consists of $M$ massless and $N-M$ mass-$m$ four-component Dirac species, each with the periodic Wilson Hamiltonian of Proposition B.3a.1 and an onsite mass term. For every odd $n\ge5$, Part 2 of the proof fixes a fine source at scale $k_U=mn^{12}$, with physical period $\ell/k_U$ and $n^3$ sites per side, and a coarse source at scale $k_I=m/n^2$, with physical period $\ell/k_I$ and $n$ sites per side; the dimensionless masses are $r_U=m/k_U=n^{-12}$ and $r_I=m/k_I=n^2$. In Definition K.10.18a take $k_1=k_U$, $k_2=k_I$, the branch family $\mathcal S_{U,n}=\{\rho_{U,n}(\theta):\theta\in[\theta_-,\theta_+]\}$ of all Gibbs states of the fine source at inverse temperature $\theta/k_U$, and the channel $\mathcal E_n$ of Part 3: a fixed mode transfer followed by the partial trace over the $N-M$ massive species and over the light momentum shell outside the coarse grid. No step of $\mathcal E_n$ depends on $\theta$, and the receiver retains the full light field algebra.

For a mesh $\delta$ with $\ell/\delta$ an odd integer and a mass ratio $r\ge0$ let $\Gamma_\delta=(2\pi/\ell)\mathbb Z^3\cap(-\pi/\delta,\pi/\delta)^3$ be the momentum grid and
$$
E_{\delta,r}(p)=\Bigl[\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{\sin^2(\delta p_i)}{\delta^2}
 +\Bigl(r+\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{1-\cos(\delta p_i)}{\delta}\Bigr)^2\Bigr]^{1/2}
$$
the dimensionless Wilson excitation energy. Write $\delta_f=\ell/n^3$, $\delta_c=\ell/n$, $\Gamma_f=\Gamma_{\delta_f}$, $\Gamma_c=\Gamma_{\delta_c}\subset\Gamma_f$, and put
$$
d(e)=\frac{(\theta_+-\theta_-)e}{1+e^{\theta_-e}}
 +\log(1+e^{-\theta_+e})-\log(1+e^{-\theta_-e}),\qquad
q_\delta(r)=4\sum_{p\in\Gamma_\delta}d(E_{\delta,r}(p)),\qquad
q=4\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}}d(2\pi|z|/\ell).
\tag{K.10.18h.1}
$$
The number $q$ is finite and positive. Write $C_{U,n}$ and $C_{I,n}$ for the diameters (K.10.23) of $\mathcal S_{U,n}$ and of $\mathcal E_n(\mathcal S_{U,n})$.

1. At every finite stage both diameters are attained at the hot-to-cold pair, $C_{U,n}=D(\rho_{U,n}(\theta_-)\Vert\rho_{U,n}(\theta_+))$ and $C_{I,n}=D(\mathcal E_n\rho_{U,n}(\theta_-)\Vert\mathcal E_n\rho_{U,n}(\theta_+))$, and
$$
C_{U,n}=Mq_{\delta_f}(0)+(N-M)q_{\delta_f}(r_U),\qquad
C_{I,n}=4M\sum_{p\in\Gamma_c}d(E_{\delta_f,0}(p)).
\tag{K.10.18h.2}
$$
The loss is $C_{U,n}-C_{I,n}=(N-M)q_{\delta_f}(r_U)+4M\sum_{p\in\Gamma_f\setminus\Gamma_c}d(E_{\delta_f,0}(p))>0$.

2. With the explicit convergence bounds of Part 4,
$$
C_U=\lim_{n\to\infty}C_{U,n}=Nq,\qquad
C_I=\lim_{n\to\infty}C_{I,n}=Mq,\qquad
C_U-C_I=(N-M)q.
\tag{K.10.18h.3}
$$
The Gibbs family of one mass-$m$ species on the coarse lattice has diameter $q_{\delta_c}(r_I)\le4n^3(\theta_+-\theta_-)\bigl[r_I+B\sqrt3\,\pi n/\ell\bigr]e^{-\theta_-r_I}$ with $B=1+\sqrt3\,\pi/2$, which tends to zero; hence the Gibbs family of all $N$ species on the coarse lattice has the same limiting diameter $Mq$ as the channel image.

3. At every finite stage the loss is positive and no channel recovers both states of the maximizing pair from their images. The limiting loss $(N-M)q$ is positive exactly when $N>M$; for $N=M$ the finite loss is that of the removed light shell and tends to zero, so $C_U=C_I$. The Petz map $\mathcal R_n$ of $\mathcal E_n$ at the reference state $\rho_{U,n}(\theta_+)$ satisfies $\lVert\mathcal R_n\mathcal E_n\rho_{U,n}(\theta)-\rho_{U,n}(\theta)\rVert_1\le\sqrt{2(C_{U,n}-C_{I,n})}$ for every $\theta\in[\theta_-,\theta_+]$, a bound that tends to zero exactly when $N=M$.

4. Let $e_j$ be the $4Mn^3$ excitation energies of the light output and $\mu_n=2^{-4Mn^3}\exp[-\theta_+\sum_je_j]$. If states $\rho'(\theta)$ satisfy $\lVert\rho'(\theta)-\mathcal E_n\rho_{U,n}(\theta)\rVert_1\le\epsilon_n\le\mu_n/4$ for every $\theta$, then every ordered relative entropy of the family $\{\rho'(\theta)\}$ differs from the corresponding one of $\mathcal E_n(\mathcal S_{U,n})$ by at most $\epsilon_n[2|\log(\mu_n/2)|+4/\mu_n]$.

For $\ell=m=1$, $[\theta_-,\theta_+]=[1,2]$, $N=2$, $M=1$ one has $q=0.2969645\ldots$, $C_{U,5}=0.5939500\ldots$ and $C_{I,5}=0.2969656\ldots$. The limits (K.10.18h.3) are multiples of one species diameter because the Gibbs family is a product over species and modes and the channel traces whole species; the scale exponents, the temperature interval and the channel are chosen by the construction. Consequently any datum that is additive over independent species and takes the value $c_\psi$ on one massless Dirac species equals $(c_\psi/q)\,C_i$, $i\in\{U,I\}$, on the endpoint theories of $N$ and of $M$ massless species: for the limiting data the conversion constants of (K.10.18e.1) are $c_\psi/q$ for $c$ and $a_\psi/q$ for $a$ at both endpoints, where the per-species central values $c_\psi$ and $a_\psi$ are inputs.

*Proof.* Parts 1–3 fix the field family, the scale sequence and the channel. Part 4 computes the finite diameters and proves their limits and the heavy comparison bound. Part 5 relates the sequence to the free mass flow. Part 6 proves the stability bound of item 4 and Part 7 the strictness, equality and recovery statements of item 3.

#### 1. Parameters and field family

Fix integers $N\ge M\ge 1$, a physical mass $m>0$, a reference coordinate period $\ell>0$, and an entire nondegenerate compact inverse-temperature interval $0<\theta_-<\theta_+$. Natural units $\hbar=c=1$ are those of Proposition B.3a.1.

The source has $M$ massless four-component Dirac species and $N-M$ species with the same fixed physical mass $m$. All have the standard normalized first-order kinetic term. On a periodic cube of physical period $L$ with an odd number $n_s\ge 5$ of sites per side and mesh $a=L/n_s$, each species has the one-particle Hamiltonian

$$
h_{a,L,m_s}(p) = \sum_i \alpha_i \sin(a p_i)/a + \beta_D [m_s + \sum_i (1-\cos(a p_i))/a],
$$

where $m_s$ is $0$ or $m$, $p$ runs over the $n_s^3$ momenta of $(2\pi/L)\mathbb{Z}^3$ in the Brillouin cube, and the many-body Hamiltonian is $d\Gamma(h)$. At $m_s=0$ the symbol is (B.3a.1.1). The Clifford relations give $h^2=[\sum_i\sin^2(ap_i)/a^2+(W_a(p)+m_s)^2]\,I$ with $W_a(p)=\sum_i(1-\cos(ap_i))/a$, so each momentum carries the eigenvalues $+E$ and $-E$ of the traceless matrix $h$, each twice, where $E\ge 0$ is the square root of the bracket. In particle/hole coordinates the Gibbs state of $d\Gamma(h)$ at inverse temperature $\beta$ is therefore the product, over the four excitation modes of every momentum, of Bernoulli occupations $f_\beta(E)$, $f_\beta(e)=1/(1+\exp(\beta e))$. A scalar shift of the Hamiltonian cancels from every normalized density.

#### 2. Scale sequence

For every odd integer $n\ge 5$, put

$$
n_c=n,\quad n_f=n^3,\quad \delta_c=\ell/n,\quad \delta_f=\ell/n^3,
$$

$$
k_U=m n^{12},\quad k_I=m/n^2,\quad r_U=m/k_U=n^{-12},\quad r_I=m/k_I=n^2.
$$

The fine and coarse physical geometries and thermal parameters are

$$
L_U=\ell/k_U,\quad a_U=\delta_f/k_U,\quad \beta_U(\theta)=\theta/k_U,
$$

$$
L_I=\ell/k_I,\quad a_I=\delta_c/k_I,\quad \beta_I(\theta)=\theta/k_I.
$$

Write $h_\delta(r)$ for the symbol of Part 1 with mesh $\delta$, period $\ell$ and mass $r$, $E_{\delta,r}(p)$ for its excitation energy, $W_\delta(p)$ for its Wilson term and $\Gamma_\delta$ for its momentum grid, a subset of $(2\pi/\ell)\mathbb{Z}^3$. Then $h_{a_U,L_U,m_s}(k_Up)=k_U\,h_{\delta_f}(m_s/k_U)(p)$, and likewise at the coarse scale. The fine field Hamiltonian is

$$
H_{U,\mathrm{field}}=k_U\Bigl[\sum_{s\le M} d\Gamma_s(h_{\delta_f}(0))+\sum_{M<s\le N} d\Gamma_s(h_{\delta_f}(r_U))\Bigr],
$$

and the coarse field Hamiltonian is

$$
H_{I,\mathrm{field}}=k_I \sum_{s\le M} d\Gamma_s(h_{\delta_c}(0)).
$$

Since $\beta_U(\theta)H_{U,\mathrm{field}}$ is $\theta$ times the dimensionless generator in brackets, the Gibbs state $\rho_{U,n}(\theta)$ of the fine source at $\beta_U(\theta)$ is the dimensionless Gibbs state at $\theta$. The input family $S_{U,n}$ consists of these states for $\theta$ in $[\theta_-,\theta_+]$. The massive symbol $h_{\delta_c}(r_I)$ is used only in the heavy comparison of Part 4, not as a retained coarse quantum field.

The fine physical momentum cutoff is of order $k_U/\delta_f$, which tends to infinity. The coarse physical cutoff is of order $k_I/\delta_c=m/(\ell n)$, which tends to zero and is eventually below $m$. Both dimensionless momentum cutoffs diverge. The physical boxes change with $n$.

The parameter $k$ sets the thermal and geometric probe scale; the finer/coarser resolution ordering is witnessed by the physical meshes. Each finite pair has $k_U>k_I$, $a_U<a_I$ and a literal momentum shell removed in Part 3. Definition K.10.18a is applied with $k_1=k_U$ and $k_2=k_I$.

#### 3. The channel and its retained algebra

Use the excitation-mode basis of each finite Hamiltonian, including its filled-negative reference. The fine and coarse dimensionless Fourier grids contain the same coarse labels $p=2\pi z/\ell$, $z_i=-(n-1)/2,\dots,(n-1)/2$; these labels form the coarse grid $\Gamma_c=\Gamma_{\delta_c}$, a literal subset of the fine grid $\Gamma_f=\Gamma_{\delta_f}$, and the fine shell is its complement in $\Gamma_f$.

The channel `E_n` is defined on every density matrix of the fine carrier:

1. Apply the fixed finite mode-separation unitary `U_n` for the fine Hamiltonian.
2. Transfer the four excitation modes of every coarse momentum label for each of the `M` massless species to their assigned target modes.
3. Trace over all `N-M` massive fine species and the retained species' fine shell.
4. Apply the fixed coarse mode rotation. The retained output is the full light field algebra only; the massive factors and the shell form the discarded complement.

In formulas $E_n(\omega)=V_n\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{dis}}(U_n\omega U_n^*)V_n^*$, where $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{dis}}$ is the partial trace of step 3 and $V_n$ is the unitary identification of steps 2 and 4, which acts on the retained modes only.

The fine/coarse spinor identification is fixed canonically. At each nonzero retained momentum $p$ write $h_f=h_{\delta_f}(0)(p)$, $h_c=h_{\delta_c}(0)(p)$ with energies $E_f,E_c$, and let $P=(I+h_f/E_f)/2$, $Q=(I+h_c/E_c)/2$, $A=QP+(I-Q)(I-P)$, and $T=A(A^*A)^{-1/2}$. On the coarse labels $|\delta_cp_i|<\pi$, so both sine vectors have the signs of the components of $p$, and both Wilson terms are nonnegative. The normalized fine/coarse Wilson Clifford vectors therefore have nonnegative dot product, so $\lVert P-Q\rVert\le 1/\sqrt{2}$, $A^*A=I-(P-Q)^2\ge I/2$, and the inverse square root exists uniformly. The unitary $T$ maps the spectral subspaces of $h_f$ onto those of $h_c$. Put $T=I$ on the original zero block. Its finite second quantization on the retained modes is the identification $V_n$. By (K.10.18g.3) the diameters of Part 4 are the same for every fixed unitary identification.

No step of the channel depends on `theta`.

The retained coarse algebra is the full light field algebra of the target, with every field outcome and every noncommuting response retained. Labels that are the same for every `theta` can be adjoined and contribute zero relative entropy. If an implementation exposes a `theta`-dependent record at the receiver, it is a different retained algebra and the diameter below must be recomputed.

By Part 1 every input state is a product of Bernoulli occupations over the fine excitation modes, and the channel keeps the factors of the light species on the coarse labels. In excitation coordinates the exact output family on the light carrier is therefore

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{out},n}(\theta) = \bigotimes_{s\le M,\,p\in\Gamma_c,\,\mathrm{polarization}} \operatorname{Bernoulli}[f_\theta(E_{\delta_f,0}(p))].
$$

The coarse Wilson Gibbs state instead uses $E_{\delta_c,0}(p)$; the two are not equated at finite $n$. The family at the coarse endpoint is $E_n(S_{U,n})$, as Definition K.10.18a prescribes.

#### 4. Exact finite predictive diameters and endpoint convergence

For an excitation energy $e\ge 0$, set

$$
d(e) = (\theta_+-\theta_-)\,e/(1+\exp(\theta_- e)) + \log(1+\exp(-\theta_+ e)) - \log(1+\exp(-\theta_- e)).
$$

By (K.10.18g.5), $d(e)=D(\rho(\theta_-)\,\|\,\rho(\theta_+))$ for one excitation mode of energy $e$; it is positive for $e>0$. For $e=0$ it is zero: every periodic zero mode is a maximally mixed two-level factor at the massless endpoint for every $\theta$.

For a finite spectrum, the corner proof of Proposition K.10.18g applies to its positive energies; fixed zero-energy factors contribute zero. Write $q_\delta(r)=4\sum_{p\in\Gamma_\delta}d(E_{\delta,r}(p))$. Then the full fine diameter and the output diameter are exactly

$$
C_{U,n} = M q_{\delta_f}(0) + (N-M)\,q_{\delta_f}(r_U),
$$

$$
C_{I,n} = 4M \sum_{p\in\Gamma_c} d(E_{\delta_f,0}(p)).
$$

Both suprema are attained at the hot-to-cold pair, the states at $\theta_-$ and $\theta_+$ in the order $D(\rho(\theta_-)\,\|\,\rho(\theta_+))$. The data-processing loss is exactly

$$
C_{U,n}-C_{I,n} = (N-M)\,q_{\delta_f}(r_U) + 4M \sum_{p\in\text{fine shell}} d(E_{\delta_f,0}(p)).
$$

This identity uses the entire input and output density families; it is (K.10.18g.3) with the massive species and the fine shell as the discarded mode set. The fine shell is nonempty and all its energies are positive, so the loss is strictly positive at every finite stage.

Define the fixed compact-volume continuum datum

$$
q = 4 \sum_{z\in\mathbb{Z}^3,\ z\ne 0} d(2\pi|z|/\ell).
$$

It is finite and positive: the bound $d(e)\le(\theta_+-\theta_-)\,e\,\exp(-\theta_-e)$ proved below and the cubic growth of the number of lattice points in a ball give convergence, and any nonzero momentum supplies a strictly positive summand. It is independent of $N,M,m,k_U,k_I$.

##### Full-band estimates

For $p$ in $\Gamma_\delta$ and $r_p=|p|$, the massless Wilson energies satisfy the full-band bounds

$$
(2/\pi)\, r_p \le E_{\delta,0}(p) \le B r_p,\quad B=1+\sqrt{3}\,\pi/2,
$$

$$
|E_{\delta,0}(p)-r_p| \le (7/12)\,\delta^2 r_p^3.
$$

The lower bound and the remainder are (B.3a.3.6) at mesh $\delta$. The upper bound follows from $|\sin(\delta p_i)|/\delta\le|p_i|$ and $W_\delta(p)\le\delta|p|^2/2$, with $\delta|p|\le\sqrt{3}\pi$ throughout the band. Since $d'(e)=\theta_+[f_{\theta_-}(e)-f_{\theta_+}(e)]-(\theta_+-\theta_-)\theta_-e\,f_{\theta_-}(e)[1-f_{\theta_-}(e)]$ and $0\le f_{\theta_+}(e)\le f_{\theta_-}(e)\le\exp(-\theta_-e)$,

$$
|d'(e)| \le [2\theta_+ +(\theta_+-\theta_-)\theta_- e]\exp(-\theta_- e).
$$

Moreover $0\le d(e)\le(\theta_+-\theta_-)\,e\,\exp(-\theta_-e)$, because $d$ is a relative entropy, its two logarithmic terms have nonpositive sum and $f_{\theta_-}(e)\le\exp(-\theta_-e)$. Every energy between $E_{\delta,0}(p)$ and $r_p$ lies in $[(2/\pi)r_p,Br_p]$, so the mean-value theorem gives

$$
|d(E_{\delta,0}(p))-d(r_p)| \le (7/12)\,\delta^2 r_p^3 [2\theta_+ +(\theta_+-\theta_-)\theta_- B r_p]\exp[-(2/\pi)\theta_- r_p].
$$

Summing over `Gamma_delta` and bounding the terms of `q` outside it,

$$
\begin{aligned}
|q_\delta(0)-q| &\le (7/3)\,\delta^2 \sum_{p\in\Gamma_\delta} r_p^3 [2\theta_+ +(\theta_+-\theta_-)\theta_- B r_p]\exp[-(2/\pi)\theta_- r_p] \\
&\quad + 4(\theta_+-\theta_-) \sum_{p\notin\Gamma_\delta} r_p\exp(-\theta_- r_p).
\end{aligned}
$$

The first sum is at most the convergent sum over $(2\pi/\ell)\mathbb{Z}^3$, and the second is the tail of a convergent series; both depend only on $\ell,\theta_-,\theta_+$. Hence $q_\delta(0)\to q$ as $\delta\to 0$.

For every $r\ge 0$, $0\le E_{\delta,r}(p)-E_{\delta,0}(p)\le r$, because $E_{\delta,r}^2-E_{\delta,0}^2=2rW_\delta+r^2$ and $E_{\delta,0}\ge W_\delta\ge 0$. For $0\le r\le 1$ every energy between them is at least $(2/\pi)r_p$ and at most $Br_p+1$, so the same derivative estimate gives the cutoff-uniform bound

$$
|q_\delta(r)-q_\delta(0)| \le 4r \sum_{p\in(2\pi/\ell)\mathbb{Z}^3} [2\theta_+ +(\theta_+-\theta_-)\theta_- (B r_p+1)]\exp[-(2/\pi)\theta_- r_p],
$$

which includes the four zero modes. Hence $q_{\delta_f}(r_U)\to q$.

A removed light shell lies outside a cube whose smallest excluded $|p|$ grows linearly in $n$. By the bound on $d$ and the full-band bounds, its exact diameter is at most

$$
4M(\theta_+-\theta_-)B \sum_{p\notin\Gamma_c} r_p\exp[-(2/\pi)\theta_- r_p],
$$

the tail of a convergent lattice series, and tends to zero.

Consequently

$$
C_U=\lim C_{U,n}=Nq,\quad C_I=\lim C_{I,n}=Mq,\quad C_U-C_I=(N-M)q.
$$

These are direct relative-entropy formulas.

##### Heavy comparison family at the coarse scale

For the comparison Gibbs family of one massive species on the coarse lattice at mass ratio $r_I$, every excitation energy obeys $E_{\delta_c,r_I}(p)\ge r_I$, and

$$
E_{\delta_c,r_I}(p)\le r_I+B|p| \le r_I+B\sqrt{3}\,\pi/\delta_c.
$$

The coarse source contains only the $M$ light fields. The coarse lattice has $4n^3$ excitation modes per species, so by the bound on $d$ the comparison family's entire thermal diameter satisfies

$$
q_{\delta_c}(r_I) \le 4n^3(\theta_+-\theta_-)[r_I+B\sqrt{3}\,\pi/\delta_c]\exp(-\theta_- r_I).
$$

With $r_I=n^2$ and $\delta_c=\ell/n$, this tends to zero: the massive species carry vanishing thermal distinguishability at the coarse scale, even though $D(\rho_{\mathrm{thermal}}\,\|\,\text{ground})=\infty$ at every finite stage. The massless estimate at $\delta=\delta_c$ gives $q_{\delta_c}(0)\to q$, so the Gibbs family of all $N$ species on the coarse lattice has diameter $Mq_{\delta_c}(0)+(N-M)q_{\delta_c}(r_I)\to Mq$, the limit of the channel image.

#### 5. Relation to the relevant mass flow

The continuum action of the source, in fixed physical units, is the free Dirac action with masses $0$ and $m$. Under the explicit coordinate/field identification $y=kx$, $\psi(x)=k^{3/2}\psi_k(y)$, its dimensionless mass is $r=m/k$. The kinetic coefficient stays one. The operator $\bar{\psi}\psi$ has engineering dimension three, so the free relevant mass has exact dimension one and $dr/d\log k=-r$; there is no interaction correction in this free source.

The scale sequence evaluates this flow at $r_U=n^{-12}$ and $r_I=n^2$. The ultraviolet scaling limit $r\to 0$ is the $N$-species massless Dirac action; at the infrared end the massive species have the vanishing thermal diameter of Part 4.

The channel of Part 3 additionally removes a literal light momentum shell. Its positive thermal loss tends to zero because that shell escapes every fixed dimensionless thermal budget. The massive-sector loss tends to $(N-M)q$. The species and shell trace thereby realizes the endpoint channel between the operational scales $k_U>k_I$.

#### 6. Stability of the finite diameters under trace-norm error

Preserving the relative-entropy diameter requires a spectral floor in addition to uniform trace-norm error. On the finite light output, the family of Part 3 has a uniform positive eigenvalue floor. Let $e_j$ be its $4Mn^3$ excitation energies. Every eigenvalue is a product of factors $f_\theta(e_j)$ or $1-f_\theta(e_j)$, each at least $\exp(-\theta_+e_j)/2$, so one explicit floor is

$$
\mu_n=2^{-4Mn^3}\exp[-\theta_+ \sum_j e_j].
$$

Let a delivered family lie within trace norm $\epsilon_n\le\mu_n/4$ of this family, state by state. The operator norm is at most the trace norm, so ideal and delivered eigenvalues are at least $\mu_n/2$. For positive matrices $A,B\ge\mu_n/2$, the logarithm integral $\log A-\log B=\int_0^\infty(B+s)^{-1}(A-B)(A+s)^{-1}\,ds$ gives $\lVert\log A-\log B\rVert\le 2\lVert A-B\rVert/\mu_n$. Write $\rho',\sigma'$ for delivered and $\rho,\sigma$ for ideal states. Then $D(\rho'\,\|\,\sigma')-D(\rho\,\|\,\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho'-\rho)(\log\rho'-\log\sigma')+\operatorname{Tr}\rho[(\log\rho'-\log\rho)-(\log\sigma'-\log\sigma)]$; the first term is at most $2\epsilon_n|\log(\mu_n/2)|$ and the second at most $4\epsilon_n/\mu_n$, which gives the uniform continuity bound

$$
|D(\rho'\,\|\,\sigma')-D(\rho\,\|\,\sigma)| \le \epsilon_n [2|\log(\mu_n/2)|+4/\mu_n].
$$

With errors for which the right-hand side is at most $2^{-n}$, the delivered finite diameters converge to the same endpoint $Mq$. This is a finite precision requirement at every stage. No pure appended heavy factor is retained, so the spectral-floor bound applies to the entire light output.

#### 7. Strictness, equality and recovery

At every finite stage the loss of Part 4 is strictly positive. If a channel recovered both states of the maximizing hot-to-cold pair from their images, monotonicity of relative entropy under that channel would give $C_{U,n}\le C_{I,n}$; hence the pair has no recovery channel. For $N>M$ the limiting loss $(N-M)q$ is strictly positive. If $N=M$, the channel removes only the escaping light shell, whose loss tends to zero, so $C_U=C_I$. In excitation coordinates the input state is $\rho_{\mathrm{ret}}(\theta)\otimes\rho_{\mathrm{dis}}(\theta)$, the retained and the discarded factor, and the reference $\rho_{U,n}(\theta_+)$ is faithful. The adjoint of $E_n$ is $X\mapsto U_n^*(V_n^*XV_n\otimes I)U_n$, so the Petz map of $E_n$ at this reference is $R_n(\tau)=U_n^*(V_n^*\tau V_n\otimes\rho_{\mathrm{dis}}(\theta_+))U_n$: it undoes the output unitary and appends $\rho_{\mathrm{dis}}(\theta_+)$. Applied to the image of the input state at $\theta$, it returns $\rho_{\mathrm{ret}}(\theta)\otimes\rho_{\mathrm{dis}}(\theta_+)$ in excitation coordinates, whose trace-norm distance from the input is

$$
\lVert\rho_{\mathrm{dis}}(\theta)-\rho_{\mathrm{dis}}(\theta_+)\rVert_1 \le \sqrt{2D(\rho_{\mathrm{dis}}(\theta)\,\|\,\rho_{\mathrm{dis}}(\theta_+))} \le \sqrt{2(C_{U,n}-C_{I,n})}
$$

by Pinsker's inequality and because the loss is the diameter of the discarded family, (K.10.18g.3). For $N=M$ this recovery error tends to zero uniformly on the interval. The map returns $\rho_{U,n}(\theta_+)$ exactly; it returns the other maximizing state $\rho_{U,n}(\theta_-)$ exactly only if no positive-energy factor is discarded, which holds at no finite stage. This is the source-specific strict/equality result; Corollary K.10.18d owns the general fact that equal diameters do not force family sufficiency.

The source has a dimension-one relevant mass, and the channel removes whole independent massive species together with an escaping light momentum shell. Part 4 proves items 1 and 2, Part 7 item 3 and Part 6 item 4. ∎

<a id="proposition-k1018i"></a>

<a id="proposition-k1018i-separated-static-shear-excludes-lapse-only-calibration"></a>**Proposition K.10.18i (Separated Static Shear Excludes Lapse-Only Calibration).** Retain the flat source, the complete Gibbs family and the channel of Theorem K.10.18h. An extension in which the fermionic Hamiltonian couples to the lapse alone can reproduce the symmetric allocation (B.3a.1.2) exactly on every lattice. Its static metric Hessian differs from that of the covariant massless Dirac action at the infrared endpoint on two disjoint spatial shear supports, at every temperature in the prescribed interval. The same obstruction applies when the spatial shear reaches the fermions through a local scalar lapse encoding that is equivariant under translations along the shear slabs and reflection of one transverse coordinate. Metric-only local controls contribute zero on the witness pair.

*Proof.* Use dimensionless box and time coordinates as in Theorem K.10.18h. At either regulator write $h_a$ for the full flat Wilson one-particle Hamiltonian, including the onsite species masses, and let $N_a=\sum_x N(x)P_x$ for a positive lapse $N$. The extension
$$
h_a(N,\gamma)=N_a^{1/2}h_aN_a^{1/2},\qquad
\left.\frac{\partial h_a}{\partial N(x)}\right|_{N=1,\gamma=\delta}=\tfrac12\{P_x,h_a\}
\tag{K.10.18i.1}
$$
is Hermitian and has the same spatial range as $h_a$. At the flat input it gives $h_a$ exactly, so the original preparation record, energy current and channel are all available with the same values. At fixed lapse it is constant in the spatial metric $\gamma$. A metric-only local control, including a contact term with finitely many derivatives, has its Hessian supported on the spatial diagonal. A finite-range lattice scalar control with fixed range in lattice units also has zero mixed variation on two fixed separated supports once its stencil diameter is smaller than their separation.

For the continuum witness let $x=(\tau,x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with periodic space of period $\ell$ and thermal antiperiodic spinors of time period $\theta\in[\theta_-,\theta_+]$. Write $W=-\log Z$ for the covariant Dirac functional. A static direction $\delta\gamma_{23}=\delta\gamma_{32}=f(x_1)$ at fixed lapse couples linearly to $\int fT_{23}$. For two disjoint supports the mixed Hessian of $W$ is the negative integrated connected $T_{23}$ covariance: the second action derivative and local changes of prescription are supported on the diagonal. The shear directions are transverse and traceless at the flat metric. For one Dirac species define the covariance integrated over relative time and the two transverse coordinates,
$$
B_\theta(r)=\int_{-\theta/2}^{\theta/2}\!d\tau\int_{\mathbb T^2_\ell}\!d^2v\;
\langle T_{23}(\tau,r,v)T_{23}(0)\rangle_{\theta,c},\qquad 0<|r|<\ell/2.
\tag{K.10.18i.2}
$$

In flat Euclidean space the covariant Dirac stress two-point function at separated points has coefficient $C_T=2/\pi^4$ in the tensor $(I_{\mu\rho}I_{\nu\sigma}+I_{\mu\sigma}I_{\nu\rho})/2-\delta_{\mu\nu}\delta_{\rho\sigma}/4$, times $|x|^{-8}$, where $I_{\mu\nu}=\delta_{\mu\nu}-2x_\mu x_\nu/|x|^2$. This is the canonical symmetric Dirac stress from the minimally coupled spin action. The flat stress and its free-field normalization are given in Osborn and Petkou (1994, equations (2.23), (5.2) and (5.6)). In the $23,23$ component write $A=\tau^2+r^2$ and $\rho=|v|$. Angular averaging over $v$ gives $C_T A^2/[2(A+\rho^2)^6]$, using the angular mean $\langle v_2^2v_3^2\rangle=\rho^4/8$. The transverse integral is $\pi C_T/(10A^3)$ and $\int_{\mathbb R}d\tau\,(\tau^2+r^2)^{-3}=3\pi/(8|r|^5)$. The flat integrated result is therefore $3\pi^2C_T/(80|r|^5)$.

To compare at the finite thermal period, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in the four-dimensional ball of radius $2\eta$ and equal to one in the ball of radius $\eta$, with $0<8\eta<\min(\theta_-,\ell)$. Let $D=\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu$, $S_0(x)=\gamma\cdot x/(2\pi^2|x|^4)$ and $F=(\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\chi)S_0$. The thermal Dirac Green function is $S_\theta=\chi S_0-D_\theta^{-1}F$. Indeed $D(\chi S_0)=\delta+F$, and all Fourier momenta obey $|p|\ge\pi/\theta_+$. The spinor Fourier multiplier of $D_\theta^{-1}$ has norm at most $\theta_+/\pi$. For derivatives through order two a common bound on $D_\theta^{-1}F$ is
$$
L=\frac{\theta_+\|(1-\Delta)^5F\|_{L^1}}{\pi\theta_-\ell^3}
\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z,\,b\in\mathbb Z^3}
\left[1+\frac{\pi^2(2j+1)^2}{\theta_+^2}+\frac{4\pi^2|b|^2}{\ell^2}\right]^{-4}<\infty.
\tag{K.10.18i.3}
$$
Here the $L^1$ norm uses the fixed cutoff chart. Each differentiated factor contributes at most $(1+|p|^2)$, accounted for by the exponent $-4$ in the bound.

At separated points the connected Wick contractions of the two stress insertions contain products of two propagator factors with two derivatives distributed between them. Inside the inner ball replacing $S_0$ by $S_\theta$ thus changes the covariance by a sum bounded by a constant times $1+|x|^{-5}$. The bound follows from $L$ and the first two derivatives of $S_0$, which are homogeneous of degrees $-4$ and $-5$. Outside that ball the differentiated thermal propagators are uniformly bounded by (K.10.18i.3) and the derivatives of $\chi S_0$ on the cutoff annulus. For $|r|<\eta/2$ the flat covariance integral outside the inner ball is uniformly bounded as well, by integrating its $|x|^{-8}$ decay away from the ball. Finally $\int_{\mathbb R^3}(|r|^2+|w|^2)^{-5/2}\,d^3w=4\pi/(3|r|^2)$. It follows that
$$
B_\theta(r)=\frac{3}{40\pi^2|r|^5}+O_{\theta_-,\theta_+,\ell,\chi}(|r|^{-2})
\tag{K.10.18i.4}
$$
uniformly in $\theta$ as $r\to0$. This uses the local Dirac singularity on the actual compact geometry and requires no limit of the temperature or period.

Choose a fixed $r_*>0$ so small that the leading term in (K.10.18i.4) bounds twice the error for $r\in[r_*/2,3r_*/2]$. Choose nonzero nonnegative smooth periodic $f,g$ supported in intervals of radius $r_*/8$ about $r_*$ and $0$, respectively. The mixed static Hessian of $W$ on these directions is $-M\theta\ell^2\int f(x_1)g(y_1)B_\theta(x_1-y_1)\,dx_1\,dy_1$, strictly negative on the entire interval. The lapse-only extension gives zero on the same pair. This distinguishes the distributions and hence their Fourier coefficients, since a distribution on the compact product of spatial tori is determined by its Fourier coefficients. In particular a fixed local response cannot repair agreement even if tests are stated on trigonometric-polynomial directions. With a regulator-dependent flat translation-invariant contact response of uniformly bounded derivative order the same conclusion holds: its Fourier coefficient on a pair of opposite momenta is a bounded-degree polynomial in the momentum, and the space of those polynomials is closed under pointwise convergence on the reciprocal lattice by finite interpolation.

For the scalar encoding variant, write $N=\mathcal N(\gamma)$ with $\mathcal N(\delta)=1$. The first variation for either slab shear is independent of the transverse coordinates by translation equivariance. Reflection of $x_2$ leaves that scalar output unchanged and reverses the shear, so $D\mathcal N$ vanishes on each of the two directions. Locality gives $D^2\mathcal N[f,g]=0$ on disjoint supports. Both terms in the Hessian chain rule for $W_a[\mathcal N(\gamma)]$ then vanish, as does the contribution of the local controls. This yields the same separated witness. ∎

<a id="corollary-k1018i1"></a>

<a id="corollary-k1018i1-noncontact-weyl-coefficient-on-the-continuum-endpoints"></a>**Corollary K.10.18i.1 (Noncontact Weyl Coefficient on the Continuum Endpoints).** In the convention in which the Weyl-squared term of the four-dimensional trace anomaly is $c\,\mathcal W^2/(16\pi^2)$, the integrated static shear covariance of $n_D$ covariantly coupled massless Dirac species satisfies
$$
\frac{2\pi^2}{3}|r|^5 B_\theta^{(n_D)}(r)
=\frac{n_D}{20}+O(|r|^3),
\tag{K.10.18i.5}
$$
uniformly on the compact temperature interval of Proposition K.10.18i. The left side uses only the covariance at distinct spatial arguments and is invariant under additions of local metric counterterms. It gives the continuum readouts $c_U=N/20$ and $c_I=M/20$ on the massless species endpoints designated by the mass-flow comparison.

*Proof.* The Ward normalization relating the flat stress two-point coefficient to the Weyl-squared trace anomaly is $c=\pi^4 C_T/40$ in these conventions. This follows from the Weyl coefficient in equations (8.1) and (8.12) of Osborn and Petkou (1994), with $\beta_a=-c/(16\pi^2)$. The integrated covariance per species has leading coefficient $3\pi^2 C_T/80$ by (K.10.18i.4). Independent species add in the connected covariance. The stated rescaling gives $c$ with the uniform $O(|r|^3)$ error. A finite local metric functional changes the Hessian only at coincident points and therefore contributes zero to the separated covariance. The lattice-to-continuum convergence of the spatial shear port still requires a physical lattice metric vertex. The static two-point readout supplies the Weyl coefficient, while the Euler coefficient requires a separate response. ∎

<a id="corollary-k1018j"></a>

<a id="corollary-k1018j-separated-static-lapse-readout-of-the-dirac-euler-coefficient"></a>**Corollary K.10.18j (Separated Static Lapse Readout of the Dirac Euler Coefficient).** Use the covariant continuum endpoints and the inverse-temperature interval of Proposition K.10.18i. For $n_D$ independent four-component massless Dirac fields take three static lapse directions supported near $0$, $r e_1$ and $2r e_1$. In the stress convention of Osborn and Petkou, let $D_\theta^{(n_D)}(r)$ denote the corresponding pointwise connected $T_{00}$ three-point covariance integrated over the two relative times on the thermal circle. With the Euler term in the trace anomaly written as $-a E_4/(16\pi^2)$, one has
$$
D_\theta^{(n_D)}(r)=\frac{15 n_D}{8192\pi^4 r^{10}}+O_{\theta_-,\theta_+,\ell}(r^{-7}),\qquad
a=\frac{11264\pi^4}{675}\lim_{r\downarrow0}r^{10}D_\theta^{(n_D)}(r)=\frac{11n_D}{360}.
\tag{K.10.18i.6}
$$
The limit is uniform in $\theta$. This readout uses the declared free Dirac species class and the stress Ward conversion on that class. The corresponding endpoint values are $a_U=11N/360$ and $a_I=11M/360$ for the limiting covariant massless theories of Theorem K.10.18h. Each mixed response can be sampled on pairwise disjoint supports, so local metric counterterms contribute zero.

*Flat triangle.* Write $\{\gamma_\mu,\gamma_\nu\}=2\delta_{\mu\nu}I$, use $\langle\psi\bar\psi\rangle=D^{-1}$ for $D=\gamma\cdot\partial$, and use $T_{00}=\bar\psi\gamma_0(\partial_0-\overleftarrow\partial_0)\psi/2$. At nonzero spatial displacement the time Fourier transform of the flat propagator is
$$
S_\omega(x)=\frac{e^{-|\omega||x|}}{4\pi|x|}\left[-i\omega\gamma_0+\left(|\omega|+|x|^{-1}\right)\gamma\cdot\widehat{x}\right].
\tag{K.10.18i.7}
$$
This is $(-i\omega\gamma_0-\gamma\cdot\nabla)$ applied to the Yukawa Green function $e^{-|\omega||x|}/(4\pi|x|)$. In a static insertion the two adjacent propagators have the same loop frequency, giving the stress vertex $i\omega\gamma_0$. The two connected Wick contractions are the two directed triangle traces with one fermion-loop minus sign each. Put $w=|\omega|$ and $K=\gamma_0\gamma_1$, so $K^2=-I$ and $\operatorname{tr}K=0$. Suppressing the three Yukawa scalar factors, the trace of the orientation with displacements $re_1,re_1,-2re_1$ is
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\operatorname{tr}\bigl[(w^2 I+i\omega(w+r^{-1})K)^2(w^2 I-i\omega(w+(2r)^{-1})K)\bigr]\\
&\hspace{3em}=4w^4\bigl[w^2+(w+r^{-1})^2-2(w+r^{-1})(w+(2r)^{-1})\bigr]
=-4w^5/r.
\end{aligned}
\tag{K.10.18i.8}
$$
Reversing the triangle replaces $K$ by $-K$ and gives the same trace. Including the scalar factors and integrating $d\omega/(2\pi)$, the covariance for one species is
$$
\frac{8/r}{2r^3(4\pi)^3\pi}\int_0^\infty w^5 e^{-4rw}\,dw=\frac{15}{8192\pi^4r^{10}}.
\tag{K.10.18i.9}
$$
Integrating the third time in the static third variation contributes the overall factor $\theta$. The sign of the third derivative with respect to the chosen lapse coordinate is fixed by the linear stress convention. With $N$ in $g_{00}=N^2$, $W=-\log Z$ and $T^E_{\mu\nu}=2\,\delta S_E/(\sqrt g\,\delta g^{\mu\nu})$, one has $\delta S_E=-\int\delta N\,T_{00}$ at flat metric, so $-\theta^{-1}\delta^3 W$ gives the integrated covariance at separated supports. Higher action derivatives are supported on a partial diagonal. Smooth bump tests approaching the distinct spatial arguments recover the integrated pointwise covariance at fixed $r>0$.

*Compact thermal estimate.* Use the cutoff and uniformly bounded propagator remainder in (K.10.18i.3), extending the bound through derivative order three by replacing the Fourier summability exponent $-4$ by $-7/2$. A connected Wick product has three propagator factors and three time derivatives distributed among them. Write their derivative orders as $d_1,d_2,d_3$ with $d_1+d_2+d_3=3$. In a fixed small chart of the two relative times where all three time differences lie within the inner cutoff radius, the difference between the thermal and flat product has a smooth remainder on at least one edge. The other two edges form a spanning tree of the three vertices. Their two time differences are independent linear coordinates of Jacobian one in absolute value. For an edge of spatial length $s\in\{r,2r\}$,
$$
\int_{\mathbb R}(s^2+t^2)^{-(3+d)/2}\,dt\ 
\le r^{-(2+d)}\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^{-(3+d)/2}\,dt.
\tag{K.10.18i.10}
$$
The two singular factors thus give at most $O(r^{-7})$ and the smooth factor is uniformly bounded. Terms with fewer singular factors obey the same estimate by bounded chart volume. Outside the chart at least one of the three time differences has fixed positive distance from zero on the circle. Its propagator and derivatives are uniformly bounded. Integration over the other two edge differences, now in circle coordinates, uses (K.10.18i.10) and gives the same bound. The analogous flat integral outside the chart has at least one edge a fixed distance from zero, and the other two independent edge times can again be integrated over $\mathbb R^2$ by (K.10.18i.10). All constants depend only on the cutoff, the positive lower thermal period, the upper thermal period and $\ell$. This establishes the uniform leading term in (K.10.18i.6). Independent species add in the connected covariance.

*Ward conversion on the Dirac class.* Let $(a_{\mathrm{OP}},b_{\mathrm{OP}},c_{\mathrm{OP}})$ be the separated stress three-point tensor coefficients in Osborn and Petkou's conventions, distinct from the trace-anomaly coefficients. Their canonical free Dirac contractions give $a_{\mathrm{OP}}=0$, $b_{\mathrm{OP}}=-n_D/(2\pi^6)$ and $c_{\mathrm{OP}}=-n_D/\pi^6$. Their trace Ward normalization in four dimensions gives
$$
a=16\pi^2\beta_b=\frac{\pi^6}{360}(9a_{\mathrm{OP}}-2b_{\mathrm{OP}}-10c_{\mathrm{OP}}).
\tag{K.10.18i.11}
$$
These are the separated free-field calculation and conversion of equations (5.2), (5.13), (8.1) and (8.37). The lapse readout (K.10.18i.9) independently fixes the scale of this one-dimensional Dirac tensor family. Substituting $n_D=\frac{8192\pi^4}{15}\lim_{r\downarrow0} r^{10}D_\theta^{(n_D)}(r)$ into (K.10.18i.11) gives (K.10.18i.6). The conversion imports the free Dirac tensor shape and the Ward identity. A single lapse triangle does not separate the tensor coefficients of a general CFT with independent stress three-point structures. See Osborn and Petkou (1994).

A finite local metric functional changes only coincident-support terms and therefore leaves (K.10.18i.6) unchanged. The readout is applied after the endpoint theory has been selected. On a continuum compact box with a fixed finite massive species, sending $r$ to zero first instead probes that species at short distances. The corresponding continuum fixed-separation heavy limit is given below. The full Wilson comparison and the physical channel are realized in Theorem K.10.18p. ∎

<a id="corollary-k1018j1"></a>

<a id="corollary-k1018j1-heavy-continuum-species-at-fixed-separated-supports"></a>**Corollary K.10.18j.1 (Heavy Continuum Species at Fixed Separated Supports).** At fixed positive spatial separation $d$ on the dimensionless thermal torus, the massive Dirac propagator and its spacetime derivatives of orders up to three have the uniform bound $C_d(1+\mu)^4 e^{-\mu d/(2\sqrt2)}$, for dimensionless mass $\mu\ge1$ and $\theta\in[\theta_-,\theta_+]$. Consequently the massive contribution to either separated static covariance used in Corollaries K.10.18i.1 and K.10.18j vanishes uniformly at fixed separation as $\mu\to\infty$. This establishes heavy-species decoupling for these two continuum noncontact responses with the separation limit taken after the mass limit.

*Proof.* Write $\omega_j=\pi(2j+1)/\theta$, $\lambda_j=(\mu^2+\omega_j^2)^{1/2}$ and $Y_\lambda(y)=e^{-\lambda|y|}/(4\pi|y|)$. The inverse of $\gamma\cdot\partial+\mu$ is given at separated spatial arguments by the Matsubara series of the periodic spatial image kernels
$$
\frac1\theta\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}e^{i\omega_j\tau}
\sum_{b\in\mathbb Z^3}(\mu-i\omega_j\gamma_0-\gamma\cdot\nabla)Y_{\lambda_j}(x+\ell b).
\tag{K.10.18i.12}
$$
Indeed the scalar image sum is the periodic Green function of $-\Delta+\lambda_j^2$, and the first-order numerator gives the Dirac inverse. Put $R=|x+\ell b|\ge d$. Each derivative of $Y_\lambda$ through order $q\le4$ is bounded by a constant depending on $d$ times $(1+\lambda)^q e^{-\lambda R}$: differentiating only produces powers of $\lambda$, bounded direction cosines and inverse powers of $R$. After the first-order numerator and at most three further derivatives, each summand is bounded by $C_d(1+\mu+|\omega_j|)^4e^{-\lambda_jR}$. Use $\lambda_j\ge(\mu+|\omega_j|)/\sqrt2$ and $\mu\ge1$ to obtain
$$
e^{-\lambda_jR}\le e^{-\mu d/(2\sqrt2)} e^{-R/(2\sqrt2)} e^{-|\omega_j|d/\sqrt2}.
\tag{K.10.18i.13}
$$
The middle factor sums over images uniformly for $x$ in a spatial fundamental cube. The last factor times $(1+|\omega_j|)^4$ sums uniformly by $\pi|2j+1|/\theta_+\le |\omega_j|\le\pi|2j+1|/\theta_-$. Factor $(1+\mu)^4$ out of the polynomial, and use $\theta^{-1}\le\theta_-^{-1}$. This gives the stated bound and absolute differentiated convergence. The connected two- and three-point stresses are finite Wick products of propagators with two and three total derivatives, respectively. Additional explicit mass factors in an equivalent off-shell stress convention contribute only polynomial growth. Since the corresponding spatial pairs stay at least $d$ apart, every term decays exponentially under the uniform bound, including after integration over the compact relative time variables. Contact and partially coincident terms vanish on the supports under consideration. ∎

<a id="proposition-k1018k"></a>

<a id="proposition-k1018k-separated-heavy-response-on-the-coarse-wilson-lattice"></a>**Proposition K.10.18k (Separated Heavy Response on the Coarse Wilson Lattice).** Use the coarse Wilson comparison source of Theorem K.10.18h in dimensionless coordinates, with mesh $\delta_n=\ell/n$ and heavy mass $\mu_n=n^2$. Consider one species and any smooth static Hermitian metric extension with the same flat matrix. For $k=2$ or $3$, choose fixed smooth metric directions whose closed spatial supports are pairwise at least $s>0$ apart on the torus. Assume the first vertex for each direction is supported on the lattice sites within $R$ graph steps of its spatial support, with $R$ fixed, and that all mixed vertices involving two distinct directions vanish once these neighborhoods are disjoint. Assume the first-vertex norms are bounded by $P_n$, polynomial in $n$. Then the separated $k$th derivative of the full canonical free energy $-\log Z_{n,\theta}$ tends to zero uniformly over $\theta\in[\theta_-,\theta_+]$. The bound includes the negative-energy sea response. It applies to the native lapse port of Proposition B.3a.1 and the finite-range tetrad extension below.

*Proof.* Let $d_n=\lceil sn/\ell\rceil-2R$ and restrict first to $n$ with $d_n\ge1$ and $9/(\ell n)\le1/2$. Any path of graph length $j$ covers physical torus distance at most $j\delta_n$. Thus any two vertex neighborhoods are at graph distance at least $d_n$. Write the flat matrix as $H_{0,n}=\mu_n\beta+K_n$, with $K_n$ the massless Wilson matrix. Its range is one in graph steps and $\|K_n\|\le 9/\delta_n$: the three central differences have norms at most $\delta_n^{-1}$ each and the three Wilson difference terms have norms at most $2\delta_n^{-1}$ each. For a Matsubara frequency $\omega_j=\pi(2j+1)/\theta$, put $\lambda_j=(\omega_j^2+\mu_n^2)^{1/2}$ and $R_j=(i\omega_j+H_{0,n})^{-1}$. The onsite inverse $(i\omega_j+\mu_n\beta)^{-1}$ has norm $\lambda_j^{-1}$. Expanding $R_j$ in a Neumann series around this onsite inverse, terms with fewer than $d_n$ powers of $K_n$ have zero block between distinct vertex neighborhoods $U,V$. With $\rho_n=9/(\ell n)$ one gets
$$
\|P_U R_j P_V\|\le\lambda_j^{-1}\frac{(9/(\delta_n\lambda_j))^{d_n}}{1-9/(\delta_n\lambda_j)}
\le\lambda_j^{-1}\frac{\rho_n^{d_n}}{1-\rho_n}.
\tag{K.10.18k.1}
$$

For a smooth finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix $H$, the Fock trace is $\det(I+e^{-\theta H})$. Its logarithm has the exact finite-carrier frequency representation
$$
\log Z_{n,\theta}=-\tfrac{\theta}{2}\operatorname{Tr}H+(4n^3)\log 2
+\sum_{j\ge0}\log\det(I+H^2/\omega_j^2).
\tag{K.10.18k.2}
$$
This follows by diagonalization and the product for $\cosh$. At a fixed stage, the paired summands and their first three parameter derivatives have $O(\omega_j^{-2})$ tails on any compact smooth parameter neighborhood, as follows by differentiating the matrix-log series for $\|H\|^2/\omega_j^2<1/2$. For a mixed derivative on disjoint supports the linear trace term and all mixed matrix vertices vanish. Differentiating the determinants of $i\omega_j+H$ and $-i\omega_j+H$ gives a sum over all signed Matsubara frequencies and the $(k-1)!$ cyclic arrangements of first vertices $V_1,\ldots,V_k$ in traces $\operatorname{Tr}(R_j V_1 R_j V_{\pi(2)}\cdots R_j V_{\pi(k)})$, up to an overall sign. Writing $V_i=P_{U_i}V_iP_{U_i}$ inside each cyclic trace replaces every resolvent by a block between two distinct supports. The absolute value of each trace is bounded by $4n^3P_n^k(\lambda_j^{-1}\rho_n^{d_n}/(1-\rho_n))^k$. Finally, comparison of the positive Matsubara sum with the integral of the decreasing function $(\mu_n^2+t^2)^{-k/2}$ gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\lambda_j^{-k}
&\le 2\mu_n^{-k}+\frac{\theta_+}{\pi}\mu_n^{1-k}\int_0^\infty(1+t^2)^{-k/2}\,dt,\\
\left|D^k(-\log Z_{n,\theta})[u_1,\ldots,u_k]\right|
&\le 4(k-1)!\left(2+\frac{\theta_+}{\pi}I_k\right)n^3 P_n^k\mu_n^{1-k}
\left(\frac{\rho_n^{d_n}}{1-\rho_n}\right)^k,
\qquad I_2=\pi/2,\quad I_3=1.
\end{aligned}
\tag{K.10.18k.3}
$$
The right side tends to zero since $d_n$ grows linearly with $n$ and $\rho_n$ is proportional to $1/n$. A finite scalar control supported on fixed-range metric stencils gives zero mixed derivative once its stencil diameter is below $s$. Multiplying the bound by the fixed number of heavy species proves the same statement for their sum.

*One spatial extension in this class.* Use $\alpha_i,\beta$ as in (B.3a.1.1). For spatial metric $\gamma$ near the identity, let $A^i=\sum_a\alpha_a(\gamma^{-1/2})_{ai}$ and let $\Omega_i=\tfrac14\sum_{a,b}\omega_i^{ab}\alpha_a\alpha_b$ be the spatial spin connection in the symmetric frame. Sample these coefficients and a positive lapse $N$ on the lattice. Let $D_{n,i}=(T_i-T_i^*)/(2\delta_n)$ and let $W_n$ be the Wilson operator of (B.3a.1.1). The finite matrix
$$
H_n(N,\gamma)=N_n^{1/2}\left[-\tfrac i2\sum_i\{A_n^i,D_{n,i}\}-\tfrac i2\sum_i\{A_n^i,\Omega_{i,n}\}+\mu_n\beta+\beta W_n\right]N_n^{1/2}
\tag{K.10.18k.4}
$$
is Hermitian with range one and gives exactly $H_{0,n}$ at the flat input. Its first lapse derivative there is $\{f_n,H_{0,n}\}/2$, the native symmetric allocation. For a direction $u=(f,h)$ with $\dot N=f$ and $\dot\gamma=h$, let $\|h\|_\infty$ and $\|\partial h\|_\infty$ be componentwise maxima. At the flat input, $\dot A^i=-\tfrac12\sum_a\alpha_a h_{ai}$, and each component of the linearized spin connection $\dot\omega_i^{ab}$ has absolute value at most $\|\partial h\|_\infty$ by the Levi-Civita connection formula in the symmetric frame. The first vertex therefore has bound
$$
\|V_u\|\le (\mu_n+9/\delta_n)\|f\|_\infty+\frac{9}{2\delta_n}\|h\|_\infty+\frac{27}{4}\|\partial h\|_\infty.
\tag{K.10.18k.5}
$$
The support radius is one. All coefficients are pointwise functions of the metric and its first derivatives, with the only two-site products supplied by a nearest-neighbor bond. Mixed vertices vanish when the support neighborhoods are disjoint. This verifies the hypotheses with a polynomial $P_n$ for a concrete spatial vertex on the original flat Wilson regulator. ∎

<a id="proposition-k1018l"></a>

<a id="proposition-k1018l-separated-light-metric-jets-of-the-wilson-extension"></a>**Proposition K.10.18l (Separated Light Metric Jets of the Wilson Extension).** Use the metric vertex (K.10.18k.4) on the fixed dimensionless spatial torus and let $\delta=\ell/L$ with $L$ odd. For $0\le\mu\le1$, compare the resulting canonical lattice response with the covariant continuum Dirac response of the same mass, using the same lapse and symmetric spatial frame. For $k=2,3$ and any fixed $k$ smooth static metric directions whose supports have mutual spatial separation at least $s>0$, their mixed free-energy derivatives differ by at most $C\delta$ for all sufficiently small $\delta$ with $\delta\le\min(1,s/8)$. The constant is uniform in $\mu$ and $\theta\in[\theta_-,\theta_+]$. The continuum separated response differs from its massless value by at most $C\mu$ on the same interval. Thus the fine sequence $\delta_f=\ell/n^3$, $\mu_f\in\{0,n^{-12}\}$ converges to the $N$-species continuum jets on these tests, and the coarse sequence $\delta_c=\ell/n$ converges to the $M$-species jets after the coarse comparison of Proposition K.10.18k. This compares the canonical equilibrium response of each Wilson regulator with its continuum reference.

*Operators and support.* The continuum one-particle operator in the spatial coordinate Hilbert space is the continuum version of (K.10.18k.4), replacing $D_{n,i}$ by $\partial_i$ and omitting $W_n$. Indeed, the spatial density transform of the spin Dirac operator gives the two displayed anticommutators by the frame compatibility identity
$$
\sum_i\bigl[\partial_i A^i+[\Omega_i,A^i]+\tfrac12(\partial_i\log\det\gamma)A^i\bigr]=0.
\tag{K.10.18l.1}
$$
For a static lapse, the spin connection and density transform supply the symmetrized operator $N^{1/2}K(\gamma)N^{1/2}$ in the same coordinate clock. Equivalently, in the spatial density variables the Euclidean time term is $\partial_\tau$ and the spatial operator is the lapse-symmetrized one. The geometric spinor measure changes only local coincident terms in the comparison of separated jets. Along disjoint directions all mixed action vertices vanish. The separated continuum variations are therefore the finite sums of connected cycles of two or three first-order static vertices, with spatial kernels evaluated only off the diagonal. At finite lattice size they are the same signed Matsubara traces derived from (K.10.18k.2).

To compare the cycles, expand a first vertex into a finite sum of terms $M_b Q M_c$, where $M_b,M_c$ are smooth matrix multiplication operators and $Q$ is one of $I,D_{n,i},W_{n,i}$, the last denoting the Wilson term of direction $i$. The continuum terms have $I,\partial_i,0$ in the corresponding slots. For example the lapse variation of a derivative operator gives $M_f D_{n,i}$ and $D_{n,i}M_f$. Each term can be expressed as $M_d Q$ plus a finite number of zeroth-order terms containing a shift by at most one mesh step: this is the discrete product rule for $D_{n,i}$ or $W_{n,i}$. The coefficients of the shifted zeroth-order terms are sampled difference quotients of a smooth coefficient. They and their limiting derivatives are uniformly bounded, with difference at most $C\delta$ by Taylor's formula. For the Wilson commutator the two opposite shifts give cancelling zeroth-order continuum limits. Such a cancellation is only needed after replacing the adjacent separated kernels by their continuum limits. In the trace, move each $Q$ onto its following resolvent by grouping it with that factor. Every multiplication coefficient restricts its site argument to within one mesh step of the corresponding support, and the extra shifts alter an edge separation by at most two mesh steps. For $\delta\le s/8$, all the kernels used this way have spatial separation at least $s/2$.

*Separated resolvent comparison.* Put $p_b=2\pi b/\ell$, $\Lambda_\delta=\{p_b: b\in\mathbb Z^3,\ |b_i|\le(L-1)/2\}$ and $t=(1+\omega^2+|p|^2)^{1/2}$. For a signed thermal Matsubara frequency $\omega$ the symbols of the resolvent and of the differentiated factors are
$$
r_\delta(\omega,p)=\frac{h_\delta(p)-i\omega}{\omega^2+E_\delta(p)^2},\quad
q_\delta(p)r_\delta(\omega,p),\qquad
q_\delta\in\left\{1,\ i\frac{\sin(\delta p_i)}\delta,\ \frac{1-\cos(\delta p_i)}\delta\right\}.
\tag{K.10.18l.2}
$$
The continuum symbols $r_0,q_0r_0$ use $h_0(p)=\alpha\cdot p+\mu\beta$ and $q_0=1,ip_i,0$. For every derivative order $j\le8$ there are constants $C_j$ depending on the positive Matsubara lower bound and the indicated order such that in the Brillouin cube, for $\delta|\omega|\le1$,
$$
|\partial_p^j(q_\delta r_\delta)|\le C_j t^{-j},\qquad
|\partial_p^j(q_\delta r_\delta-q_0r_0)|\le C_j\delta t^{1-j}.
\tag{K.10.18l.3}
$$
The uniform symbol estimates follow from $\|\partial_p^j h_\delta\|\le C_j(1+|p|)^{1-j}$ and $\|\partial_p^j(h_\delta-h_0)\|\le C_j\delta(1+|p|)^{2-j}$, with the same respective bounds for the three multiplier symbols. At $j=0,1$ these follow from the sine and cosine Taylor inequalities. At $j\ge2$ they follow from the explicit derivatives, using $\delta(1+|p|)\le 1+\sqrt3\pi$. The resolvent denominator obeys $\omega^2+E_\delta^2\ge c(\omega^2+|p|^2+\mu^2)$, with $c$ independent of $\delta$, by the Wilson band bound and $\mu\ge0$. When $\delta|\omega|\le1$ the explicit $\delta^{j-1}$ bound for $j\ge2$ gives $C_j t^{1-j}$, and for the difference derivatives it gives $C_j\delta t^{2-j}$. The positive lower frequency bound gives $\|r_\delta\|,\|r_0\|\le C_0/t$. Applying $r_\delta-r_0=r_\delta(h_0-h_\delta)r_0$ and the differentiated inverse identity proves (K.10.18l.3).

If $\delta|\omega|>1$, use the same derivative proof with $T=(1+\delta^{-2})^{1/2}$ in place of $t$. The first resolvent and every term in its derivatives contribute at least one factor $|\omega|^{-1}$, while $\|q_\delta\|\le C T$. Hence on the entire Brillouin cube
$$
|\partial_p^j(q_\delta r_\delta)|\le C_jT^{1-j}/|\omega|.
\tag{K.10.18l.4}
$$
In the remainder of the proof (K.10.18l.3) is used only when $\delta|\omega|\le1$.

The real-space lattice operator entries of $q_\delta r_\delta$ are $\delta^3$ times the kernels normalized with $\ell^{-3}\sum_{p\in\Lambda_\delta}e^{ip\cdot x}$. If $x$ has torus distance at least $s/2$ from the origin, at least one component has distance at least $s/(2\sqrt3)$ modulo $\ell$. Apply finite summation by parts eight times in that momentum coordinate. This extracts a divisor $(e^{2\pi ix_i/\ell}-1)^8$ with magnitude bounded below on the stated set. A reciprocal-step difference of order eight is the integral of the eighth derivative over eight independent shifts, each in $[0,2\pi/\ell]$. For the low frequency estimate use a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi(\delta p)$ equal to one in a cube about zero and supported in the interior of the Brillouin cube. Apply the difference estimate to the low part of the lattice-minus-continuum symbols and to each high part separately. In the cutoff transition $|p|\ge c/\delta$, each derivative of the cutoff contributes a factor $O(\delta)$, of the same order as $O(t^{-1})$ when $\delta|\omega|\le1$. Across a lattice Brillouin seam the high part is smooth periodic, so the finite differences retain these bounds. Continuum summation is over the whole reciprocal lattice. The differentiated continuum tails are absolutely summable and give the continuum off-diagonal kernels, by the distributional summation by parts identity. In the cubic sum estimate $\sum_{b\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+\omega^2+|p_b|^2)^{-j/2}\le C_j(1+|\omega|)^{3-j}$ for $j>3$, one can take $C_j$ from integrating the radial majorant over cubic cells. For cells of side $2\pi/\ell$ centered at $p_b$, the inequality $1+\omega^2+|p|^2\le 2(1+3\pi^2/\ell^2)(1+\omega^2+|p_b|^2)$ on the cell gives an explicit comparison with the integral on $\mathbb R^3$.

Consequently the difference of the normalized kernels at matching separated lattice arguments is at most $C_s\delta(1+|\omega|)^{-4}$ in the range $\delta|\omega|\le1$: the low symbol error contributes $C_s\delta\sum_p t^{-7}$ and each high tail is bounded by the same expression since $t\ge c/\delta$ there. Each individual kernel is bounded by $C_s(1+|\omega|)^{-5}$ in this range. The continuum estimates hold also at higher frequencies, where (K.10.18l.4) and the finite number $L^3$ of modes give the lattice bound $C_s\delta^4/|\omega|$ after eight differences. All constants can be chosen from the sine/cosine derivative bounds, the fixed cutoff derivative norms, the lower bound on the extracted divisor and the convergent radial integrals. The same argument gives uniform first spatial derivatives of the continuum kernel, with bounds $C_s(1+|\omega|)^{-4}$, by inserting the multiplier $ip_i$ before the eight differences. It also gives the $O(\mu)$ difference of the massive and massless continuum kernels with the same summable frequency majorant, using the inverse identity with $h_\mu-h_0=\mu\beta$.

*Cycles and quadrature.* At low frequencies telescope the difference of the products of separated kernels around each cycle. All factors are bounded by the stated summable majorants, and the kernel difference and each one-mesh shift error contribute at most $C_s\delta(1+|\omega|)^{-4}$. The coefficients are uniformly bounded fixed smooth functions or their difference quotients. The factor $\delta^{3k}$ from the $k$ kernels is precisely the product integration weight in the trace over the $k$ spatial sites. The periodic Riemann sum for the product continuum integrand has error at most $C_s\delta(1+|\omega|)^{-4}$ by the first spatial derivative bound and the cellwise mean-value inequality. The integrand may be set to zero near the partial spatial diagonals because the support factors already vanish there. The finitely many low-frequency cycle errors thus sum to at most $C_s\delta$. For $\delta|\omega|>1$ the lattice cycle is bounded by $C_s(\delta^4/|\omega|)^k$, and the continuum cycle by $C_s(1+|\omega|)^{-5k}$. Their sums are $O(\delta^{5k-1})$ by the uniform Matsubara spacing, which is sufficient for both $k=2$ and $k=3$. The continuum cycle represents the static connected Wick response after integrating all relative times, which identifies the loop frequencies. Absolute convergence on separated supports permits this identification and the sums above. The fixed number of Wick cycles and the finite coefficient expansions are absorbed into $C$. This gives the claimed comparisons. ∎

<a id="proposition-k1018m"></a>

<a id="proposition-k1018m-volume-preserving-shear-contact-of-the-wilson-stencil"></a>**Proposition K.10.18m (Volume-Preserving Shear Contact of the Wilson Stencil).** On either Wilson lattice of Theorem K.10.18h, use the metric extension (K.10.18k.4) and the constant spatial metric $\gamma_t=\operatorname{diag}(e^{2t},e^{-2t},1)$ at unit lapse. For one species of dimensionless mass $0\le\mu\le1$, the flat shear Hessian of the canonical free energy $W_{\delta,\theta}=-\log Z_{\delta,\theta}$ diverges at least as $-c\theta_-\ell^3\delta^{-4}$ for an explicit $c>0$, uniformly over $\theta\in[\theta_-,\theta_+]$. Every diffeomorphism-covariant local scalar functional of the metric has zero shear Hessian along this family. Therefore local controls of that covariant class alone cannot match the raw stencil to the covariantly renormalized continuum Hessian. A regulator-frame-dependent local control or a change in the stencil is required for this response.

*Proof.* The symmetric spatial frame for this family is constant in space, so its spin connection vanishes. Put $s_i=\sin(\delta p_i)/\delta$ and $B=\mu+\delta^{-1}\sum_i(1-\cos(\delta p_i))$. At each momentum the eigenvalues are $\pm E_t$, each with multiplicity two, where
$$
E_t=\bigl(e^{-2t}s_1^2+e^{2t}s_2^2+s_3^2+B^2\bigr)^{1/2}.
\tag{K.10.18m.1}
$$
The Wilson term in (K.10.18k.4) is independent of $t$. At $t=0$, writing $S=s_1^2+s_2^2$ and $E=E_0$, one obtains
$$
E'=\frac{s_2^2-s_1^2}{E},\qquad
E''=\frac{2S}{E}-\frac{(s_2^2-s_1^2)^2}{E^3}\ge\frac{S}{E}.
\tag{K.10.18m.2}
$$
An identically zero mode contributes zero and can be handled directly. The momentum contribution to $W_{\delta,\theta}$ is $-4\log[2\cosh(\theta E_t/2)]$. Its second derivative is
$$
-2\theta\tanh(\theta E/2) E''-\theta^2\operatorname{sech}^2(\theta E/2)(E')^2.
\tag{K.10.18m.3}
$$
Both summands are nonpositive. Restrict the momentum sum to $\delta p_i\in[\pi/6,\pi/3]$ for all three components. There $S\ge1/(2\delta^2)$, and $\delta\le1$, $\mu\le1$ give $E\le10/\delta$ from the full-band sine and Wilson bounds. Also $E\ge1/(2\delta)$, so for $\delta\le\theta_-/4$ the hyperbolic tangent is at least $1/2$. With $L=\ell/\delta\ge24$, the reciprocal grid has at least $L/24$ samples per component in this interval. Equations (K.10.18m.2) and (K.10.18m.3) then yield
$$
\left.\frac{d^2 W_{\delta,\theta}}{dt^2}\right|_{0}\le -\frac{\theta_-\ell^3}{20\,24^3\,\delta^4}.
\tag{K.10.18m.4}
$$

The four-dimensional Euclidean product metric $d\tau^2+\gamma_t$ is flat and its volume is $\theta\ell^3$ for all $t$. Locally the metrics are isometric to the same flat metric. An invariant local scalar density formed solely from the metric and its derivatives therefore takes the same integrated value for each $t$. A finite dependence on the torus shape is permitted for the continuum action. Its covariantly renormalized Hessian is finite uniformly on the compact temperature interval and $0\le\mu\le1$: in the proper-time heat representation the identity winding term is independent of $t$, the differentiated nonidentity windings have exponentially small small-time bounds, and the antiperiodic time spectrum gives a uniform large-time gap. This comparison leaves the divergent lattice term (K.10.18m.4) intact under covariant local controls. The test uses the constant spatial zero-momentum mode, which was outside the separated support proof of Proposition K.10.18l. ∎

<a id="corollary-k1018m1"></a>

<a id="corollary-k1018m1-vacuum-subtraction-for-the-uniform-shear-contact"></a>**Corollary K.10.18m.1 (Vacuum Subtraction for the Uniform Shear Contact).** Keep the constant volume-preserving shear and the canonical Wilson response of Proposition K.10.18m. For $0\le\mu\le1$ define the energy density from the infinite-volume Wilson band at the same dimensionless mesh and mass,
$$
\mathcal E^{\mathrm{vac}}_{\delta,\mu}(\gamma)=-2\int_{[-\pi/\delta,\pi/\delta]^3} E_{\delta,\mu}(p;\gamma)\,\frac{d^3p}{(2\pi)^3},
\tag{K.10.18m.5}
$$
where the energy for a constant positive spatial metric uses the same Wilson term and symmetric inverse frame as (K.10.18k.4). Extend this energy density pointwise in the marked regulator frame and add the opposite density to the source energy. Its contribution to $W=-\log Z$ on the constant family is $-\theta\ell^3\mathcal E^{\mathrm{vac}}_{\delta,\mu}(\gamma)$. The corrected second derivative on $\gamma_t$ converges to the covariantly renormalized continuum shear Hessian, uniformly in $\mu\in[0,1]$ and $\theta\in[\theta_-,\theta_+]$. It uses a local control independent of temperature and torus period, fixed by the vacuum band. The absolute error is $O(\delta^{1/6})$ with the constants specified by the bounds below.

*Proof.* Let $F_{\delta,\mu}(p)=\partial_t^2 E_{\delta,\mu}(p;\gamma_t)|_{0}$, the expression in (K.10.18m.2), and let $F_{0,\mu}$ be its continuum counterpart obtained by substituting $s_i=p_i$ and $B=\mu$. The vacuum part of the corrected Hessian is
$$
-2\theta\left[\sum_{p\in\Lambda_\delta} F_{\delta,\mu}(p)-\frac{\ell^3}{(2\pi)^3}\int_{\mathrm{BZ}_\delta}F_{\delta,\mu}(p)\,d^3p\right].
\tag{K.10.18m.6}
$$
The remaining thermal part is the difference between the Hessian (K.10.18m.3) and $-2\theta\sum F_{\delta,\mu}(p)$. This splitting follows from $-4\log[2\cosh(\theta E/2)]=-2\theta E-4\log(1+e^{-\theta E})$. The derivative terms are continuous in $(p,\mu)$ at $(0,0)$, where $E_t$ is identically zero. The continuum density in (K.10.18m.5) is not used as a finite scalar coefficient, since its infinite-volume momentum integral diverges. On the volume-preserving family the continuum infinite-volume heat trace density is independent of $t$ by the linear change of spatial momenta of determinant one.

For a fixed smooth radial ultraviolet partition $\chi_Q(p)=\chi(p/Q)$ with $\chi=0$ on $|p|\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on $|p|\ge2$, split each term of (K.10.18m.6) at $Q\ge1$. Assume $2Q\delta\le1$. Uniform symbol estimates on the Brillouin cube give, for $|p|\ge Q$ and $0\le j\le6$,
$$
|\partial_p^j F_{\delta,\mu}(p)|+|\partial_p^j F_{0,\mu}(p)|\le C_j|p|^{1-j}.
\tag{K.10.18m.7}
$$
Indeed $E_{\delta,\mu}\ge (2/\pi)|p|$, the lattice derivatives of $s_i,B$ satisfy $|\partial^j(s_i,B)|\le C_j|p|^{1-j}$ there, and each term of (K.10.18m.2) is a quotient of the indicated homogeneous degrees. The constants can be taken from these sine and cosine bounds by the product and inverse rules. The same statements follow directly for the continuum. Near $p=0$, where low momenta are treated without derivatives, the elementary Taylor inequalities and the lower bound $E_{\delta,\mu},E_{0,\mu}\ge c(|p|+\mu)$ give
$$
|F_{\delta,\mu}(p)-F_{0,\mu}(p)|\le C\delta |p|^2,\qquad |p|\le2Q.
\tag{K.10.18m.8}
$$
For example $|h_\delta-h_0|\le C\delta|p|^2$ bounds the energy difference. In (K.10.18m.2), the degree-two and degree-four numerators vanish respectively as $|p|^2$ and $|p|^4$.
