Inserting this energy error in the inverse denominators and using the sine numerator error gives (K.10.18m.8), with the same bound at $(0,0)$ by continuity.

The high part $\chi_Q F_{\delta,\mu}$ extends smoothly across the periodic Brillouin seam. Its sixth pure momentum derivatives have $L^1$ norm at most $C Q^{-2}$, from (K.10.18m.7), the cutoff derivative bounds, and the radial integral of $r^{-5}$ on three-dimensional space outside $Q$. The periodic lattice sampling identity expresses the high sum-minus-integral as its Fourier coefficients at nonzero windings $\ell b$. Integrating by parts six times in a coordinate where $|b_i|\ge |b|/\sqrt3$ bounds its absolute value by $C'\ell^{-3}Q^{-2}\sum_{b\ne0}|b|^{-6}$. Here $\ell^{-3}$ includes the $\ell^3$ factor from the integral normalization. The same high bound applies in the continuum first with the smoothing multiplier $e^{-\varepsilon E_{0,\mu}^2}$ and then as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Its derivatives satisfy the same symbol estimates uniformly, since each power of $\varepsilon E_{0,\mu}^2$ times the exponential is uniformly bounded. The high winding coefficients converge by dominated convergence of the sixth derivatives. The low part converges ordinarily. This gives a well-defined continuum winding sum and the same bound on its high tail. The low lattice-continuum difference of sums and integrals is bounded by $C_\ell\delta Q^5$ by (K.10.18m.8) and the number or volume of momenta in a ball of radius $2Q$.

This continuum winding prescription gives the covariantly renormalized Hessian. To see the connection to the proper-time heat integral, the same argument applies to $\partial_t^2[E_t\operatorname{erfc}(\sqrt\varepsilon E_t)]|_0$. The displayed symbol bounds remain uniform in $\varepsilon$. At fixed $p$ this tends to $F_{0,\mu}(p)$. For the vacuum energy one can use the exact scalar identity
$$
\int_\varepsilon^\infty t^{-3/2}e^{-tE^2}\,dt
=2\varepsilon^{-1/2}e^{-\varepsilon E^2}-2\sqrt\pi E\operatorname{erfc}(\sqrt\varepsilon E).
\tag{K.10.18m.9}
$$
The zero-winding heat contribution cancels identically on the constant unit-volume family, and the first term on the right has vanishing shear derivative of its nonzero winding sum as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ by the Gaussian winding formula. The $\operatorname{erfc}$ term gives the stated winding prescription. The finite-temperature heat windings are the canonical thermal term, as follows by the antiperiodic heat sum or the equivalent product for $\cosh$. Any local covariant heat subtraction on this flat constant-volume family has zero derivative, as in Proposition K.10.18m.

The thermal tails above $Q$ are bounded uniformly by $C_\ell(1+Q)^C e^{-c\theta_-Q}$ using (K.10.18m.3), the band energy bound and the decay of $1-\tanh$ and $\operatorname{sech}^2$. Below $2Q$, differentiating the scalar thermal factors with respect to $E$ gives a uniform bound because $\theta\le\theta_+$, and (K.10.18m.8), its first-derivative analogue and the same energy comparison bound the total low thermal error by $C_\ell\delta(1+Q)^6$. Take $Q=\delta^{-1/12}$ for all sufficiently small $\delta$ to give $O(\delta^{1/6})$ for both the vacuum and thermal parts. All constants come from the fixed cutoff through order six, the flat symbol bounds, $\ell$, and the compact temperature interval. The subtraction matches the second derivative on this declared constant shear family. Metric contacts at nonzero momenta, higher orders and physical realization require additional response records. ∎

<a id="proposition-k1018n"></a>

<a id="proposition-k1018n-complete-static-metric-jets-of-the-temperature-contrast"></a>**Proposition K.10.18n (Complete Static Metric Jets of the Temperature Contrast).** Use the Wilson extension (K.10.18k.4) at a fixed dimensionless torus of period $\ell$, with mass $0\le\mu\le1$. Fix any finite list of real trigonometric-polynomial lapse and spatial metric directions. Let $W_{\delta,\theta}$ be its canonical free energy $-\log Z$ and $W_{0,\theta}$ the covariantly renormalized continuum free Dirac functional. For each mixed jet of order $1\le r\le3$ at the flat input, including overlapping supports, one has
$$
\left|D^r\left[\frac{W_{\delta,\theta}}{\theta}-\frac{W_{\delta,\theta'}}{\theta'}
-\frac{W_{0,\theta}}{\theta}+\frac{W_{0,\theta'}}{\theta'}\right]\right|\le C\delta,
\qquad \theta,\theta'\in[\theta_-,\theta_+].
\tag{K.10.18n.1}
$$
The constant is independent of the lattice spacing and mass in these ranges. A temperature-independent static local energy functional has zero contribution to this contrast. In particular the estimate gives all thermal contact and partial-diagonal contributions in these directions. Matching the absolute jets at one reference temperature would therefore give their uniform matching throughout the interval.

*Spectral function.* Define the even holomorphic function on $|\operatorname{Im}z|<\pi/\theta_+$ by
$$
g_{\theta,\theta'}(z)=-\frac1\theta\log[2\cosh(\theta z/2)]+\frac1{\theta'}\log[2\cosh(\theta'z/2)],
\tag{K.10.18n.2}
$$
with logarithms real on the real axis. The zeros of the hyperbolic cosines lie outside the open strip. On any closed smaller strip this function obeys $|g_{\theta,\theta'}(x+iy)|\le C e^{-\theta_-|x|}$. At positive or negative $x$ the linear term of each logarithm cancels, and the remaining logarithms are of $1+e^{-\theta z}$ or $1+e^{\theta z}$. The bound on the remaining compact part is uniform by continuity. At finite lattice size the contrast is exactly $\operatorname{Tr}g_{\theta,\theta'}(H)$ by the Fock determinant. The term proportional to $\operatorname{Tr}H$ in (K.10.18k.2) cancels.

*Covariant and canonical temperature contrast.* In coordinate density variables and up to a fixed unitary time Clifford factor, the covariant Dirac operator is the static congruence $N^{-1/2}D_0N^{-1/2}$ of $D_0=\partial_\tau+H$, with $H$ the lapse-symmetrized self-adjoint operator of Proposition K.10.18l. The time coefficient is $N^{-1}$ and the two lapse factors in $H$ cancel the two outer factors in the spatial term. To check the determinant in these variables, set $R_s=N^{-s/2}$, $D_s=R_sD_0R_s$, $A=\dot R_sR_s^{-1}$ and $T_s=D_s^*D_s$. Invertibility follows from the antiperiodic time spectrum of $D_0$ and the invertible $R_s$. The identity $\dot T_s=2D_s^*AD_s+AT_s+T_sA$ gives
$$
\frac{d}{ds}\log|\det\nolimits_\zeta D_s|
=\operatorname{FP}_{z=0}\bigl[
\operatorname{Tr}(AT_s^{-z})+\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(A(D_sD_s^*)^{-z}\bigr)\bigr].
\tag{K.10.18n.3}
$$
Here $\log|\det_\zeta D_s|=\tfrac12\log\det_\zeta T_s$, and the traces follow by cyclicity for large $\operatorname{Re}z$ and continuation. The two values at zero are the inserted heat coefficients in dimension four, with no kernel contribution. Their local densities are static, so they scale exactly with the period $\theta$. The normalized contrast is invariant along this congruence. Local covariant finite subtractions scale in the same way. For the canonical operator $D_0^*D_0=-\partial_\tau^2+H^2$, the zero temporal winding in the heat trace cancels from the normalized contrast. The nonzero windings give $-\theta^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}\log(1+e^{-\theta |H|})$ at each period, by the antiperiodic frequency sum. Their difference is $\operatorname{Tr}g_{\theta,\theta'}(H)$. This trace is absolutely convergent by compact elliptic spectral growth and the exponential decay of $g$. The even holomorphic expression covers the spatial zero modes without differentiating an absolute-value cusp.

*Complete vertices and estimates.* Write $V_I$ for the mixed metric vertex differentiated in any nonempty subset $I$ of the $r$ directions. The vertex is obtained by differentiating (K.10.18k.4) and its continuum version, so all terms from the lapse factors, frame and spin connection are included. Because the directions are finite Fourier lists, these vertices have a fixed finite set of momentum transfers, independent of mesh. Let $K$ bound the sum of transfer norms around any cycle. For each initial momentum $p$, every vertex in a resulting cycle obeys the bound $C_K(1+|p|)$ in both models. On $\delta|p|\le1/2$ its lattice-continuum difference is at most $C_K\delta(1+|p|)^2$. These bounds follow termwise from the sine and cosine Taylor inequalities and the smooth finite Fourier coefficients of the differentiated symmetric frame and connection. The Wilson vertex contributes at most $C_K\delta(1+|p|)^2$ on the low region. Outside it, centered representatives obey the uniform linear full-band bound and transfers are taken modulo the reciprocal lattice.

Differentiating the holomorphic functional calculus gives all orders through three as a finite sum of loops. Every ordered partition $(I_1,\dots,I_j)$ of the $r$ differentiation indices supplies a term with the $j$ vertices $V_{I_1},\dots,V_{I_j}$ and $j+1$ resolvents. This follows by differentiating $(z-H)^{-1}$ and using $D(z-H)^{-1}=(z-H)^{-1}(DH)(z-H)^{-1}$. For each Fourier loop take a contour consisting of rectangles enclosing its positive and negative flat one-particle energies. For $|p|$ sufficiently large compared with $K+1$, all shifted magnitudes lie in $[c|p|,C(1+|p|)]$, uniformly in mesh by the Wilson band bounds and the torus-distance triangle inequality at a Brillouin seam. The rectangles have heights $\pm\pi/(2\theta_+)$, inner real boundaries at $\pm c|p|/2$, and outer real boundaries beyond all energies by at least one. The loop length is $O(1+|p|)$ and every resolvent has norm bounded by a uniform constant on the contour. The integrand is at most a polynomial in $1+|p|$ times $e^{-c\theta_-|p|/2}$. For the finite low block use one rectangle enclosing both signs, with the same fixed heights and real boundaries a fixed distance beyond the maximum energies. Its bounds include the zero modes.

For the momenta with $\delta|p|\le1/2$ use a common contour enclosing the energies of both models. The inverse identity and the flat band Taylor bound give a resolvent difference at most $C\delta(1+|p|)^2$ there. Telescoping all vertex and resolvent differences and integrating gives a per-loop difference bounded by $C\delta(1+|p|)^B e^{-c\theta_-|p|/2}$ on the high part of this region, and by $C\delta$ on the fixed low block. The remaining lattice or continuum tail has absolute sum $O(e^{-c'/\delta})$ by the same exponential contour estimate. This also handles momentum wrap, which is confined to that tail for sufficiently small mesh. The sign and multiplicities of all terms are identical, because the same differentiated resolvent formula was used. Summing over the spatial reciprocal lattice proves (K.10.18n.1).

For continuum differentiation factor $g(H)=(H+i\eta)^{-4}\,g_4(H)$ with $g_4(z)=(z+i\eta)^4g(z)$ and $\eta>\pi/\theta_+$. The inverse fourth power and its first three metric derivatives map $L^2$ into $H^4$ on the common elliptic domain. This follows by differentiating the four resolvent factors, since every metric vertex is first order and each extra resolvent recovers one derivative. The embedding $H^4\hookrightarrow L^2$ on this three-torus is trace class. The $g_4$ functional calculus and its derivatives converge in operator norm on the two fixed-height lines: a resolvent has bounded $L^2$ norm there, its $L^2\to H^1$ norm grows at most polynomially in $|z|$ by the uniform elliptic estimate, and $g_4$ decreases exponentially. This justifies trace differentiation. The resulting Fourier loop formula follows by scalar holomorphic calculus on each finite loop, or by taking finite flat momentum cutoffs. With finite momentum transfers, any discrepancy involving a cutoff boundary has a loop entirely at high momentum and vanishes by the same exponentially summable estimate. All constants can be bounded from the finite coefficient lists, the strip height, the linear band bounds, and convergent sums of $(1+|p|)^B e^{-c\theta_-|p|/2}$, uniformly on the compact temperature interval. ∎

<a id="proposition-k1018o"></a>

<a id="proposition-k1018o-complete-absolute-static-jet-matching-on-the-wilson-scale-sequence"></a>**Proposition K.10.18o (Complete Absolute Static Jet Matching on the Wilson Scale Sequence).** Fix a covariant proper-time finite part at a positive physical scale $\mu_*$, and use the static Wilson metric extension (K.10.18k.4) on the branches of Theorem K.10.18h. There is one real regulator-frame-dependent local metric energy control of metric order at most three and spatial derivative order at most four. Its coefficients are fixed by the flat infinite-volume vacuum symbols, the actual mesh and species mass, and the covariant proper-time prescription. They are independent of the temperature interval, the torus period, and the endpoint central data. After this control, every mixed static jet of orders one through three on any fixed finite list of trigonometric-polynomial directions converges to the covariant continuum jet at the same mass and proper-time scale. In the dimensionless torus coordinates the error is bounded by
$$
C\delta[1+|\log\delta|]\quad (0\le r\le1),\qquad
C(\delta+r^{-1})\quad (r\delta\ge1,\ r\ge1),
\tag{K.10.18o.1}
$$
uniformly on the compact temperature interval. In this statement $\delta$ is the dimensionless lattice spacing and $r$ the dimensionless species mass. The first estimate applies to the fine light and heavy species and to the coarse light species. The second applies to the coarse massive comparison. The matched local heavy threshold terms remain in the response. The theorem concerns canonical equilibrium jets and their local energy control.

*Response conventions.* Put $W=-\log Z$ and use the energy response $W/\theta$. The vacuum part for a finite one-particle Hamiltonian $H$ is $-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}|H|+\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}H$. The trace term vanishes for the stencil (K.10.18k.4) at every metric, because all its spin matrix coefficients have zero spin trace. The even thermal plus vacuum expression can equivalently be differentiated by the paired Matsubara formula (K.10.18k.2), which includes the possible zero modes without differentiation of a cusp. The continuum uses the spatial density variables and lapse symmetrization of Proposition K.10.18l. For static coefficients this puts the canonical Euclidean operator in the form $\partial_\tau+H$. Finite local differences between this prescription and the covariant geometric density and heat prescription are accounted for below. They are independent of the time period after division by $\theta$.

*Complete vacuum amplitudes.* Write $q$ for all independent external spatial momenta, with the last determined by conservation, and $p$ for the internal momentum. At fixed metric order $j\le3$, differentiate the exact determinant. Each ordered partition of the directions into $s$ nonempty blocks supplies a cyclic trace with $s$ resolvents and $s$ vertices, one vertex for each block. The vertices are the actual mixed derivatives of (K.10.18k.4). In particular the one-propagator terms and the second- and third-order mixed Hamiltonian derivatives are included. Let $I_\delta(p;q)$ and $I_0(p;q)$ be the signed vacuum-frequency integrands for the energy jets after the real-frequency integral $\int d\omega/(2\pi)$ and the indicated finite cyclic sum. Use the complete antiperiodic sum in place of this frequency integral for the thermal torus. All statements are coefficientwise in the constant tensor components of the directions. Near a massless vacuum zero the unregularized amplitude is used as an integrable distribution, with the explicit ultraviolet partition below.

The following bounds give the needed power count. If $|p|\ge 2K+2$, where $K$ bounds the external momenta and shifts throughout the Taylor segment, the shifted continuum energies are comparable to $P=1+|p|+r$. The shifted Wilson energies are also comparable to $P$ in the Brillouin cube, with momentum representatives taken modulo the reciprocal grid near its faces. The lower bound follows from (B.3a.3.6) and the nonnegative Wilson mass. A vertex of external and internal derivative order $a$ has norm at most $C_a P^{1-a}$ if $r\delta\le1$. For a term differentiated in at least one momentum its pure onsite mass part vanishes. The free derivative symbols have size at most $|p|$ and the differentiated trigonometric symbols have bounds $C_a\delta^{a-1}$ for $a\ge1$. Spin-connection terms are first order in the external momenta and have the same count. For the continuum these facts follow directly from its linear internal symbol and the same first-order connection. The estimates hold through any fixed finite differentiation order. They also apply to derivatives with respect to fixed bounded external components after replacing one of the centered momentum representatives by a neighboring periodic representative, since these have comparable norms at a seam.

The resolvent norm is at most $C(\omega^2+P^2)^{-1/2}$. In a term where derivatives create $u$ extra resolvents, the corresponding extra differentiated Hamiltonians supply at most $P^{u-a}$ after their derivative orders are counted. The integrated frequency majorant is $C P^{1-s-u}$ for $s+u\ge2$. This follows by the change of variable $\omega=Py$ in the absolutely convergent real-frequency integral. In the single-propagator term before differentiation use the symmetric pair $(i\omega+H)^{-1}+(-i\omega+H)^{-1}=2H(\omega^2+H^2)^{-1}$, which has the same integrated degree. Differentiating this paired expression preserves its frequency integrability. The same estimates hold for the antiperiodic sum on any compact positive interval by comparison with the decreasing integrable frequency majorants. Thus, for each joint multi-index $a$ in $p,q$ and $r\delta\le1$,
$$
|\partial^a I_\delta|+|\partial^a I_0|\le C_a P^{1-|a|}.
\tag{K.10.18o.2}
$$
On $\delta |p|\le\eta$ with fixed $\eta<1/4$, the flat symbol difference and each metric vertex difference gain $C\delta P$ relative to this order, by the trigonometric Taylor inequalities and the inverse identity. This gives $|\partial^a(I_\delta-I_0)|\le C_a\delta P^{2-|a|}$ there. These inequalities use no bound on the temporal frequencies in terms of the spatial cutoff.

*Vacuum normalization at infinite volume.* Fix a smooth radial cutoff $\chi(p)$, zero below one fixed positive radius and one above twice that radius. Let $T_q^4$ be the Taylor polynomial of total degree four at $q=0$. Define the lattice and continuum ultraviolet-subtracted vacuum amplitudes by inserting $1-\chi(p)T_q^4$ into their respective integrands. At each finite $\delta$ the removed lattice coefficients are actual Brillouin integrals, and the continuum subtracted amplitude is finite. For an arbitrary mass and a fixed external-momentum budget, the continuum integral is justified by (K.10.18o.2), with the low region kept unexpanded. The Taylor identity is the integral remainder along the segment from zero to $q$. The ultraviolet part has fifth derivatives and spatial degree $-4$.

Here is a local comparison of this continuum prescription with the geometric heat prescription. Work first at strictly positive mass. Use $D=\partial_\tau+H$ and $T=D^*D$ in the canonical density variables. For fixed external momenta the flat Fourier coefficients of a $j$th metric derivative of $\operatorname{Tr}e^{-tT}$ follow by the Duhamel identity. Each term with $s$ differentiated $T$ factors has a factor $t^s$ times a simplex integral, $s$ polynomial vertices of internal and external momentum degree at most two, and Gaussian factors. At flat input their weighted exponent obeys $\sum_i u_i |P+Q_i|^2\ge |P|^2/2-C_K$ for $P=(\omega,p)$ and bounded $Q_i=(0,q_i)$, since $u_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i u_i=1$. Each external derivative lowers the polynomial degree by one or brings a Gaussian derivative with its compensating factor $\sqrt t$ after rescaling $P$ by $t^{-1/2}$. Thus five external derivatives give a uniform bound $C_K t^{1/2}$ for the integrated four-dimensional differentiated heat trace at $0<t\le1$. At large proper time the strictly positive mass gives exponential convergence.

To identify the same fifth derivatives with the canonical vacuum loops, use a smooth auxiliary compression of the metric perturbation. In flat momentum coordinates put $H_B(u)=H(0)+M_B(H(u)-H(0))M_B$, with $M_B$ multiplication by $\varphi(p/B)$, where $\varphi=1$ on the unit ball and has compact support. On a finite torus the metric-dependent part of this operator is a finite matrix block. The canonical proper-time response on that block equals the paired time determinant after removing the metric-independent reference. Indeed the spatial block and temporal Fourier modes diagonalize separately, and the heat identity (K.10.18m.9) gives the vacuum part. The same identities hold for its flat infinite-volume coefficient densities: for a fixed cutoff all loop momenta lie in a compact set, and one can either pass the torus Riemann sums to the integrals at commensurate external momenta or use the finite loop matrix calculus directly. For $|p|\le B-K$, every shifted vertex is unchanged. The remaining differentiated terms have $|p|\ge B-K$; every derivative of a nonconstant cutoff multiplier supplies $O(B^{-1})$ on its transition shell. For the canonical loops the integrated fifth-derivative error is bounded by $C/B$ from (K.10.18o.2). For the heat terms the same power count gives $C t^{1/2}(1+tB^2)^J e^{-c t B^2}$ for $0<t\le1$, for a fixed finite $J$: factors $B^{-1}$ from the cutoff derivatives are at most $C|p|^{-1}$ on their shell and are handled by the same Gaussian moment integral. Its integral with $dt/t$ is $O(B^{-1})$. The large-time tail is exponentially small in $B$ on the high band. Thus removal of the auxiliary cutoff identifies the fifth derivatives of the two unrestricted vacuum prescriptions. No hard cutoff on a moving momentum boundary is differentiated.

After the unitary density identification of the geometric and coordinate spinor Hilbert spaces, the geometric operator is $N^{-1/2}\beta(\partial_\tau+H)N^{-1/2}$, up to a fixed choice of Euclidean spin frame. The factor $\beta$ is a constant unitary and commutes with the lapse multiplier. This identity follows from the spatial compatibility formula (K.10.18l.1) and the lapse spin-connection term. Thus only a local positive scalar congruence remains when comparing the squared singular-value determinants. For a multiplication path $D_s=R_sD_0R_s$ and $A=\dot R_sR_s^{-1}$ the analytic determinant variation is the finite part at $z=0$ of
$$
\operatorname{Tr}\big[A(D_s^*D_s)^{-z}\big]+\operatorname{Tr}\big[A(D_sD_s^*)^{-z}\big].
\tag{K.10.18o.3}
$$
This follows by differentiating $D_s^*D_s$, then cyclically moving one $D_s$ through the complex power. The two inserted heat coefficients at $z=0$ are local of derivative order at most four. Consequently this change of variables contributes zero after five external derivatives. Local proper-time subtractions have the same derivative bound. This proves equality of fifth external derivatives in the two prescriptions.

The difference is therefore a polynomial $P_\mathrm{cov}(q)$ of degree at most four. At strictly positive mass it may be computed at $q=0$. For zero mass compute it on a fixed finite unisolvent set, choosing at each interpolation point the nonzero proper partial sums of the external momenta whenever the metric order allows. Such lists form an open dense set, and no individual fourth momentum derivative at the massless vacuum origin is taken. For continuity of the canonical subtracted amplitudes at those points, in the bounded internal-momentum region each cycle has at most three resolvents, all uniformly integrable by Hölder in four internal dimensions, and the high Taylor integrals stay away from zero. The continuum heat finite part has the same continuity. For the latter, at large proper time a Gaussian simplex term with $s\ge2$ can be large only near simplex faces where the simplex weight concentrates at one of its distinct shifted internal momenta. Splitting by the largest simplex weight, each of the other $s-1$ weights costs $O(t^{-1})$ by the strictly positive separation of the shifts. At the repeated starting momentum combine its two adjacent weights first. The trace integral thus has the large-time factor $t^s t^{-(s-1)} t^{-2}=t^{-1}$ times a bounded vertex factor. The $s=1$ term also has $t^{-1}$ by the four-dimensional Gaussian integral. The positive mass factor only improves the bound, so the proper-time measure $dt/t$ gives a uniform integrable tail as the mass tends to zero. Uniform small-time subtractions follow from the same Duhamel expansion with mass in a compact interval. Finite interpolation now yields the massless polynomial and an effective coefficient rule. The same polynomial applies to a finite torus and compact positive temperature: local heat terms depend only on the local symbol, while all nonidentity windings give finite differences independent of the ultraviolet subtraction. The quantitative sum and integral estimates below justify the latter transfer.

*Choice of lattice local energy.* In the actual physical variables let the ultraviolet transition radius be $\lambda(a)=\min(\mu_*,\eta/(4a))$, with $a$ the physical mesh. Apply the preceding prescription with $\chi(p/\lambda(a))$ and the actual mass. In addition to removing the high-band lattice Taylor integral and adding $P_\mathrm{cov}$, add the low-band polynomial
$$
\int (1-\chi(p/\lambda(a)))\,T_q^4[I_0(p;q)-I_a(p;q)]\,\frac{d^3p}{(2\pi)^3}.
\tag{K.10.18o.4}
$$
Its support is inside the lattice band. At mass zero, for the degree-four coefficient the extra $a|p|$ from the lattice-continuum symbol difference improves $|p|^{-3}$ to $a|p|^{-2}$, integrable in three dimensions. Indeed the proof of (K.10.18o.2) applies homogeneously for $|p|>0$ at $q=0$ after rescaling frequency by $|p|$, with the trigonometric difference bounds relative to $|p|$ and no added unit scale. The lower degrees are easier by the same estimate. The scalar Taylor terms therefore give one finite real local energy functional: replace external momenta by spatial derivatives of the corresponding metric perturbations and integrate the real symmetrized cubic polynomial over the physical volume. Set higher metric orders of this control to zero. The construction is local in the marked regulator frame and its fixed coefficients use no temperature or torus data. This low-band term ensures exact comparison of the polynomial pieces even when the dimensionless transition radius grows or shrinks along the scale sequence.

*Quantitative nonpolynomial matching.* After rescaling to the fixed dimensionless torus, use a separate fixed smooth partition at $Q>2K+2$ in the estimates, independent of the control's transition radius. The corrected infinite-volume vacuum defect is the integral of $(1-T_q^4)(I_\delta-I_0)$ on the common band and of $-(1-T_q^4)I_0$ outside it. Indeed the lattice high polynomial is removed, the continuum finite part restores its own high polynomial with the covariant correction, and (K.10.18o.4) subtracts the low Taylor difference on the common band. The low-region integrals converge with $O(\delta)$ for bounded mass. All shifted internal momenta stay bounded, and the possible coincident massless zeros have an integrable frequency and spatial measure after the actual vertices are included. A direct bound for the difference uses the inverse identity and the estimate $\|h_\delta(p+q)-h_0(p+q)\|\le C\delta |p+q|^2$. Each extra singular resolvent is accompanied by this quadratic zero. For a cycle with up to three resolvents, the worst remaining product is bounded by $C\prod_{i=1}^3(\omega^2+|p+q_i|^2)^{-1/2}$ on the compact four-dimensional integration block. Hölder's inequality with exponent three bounds the integral of this product uniformly in the shifts and $r$. The low-region Taylor polynomial of the difference is controlled through degree four by the homogeneous bound above. The high remainder in the region $Q<|p|<\eta/\delta$ has bound $C\delta|p|^{-3}$ from (K.10.18o.2) with five external derivatives. In the remaining band and outside it the individual bounds are $C|p|^{-4}$. The radial integrals give $C\delta[1+|\log\delta|]$.

For the spatial-period and temperature transfer, split at the separate fixed smooth high cutoff $Q$. On its high part the finite torus vacuum sum minus the corresponding integral is the sum of nonzero spatial windings. To compare the lattice and continuum high windings use six pure internal momentum derivatives and periodic summation by parts, with a smooth shared cutoff supported inside the band for the common portion. From (K.10.18o.2) the sixth derivative of the difference has $L^1$ bound $C\delta$ there, since $\delta |p|^{-4}$ is integrable at infinity. The two remaining high tails have bound $C\delta^2$ for their sixth derivatives. The summable nonzero winding factor is $C_\ell\sum_{b\ne0}|b|^{-6}$. The continuum high winding prescription is the same as its heat finite part: the small-proper-time nonzero spatial windings in the Duhamel expansion are exponentially small before the proper-time integral by Gaussian Poisson summation with the shifted internal centers. Their value after the proper-time integral agrees with the six-derivative winding prescription by the same auxiliary smooth compression and absolute derivative bounds. For the high thermal terms the contour estimates of Proposition K.10.18n apply to the difference between the Matsubara energy and the vacuum energy, using $-\theta^{-1}\log(1+e^{-\theta z})$ and $-\theta^{-1}\log(1+e^{\theta z})$ on the two separate energy rectangles. This supplies an exponential majorant and an $O(\delta)$ lattice-continuum difference. In the low region combine the low vacuum integral with the correction from it to the actual finite torus response before comparing. The low vacuum integrals cancel in this decomposition. The finitely many actual low modes use the paired Matsubara sum, whose positive frequency gap gives the $O(\delta)$ error. This also retains the possible massless $p=0$ block. The vacuum subtraction coefficients are consequently unaffected by the temperature or spatial period. The above local contributions and their errors prove the first bound in (K.10.18o.1), including all mixed metric vertices.

For $r\delta\ge1$, each undifferentiated lattice vertex costs at most $Cr$. Every differentiated factor with $v\ge1$ external or internal momentum derivatives costs at most $C_v\delta^{v-1}$; the onsite mass term has no momentum derivative. If $u\ge1$ factors carry a total of five derivatives, frequency integration gives $C\delta^{5-u}r^{1-u}\le C\delta^4$. Integrating over the Brillouin volume gives $C\delta$. For six internal derivatives the same calculation gives $C\delta^5$ per integrand and $C\delta^2$ after integrating. Thus the nonzero spatial windings contribute at most $C_\ell\delta^2$ by periodic Poisson, without removing a low block in this gapped sector. The continuum integrand estimates give $Cr^{-1}$ for the integrated fifth derivative and $Cr^{-2}$ for the integrated sixth derivative, by rescaling internal momentum and frequency by $r$. The low-band polynomial and covariant polynomial have already been matched exactly. Thermal terms in either model have bounds polynomial in $r,\delta^{-1}$ times $e^{-c\theta_-r}$ by the same separated spectral contours; since $r\delta\ge1$, this is bounded by $C/r$. This proves the second estimate in (K.10.18o.1).

All constants arise from fixed finite tensor coefficient lists, a finite order of sine, cosine and cutoff derivative bounds, a finite external-momentum budget, the convergent frequency integrals, the compact thermal interval, and the spatial winding sum. The scalar control changes the absolute energy and its metric derivatives. Its implementation requires a separately prepared and calibrated source-energy reference, since the flat normalized Gibbs state does not record that scalar. ∎

<a id="theorem-k1018p"></a>

<a id="theorem-k1018p-realized-wilson-mass-flow-channel-and-endpoint-calibration"></a>**Theorem K.10.18p (Realized Wilson Mass-Flow Channel and Endpoint Calibration).** Fix effectively specified $m,\ell,\theta_-,\theta_+$ as in Theorem K.10.18h and the independent proper-time scale of Proposition K.10.18o. There is a registered sequence of finite local hosts with the Wilson metric coupling (K.10.18k.4), the scalar energy controls of Proposition K.10.18o, and a paid causal realization of the state-independent map of Theorem K.10.18h on the complete retained light field algebra. The canonical calibration and the actual output instruments use the same coarse field register and native metric controls. Their states are joined by the uniform flat comparison (K.10.18p.1) below. The calibrated continuum endpoint values and predictive diameters are
$$
(c_U,a_U,C_U)=(N/20,11N/360,Nq),\qquad
(c_I,a_I,C_I)=(M/20,11M/360,Mq).
$$
The common conversion constants in (K.10.18e.1) are $1/(20q)$ and $11/(360q)$, respectively. The strict/equality and recovery conditions are those of Theorem K.10.18h. The construction uses the declared finite local control and finite precision regime of Construction F.10.12i.7. No uniform bound on apparatus size, running time, or work is needed along the scale sequence.

*Field and control host.* At each fine site of every species, and at each coarse light-field site, put the seven-mode site block of Construction F.10.12i.4. The coarse heavy comparison, when used, is a separate prepared finite block under the same coefficient rule. It has no receiver port. Mark the periodic edges with their actual lengths $a_U$ or $a_I$ and register the spin boundary condition and orientations. Use the complete periodic auxiliary matching sector of that construction. The field Hamiltonian is the dressed nearest-neighbor form of (K.10.18k.4), in physical energy units at that scale. For any static control profile each onsite or link coefficient is an actual programmed matrix on its fixed one- or two-site support. Onsite spin-connection, mass and Wilson coefficients and both endpoint lapse factors are included. On the prepared code the lifted operators obey $\widehat H(u)J=Jd\Gamma(H(u))$ exactly for the prescribed matrices, where $J$ is the code isometry. This holds for all profiles, so it holds for the first, second and third differentiated matrices. The flat current and lapse normalization are (K.10.18k.5) and (B.3a.1.2). All metric jets are obtained by comparing runs on the same native controls in the original coordinate clock.

The scalar density of Proposition K.10.18o is a cubic local polynomial in the metric perturbations and their retained spatial derivatives. On the finite torus program its exact quadrature on each tested Fourier list: choose a controller grid with strictly more nodes per axis than twice the maximum total Fourier degree in the cubic density, then the integral is the discrete sum by exact Fourier orthogonality. The controller grid is a separate owned classical/energy stock and its cells use the prescribed external profiles, the stencil's independently computed coefficients, and the actual geometry. Its quadrature is exact for the tested orders, and each larger Fourier list can use a finer finite grid under the same density rule. The fixed finite counterterm coefficients can be evaluated to arbitrary certified precision by the vacuum integrals and heat estimates of Proposition K.10.18o. Let $s_x(u)$ denote a cell's physical scalar energy contribution. Supply one occupied control level at that cell with a gap $B_x+s_x(u)$ and a reference level of gap $B_x$, where $B_x>1+\sup|s_x|$ on the registered compact parameter box. The ready level is invariant during the native field response. The zero-profile reference and both actual gaps are retained. The gap difference and its changes are read with a co-located Ramsey reference that calibrates phase in the original clock, using pulses and, for large gaps, short interrogations fixed from the known uniform bound. Equivalently the static work difference in the occupied level gives $s_x(u)-s_x(0)$. Its Hamiltonian is a genuine scalar addition to the source in the occupied sector, independent of the Gibbs normalization, and its metric work derivatives are included once. No temperature label enters the programmed density or reference. This joins the independently determined local control to an actual scalar energy port.

*Channel and complete receiver.* Give each field and auxiliary qubit to be captured its own blank co-located capture qubit. Use the parallel exchange pulses of Construction F.10.12i.7 and retain their complete gauge constraints. Choose a marked routing tree joining the capture cells, a decoder, coarse load cells and owned sink cells. For each actual route hop of length $d_e$ use time at least $d_e/c+1$ in the registered physical units. Store transported registers in owned finite carrier blocks with a scalar storage Hamiltonian and no logical drift. Gates use physically co-located carrier blocks. No operation at the decoder is assigned to the earlier cut. At the decoder apply the inverse code isometry on its transported code and the inverse fine mode rotation, then separate the retained labels from the discarded species and shell. The mode rotation, retained polar map of Theorem K.10.18h and coarse encoding are implemented by a fixed finite rotation list for that $n$. The map on the ideal code is precisely the isometry followed by the declared partial trace, on every input of the complete field register. There is no use of the preparation parameter. All unused factors, correlations, purifiers, actual work records and preparation labels remain in the owned sink or supplier. They have no return port at the receiver. Restore the selected modes to the actual coarse torus cells, and load their auxiliary matching sector. With native links disabled during loading, turn on the actual coarse Hamiltonian by a registered scalar ramp. The image state is diagonal in its flat signed-mode basis, so it commutes with this ramp and is unchanged in the ideal protocol. All switch times and energies enter the ledger.

The receiver contains the complete light logical field register, including both physical parity sectors, with its fixed code. The native stress and metric vertices are even and have the stated local spin support. To implement a general finite receiver matrix instrument, transport a complete register to its own future decoder and decode it as a finite physical spin register. All logical CAR matrices can then be read by a finite co-located spin instrument. This uses co-location for the odd distributed CAR matrices. A charged instrument can equivalently use its explicitly prepared parity reference. The supplier purification and readable preparation parameter remain at their separately owned ports. The only appended bookkeeping is the fixed parameter-independent controller schedule and the padded invoice.

*Finite resources and accuracy.* The following is a generating ledger, with all its entries determined before evaluating the continuum endpoint coefficients. A deterministic fine and coarse one-particle Fourier basis and the known Wilson symbol give their exact signed-mode matrices, with the full periodic zero block retained. Lexicographic elimination of a $d\times d$ mode unitary uses at most $d(d-1)/2$ two-mode rotations and $d$ phases. The auxiliary matching state is prepared by a recorded finite Gaussian/stabilizer circuit with the actual orientations. A Gibbs state of a controlled finite matrix is prepared by diagonalizing that matrix and preparing one owned system/purifier pair for every occupation. A pair with probability $f=(1+e^{\theta E})^{-1}$ uses a controlled two-mode rotation on an owned even pair. Degenerate eigenvalues are implemented by any certified spectral-block preparation within the declared tolerance. More directly one can approximate the thermal covariance as a matrix function and diagonalize a finite rational approximation to it, which does not require deciding equality of eigenvalues. The code map and decoding circuit are the finite basis permutation and matching-state preparation of Construction F.10.12i.4. All these finite lists may be decomposed into co-located elementary controlled spin gates. Each two-block gate is routed along the unique recorded tree path, with its actual pickup, co-location and return stages. Program evaluation, ready states, reference states, switches, storage and the unused sectors are included.

For an actual pulse $j$, with unit-normalized generator $G_j$, choose a smooth amplitude $b_j(t)$ with the prescribed action. A bound $L_j$ on the native and auxiliary drift over its support is the sum of the explicit actual term norm bounds during that pulse, including contemporaneous controls. The approximation errors satisfy
$$
\|U_{\rm actual}-U_{\rm ideal}\|\le \sum_j\bigl(\eta_j+\tau_j L_j\bigr)+\sum_j\zeta_j,
$$
where $\eta_j$ is the gate-angle synthesis error, $\tau_j$ is the pulse duration, and $\zeta_j$ bounds the physical timing and ramp error by the generator norm times the actual timing error. Causal transport is not assigned a short pulse duration. The zero-logical-drift storage rule holds throughout those intervals. Use the clocks of Construction F.10.12i.7 and choose every paid tolerance so the sum is below the branch error budget. The actual peak $\|G_j\|\sup|b_j|$, duration, action and reference switching work are recorded. A usable work bound for the pulse is the sum of the variation of its control amplitude times $\|G_j\|$ and the integral of the actual Hamiltonian coefficient variation over that interval. This follows from $d\langle H(t)\rangle/dt=\langle\partial_tH(t)\rangle$. Include each signed ramp and gap change, and bound it by the corresponding actual finite operator norm variation. No reset or erased spent stock is used.

The cost record uses the supplied ready prices $P_v$ and holding powers $Q_v$ of the host cells, frozen before the response run. For a prepared run with known maximal horizon $T$ its stock invoice is $\sum_v S_v(P_v+TQ_v)$, where each $S_v$ is the integer stock count of the registered cell or stock type. A concrete supplied tariff is $P_v=Q_v=1$ in fixed ready and holding units. Add all actual pulse peaks, integrated switching-work bounds, courier work and storage entries, numerical precision operations and the scalar reference stocks with their baselines. The generated pulse, stock, path and control coefficient lists evaluate every entry. Padding to a worst-case common schedule across the finite preparation grid does not expose its label. Every coefficient and pulse tolerance is determined by an effective finite algorithm. The stock and work can grow with $n$.

The full continuum inverse-temperature interval is obtained from finite preparation grids with spacing at most $\epsilon/(4(1+\|H_F\|))$, where $H_F$ is the actual dimensionless many-body field Hamiltonian. The trace derivative of its Gibbs state has norm at most $2\|H_F\|$. A grid error and a pulse or preparation error can therefore each be funded below a requested $\epsilon$. At a fixed stage the ideal physical map is an exact partial trace after the fixed input/output mode identifications. The actual paid errors are uniform in all input matrices on the declared code when only the channel operations are compared, by the unitary norm error and trace-norm contraction. *Absolute jets on smooth directions.* The estimates of Proposition K.10.18o are polynomial in the Fourier momentum budget when specialized to the actual scale sequence. <a id="theorem-k1019a-exact-relational-clock-on-the-deparametrizable-constraint-class"></a>**Theorem K.10.19a (Exact Relational Clock on the Deparametrizable Constraint Class).** Let
$$
\mathcal M=T^*\mathbb R\times\mathcal P
$$
carry canonical coordinates $(T,p_T,z)$ and the single first-class constraint
$$
\mathcal C=p_T+H(z)=0,
\tag{K.10.19a.1}
$$
where the Hamiltonian flow $\Phi_H^s$ is complete on $\mathcal P$. Then $T$ is a global phase-space clock because
$$
\{T,\mathcal C\}=1,
\tag{K.10.19a.2}
$$
and every gauge orbit meets each slice $T=s$ exactly once. For every continuously differentiable phase-space function $f$ on $\mathcal P$, the relational observable
$$
O_f(s)(T,p_T,z)=f\!\left(\Phi_H^{\,s-T}(z)\right)
\tag{K.10.19a.3}
$$
is gauge invariant and restricts to $f(z)$ on $T=s$.

More generally, a differentiable candidate clock $\tau$ has no differentiable local inverse along an orbit at a point where $\{\tau,\mathcal C\}=0$. This does not by itself imply failure of local or global injectivity. It is a global clock in the sense of unique orbit-slice intersections exactly when its restriction to every orbit is strictly monotone, has the declared common range, and each level set intersects each orbit once.

*Proof.* The constraint flow advances $T$ by the gauge parameter and advances $z$ by the same Hamiltonian time. These two changes cancel in (K.10.19a.3), so $\{O_f(s),\mathcal C\}=0$. Completeness and (K.10.19a.2) give one intersection with every slice. If a differentiable inverse along an orbit existed where $\{\tau,\mathcal C\}=0$, differentiating the inverse identity would give $1=0$ by the chain rule. Nevertheless, $\tau=T^3$ is strictly increasing along every orbit and has range $\mathbb R$, despite its zero derivative at $T=0$; its inverse there is not differentiable. Strict monotonicity plus the common-range condition is sufficient and necessary for unique intersection with every declared level. ∎

This theorem supplies the clock and Dirac observables for the deparametrizable class and distinguishes regular local invertibility from unique global orbit-slice intersections. A PU continuum branch must still construct its constraint in the form (K.10.19a.1), or supply a different globally covered clock atlas.

<a id="theorem-k1019b-projective-cosmological-measure-and-regulator-independence-criterion"></a>**Theorem K.10.19b (Projective Cosmological Measure and Regulator-Independence Criterion).** Let $(\Omega_n,\pi_{n+1,n})$ be nonempty finite sample spaces with surjective coarse-graining maps, and let $\mu_n$ be probability measures. There is a unique probability measure on the inverse-limit cylinder algebra with marginals $\mu_n$ exactly when
$$
(\pi_{n+1,n})_*\mu_{n+1}=\mu_n
\quad\text{for every }n.
\tag{K.10.19b.1}
$$
On the compact inverse limit this cylinder measure extends uniquely to the generated Borel sigma-algebra. Hence the probability of every finite-level event is regulator independent precisely when its values are compatible under (K.10.19b.1).

Assume (K.10.19b.1), and let $w_n:\Omega_n\to[0,\infty)$ be observer-selection weights with $0<Z_n:=\sum_{\omega}w_n(\omega)\mu_n(\omega)<\infty$. The conditioned measures
$$
\nu_n(A)=\frac1{Z_n}\sum_{\omega\in A}w_n(\omega)\mu_n(\omega)
\tag{K.10.19b.2}
$$
are regulator independent exactly when the normalized densities
$$
\bar w_n:=\frac{w_n}{Z_n}
\quad\text{satisfy}\quad
\bar w_n
=\mathbb E_{\mu_{n+1}}
\!\left[\bar w_{n+1}\mid\pi_{n+1,n}\right]
\quad\mu_n\text{-almost surely}.
\tag{K.10.19b.3}
$$

*Proof.* Necessity of (K.10.19b.1) follows by evaluating the same cylinder event at two adjacent levels. Consistency makes the cylinder assignment well defined and finitely additive; the finite spaces and compact inverse limit give the unique countably additive extension. Applying the same pushforward calculation to the weighted measures gives (K.10.19b.3), and conditional expectation proves sufficiency. Conversely, equality of all weighted cylinder probabilities is the defining integral identity for (K.10.19b.3). ∎

The theorem completely resolves normalization, regulator independence, conditioning, and observer weighting for the declared projective finite class. Theorem K.10.19d supplies these physical fields for one named compact-torus qualified-observer survey, with its complete source premise and cylinder interface explicit.

<a id="theorem-k1019c-clock-atlas-gluing-criterion-and-periodic-orbit-obstruction"></a>**Theorem K.10.19c (Clock-Atlas Gluing Criterion and Periodic-Orbit Obstruction).** Let $\mathcal M$ be a smooth symplectic manifold, and let $\mathcal C\in C^\infty(\mathcal M)$ have $0$ as a regular value with $\Sigma:=\mathcal C^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing$. The Hamiltonian vector field $X_{\mathcal C}$, defined by $X_{\mathcal C}f=\{f,\mathcal C\}$, is tangent to $\Sigma$; assume its flow $\Phi^s$ on $\Sigma$ is complete. A clock chart is a pair $(U,\tau_U)$ with $U\subset\Sigma$ open and $\Phi$-invariant and $\tau_U\in C^\infty(U)$ satisfying $\{\tau_U,\mathcal C\}=1$ on $U$; a clock atlas is a family of clock charts whose domains cover $\Sigma$; a global clock is a clock chart with domain $\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ admits a global clock if and only if it admits a clock atlas and its orbit space $\Sigma/\Phi$ is Hausdorff;

2. a global clock $\tau$ satisfies $\tau(\Phi^sx)=\tau(x)+s$, every orbit meets every level set $\{\tau=s\}$ exactly once, and for every $f\in C^1(\Sigma)$ the relational observable $O_f(s)(x):=f(\Phi^{\,s-\tau(x)}x)$ is constant along orbits and equals $f$ on $\{\tau=s\}$;

3. if $\Phi^Px=x$ for some $x\in\Sigma$ and $P>0$, then no clock chart contains $x$ and no continuous function on $\Sigma$ is strictly increasing along every orbit; for $\mathcal C=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^2(p_i^2+q_i^2)-E$ with $E>0$ on $T^*\mathbb R^2$, every orbit in $\Sigma\cong S^3$ has period $2\pi$;

4. the Hausdorff condition cannot be removed: on $T^*(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\})$ with canonical coordinates $(x,y,p_x,p_y)$ and $r:=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, the constraint $\mathcal C=p_yr$ has $\Sigma=\{p_y=0\}$ and the clock atlas
$$
\tau_+=\ln(r+y)\ \text{ on }\ \Sigma\setminus\{x=0,\ y<0\},
\qquad
\tau_-=-\ln(r-y)\ \text{ on }\ \Sigma\setminus\{x=0,\ y>0\},
\tag{K.10.19c.1}
$$
but no continuous function on $\Sigma$ whose restriction to every orbit is a strictly increasing bijection onto $\mathbb R$.

For the deparametrizable class of Theorem K.10.19a, $T$ is a global clock by (K.10.19a.2).

*Proof.* On a clock chart, $\frac{d}{ds}\tau_U(\Phi^sx)=(X_{\mathcal C}\tau_U)(\Phi^sx)=1$ along the complete orbit inside the invariant set $U$, so $\tau_U(\Phi^sx)=\tau_U(x)+s$. For a global clock, $s\mapsto\tau(x)+s$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R$, which gives the level-set statement of item 2, and $O_f(s)(\Phi^{s'}x)=f(\Phi^{\,s-\tau(x)-s'}\Phi^{s'}x)=O_f(s)(x)$, with $O_f(s)(x)=f(x)$ when $\tau(x)=s$.

For item 1, let $\varpi:\Sigma\to Q:=\Sigma/\Phi$ be the quotient map. It is open, because the saturation of an open set is the union of its flow translates, so $Q$ is second countable. For a clock chart $(U_\alpha,\tau_\alpha)$, the level $S_\alpha:=\tau_\alpha^{-1}(0)$ is an embedded hypersurface of $U_\alpha$, since $d\tau_\alpha(X_{\mathcal C})=1$, and $\varrho_\alpha(x):=\Phi^{-\tau_\alpha(x)}x$ is a smooth retraction of $U_\alpha$ onto $S_\alpha$ that is constant on orbits. Hence $\varpi|_{S_\alpha}$ is a homeomorphism onto the open set $\varpi(U_\alpha)$, and on overlaps the transition maps $\varrho_\beta|_{S_\alpha\cap U_\beta}$ are smooth with smooth inverses $\varrho_\alpha|_{S_\beta\cap U_\alpha}$. If $Q$ is Hausdorff, these charts make $Q$ a smooth manifold on which $\varpi$ is smooth, and $Q$ carries a smooth partition of unity $\{\psi_\alpha\}$ subordinate to $\{\varpi(U_\alpha)\}$. The functions $\varphi_\alpha:=\psi_\alpha\circ\varpi$ are smooth, $\Phi$-invariant and locally finite, are supported in $\varpi^{-1}(\varpi(U_\alpha))=U_\alpha$, and sum to one. The function $\tau:=\sum_\alpha\varphi_\alpha\tau_\alpha$, each term extended by zero off the support of $\varphi_\alpha$, is smooth and satisfies $X_{\mathcal C}\tau=\sum_\alpha\bigl[(X_{\mathcal C}\varphi_\alpha)\tau_\alpha+\varphi_\alpha X_{\mathcal C}\tau_\alpha\bigr]=\sum_\alpha\varphi_\alpha=1$, so it is a global clock. Conversely, a global clock is a one-chart atlas, and $\varrho(x):=\Phi^{-\tau(x)}x$ induces a continuous bijection from $Q$ onto the Hausdorff subspace $\tau^{-1}(0)\subset\Sigma$ with continuous inverse $\varpi|_{\tau^{-1}(0)}$.

For item 3, a clock chart containing $x$ would give $\tau_U(x)=\tau_U(\Phi^Px)=\tau_U(x)+P$, and a function strictly increasing along the orbit of $x$ would take different values at $x$ and at $\Phi^Px=x$. For the two-oscillator constraint, $d\mathcal C$ vanishes only at the origin, where $\mathcal C=-E\ne0$, and Hamilton's equations $\dot q_i=p_i$, $\dot p_i=-q_i$ make every orbit $2\pi$-periodic on the sphere $\Sigma$ of radius $\sqrt{2E}$.

For item 4, $d\mathcal C=r\,dp_y+p_y\,dr$ equals $r\,dp_y\ne0$ on $\Sigma$. On $\Sigma$, Hamilton's equations give $\dot x=\dot p_x=\dot p_y=0$ and $\dot y=r$. The orbits are therefore the lines $\{x=h,\ p_x=p\}$ with $h\ne0$, on which $y=|h|\sinh(s+s_0)$ ranges over $\mathbb R$, and the half-lines $\{x=0,\ y>0,\ p_x=p\}$ and $\{x=0,\ y<0,\ p_x=p\}$, on which $y=y_0e^{s}$ and $y=y_0e^{-s}$ respectively. The two domains in (K.10.19c.1) omit whole orbits, the functions are smooth where $r\pm y>0$, and $X_{\mathcal C}\tau_\pm=r\,\partial_y\tau_\pm=1$. Suppose $g$ is continuous on $\Sigma$ and restricts to a strictly increasing bijection onto $\mathbb R$ along every orbit, and write points of $\Sigma$ as $(x,y,p_x)$. Along the half-line $\{x=0,\ y<0,\ p_x=0\}$, $y$ increases with the flow and $g$ is unbounded above, so some $y'<0$ has $g(0,y',0)>g(0,1,0)$. For $h\ne0$, the points $(h,y',0)$ and $(h,1/2,0)$ lie on one orbit in increasing flow order, so $g(h,y',0)<g(h,1/2,0)$, and letting $h\to0$ gives $g(0,y',0)\le g(0,1/2,0)$. On the half-line $\{x=0,\ y>0,\ p_x=0\}$, $g(0,1/2,0)<g(0,1,0)$, which contradicts $g(0,y',0)>g(0,1,0)$. For the deparametrizable class, $\Sigma=\{p_T=-H\}$, $0$ is a regular value because $\partial\mathcal C/\partial p_T=1$, and (K.10.19a.2) states $\{T,\mathcal C\}=1$ on all of $\Sigma$. ∎

## 3. Five-slot physical schedule and exact state law

Each fresh trial uses exactly five slots of duration $\tau$:

1. Fresh-reference entrance, source/calibration checks and descriptor installation.
2. Charged system/ancilla preparation with the prescribed positive waveform.
3. Free system drift and paid clock/holding interval; this is the observation window.
4. Neutral detector/instrument slot.
5. Copy, validation and durable retention of the outcome and flags.

The observation clock is $s=s_{\mathrm{lab}}-s_{\mathrm{prep\_end}}$ in slot 3, with $0<s<\tau$. The installed clock records a nondisturbing service timestamp at the registered interior $s^*$, and its finite descriptor includes the paid evaluation of $\log[s/(\tau-s)]$. This reads the clock service, not the CAR field. Its origin is the actual recorded slot-2 endpoint, not a fitted or Euclidean time. No interaction with a test detector occurs inside this window. Relational observables at an interior $s^*$ are measured through a specified endpoint Heisenberg transfer in slot 4, as below. Hence the unmeasured dynamical history is not disturbed by an undeclared intermediate instrument.

On the system, let $h_N=\hbar cB_{N}$ with the original retained scalar many-body excitation offset. For preparation set

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{z_0,N}&=\exp(ih_N\tau/\hbar)\,C_{z_0,N}\exp(-ih_N\tau/\hbar),\\
\Theta_{z_0,N}&=\arcsin\sqrt{D_{z_0,N}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the original empty-system/filled-matching-charge-ancilla entrance state, mixing generator $G_{\Theta}$, and positive shift $\kappa_{N}$. The supplied total waveform is $H_{0,N}+F_N(s)(G_\Theta+\kappa_NI)F_N(s)^*$. Its endpoint reduced covariance is exactly $C_{z_0,N}$; its full purification and scalar phase are retained. The angle norm is at most $\pi/2$, so the previously proved peak bound applies. No physical drift cancellation or discard of the correlated preparation ancillas occurs.

During slot 3 the actual full state is evolved by the system drift tensored with the ancillary idle identity. Thus $z_N(s)=\exp(-ih_{R,N}s/\hbar)z_0\exp(ih_{R,N}s/\hbar)$. The complementary system covariance remains thermal; its multi-time CAR correlations retain the original source law. System-ancilla correlations evolve and are retained. The field/controller/calibration services and every previously installed source stock remain installed and paid throughout.

All commute with the flavour charge and fermion parity. Each has norm at most one. Their expectations give every diagonal entry and every real/imaginary off-diagonal entry of z. equals its actual source expectation and its endpoint-transferred CP instrument law. It is constant on constraint leaves. System tomography separates z0 and hence the reduced histories.
