<a id="theorem-k1025a-separation-entropy-tracking-budget"></a>**Theorem K.10.25a (Separation-Entropy Tracking Budget).** Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and $F:K\to K$ continuous. Equip length-$n$ histories with the maximum metric, and let $s_n(K,2\varepsilon)$ be the maximum number of initial states whose histories are pairwise more than $2\varepsilon$ apart. Any fixed-width binary encoder and decoder that approximate every history within $\varepsilon$ require

$$
B_n\ge\left\lceil\log_2s_n(K,2\varepsilon)\right\rceil.
$$

**Proof.** Two histories separated by more than $2\varepsilon$ cannot have the same decoded approximation: the triangle inequality would bound their distance by $2\varepsilon$. Encoding is therefore injective on a separated set, and $2^{B_n}\ge s_n$. This proves the bound. Define $h_{\mathrm{sep}}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\ln s_n(K,2\varepsilon)$. Taking limit superiors gives $\limsup B_n/n\ge h_{\mathrm{sep}}/\ln2$. Positive fixed-scale separation entropy excludes a fixed bit budget that works for every horizon.

**Example (An Exact Tracking-Cost Witness).** Let $K=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N_0}$, let $F$ be the left shift, and set
$$
d(x,y)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}2^{-j-1}|x_j-y_j|.
$$
This compact system has $2^n$ initial states formed by an arbitrary length-$n$ binary prefix followed by zeros. Two different prefixes differ at some position $j<n$; after $j$ shifts their distance is at least $1/2$. Thus for $0<\varepsilon<1/4$ these states are more than $2\varepsilon$ separated in the history metric, and Theorem K.10.25a gives $B_n\ge n$.

For an upper bound, transmit the first $n+L$ bits, where $2^{-L-1}\le\varepsilon$, and decode each retained history using a zero tail. At every time $j<n$, the first $n+L-j$ output bits are exact and the remaining metric weight is at most $2^{-L-1}$. Hence $B_n=n+O_\varepsilon(1)$ suffices. The asymptotic tracking cost is exactly one bit per step, even though the shift rule has a fixed finite description. A periodic initial state also has a short description. The uniform cost comes from covering all retained histories.

**Application to Classical Dynamics.** A compact invariant subsystem with a certified positive-entropy symbolic model supplies the hypotheses of Theorem K.10.25a at sufficiently fine resolution. Bolotin and MacKay's restricted-three-body construction provides such symbolic dynamics on its stated small-mass and near-collision regime [Bolotin, MacKay 2006]. Applying the tracking theorem registers that subsystem, its return map and metric, and the time per return. The return count becomes physical time only through this additional timing record.

Three different classical questions then have separate answers. Non-integrability concerns the existence of first integrals in a stated function class; for example, Tsygvintsev proves the absence of a complete set of complex meromorphic first integrals near the Lagrangian solution (Tsygvintsev 2001). A convergent series represents solutions on its stated domain. The separation bound instead counts how many distinguishable histories a uniformly accurate finite code must represent. Neither an integrability obstruction nor a series representation alone determines that count. For a causal observer receiving continual measurements, the channel and estimation assumptions convert entropy into an information-rate bound [Kawan, Yüksel 2020]. Almost-sure symbolic complexity and uniform history coverage are likewise different quantifiers; the present theorem uses the latter.

<a id="theorem-k1025b-finite-quotient-descent"></a>**Theorem K.10.25b (Finite Quotient Descent).** For a finite partition with quotient map $q$, exact deterministic descent exists precisely when

$$
q(x)=q(y)\ \Longrightarrow\ q(Fx)=q(Fy).
$$

If it exists, each initial quotient state determines its entire itinerary. A partition with $N$ cells of diameter at most $2\varepsilon$ then permits at most $N$ pairwise more than $2\varepsilon$-separated histories, so $h_{\mathrm{sep}}(F,K,2\varepsilon)=0$. Positive separation entropy therefore obstructs exact deterministic descent to every finite partition meeting that diameter bound.

*Proof.* If $qF=\bar Fq$, then $q(x)=q(y)$ implies $q(Fx)=\bar F(q(x))=\bar F(q(y))=q(Fy)$. Conversely, the displayed fiber condition makes $\bar F(q(x)):=q(Fx)$ independent of the chosen representative, so it defines the required deterministic quotient map. Induction gives $q(F^j x)=\bar F^{\,j}(q(x))$ for every integer $j\ge0$. Hence two initial states in the same cell remain in the same cell at every step, and their distance in every finite history metric $d_n$ is at most $2\varepsilon$. A set with pairwise $d_n$-distances greater than $2\varepsilon$ contains at most one representative from each of the $N$ initial cells. Thus $1\le s_n(F,K,2\varepsilon)\le N$ on the nonempty state space of the tracking theorem, and $\limsup_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\ln s_n=0$. ∎

**Interpretation.** The obstruction identifies a failure of the chosen finite state description to determine its successor. Exact dynamics supplies the set-valued map $i\mapsto\{q(Fx):x\in P_i\}$. A stochastic kernel additionally specifies a measure and the treatment of memory; a deterministic refinement adds retained distinctions; continual observation supplies new information. Each construction answers a different modeling task. An ontic reading in which the finite quotient exhausts physical state is a separately stated physical principle.

**Physical Finite-Information Hypothesis.** A finite-information interpretation takes the registered finite state as the complete physical state and specifies how previously unresolved quantities become actual. Del Santo and Gisin develop a classical indeterministic model using finite information quantities [Del Santo, Gisin 2019]. Within the present framework, this is a candidate realization of the quotient obstruction: its update law, probability assignment, and response map specify the physical hypothesis. The deterministic and set-valued quotient constructions provide comparison models with the same retained observations. Distinguishing them experimentally requires a predicted difference in an accessible response statistic.

<a id="corollary-k1025c-certified-finite-time-separation"></a>**Corollary K.10.25c (Certified Finite-Time Separation).** Let $\delta_0:=d(x,y)>0$ and $\ell>\delta_0$. Suppose $D(t):=d(\Phi^t x,\Phi^t y)$ is continuous on $[0,t_+]$, where
$$
0<c\le1\le C,\qquad \lambda>0,\qquad
t_+:=\lambda^{-1}\ln\frac{\ell}{c\delta_0},
$$
and the certified bounds
$$
c\delta_0e^{\lambda t}\le D(t)\le C\delta_0e^{\lambda t}
$$
hold throughout that interval. Then the first crossing $T_\ell:=\inf\{t\in[0,t_+]:D(t)\ge\ell\}$ exists in $[0,t_+]$ and satisfies
$$
\max\left\{0,\lambda^{-1}\ln\frac\ell{C\delta_0}\right\}
\le T_\ell\le
\lambda^{-1}\ln\frac\ell{c\delta_0}.
$$

*Proof.* The lower estimate gives $D(t_+)\ge\ell$, whereas $D(0)=\delta_0<\ell$. Continuity gives a first crossing in the certified interval. For $t<\lambda^{-1}\ln(\ell/(C\delta_0))$, the upper estimate gives $D(t)<\ell$, proving the lower bound, with the nonnegative-time clamp. The lower endpoint therefore uses the upper expansion estimate, and the upper endpoint uses the lower estimate. A positive asymptotic Lyapunov exponent alone supplies neither these uniform finite-time estimates nor their interval of validity. With $c,C,\lambda,\ell$ unchanged and admissible positive seeds $\delta_0,\delta'_0<\ell$, each unclamped logarithmic threshold changes by exactly $-\lambda^{-1}\ln(\delta'_0/\delta_0)$. The clamped lower endpoint can have a smaller change in magnitude, and the bounds do not determine an exact sensitivity of the actual crossing time. The same logarithmic formula applies to the nominal threshold $\lambda^{-1}\ln(\ell/\delta_0)$. ∎

For example, a registered scale ratio $\ell/\delta_0=e^{100}$ gives a nominal horizon $100/\lambda$. Multiplying the seed by two changes that nominal value by $(\ln2)/\lambda$, or about $0.693\%$; multiplying it by ten changes it by about $2.303\%$. Thus the percentage sensitivity depends on the specified change in the seed. Using a PU spatial cutoff as $\delta_0$ additionally requires a phase-space metric, a coarse-graining map, and a bound on its projection onto the unstable direction. These are the bridge data connecting the operational spacing to the dynamical estimate.

<a id="theorem-k1019f-future-complete-source-with-finite-calibrated-material-time"></a>**Theorem K.10.19f (Future-Complete Source with Finite Calibrated Material Time).** Use the complete effective-action source of Theorem R.8.2b, parts A.1–A.5, with its fixed positive constants
$$
G,\beta,m,v,L,q>0,\qquad \alpha=\beta G,\quad \kappa=8\pi G,
\quad k=2\pi v/L>0,\quad 0<\varepsilon\le1,
\quad c=\hbar=1.
\tag{K.10.19f.1}
$$
Set its constitutive program $J=0$, a member of the same admitted source ball. Keep all material-clock stress and the scalaron of the original $R+\alpha R^2$ action. In Einstein proper time $t$, take the original homogeneous torus data
$$
a(0)=a_0>0,\quad \phi(0)=\dot\phi(0)=0,\quad
X^0(0)=0,\quad\dot X^0(0)=q,\quad X^j=kx^j,
\quad y(0)=\dot y(0)=0,
\tag{K.10.19f.2}
$$
with positive expanding $H(0)=H_0$ fixed by the constraint. Define
$$
\begin{gathered}
b=\sqrt{2\kappa/3},\quad F=e^{b\phi},\quad
V(\phi)=\frac{(1-F^{-1})^2}{8\kappa\alpha},\quad
\mathcal S=q^2+3k^2/a_0^2,\\
E_0=\varepsilon^2\mathcal S/2,\quad H_0=\sqrt{\kappa E_0/3},\quad
V_\infty=\frac1{8\kappa\alpha},\quad
\delta=\sqrt{8\kappa\alpha E_0}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{K.10.19f.3}
$$
If $\delta<1$, this same source solution exists for all future Einstein and Jordan proper time, with bounded positive $F$, and is future timelike and null geodesically complete. Its original calibrated material time $T=X^0/q$ has positive derivative and nonzero material Jacobian at every finite time, but finite future range $[0,T_\infty)$. Its positive-clock-branch homogeneous reduced Hamiltonian flow is incomplete at $T_\infty$. Every fixed nonconstant periodic tilt $T+f(Z)$ eventually loses timelikeness somewhere. These conclusions are future and source-specific; they do not exclude other clocks or refute the explicit completeness premises of Theorems K.10.19a/c.

*Proof.* The family is nonempty with fixed positive $\varepsilon$: choose
$$
\varepsilon=\min\{1,[4\sqrt{\kappa\alpha\mathcal S}]^{-1}\}.
\tag{K.10.19f.4}
$$
Then $\delta\le1/2$. No zero-source limit or change of time, coupling or energy units is used. At $J=0$, zero data keep $y=0$ by its homogeneous linear equation. The winding fields solve their full equations but retain their nonzero gradient energy. The exact Einstein-frame equations of Theorem R.8.2b reduce to
$$
\ddot X^0+(3H-b\dot\phi)\dot X^0=0,\quad
 a^3F^{-1}\dot X^0=a_0^3q,\quad \dot T=a_0^3F/a^3,
\tag{K.10.19f.5}
$$
$$
\begin{gathered}
\rho_t=\frac{\varepsilon^2q^2a_0^6F}{2a^6},\quad
\rho_s=\frac{3\varepsilon^2k^2}{2Fa^2},\quad
E=\dot\phi^2/2+V+\rho_t+\rho_s,\\
\dot a=aH,\quad 3H^2=\kappa E,\quad
\dot H=-\frac\kappa2(\dot\phi^2+2\rho_t+2\rho_s/3),\\
\ddot\phi+3H\dot\phi+V'=-b\rho_t+b\rho_s.
\end{gathered}
\tag{K.10.19f.6}
$$
The physical clock momentum density is $\varepsilon^2a^3F^{-1}\dot X^0=\varepsilon^2a_0^3q$; its $\varepsilon^2$ factor has not been discarded. In particular $\ddot\phi(0)=b\varepsilon^2(3k^2/a_0^2-q^2)/2$; freezing $F$ or deleting the spatial clocks is not this solution.

Differentiation gives $\dot\rho_t=(b\dot\phi-6H)\rho_t$, $\dot\rho_s=(-b\dot\phi-2H)\rho_s$, and
$$
\dot E=-3H(\dot\phi^2+2\rho_t+2\rho_s/3).
\tag{K.10.19f.7}
$$
Thus the Friedmann constraint propagates. As long as $H>0$, $H$ and $E$ do not increase. Since $V\le E\le E_0<V_\infty$,
$$
F_{\min}=\frac1{1+\delta}\le F\le\frac1{1-\delta}=F_{\max},
\qquad |\dot\phi|\le\sqrt{2E_0}.
\tag{K.10.19f.8}
$$
In particular $\phi$ stays in a compact interval. The retained spatial-clock term gives
$$
H^2\ge\frac{\kappa\varepsilon^2k^2}{2Fa^2}\ge\frac{v_*^2}{a^2},\quad
v_*:=\varepsilon k\sqrt{\frac\kappa{2F_{\max}}}>0,
\quad a_0+v_*t\le a(t)\le a_0e^{H_0t}.
\tag{K.10.19f.9}
$$
The expanding branch cannot reach $H=0$ at finite regular time, since $H\ge v_*/a>0$ there.

If a finite maximal future endpoint existed, (K.10.19f.8)–(K.10.19f.9) would bound $a,H,\phi,\dot\phi$ in a compact regular set with $a,F,H>0$. Equation (K.10.19f.5) bounds $\dot X^0\le qF_{\max}$ and $X^0$ on that finite interval. The smooth finite ODE is bounded and locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of this set; its solution has a regular limit and extends, contradicting maximality. Hence $t\in[0,\infty)$ on the same original solution. This is finite energy on every finite-time compact slice, not a uniform bound on total energy over an infinitely expanding history.

The Jordan proper time and scale factor satisfy
$$
d\tau=F^{-1/2}dt,\quad a_J=a/\sqrt F,\quad
\frac{t}{\sqrt{F_{\max}}}\le\tau(t)\le\frac{t}{\sqrt{F_{\min}}},\quad
 a_J(\tau)\ge\frac{a_0+v_*\sqrt{F_{\min}}\tau}{\sqrt{F_{\max}}}.
\tag{K.10.19f.10}
$$
Thus $\tau$ tends to infinity and both metrics are smooth at every finite proper time. The exact Jordan scalar curvature $R=(F-1)/(2\alpha)$ stays bounded. In either homogeneous torus metric, causal geodesics have conserved spatial covector $P_i$. For a timelike geodesic, $d\tau/ds=\sqrt{1+|P|^2/a_J^2}$ is bounded above, so infinite cosmic time requires infinite proper length $s$. For a null geodesic, $P\ne0$ and $d\lambda/d\tau=a_J/|P|$ has divergent integral by (K.10.19f.10). Smooth finite-time coefficients allow every finite continuation. The same argument with $a(t)$ proves future causal completeness in the Einstein metric. Past completeness is not asserted.

Nevertheless, (K.10.19f.5) and the growth bounds give
$$
0<\dot T\le\frac{a_0^3F_{\max}}{(a_0+v_*t)^3},\qquad
\frac{F_{\min}}{3H_0}\le T_\infty
=\int_0^\infty\frac{a_0^3F(t)}{a(t)^3}dt
\le\frac{F_{\max}a_0}{2v_*}<\infty.
\tag{K.10.19f.11}
$$
At every finite time the full material Jacobian is $\dot X^0k^3>0$, $-g_E^{-1}(dT,dT)=\dot T^2>0$, and the winding material map is one-to-one onto its actual time interval and circle target. There is no finite-time clock caustic. Yet $\dot T\to0$ and $dT/d\tau=a_0^3F^{3/2}/a^3\to0$. The calibration $\dot T(0)=1$ is unchanged. Its physical canonical density $p_T=\varepsilon^2q^2a_0^3$ stays positive; this does not give a uniform positive geometric bracket as volume grows.

For an actual incomplete reduced flow, let $V_c=L^3$ and use
$$
p_a=-\frac{6V_ca\dot a}{\kappa N},\quad
p_\phi=\frac{V_ca^3\dot\phi}{N},\quad
P=\frac{V_c\varepsilon^2q^2a^3F^{-1}\dot T}{N}.
\tag{K.10.19f.12}
$$
The homogeneous winding branch has zero angular momenta but retains their gradient energy in
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal C_{\mathrm{hom}}&=\mathcal B+\frac{FP^2}{2V_c\varepsilon^2q^2a^3}=0,\\
\mathcal B&=-\frac{\kappa p_a^2}{12V_ca}
+\frac{p_\phi^2}{2V_ca^3}+V_ca^3V
+\frac{3V_c\varepsilon^2k^2a}{2F}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{K.10.19f.13}
$$
On the positive-clock branch its exact root and reduced Hamiltonian are
$$
P=\mathcal P:=\sqrt{-\frac{2V_c\varepsilon^2q^2a^3\mathcal B}{F}}>0,
\qquad H_T=-\mathcal P,\quad
\Omega_T=da\wedge dp_a+d\phi\wedge dp_\phi.
\tag{K.10.19f.14}
$$
Its domain is $a,F>0$, $\mathcal B<0$. This is an autonomous $J=0$ reduction; on the actual solution $\mathcal P=V_c\varepsilon^2q^2a_0^3$. Its positive Einstein lapse is $dt/dT=a^3/(a_0^3F)$. As $T\uparrow T_\infty$, $a\to\infty$ and $p_a=-6V_ca^2H/\kappa\le-6V_cv_*a/\kappa\to-\infty$. There is no finite endpoint in the uncompactified canonical domain and no continuous extension through this finite Hamiltonian time. Any full inhomogeneous domain containing the invariant homogeneous trajectory likewise cannot have complete flow on that uncompactified smooth-metric phase space. This is compatible with spacetime completeness and with Theorem K.10.19a's separate complete-flow premise. Adding a point at $a=\infty$ requires a different symplectic/source construction.

Finally a fixed periodic smooth $f(Z)$, with $Z=x$ on this branch, gives
$$
g_E^{-1}(d[T+f(Z)],d[T+f(Z)])
=-F^2a_0^6/a^6+|df|_\delta^2/a^2.
\tag{K.10.19f.15}
$$
For nonconstant $f$, choose a point with $d=|df|_\delta>0$. Timelikeness needs $d^2<F^2a_0^6/a^4\le F_{\max}^2a_0^6/a^4$, which fails at finite time once $a^2>F_{\max}a_0^3/d$. A tilt initially timelike must become null and then spacelike somewhere. Constant tilts stay timelike but retain the finite range. Other clocks or atlases are not excluded. These conclusions concern this nonempty fixed-positive-source low-energy family, not all energies, past development, a microscopic quantum realization or the whole clock predicate. $\square$

<a id="theorem-k1019g-a-forward-complete-geometric-clock-on-the-same-low-energy-source"></a>**Theorem K.10.19g (A Forward-Complete Geometric Clock on the Same Low-Energy Source).** Retain Theorem K.10.19f's action, constants, fixed positive $\varepsilon$, $J=0$ and homogeneous $y=0$ winding sector. The calibrated material time $T=X^0/q$ remains a canonical observable. The distinct geometric clock $S=\log(a/a_0)$ has unlimited future range on that theorem's actual low-energy branch. Its exact reduction and canonical overlap are as follows.

Let $V_c=L^3$ and allow a positive conserved total material-clock momentum $P$. The full homogeneous densities are
$$
\dot T=\frac{FP}{V_c\varepsilon^2q^2a^3},\quad
\rho_t=\frac{FP^2}{2V_c^2\varepsilon^2q^2a^6},\quad
\rho_s=\frac{3\varepsilon^2k^2}{2Fa^2},\quad
E=\dot\phi^2/2+V+\rho_t+\rho_s.
\tag{K.10.19g.1}
$$
The same Einstein/scalaron equations (K.10.19f.6) hold. At $a=a_0$ consider the open section
$$
\mathcal U_0=\left\{(T,P,\phi,p_\phi):P>0,\quad
E_0=\frac{p_\phi^2}{2V_c^2a_0^6}+V(\phi)
+\frac{FP^2}{2V_c^2\varepsilon^2q^2a_0^6}
+\frac{3\varepsilon^2k^2}{2Fa_0^2}<V_\infty\right\},
\tag{K.10.19g.2}
$$
with $p_a$ chosen by the expanding negative root. It contains the original data, where $P=V_c\varepsilon^2q^2a_0^3$. Its neighbors use the same action and units, but need not have the original zero scalaron data or unit initial $\dot T$; they are not the same fixed-data retarded chart. This is open within the homogeneous $y=0$ reduced section, not the full inhomogeneous phase space. Arbitrary $T$ is allowed because $J=0$ has exact material-time shift symmetry.

*Proof.* The exact energy balance (K.10.19f.7) preserves $E\le E_0$. With $\delta=\sqrt{8\kappa\alpha E_0}<1$, the bounds $F_{\min}\le F\le F_{\max}$, $H\ge v_*/a$ and $a\ge a_0+v_*t$ hold with $v_*=\varepsilon k\sqrt{\kappa/(2F_{\max})}$. The same compact-set ODE proof gives all future proper time for every datum in (K.10.19g.2). These bounds are uniform on compact subsets below a fixed energy less than $V_\infty$.

##### 1. Exact root, sign and reduced equations

The canonical change
$$
S=\log(a/a_0),\quad p_S=ap_a,\quad p_a\,da=p_S\,dS,\quad a=a_0e^S
\tag{K.10.19g.3}
$$
keeps $(T,P)$ and $(\phi,p_\phi)$. Multiplying the full constraint (K.10.19f.13) by $12V_ca^3/\kappa$ gives $-p_S^2+\mathcal Q=0$, with
$$
\mathcal Q=\frac6\kappa\left[p_\phi^2+\frac{FP^2}{\varepsilon^2q^2}\right]
+\frac{12V_c^2}{\kappa}a^6V
+\frac{18V_c^2\varepsilon^2k^2}{\kappa F}a^4.
\tag{K.10.19g.4}
$$
All summands are nonnegative and the winding term is strictly positive. On the expanding branch $p_S<0$, set $H_S=\sqrt{\mathcal Q}>0$. Then
$$
\mathcal C=-\frac{\kappa(p_S-H_S)(p_S+H_S)}{12V_ca^3},\quad
\mathcal C_S=p_S+H_S=0,\quad
\{S,\mathcal C_S\}=1,\quad \{S,\mathcal C\}=H>0,
\quad N_S=\frac{dt}{dS}=\frac{6V_ca^3}{\kappa H_S}=\frac1H.
\tag{K.10.19g.5}
$$
On a fixed $S$ section the pulled-back canonical potential and form are $\Theta_S=p_\phi\,\delta\phi+P\,\delta T$ and
$$
\Omega_S=d\phi\wedge dp_\phi+dT\wedge dP.
\tag{K.10.19g.6}
$$
The history action is $\int[p_\phi\phi'+PT'-H_S]dS$, and hence
$$
\phi'=\frac{6p_\phi}{\kappa H_S},\quad
T'=\frac{6FP}{\kappa\varepsilon^2q^2H_S}>0,\quad
P'=0,\quad p_\phi'=-\partial_\phi H_S.
\tag{K.10.19g.7}
$$
Using $H_S=6V_ca^3H/\kappa$ recovers $\dot\phi/H$ and $\dot T/H$. Differentiating every $F$ and $V$ term in (K.10.19g.4) retains both $-b\rho_t$ and $+b\rho_s$ in the scalaron equation. Even at $J=0$,
$$
\partial_SH_S=\frac{36V_c^2}{\kappa H_S}
[a^6V+\varepsilon^2k^2a^4/F]>0.
\tag{K.10.19g.8}
$$
Thus $H_S$ is explicitly time dependent, unlike the autonomous premise of Theorem K.10.19a. Its positive sign comes from the expanding geometric momentum, and does not reverse the correct $H_T=-\mathcal P$ of the material chart. In natural units $S,p_S,H_S$ are dimensionless, whereas $P$ is conjugate to the time-dimensional $T$. Positive $H_S$ is not a positive physical energy in the original proper-time units.

##### 2. Forward completeness with the material observable retained

For every datum in $\mathcal U_0$,
$$
S(t)\ge\log(1+v_*t/a_0)\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad
\frac{dS}{dt}=H>0.
\tag{K.10.19g.9}
$$
Every finite $\sigma\ge0$ is reached once at a finite $t_\sigma\le a_0(e^\sigma-1)/v_*$. On $0\le S\le\sigma$, $a\in[a_0,a_0e^\sigma]$, $\phi$ stays in its fixed compact interval, $|p_\phi|\le V_ca_0^3e^{3\sigma}\sqrt{2E_0}$ and $H\ge v_*/(a_0e^\sigma)>0$. The original material observable still has finite total increment,
$$
0<T_\infty-T(0)\le\frac{F_{\max}P}{2V_c\varepsilon^2q^2v_*a_0^2}<\infty.
\tag{K.10.19g.10}
$$
Thus all coordinates stay in a compact regular neighborhood on each finite $S$ interval, and $H_S$ is separated from zero there. Smooth Hamiltonian ODE continuation proves forward completeness, rather than assuming that changing clock labels repairs it.

More generally, at any finite $S_0$, the expanding domain $P>0$ and
$$
E(S_0,z)=\frac{p_\phi^2}{2V_c^2a^6}+V
+\frac{FP^2}{2V_c^2\varepsilon^2q^2a^6}
+\frac{3\varepsilon^2k^2}{2Fa^2}<V_\infty,\qquad a=a_0e^{S_0},
\tag{K.10.19g.11}
$$
is forward invariant: $E'=-3[\dot\phi^2+2\rho_t+2\rho_s/3]\le0$. The same continuation holds for all $S\ge S_0$. No arbitrarily negative $S$, higher-energy data or full-phase-space coverage follows.

##### 3. The actual canonical transition to the calibrated clock

The $T$ chart has $(a,p_a,\phi,p_\phi)$ and reconstructs $P=\mathcal P>0$ by (K.10.19f.14); the $S$ chart has $(T,P,\phi,p_\phi)$ and reconstructs $p_S=-H_S$. For fixed material value $\tau$ and volume value $\sigma$, define their transition by reconstructing the full state on $T=\tau$, evolving the exact equations with all clock and scalaron terms, taking its unique event at $a=a_0e^\sigma$, and reading $(T,P,\phi,p_\phi)$ there. The inverse develops that same solution to $T=\tau$. It exists only if $\tau$ belongs to its actual material-clock range. Backward comparison uses only the known finite common segment; no formula is extended beyond $T_\infty$.

This is an exact Cauchy/hitting map, not a claim of an elementary closed solution. Its hitting time depends on initial data. The implicit function theorem applies because $dS/dt=H>0$ at each finite hit and $dT/dt>0$ for its inverse. A tangent variation at the target needs the constraint-flow correction $-\delta S/\{S,\mathcal C\}$, with denominator $H$.

For completeness, restrict
$$
\Omega=da\wedge dp_a+d\phi\wedge dp_\phi+dT\wedge dP
\tag{K.10.19g.12}
$$
to $\mathcal C=0$. Its null direction is $X_{\mathcal C}$. A hitting map $x\mapsto\Phi_{\mathcal C}^{u(x)}x$ differentiates as $D\Phi_{\mathcal C}^u v+X_{\mathcal C}du(v)$. The extra terms vanish when paired with constrained tangents because $\Omega(X_{\mathcal C},v)=d\mathcal C(v)=0$, and fixed-time constraint flow preserves $\Omega$. Hence the true state-dependent hitting map satisfies
$$
\Psi_{(S,\sigma)\leftarrow(T,\tau)}^*\Omega_S=\Omega_T.
\tag{K.10.19g.13}
$$
No completeness of $X_{\mathcal C}$ is used. Uniqueness on three common segments gives exact composition, inverse and identity laws. These source overlaps do not continue the material chart through its missing endpoint; $T(S)\to T_\infty$ only as $S\to\infty$.

Finally,
$$
S=\frac13\log\frac{\operatorname{Vol}_E}{V_ca_0^3},\qquad
\operatorname{Vol}_E=\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\sqrt{h_E}
=\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}F^{3/2}\sqrt{h_J}.
\tag{K.10.19g.14}
$$
It is a metric-plus-scalaron observable on the winding-labeled homogeneous slices, with $dS/d\tau=\sqrt F H>0$ in Jordan proper time. It is neither the material clock nor the Jordan-volume logarithm, whose derivative has an additional scalaron term. It adds no external force, but this continuum definition supplies no microscopic volume/scalaron instrument, quantum clock operator or resource invoice. The conclusion is an actual same-source homogeneous forward-global clock and canonical overlap, not a two-sided complete inhomogeneous clock atlas or full microscopic realization. $\square$

### K.11.2 Active Development Areas

The following areas have established conceptual frameworks with detailed calculations in progress:

**Cross-domain optimality transport.** Beyond the response-preservation entries of the cross-domain certificate stated below, transporting an optimality claim from the common problem $X_*$ back to a domain $X_i$ requires the common optimum to lie in $F_i(X_i)$, and requires the domain objective $J_i$ to be the pullback of the common objective $J_*$ under $F_i$, or a declared strictly increasing reparameterization of it, on that image when both problems use the same minimization or maximization convention. A strictly decreasing reparameterization transports the claim only with the optimization direction reversed.

**Problem-of-time protocol.** An event count may be proposed as a physical clock only after the constrained model supplies a phase-space function $T$, proves the required monotonicity on the chosen branch, and shows that the relational observables $O(T)$ are gauge invariant or satisfy the appropriate Dirac condition. A discrete count can itself be reparametrization invariant and does not remove the Hamiltonian constraint. SPAP excludes specified internal total self-models; it does not exclude the external mathematical state used to formulate a constrained theory.

**Cosmological-measure protocol.** A single realized history does not by itself define probabilities for regions or observations within that history. A measure proposal must state its sample space, event algebra, normalized measure or regulator, cutoff-removal rule, conditioning data, and observer-selection function, and must prove regulator independence at the claimed resolution. Gleason--Busch probabilities on quantum effects do not supply those cosmological entries. Fluctuation-observer claims require an independently defined production and observation model.

**Cross-domain recurrence certificate.** A common discrete structure appearing in several domains may be compared through a finite certificate
$$
\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{cross}}
=
\bigl(
X_i,F_i,\mathcal O_i,\mathcal O_*,R_i,\chi_{\mathrm{lock}}
\bigr)_{i=1}^n,
$$
where $X_i$ is the domain object, $F_i:X_i\to X_*$ is an explicit reduction to one common problem, $\mathcal O_i$ and $\mathcal O_*$ are declared response families, and $R_i$ bounds failure of response preservation. Under the objective and attainability conditions above, optimality transports to every preimage of the common optimum without requiring injectivity. For a claim on a retained response quotient, the objective and reduction must be well-defined on that quotient. If the common optimum is unique, its pullback optimum is unique on the retained response quotient exactly when the fiber over that optimum contains one quotient class. Injectivity on the entire retained response quotient is a sufficient stronger condition for this uniqueness and is required for a faithful identification of all its classes with their images. Shared integers, codes, lattices, or optimization language without these maps establish analogy, not identity.

The framework organizes branch-qualified relations among operational constraints, candidate constants, effective geometry, and biological response models. Its ultraviolet result is a certificate-gated operational cutoff, not generic UV finiteness; each cross-sector connection retains the independent hypotheses listed below.
